##### 7.5 The Critical Angle: Where Reflection Becomes Total

For light travelling from a denser medium (glass, n₁ = 1.50) to a less dense medium (air, n₂ = 1.00):

Small angle of incidence (e.g. 10°): mostly transmitted, slightly reflected (partial reflection — see section 7.3).

Approaching the critical angle: the transmitted ray bends further from the normal, and the reflected intensity increases.

At the critical angle C: the angle of refraction is 90° — the transmitted ray travels along the interface. The reflected intensity is still partial.

Above the critical angle: total internal reflection (TIR) — 100% reflection, 0% transmission.

The critical angle:

sin C = n₂ / n₁ = 1.00 / 1.50
C = sin⁻¹(0.667) = 41.8°

So for glass-to-air, TIR occurs for any angle of incidence greater than 41.8°. This is the boundary between partial reflection (spec 55) and total reflection (spec 47).

##### 7.6 Conceptual Map of Reflection/Transmission Regimes

Angle of incidence Reflection Transmission

i < critical angle Partial reflection (Fresnel) Mostly transmitted (refracted)

i = critical angle Partial reflection Refracted ray travels along interface (90° refraction)

i > critical angle Total internal reflection (100%) None

This unifies spec 47 (TIR) and spec 55 (transmission/reflection) into one conceptual picture: TIR is the limiting case of partial reflection when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

#### 8. Applications of Transmission and Reflection at an Interface

##### 8.1 Application 1: Pulse-Echo Scanning (Medical Ultrasound)

Spec 56, application of spec 55.

A transducer emits a short pulse of ultrasound (typically 2–10 MHz) into the body. At each tissue boundary (skin-fat, fat-muscle, muscle-bone, etc.) a fraction of the pulse is reflected back to the transducer. The transducer acts as both emitter and detector — it records the time delay t between emitting the pulse and detecting each echo.

Distance to each boundary:

d = (v × t) / 2

where v is the speed of sound in the relevant tissue (typically 1540 m s⁻¹ in soft tissue) and the factor of 2 accounts for the pulse travelling to the boundary and back.

Worked example (examiner-favoured, Jan 2023 Q17b):

An ultrasound pulse is emitted into the body. An echo is detected 0.080 ms after emission. The speed of sound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the distance to the reflecting boundary.

d = (v × t) / 2
  = (1540 m s⁻¹ × 0.080 × 10⁻³ s) / 2
  = 0.1232 / 2
  = 0.062 m
  = 6.2 cm

Result: the boundary is 6.2 cm below the skin.

Why coupling gel is needed (links to spec 55): without gel, the air-skin boundary reflects ~99.9% of the ultrasound (section 7.4) and almost none enters the body. The gel (acoustic impedance close to skin) reduces this mismatch.

##### 8.2 Application 2: Optical Fibres (Spec 47, 48, 55)

An optical fibre consists of a glass core (high n, e.g. 1.50) surrounded by a glass cladding (lower n, e.g. 1.46). Light entering one end of the fibre at a small enough angle undergoes total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary repeatedly, staying within the core until it emerges at the far end.

Critical angle at the core-cladding boundary:

sin C = ncₗₐddᵢₙg / ncₒᵣₑ = 1.46 / 1.50 = 0.973
C = sin⁻¹(0.973) = 76.7°

So any ray inside the core striking the cladding at an angle greater than 76.7° (measured from the normal) undergoes TIR and stays in the core.

Why cladding is used (links to spec 55):

1. Provides a clean, controlled boundary for TIR. Without cladding, the core-air boundary would be at the glass surface — scratches, dirt, or contact with other fibres would disrupt TIR and let light escape.

2. Prevents cross-talk between adjacent fibres in a bundle. Without cladding, light leaking from one fibre could enter a neighbouring fibre.

3. Reduces pulse broadening (modal dispersion). A higher critical angle (compared to the core-air case) means only rays within a narrower range of angles can propagate — this reduces the path-length differences between rays and hence reduces pulse broadening.

Worked example (Oct 2022 Q16 style, optical fibre):

A fibre has ncₒᵣₑ = 1.52 and ncₗₐddᵢₙg = 1.40. Calculate the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary.

sin C = ncₗₐddᵢₙg / ncₒᵣₑ = 1.40 / 1.52 = 0.921
C = sin⁻¹(0.921) = 67.0°

Any ray inside the core striking the cladding at an angle > 67.0° (from the normal) undergoes TIR.

##### 8.3 Application 3: Sonar (Spec 56, application of spec 55)

A sonar system on a ship emits a pulse of ultrasound (typically 30–200 kHz) into the sea. The pulse reflects off the sea floor (or off a shoal of fish, or a submarine) and returns to a detector on the ship. The depth is calculated using d = vt/2.

Speed of sound in water: ~1500 m s⁻¹ (vs ~340 m s⁻¹ in air). This is much faster than in air because water is much less compressible.

Worked example (Jun 2022 Q12c style):

A sonar pulse is emitted from a ship. The echo from the sea floor is detected 1.20 s later. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m s⁻¹. Calculate the depth of the sea.

d = (v × t) / 2
  = (1500 m s⁻¹ × 1.20 s) / 2
  = 1800 / 2
  = 900 m

Result: the sea is 900 m deep at this point.

Why ultrasound (not audible sound)?

Penetration: higher-frequency ultrasound is less attenuated in water than audible sound, so it travels further.

Directionality: shorter wavelength (λ = v/f, so for 100 kHz in water, λ = 1.5 cm) allows a narrow beam, so the source can be directional. Audible sound (λ ~ 1 m to 15 m in water) would spread in all directions.

Marine life: audible sound would disturb marine animals; ultrasound is mostly above their hearing range.

##### 8.4 Application 4: Pulse-Echo in Non-Destructive Testing (NDT)

The same principle is used to detect cracks inside metal components (e.g. aircraft wings, railway lines). An ultrasound pulse is sent into the metal; any crack (an air-metal interface, since Zₐᵢᵣ ≪ Zₘₑₜₐₗ) reflects a strong echo back. The position of the crack is found from d = vt/2, where v is the speed of sound in the metal (typically ~5000 m s⁻¹ in steel).

Worked example (Jun 2025 Q13a style — the "undetectable crack"):

An ultrasound pulse is sent into a steel rail of thickness 5.0 cm. The speed of sound in steel is 5200 m s⁻¹. A crack is present at the centre of the rail. Calculate the time delay between emitting the pulse and detecting the echo from the crack.

d = 2.5 cm = 2.5 × 10⁻² m (half the rail thickness)
t = 2d / v = (2 × 2.5 × 10⁻² m) / 5200 m s⁻¹
         = 5.0 × 10⁻² / 5200
         = 9.6 × 10⁻⁶ s
         = 9.6 µs

Result: the echo from the crack is detected 9.6 µs after emission. (Note: Jun 2025 Q13a tested why a crack parallel to the rail face is undetectable — because such a crack reflects the pulse back at a small angle, away from the transducer.)

#### 9. Common Pitfalls and Examiner Traps

##### 9.1 The "angle from surface" trap

The most common refraction error. Mark schemes (Jan 2023 Q15a, Jan 2025 Q18) give angles measured from the surface, requiring the student to subtract from 90° to obtain the angle from the normal. Always check whether the angle is from the surface or from the normal.

##### 9.2 The "factor of 2" trap in pulse-echo

The second most common error in pulse-echo questions. The pulse travels to the boundary and back, so d = vt/2, not d = vt. Forgetting the factor of 2 doubles the calculated distance.

##### 9.3 Confusing "diffraction" with "refraction"

Diffraction (spec 50) is the spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle — requires the wave to meet a gap/obstacle comparable to its wavelength. Refraction (spec 45) is the change of direction of a wave at an interface between two media — happens at every interface, regardless of wavelength. Oct 2022 Q8 MCQ tested this directly: "What does NOT occur at a glass block?" — diffraction (it occurs only at gaps/obstacles, not at flat interfaces).

##### 9.4 Forgetting "both reflection and transmission"

Spec 55 explicitly requires the understanding that both reflection and transmission occur at most interfaces. Examiner mark schemes (Jan 2024 Q18b) reward "both reflection and transmission" — describing only one loses marks.

##### 9.5 Missing one of the two TIR conditions

For TIR (spec 47, application of spec 55), both conditions must be stated:

1. Light must travel from a denser to a less dense medium (n₁ > n₂).

2. The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.

Stating only one condition loses 1 mark.

#### 10. Quick Reference: Concept Map

SPEC 50 (Diffraction + Huygens)
│
├── Huygens' construction: every point on wavefront = secondary source
│       ├── secondary wavelets spread forward at wave speed
│       └── envelope of wavelets = new wavefront
│
├── Single-slit diffraction: secondary wavelets from across slit interfere
│       ├── central maximum (brightest, twice as wide)
│       ├── first minimum at sin θ = λ/a
│       └── secondary maxima (dimmer, narrower)
│
└── Obstacle diffraction: wavelets from unblocked edges spread into shadow
        └── more diffraction when λ ≈ obstacle size

SPEC 48 (Measuring refractive index of a solid)
│
├── Apparatus: glass block + ray box + protractor + pins + paper
│
├── Method: mark incident + emergent rays, draw refracted ray, measure i and r
│       ├── vary i over 5+ angles
│       └── record i, r, sin i, sin r
│
└── Analysis: plot sin i vs sin r
        ├── straight line through origin
        └── gradient = n (refractive index)
        └── more accurate than single reading (random errors cancel, anomalies visible)

SPEC 55 (Transmission and reflection at interface)
│
├── At every interface: partial reflection + transmission
│       ├── fraction reflected depends on impedance mismatch (Z₂ − Z₁)
│       └── transmission: wave enters new medium (refracted if non-normal)
│
├── Critical angle: boundary between partial and total reflection
│       ├── sin C = n₂/n₁
│       └── above C: total internal reflection (no transmission)
│
└── Applications:
        ├── pulse-echo (medical ultrasound, d = vt/2)
        ├── optical fibres (TIR at core-cladding, ncₒᵣₑ > ncₗₐddᵢₙg)
        └── sonar (ultrasound in water, d = vt/2, v ≈ 1500 m s⁻¹)

What a full-mark QWC answer looks like (Beats — Oct 2022 Q15a(ii), 6 marks):

1. The two sound sources have slightly different frequencies, so they are NOT coherent

2. Because the frequencies differ, the phase difference between them changes continuously over time

3. This causes alternating constructive and destructive interference at the observer

4. The listener hears periodic variation in loudness (amplitude), known as beats

5. Structure marks: Use "because," "so," "this causes" to create a coherent logical chain. Listing without connective words earns only 1/2 structure marks.

Common pitfalls:

Not linking phase difference explicitly to path difference using the formula when calculations require it (Jan 2025 Q14b)

Describing beats as "interference pattern" without explaining WHY the pattern changes (missing the "changing phase difference" link)

Confusing in-phase and antiphase conditions (constructive = nλ path diff, destructive = (n+½)λ)

What a full-mark QWC answer looks like (Stationary wave in closed tube — Jun 2025 Q17a, 6 marks):

1. A progressive wave travels down the tube and reflects at the closed end (fixed boundary), inverting the wave (180° phase change)

2. The reflected wave superposes with the incident wave, creating a stationary wave pattern

3. At the closed end, a node forms because the fixed boundary inverts the wave, causing permanent cancellation

4. At the open end, an antinode forms because the wave is free to move (no phase change at open boundary)

5. The fundamental mode has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, with wavelength λ = 4L

6. Structure: Causal chain using "because," "therefore," "so" — each point leads logically to the next

Common pitfalls:

Distance between adjacent nodes = λ/2, NOT λ (Oct 2023 Q6 MCQ trap)

Thinking length change affects wave speed (Jun 2024 Q8 — length is a red herring for v = √(T/μ), though it does affect f)

Amplitude ≠ instantaneous displacement (3 papers) — an antinode has maximum amplitude but zero displacement twice per cycle

Getting the derivation wrong for f² = T/(4L²μ) — must show BOTH v = fλ AND v = √(T/μ) before combining

What a full-mark QWC answer looks like (Underwater TIR — Oct 2024 Q17b, 6 marks):

1. Light travels from water (n ≈ 1.33) to air (n = 1.0) — denser to less dense, so TIR is possible

2. The critical angle for water-air is sin⁻¹(1.0/1.33) ≈ 48.8°

3. When the angle of incidence exceeds 48.8°, all light is reflected back into the water

4. No light is transmitted into the air above — the light is totally internally reflected

5. This creates a "mirror" effect at the water surface when viewed from below at a shallow angle

6. Structure: "Because the light travels from a denser medium, TIR can occur. The angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, SO all light is reflected. THEREFORE no light escapes into the air."

Common pitfalls:

ANGLE-FROM-SURFACE TRAP (7 papers): Angles on diagrams are often measured from the SURFACE, not the normal. Always subtract from 90° before applying Snell's law. This is the single most frequent Ch 2.3 trap.

Forgetting both TIR conditions (Jun 2022 Q1): must have BOTH denser→less dense AND i > critical angle

Multiplying c by n instead of dividing (Jun 2025 Q1: v = c/n, not v = cn)

Not explaining WHY light bends (must mention speed change at boundary)

Total: 7+ appearances, ~23 marks (spec 56)

What a full-mark answer looks like (Resolution — Jun 2025 Q13a, 4 marks):

1. Speed from graph at 23°C = 4115 m s⁻¹

2. Round-trip time to crack: t = 2d/v = 2 × 0.04/4115 = 1.94 × 10⁻⁵ s = 19.4 μs

3. Since 19.4 μs < 200 μs (pulse duration), the echo returns BEFORE the transmitted pulse has finished

4. The echo and outgoing pulse overlap, so the crack cannot be distinguished — it will NOT be detected

Common pitfalls:

FACTOR-OF-2 TRAP (6+ papers): d = vt/2, NOT vt. The pulse travels to the reflector AND back.

COUNTERINTUITIVE RESOLUTION TRAP (Jun 2025 Q13a): A CLOSER crack may be HARDER to detect, not easier. If the round-trip time is shorter than the pulse duration, the echo overlaps the outgoing pulse. Students expect shorter distance = easier detection.

Not reading the wave speed from the graph at the correct temperature

Not making an explicit conclusion in "deduce" questions

Total: 6 appearances for spec 58, ~24 marks

What a full-mark answer looks like (Wave vs Particle — Oct 2023 Q17a / Jun 2025 Q19b, 6 marks):

1. Wave model prediction: Any frequency of light, given sufficient intensity and time, should eject electrons (energy accumulates gradually)

2. Observation: No electrons are emitted below the threshold frequency, regardless of intensity or duration

3. Photon model explanation: Light consists of photons, each with energy E = hf. A single photon interacts with a single electron (one-to-one interaction). If hf < φ, the photon lacks sufficient energy and the electron cannot escape — this energy cannot be accumulated.

4. Photon model explains intensity effect: Higher intensity means MORE photons per second (more photoelectrons), but each photon's energy is unchanged — so max KE depends on frequency, not intensity.

5. Photon model explains instantaneous emission: Because the interaction is one-to-one, emission is immediate when a photon with sufficient energy strikes the surface — no time delay.

6. Structure marks: Use "because," "however," "in contrast" to compare the two models explicitly.

Common pitfalls:

Only describing the particle model without contrasting it with what the wave model PREDICTS (2 papers)

Not using connective words — listing facts without causal linkages loses structure marks

Confusing intensity (number of photons) with photon energy (determined by frequency)

#### 12. Photoelectric Effect (Spec 59–62) — Highest-Yield Topic

Paper Question Marks Command Word How Tested Key Point

Jun 2025 Q18a-b 14 Mega-block UV/photon mega-block: threshold frequency, work function, stopping potential, photon counting Largest Ch 2.3 mega-block in recent papers

Jun 2025 Q19b 6 Discuss (QWC) Wave vs particle model comparison 4 IC + 2 structure

Jan 2025 Q19c 2 Calculate Stopping potential: Vₛ = KEₘₐₓ/e = (hf − φ)/e Relates to V = W/Q from Ch 2.4

Oct 2023 Q17a 6 Discuss (QWC) Photoelectric observations Same QWC framework

Jan 2022 Q13 6 Discuss (QWC) Particle nature of light Same QWC framework

Jun 2019 Q14 6 Discuss (QWC) Particle vs wave model Same QWC framework

Jun 2023 Q17(b)(ii) 6 Calculate 6 energy level differences from spectrum Multiple ΔE calculations

Oct 2022 Q17a(ii) 2 Calculate LED photon emission energy E = hf with f from wavelength

Jan 2022 Q16 12 Mega-block 12-mark block: photoelectric + internal resistance Cross-chapter question

Jun 2022 (part) 4 Calculate Photoelectric equation: find φ from graph gradient Gradient of KEₘₐₓ vs f graph = h; y-intercept = −φ

Oct 2019 (part) 3 Calculate Photoelectric equation with eV conversion Convert eV to joules: multiply by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹

Total: ~138 marks across spec 58–62 (highest-yield topic in Ch 2.3)

What a full-mark answer looks like (Photoelectric equation calculation):

1. Convert work function from eV to joules: φ = 2.3 eV × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

2. Calculate photon energy: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 8.0 × 10¹⁴ = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

3. Apply photoelectric equation: KEₘₐₓ = hf − φ = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.62 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

4. Convert back to eV if required: KEₘₐₓ = 1.62 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.01 eV

What a full-mark answer looks like (Stopping potential): "eVₛ = KEₘₐₓ, so Vₛ = KEₘₐₓ/e. The stopping potential is the minimum p.d. needed to reduce the photocurrent to zero. It depends on the frequency of the incident light, not its intensity."

Common pitfalls:

Forgetting to convert between eV and joules (1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) — appears in almost every photoelectric calculation

Confusing intensity (affects number of photoelectrons) with frequency (affects max KE)

Not comparing wave and particle models in QWC questions — must describe what the wave model predicts AND fails to explain

Using V = W/Q incorrectly for stopping potential — Vₛ = KEₘₐₓ/e, where KEₘₐₓ = hf − φ

#### 13. Atomic Line Spectra (Spec 63)

Paper Question Marks Command Word How Tested Key Point

Oct 2022 Q2 1 Select (MCQ) Longest wavelength = smallest ΔE transition Longest λ = lowest f = smallest energy gap

Jun 2025 Q5 1 Select (MCQ) Shortest wavelength emission = largest ΔE Arrow LENGTH on diagram ∝ energy, NOT wavelength

Jan 2025 Q9 1 Select (MCQ) Number of distinct frequencies from excited atom Count all possible downward transitions: n(n-1)/2

Jun 2025 Q18a 2 State Photon emission mechanism in discharge tube Excitation → de-excitation → photon emitted with E = ΔE

Jun 2023 Q17(b)(ii) 6 Calculate 6 energy level differences from line spectrum ΔE = Eᵤₚₚₑᵣ − Eₗₒwₑᵣ for each transition

Jun 2024 Q17(a)(ii) 6 Discuss (QWC) Discharge tube photon emission QWC: excitation, de-excitation, discrete energies, line spectrum

Jan 2024 (part) 2 Calculate Wavelength from energy level transition λ = hc/ΔE, with eV→J conversion

Oct 2019 (part) 2 Calculate Energy of photon from wavelength E = hc/λ

Jun 2022 (part) 2 Explain Emission vs absorption spectrum distinction Emission: bright lines on dark; absorption: dark lines on continuous

Total: 7 appearances, ~20 marks (spec 63)

What a full-mark answer looks like (Transition wavelength calculation):

1. ΔE = Eᵤₚₚₑᵣ − Eₗₒwₑᵣ = (−1.51) − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV

2. Convert to joules: ΔE = 1.89 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

3. λ = hc/ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.59 × 10⁻⁷ m = 659 nm

Common pitfalls:

LONGEST-WAVELENGTH TRAP (Oct 2022 Q2): Longest wavelength = lowest frequency = smallest ΔE. Students often select the transition with the longest arrow (largest ΔE), confusing arrow length (proportional to energy) with wavelength (inversely proportional to energy).

Forgetting to convert eV to joules before using λ = hc/ΔE

Not recognising that absorption transitions go UP (electron gains energy) while emission transitions go DOWN

Counting transitions incorrectly — from level n, the number of possible emission transitions is n(n−1)/2

Exam strategy for Ch 2.3: The top 3 topics (photoelectric effect, refraction/TIR, stationary waves) account for 340/727 marks (46.8%). These three areas alone average 26.8 marks per paper — one-third of the entire paper. Master these first, then move to intensity, diffraction grating, and de Broglie/duality. The photoelectric effect is the single most important topic in the entire WPH12 specification, appearing in EVERY paper with an average of 10.6 marks per session.

### WPH12 Extension — Waves Supplement (Exam Connections)

Scope: Cross-references every definition and concept in ext-waves-supplement-definitions.md and ext-waves-supplement-concepts.md to how it has been tested in WPH12/01 papers (Jan 2019–Jun 2025) and how it is likely to be tested. This file is the bridge between study content and exam performance. Source: 11 non-COVID WPH12/01 papers (Jan 2019–Jun 2025) + examiner reports + mark schemes + the WPH12 cross-paper analysis.

#### 1. How These Topics Are Tested — Frequency Table

Insight: The three gap areas (spec 48, 50, 55) together with their direct applications (spec 45–47, 56) account for ~22 marks per paper — over 25% of the 80-mark paper. While pure spec-50 Huygens questions are rare (only 1 paper), the understanding of Huygens is implicitly required for diffraction questions, electron diffraction (spec 53), and diffraction grating (spec 51). Similarly, spec 55's standalone testing is rare, but partial reflection is the conceptual basis for TIR (spec 47) and pulse-echo (spec 56), which together are worth ~30 marks per paper.

#### 2. Definition-by-Definition Exam Mapping

##### 2.1 Huygens' Construction (spec 50)

How tested:

"Use Huygens' construction to explain what happens to a wave when it meets a slit." (3 marks, Jun 2024 Q16b — the only direct Huygens question in 11 papers)

Implicitly tested via single-slit diffraction and electron diffraction explanations.

Full-mark answer requirements (Jun 2024 Q16b mark scheme):

1. Every point on the wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets (1 mark)

2. The new wavefront is the envelope (tangent) of these wavelets (1 mark)

3. At a slit, only the points within the slit emit wavelets; these spread out (1 mark)

Common pitfalls:

Saying "the wave bends" without explaining the secondary wavelet mechanism — does not score.

Omitting "envelope" or "tangent" — loses the second mark.

Describing interference instead of Huygens — irrelevant to the question asked.

##### 2.2 Single-Slit Diffraction (spec 50)

How tested:

"Describe the diffraction pattern produced when monochromatic light passes through a single narrow slit." (3 marks, Oct 2021 Q15c)

"Explain why the central maximum is wider than the other maxima." (2 marks, Jun 2024 Q16c)

Full-mark answer requirements:

Central maximum is the brightest and widest fringe (twice as wide as the secondary maxima)

Secondary maxima are dimmer and narrower, with intensity decreasing away from the centre

Minima occur where wavelets from across the slit interfere destructively

Common pitfalls:

Confusing single-slit pattern with double-slit pattern (double-slit has equal-intensity fringes of equal width).

Forgetting that the central maximum is twice as wide as the secondary maxima.

Stating "the pattern is the same as a double-slit pattern" — incorrect.

##### 2.3 Obstacle Diffraction / Wavelength-to-Size Ratio

How tested:

"Explain why sound waves diffract around a doorway but light waves do not." (2 marks, Jan 2022 Q12a)

QWC on harbour waves (6 marks, Jan 2023 Q15a)

QWC on harbour waves again (6 marks, Jan 2024 Q17b — examiner repeated this question type)

Full-mark answer (Jan 2022 Q12a style):

Sound wavelength (~1 m) is comparable to the doorway width (~1 m) → significant diffraction (1 mark)

Light wavelength (~500 nm) is much smaller than the doorway → negligible diffraction (1 mark)

Common pitfall: Stating "sound has a longer wavelength than light" without relating the wavelength to the obstacle size. The mark scheme requires the comparison.

##### 2.4 Measuring Refractive Index of a Solid (spec 48)

How tested:

"Describe how a student could use a glass block and a ray box to determine the refractive index of the glass." (6 marks, Jun 2024 Q14b — the most thorough test of spec 48 in the past 5 years)

"Explain why it is better to take measurements at several different angles of incidence and plot a graph, rather than use a single angle." (2 marks, Jan 2024 Q18c(ii))

Full-mark answer structure (Jun 2024 Q14b — 6 marks):

1. Place the glass block on a sheet of paper and trace around it; draw a normal at the point where the ray will meet the block (1 mark)

2. Direct a narrow ray from the ray box at a measured angle of incidence; mark the incident ray using two pins (1 mark)

3. Mark the emergent ray on the far side of the block using two more pins (1 mark)

4. Remove the block; join the pin marks to draw the incident, refracted (inside the block), and emergent rays (1 mark)

5. Measure i and r with a protractor; repeat for at least 5 different angles of incidence (1 mark)

6. Plot sin i against sin r; the gradient of the straight line through the origin equals n (1 mark)

Common pitfalls:

Forgetting to draw the normal (line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence).

Measuring the angle from the surface instead of from the normal.

Using only one or two angles (mark scheme requires "at least 5").

Plotting sin r against sin i (inverted axes) — gradient becomes 1/n, not n.

Calculating n = sin i / sin r from a single reading instead of using the graph gradient.

##### 2.5 Transmission AND Reflection at an Interface (spec 55)

How tested:

"Explain why some of the light is reflected and some is transmitted when light meets a glass-air interface." (2 marks, Jun 2022 Q14b)

"State what is meant by partial reflection." (1 mark, Jan 2024 Q12a)

MCQ: "What does NOT occur at a glass block?" — answer: diffraction (1 mark, Oct 2022 Q8)

Full-mark answer (Jun 2022 Q14b style):

At the interface, there is a change in wave speed (or impedance mismatch) (1 mark)

Both reflection and transmission occur; the proportions depend on the size of the mismatch (1 mark)

Common pitfalls:

Stating only "light is reflected" or only "light is transmitted" — mark scheme requires both.

Confusing "interface" (spec 55) with "slit" (spec 50) — Oct 2022 Q8 traps students who say diffraction occurs at a glass block.

Forgetting to mention the change in wave speed as the cause.

##### 2.6 Critical Angle as the Boundary Between Partial and Total Reflection

How tested:

"Calculate the critical angle for light travelling from glass (n = 1.50) into air." (2 marks, Jan 2022 Q5)

"Explain what happens to the light as the angle of incidence is gradually increased from 0° to 90° in the glass." (3 marks, Oct 2023 Q18c — conceptual)

Full-mark answer (Oct 2023 Q18c style):

For i < critical angle: most light is transmitted (refracted), with a small partial reflection (1 mark)

As i approaches the critical angle: the refracted ray bends further from the normal, and the reflected intensity increases (1 mark)

For i > critical angle: total internal reflection — 100% reflected, no transmission (1 mark)

Common pitfall: Treating partial reflection and TIR as separate phenomena. They are the same phenomenon at different angles of incidence — TIR is the limiting case.

##### 2.7 Pulse-Echo / Ultrasound (spec 56, application of spec 55)

How tested:

11/11 papers, 23 marks total — appears in EVERY paper.

Most common form: "Calculate the distance to the boundary given the time delay and wave speed" (3 marks).

Factor-of-2 trap: forgetting to divide vt by 2 — appears in 6 examiner reports.

Full-mark answer requirements:

1. Use d = vt/2 (state the formula explicitly)

2. Substitute values with correct units (especially convert ms to s, cm to m)

3. Quote answer with appropriate sig figs and units

Common pitfalls:

Forgetting the factor of ½ — calculates 2× the correct distance (lose 1 mark).

Using the speed of sound in air (340 m s⁻¹) instead of in water (1500 m s⁻¹) or in tissue (1540 m s⁻¹).

Mixing units (e.g. v in m/s but t in ms without conversion).

##### 2.8 Optical Fibre (spec 47, 48, 55)

How tested:

4 papers, 38 marks total — appears as a multi-part question with a real-world context.

Most common: calculate critical angle at core-cladding, predict whether TIR occurs for a given ray, explain the role of cladding, calculate pulse broadening.

Full-mark answer structure (Jan 2025 Q18 — 13 marks):

1. State ncₒᵣₑ > ncₗₐddᵢₙg and why (1 mark)

2. Calculate critical angle: sin C = ncₗₐddᵢₙg/ncₒᵣₑ (2 marks)

3. Apply: ray strikes cladding at angle > C → TIR occurs (2 marks)

4. Explain role of cladding: protects core boundary, prevents cross-talk, reduces modal dispersion (3 marks)

5. Calculate pulse broadening from path-length difference between axial and extreme rays (3 marks)

6. QWC: continuous prose, cause-and-effect connectives (2 marks)

Common pitfalls:

Forgetting ncₒᵣₑ > ncₗₐddᵢₙg (mark scheme requires this stated).

Using ncₗₐddᵢₙg/ncₒᵣₑ inverted → sin C > 1 (mathematically impossible — diagnostic of the error).

Confusing modal dispersion (different path lengths) with material dispersion (different wavelengths).

#### 3. Command Word Mapping for Spec 48, 50, 55 Questions

Command word What the examiner wants Marks Typical context

State A single term or value, no working 1 "State what is meant by partial reflection"

Describe List the features of a phenomenon 2–3 "Describe the diffraction pattern produced by a single slit"

Explain Cause-and-effect reasoning; why something happens 2–3 "Explain why sound diffracts around a doorway but light does not"

Use Huygens' construction to explain Apply the secondary-wavelet model to a specific situation 3 "Use Huygens' construction to explain what happens when a wave meets a slit"

Calculate Show working, numerical answer 2–3 "Calculate the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary"

Determine Show working from data, may involve judgment 3–4 "Determine the refractive index of the glass using the graph"

Show that Use given data, show every step, arrive at given value 2 "Show that the angle to the first minimum is 0.36°"

Discuss (QWC) Sustained prose, multiple linked points, evaluation 6 "Discuss the use of cladding in optical fibres"

Suggest Plausible application, reason, or improvement 1–2 "Suggest why coupling gel is used in ultrasound scanning"

#### 4. Recurring Examiner Report Themes (Jan 2019–Jun 2025)

##### 4.1 "Students forgot the factor of ½ in pulse-echo"

Appears in 6 examiner reports (Jun 2019, Jan 2022, Jun 2022, Oct 2023, Jan 2024, Jun 2025). The pulse travels to the boundary and back, so d = vt/2, not d = vt. Fix: write d = vt/2 (with the 2) on the formula sheet, and explicitly state "the pulse travels there and back".

##### 4.2 "Students measured the angle from the surface, not the normal"

Appears in 5 examiner reports (Jan 2022, Jan 2023, Oct 2023, Jan 2025, Jun 2025). Snell's law and the critical angle use angles measured from the normal. Fix: always check whether the question gives the angle from the surface; if so, subtract from 90°.

##### 4.3 "Students described only one of reflection or transmission"

Appears in 4 examiner reports (Jun 2022, Jan 2024, Jun 2024, Jan 2025). Spec 55 requires the understanding that both reflection and transmission occur at most interfaces. Fix: when asked about an interface, always state "both reflection and transmission occur, with the proportions depending on the impedance mismatch".

##### 4.4 "Students confused diffraction with refraction"

Appears in 3 examiner reports (Oct 2022, Jan 2023, Jan 2024). Diffraction (spec 50) requires a gap or obstacle comparable to the wavelength; refraction (spec 45) occurs at every interface regardless of wavelength. Oct 2022 Q8 MCQ directly tested this — many students said diffraction occurs at a glass block (it does not; only refraction and partial reflection occur). Fix: diffraction = spreading through a gap; refraction = bending at an interface.

##### 4.5 "Students forgot to draw the normal"

Appears in 2 examiner reports (Jun 2024, Jan 2025) — both in spec 48 method questions. The normal is the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence; angles i and r are measured from it. Fix: always draw the normal first, before measuring any angles.

##### 4.6 "Students used only one angle of incidence"

Appears in 2 examiner reports (Jun 2024, Jan 2024). The mark scheme for spec 48 explicitly requires "at least 5 different angles of incidence". Using only one or two loses the method mark. Fix: in method questions, always state "repeat for at least 5 different angles".

##### 4.7 "Students forgot both TIR conditions"

Appears in 4 examiner reports. TIR requires: (1) denser → less dense medium AND (2) i > C. Stating only one condition loses 1 mark. Fix: state both conditions, connected by "AND".

##### 4.8 "Students could not apply Huygens' construction"

Appears in 1 examiner report (Jun 2024). Students described the diffraction pattern but did not use the secondary-wavelet mechanism to explain it. Fix: Huygens questions require "every point on the wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets" and "the new wavefront is the envelope of these wavelets".

#### 5. Mark Scheme Phrasing — Exact Wording That Scores

Examiner mark schemes reward very specific phrasing. Memorise these:

Mark scheme phrase Scores the mark for

"secondary wavelets" Huygens' construction

"envelope of the wavelets" Huygens' construction (new wavefront)

"spreading of the wave" Diffraction definition

"gap width comparable to the wavelength" When diffraction is significant

"central maximum is brightest and widest" Single-slit pattern feature

"twice the width of the secondary maxima" Central maximum width

"wavelength much smaller than obstacle" Why light does not diffract around buildings

"sin i = n sin r" Snell's law (single medium)

"gradient = n" Refractive index from graph

"at least 5 different angles" Spec 48 method requirement

"both reflection and transmission" Spec 55 interface behaviour

"change in wave speed at the boundary" Cause of reflection

"impedance mismatch" Cause of partial reflection

"denser to less dense medium" TIR condition 1

"angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle" TIR condition 2

"ncₒᵣₑ > ncₗₐddᵢₙg" Optical fibre refractive index ordering

"TIR at the core-cladding boundary" Optical fibre mechanism

"d = vt/2" Pulse-echo distance formula

"pulse travels there and back" Why the factor of 2

"coupling gel reduces reflection at air-skin boundary" Ultrasound practical detail

Do NOT paraphrase these in the exam. Use the exact phrasing — examiners are looking for these keywords.

#### 7. Practice Questions (Self-Test)

##### 7.1 Huygens + Diffraction (3 marks)

Use Huygens' construction to explain what happens to a plane wavefront when it meets a narrow slit whose width is comparable to the wavelength.

Expected answer:

Every point on the wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets (1 mark)

Only the points within the slit opening emit wavelets into the region beyond the slit (1 mark)

The new wavefront (envelope of these wavelets) is curved, so the wave spreads laterally beyond the geometric shadow of the slit — diffraction (1 mark)

##### 7.2 Refractive Index Practical (8 marks)

A student is given a rectangular glass block, a ray box with a single slit, a protractor, a sheet of paper, and 4 pins. They are asked to determine the refractive index of the glass.

(a) Describe the method the student should use. (6 marks) (b) State why the student should take measurements at several different angles of incidence rather than at a single angle. (2 marks)

Expected answer:

(a)

1. Place the block on the paper; trace around it with a pencil. Draw a normal to one face at the point where the ray will meet the block (1)

2. Direct a narrow ray from the ray box at a measured angle of incidence i; mark the incident ray with two pins placed in line with the ray (1)

3. Look through the far side of the block along the ray; place two more pins in line with the emergent ray (1)

4. Remove the block; join the pin marks to draw the incident, refracted (inside the block), and emergent rays (1)

5. Measure i and r with a protractor; repeat for at least 5 different angles of incidence (1)

6. Plot sin i against sin r; the gradient of the straight line through the origin equals the refractive index n (1)

(b)

Random errors in individual angle measurements partly cancel out when the line of best fit is drawn (1)

Anomalies are visible as points off the line and can be excluded; the gradient method is more reliable than a single n = sin i / sin r calculation (1)

##### 7.3 Single-Slit Calculation (4 marks)

Monochromatic light of wavelength 580 nm is incident on a single slit of width 0.080 mm. A screen is placed 1.50 m beyond the slit.

(a) Calculate the angle to the first minimum. (2) (b) Calculate the width of the central maximum on the screen. (2)

Expected answer:

(a)

sin θ = λ / a = (580 × 10⁻⁹) / (0.080 × 10⁻³) = 7.25 × 10⁻³

θ = sin⁻¹(7.25 × 10⁻³) ≈ 0.42° (or 7.25 × 10⁻³ rad, since θ is small)

(b)

Distance from centre to first minimum: x = D × tan θ ≈ 1.50 × 7.25 × 10⁻³ = 1.09 × 10⁻² m

Width of central maximum = 2x = 2.18 × 10⁻² m = 2.18 cm

##### 7.4 Transmission, Reflection, and Critical Angle (6 marks)

Light of wavelength 500 nm travels inside a glass block of refractive index 1.60. The light meets a glass-air interface.

(a) Calculate the critical angle at the glass-air interface. (2) (b) State what happens to the light when the angle of incidence is 30° (i.e. less than the critical angle). (2) (c) State what happens when the angle of incidence is 50° (i.e. greater than the critical angle). (2)

Expected answer:

(a)

sin C = nₐᵢᵣ / ngₗₐₛₛ = 1.00 / 1.60 = 0.625

C = sin⁻¹(0.625) = 38.7°

(b) (when i = 30° < C)

Both reflection and transmission occur (partial reflection) (1)

Most of the light is transmitted (refracted) into the air, bending away from the normal; a small fraction is reflected back into the glass (1)

(c) (when i = 50° > C)

Total internal reflection occurs (no transmission into air) (1)

100% of the light is reflected back into the glass, angle of reflection = 50° (1)

##### 7.5 Pulse-Echo / Ultrasound (5 marks)

In a medical ultrasound scan, a transducer emits a short pulse of ultrasound into the body. The speed of sound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. An echo is detected 65 µs after the pulse is emitted.

(a) Calculate the distance from the transducer to the reflecting boundary. (3) (b) Explain why a coupling gel is used between the transducer and the skin. (2)

Expected answer:

(a)

d = vt/2 (state the formula) (1)

d = (1540 × 65 × 10⁻⁶) / 2 (correct substitution with µs → s conversion) (1)

d = 0.100 / 2 = 0.050 m = 5.0 cm (numerical answer with units, 2 sig figs) (1)

(b)

Without gel, the air-skin boundary reflects ~99.9% of the ultrasound (due to the large acoustic impedance mismatch between air and skin); almost none enters the body (1)

The gel has an acoustic impedance close to that of skin, so the gel-skin interface reflects very little; this allows the ultrasound to be transmitted into the body (1)

Tier 1 — FoundationIf you can't answer these instantly, revisit the chapter content.

Q1 QFR §64 1 mark · ~1 min

Define electric current.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge (the charge passing a point per unit time).

Marking Points

B1 Rate of flow of (electric) charge

NOT Accepted

"Flow of electrons" alone (describes electron flow, not the definition of current — ions can also carry current); "movement of charge" without "rate of"; "what flows in a wire".

⚠️ Common Error

Describing the mechanism (electrons moving) instead of giving the formal definition. The MS for Jan 2020 Q1(a) required "rate of flow of charge" specifically.

Q2 QFR §65 1 mark · ~1 min

Define potential difference.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: The energy transferred (work done) per unit charge between two points in a circuit.

Marking Points

B1 Energy transferred per unit charge (accept "work done per unit charge")

NOT Accepted

"The push of electricity"; "the voltage across a component" (circular definition); "energy per second" (that is power, not p.d.).

⚠️ Common Error

Confusing potential difference with current or power. "Energy per second" is a power definition, not a p.d. definition.

Q3 QFR §67a 1 mark · ~1 min

State Kirchhoff's first law.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: At any junction (node) in an electrical circuit, the sum of the currents entering the junction equals the sum of the currents leaving the junction.

Marking Points

B1 Sum of currents entering a junction = sum of currents leaving (accept "algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero")

NOT Accepted

"Voltage is the same in parallel" (that is a consequence, not the law); "Current is conserved" without mentioning a junction (too vague — the MS for Jun 2024 Q9 required explicit mention of the junction).

⚠️ Common Error

Stating Kirchhoff's second law instead. Adding "the current splits equally" (it does not necessarily split equally).

Q4 QFR §69 1 mark · ~1 min

Define electromotive force (e.m.f.).

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is the energy transferred per unit charge by the source when charge flows through it.

Marking Points

B1 Energy (transferred/converted/work done) per unit charge (by/through the source)

NOT Accepted

"The force that pushes electrons" (e.m.f. is NOT a force); "the voltage of a cell" (voltage is a p.d.); omitting "per unit charge"; "the p.d. across a cell" (terminal p.d. ≠ e.m.f. when current flows).

⚠️ Common Error

The word "force" in "electromotive force" misleads students into thinking it is a force. E.m.f. is an energy-per-charge quantity (measured in volts), not a force (measured in newtons).

Q5 TDC §69 1 mark · ~1 min

State the equation relating terminal potential difference, e.m.f., current, and internal resistance.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: V = ε − Ir

Marking Points

B1 V = ε − Ir (accept ℰ or E for e.m.f. symbol)

NOT Accepted

V = ε + Ir (wrong sign — would mean terminal p.d. exceeds e.m.f., which is physically impossible); V = IR (this is Ohm's law, not the e.m.f. equation).

⚠️ Common Error

Writing V = ε + Ir. This is the single most common sign error in Ch 2.4. The lost volts (Ir) must be subtracted from the e.m.f. to give the terminal p.d.

Tier 2 — ApplicationMulti-step calculations, explanations, and data interpretation.

Q6 EXP §64 3 marks · ~3 min

Explain, in terms of the motion of conduction electrons and lattice ions, why a metal wire has resistance.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: When a p.d. is applied across a metal wire, the free electrons are accelerated by the electric field and gain kinetic energy. However, the electrons repeatedly collide with the vibrating lattice ions. At each collision, the electrons transfer energy to the lattice (heating the wire) and lose their directed velocity. This repeated scattering randomises the electron motion and limits the mean drift velocity, which manifests macroscopically as resistance.

Marking Points

M1 Electrons are accelerated by the electric field / gain kinetic energy

M1 Electrons collide with (vibrating) lattice ions

A1 Collisions randomise electron velocity / transfer energy to the lattice / limit the drift velocity

NOT Accepted

"Electrons get stuck" or "electrons are repelled by atoms" — must reference collisions with lattice ions specifically. "Opposition to current flow" is a restatement, not a mechanism.

⚠️ Common Error

Describing resistance as "opposition to current flow" without any microscopic mechanism. The MS for Jun 2019 Q4(b) explicitly required the collision mechanism.

Q7 WTE §67a 2 marks · ~3 min

Explain how Kirchhoff's first law is a consequence of the conservation of charge.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: Conservation of charge states that electric charge cannot be created or destroyed. At a junction, the charge flowing into the junction per unit time must equal the charge flowing out per unit time. Since current is defined as the rate of flow of charge (I = ΔQ/Δt), and the time interval is the same for all branches, the sum of currents entering must equal the sum of currents leaving.

Marking Points

E1 Charge cannot be created or destroyed / is conserved

E2 Therefore charge per unit time flowing in = charge per unit time flowing out at a junction, and since I = ΔQ/Δt, the sum of currents in equals sum of currents out

NOT Accepted

"Charge is conserved so current is conserved" (too vague — must explicitly link charge conservation to current via the rate definition).

⚠️ Common Error

Stating Kirchhoff's first law without explaining why it follows from charge conservation. The key step is connecting charge (Q) to current (I) via I = ΔQ/Δt.

Q8 DIA §70 4 marks · ~5 min

Sketch separate I–V characteristic graphs for each of the following components. In each case, label both axes and indicate the key features of the graph.
(a) A metallic conductor at constant temperature (ohmic conductor).
(b) A filament lamp.
(c) A silicon diode.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: Three I–V graphs sketched (V on x-axis, I on y-axis): (a) straight line through origin; (b) symmetric curve through origin with decreasing gradient; (c) zero current until ~0.6 V forward bias, then sharp rise.

Part (a) — Ohmic conductor: A straight line through the origin with constant gradient (I is directly proportional to V).

Part (b) — Filament lamp: A curve through the origin with decreasing gradient as |V| increases (the graph becomes less steep). The curve is symmetric in the first and third quadrants (same shape for positive and negative V).

Part (c) — Silicon diode: Approximately zero current for negative p.d. and for positive p.d. below ~0.6 V. Above approximately 0.6 V in the forward-biased direction, the current increases sharply.

Marking Points

B1 Part (a): Straight line through the origin; both axes labelled

B1 Part (b): Curve through the origin with decreasing gradient; symmetric about the origin

B1 Part (c): Approximately zero current for negative V and for positive V < 0.6 V

B1 Part (c): Sharp increase in current above threshold of ~0.6 V in forward direction

NOT Accepted

Drawing the diode curve in both quadrants (diodes conduct in only one direction). Drawing the filament lamp as a straight line. Omitting axis labels.

⚠️ Common Error

For the diode, drawing a curve that rises gradually rather than showing a sharp threshold at ~0.6 V. The MS requires the near-zero current region and the sharp transition to be clearly distinguishable.

Q9 WTE §70, §79 4 marks · ~5 min

A student is asked to explain why the resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature while the resistance of an NTC thermistor decreases with temperature. Their answer is: "The resistance changes because of temperature. In both cases the atoms vibrate more, which changes the resistance." Explain what is wrong with this answer and write a correct explanation for each component.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: The student's answer is wrong because it applies the same mechanism (lattice vibrations) to both components. "Lattice vibrations" is the mechanism for metals only — it does not explain thermistor behaviour.

Metal: As temperature increases, the lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude. This increases the frequency of collisions between conduction electrons and lattice ions, increasing the scattering of electrons and therefore increasing the resistance.

NTC thermistor: As temperature increases, more charge carriers are released (promoted) into the conduction band. This increases the number density of charge carriers (n). Since resistance is inversely related to the number of charge carriers, the resistance decreases.

Marking Points

C1 Identifies the error: the student applies the same mechanism to both; "lattice vibrations" is not the mechanism for semiconductors

C2 Metal: increased lattice ion vibrations → increased electron scattering → increased resistance

C3 Thermistor: increased temperature → more charge carriers released into conduction band → increased n → decreased resistance

C4 Clear contrast between the two different mechanisms

NOT Accepted

"Both have increased vibrations so both resistances increase"; "The thermistor has more energy so resistance decreases" (no mechanism); "Electrons move faster in the thermistor" (it is charge carrier number that increases, not their speed).

⚠️ Common Error

This is the #1 exam trap in Ch 2.4, appearing in 4 of 13 past papers. The MS for Jan 2022 and Oct 2023 specifically penalised students who used "lattice vibrations" to explain thermistor behaviour. The metal mechanism (vibrations) and semiconductor mechanism (charge carrier release) are fundamentally different.

Q10 DER §65 3 marks · ~4 min

The volt is defined as 1 joule per coulomb and the ampere as 1 coulomb per second. Show that 1 V = 1 W A⁻¹, where W represents watts. (Bald answer = 0 marks — every algebraic step must be shown.)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: 1 V = 1 W A⁻¹ (shown via unit substitution: 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹ → 1 W s C⁻¹ → 1 W A⁻¹).

Starting from the definition of the volt:

1 V = 1 J C⁻¹

Since 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹, we can write 1 J = 1 W s. Substituting:

1 V = (1 W s) × C⁻¹ = 1 W s C⁻¹

Since 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹, therefore 1 s C⁻¹ = 1 A⁻¹. Substituting:

1 V = 1 W × A⁻¹ = 1 W A⁻¹ ✓

Marking Points

M1 Starts from 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹

M1 Expresses joules in terms of watts and seconds: 1 J = 1 W s (from 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹)

A1 Substitutes and uses 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹ to show 1 V = 1 W A⁻¹

NOT Accepted

Writing "1 V = 1 W A⁻¹" directly without derivation (bald answer = 0 marks). Skipping intermediate steps.

⚠️ Common Error

Students often write the final answer immediately, losing all 3 marks. Every algebraic manipulation must be shown for "show that" questions. This is a unit-derivation question, not a recall question.

Q11 CAL §73 3 marks · ~4 min

A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a current of 2.4 A. The number density of free electrons in copper is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the drift velocity of the free electrons in the wire.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: v = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ (≈ 0.12 mm s⁻¹).

v = I/(nAe) = 2.4 / (8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 2.4 / (2.04 × 10⁴) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹

Marking Points

M1 Correct rearrangement and substitution into v = I/(nAe)

M1 Correct evaluation of the denominator: nAe = 2.04 × 10⁴ (allow 2.0–2.1 × 10⁴)

A1 v = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ (allow 1.15–1.20 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹)

NOT Accepted

Answer without unit; answer with incorrect magnitude (e.g. 1.2 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ — this is faster than light!); using diameter instead of cross-sectional area.

⚠️ Common Error

Getting the magnitude completely wrong. Drift velocity in metals is always very small (~10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹), because the number density of free electrons is enormous. If your answer comes out much larger than 1 mm s⁻¹, check your calculation.

Q12 CAL §77 3 marks · ~3 min

An LED has a potential difference of 2.1 V across it and a current of 18 mA through it. Calculate the power dissipated by the LED.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: P = 0.038 W (or 38 mW).

P = VI = 2.1 × 0.018 = 0.0378 W = 0.038 W (or 38 mW)

Marking Points

M1 Conversion of 18 mA to 0.018 A

M1 Correct substitution into P = VI

A1 0.038 W or 38 mW (accept 0.0378 W for 3 s.f.)

NOT Accepted

37.8 W (failed to convert mA to A — this is 1000× too large); 2.1 × 18 = 37.8 "W" without unit conversion; answers without units.

⚠️ Common Error

The mA-to-A conversion trap. Multiplying 2.1 × 18 directly gives 37.8, which is wrong by a factor of 1000. Always convert milliamperes to amperes before substituting into P = VI.

Q13 RAT §71 3 marks · ~4 min

Wire P has length l, diameter d, and resistivity ρ. Wire Q has length 2l, diameter d, and is made of the same material. Wire R has length l, diameter 2d, and is made of the same material. State the ratio of resistances Rₚ : Rᵩ : Rᵣ.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: Rₚ : Rᵩ : Rᵣ = 4 : 8 : 1.

Working:

R = ρl/A, so Rₚ = ρl/A where A = πd²/4

Wire Q: length 2l, same A → Rᵩ = ρ(2l)/A = 2Rₚ

Wire R: same length l, diameter 2d → Aᵣ = π(2d)²/4 = 4A → Rᵣ = ρl/(4A) = Rₚ/4

Expressing as integer ratio: Rₚ : Rᵩ : Rᵣ = Rₚ : 2Rₚ : Rₚ/4 = 4 : 8 : 1

Marking Points

M1 Correct reasoning for Q: doubling length doubles resistance (Rᵩ = 2Rₚ)

M1 Correct reasoning for R: doubling diameter quadruples area, so resistance is quartered (Rᵣ = Rₚ/4)

A1 Correct final ratio: 4 : 8 : 1

NOT Accepted

1 : 2 : 0.25 (not integer ratio); 4 : 2 : 1 (wrong — confused the effect of doubling diameter); 1 : 2 : 4 (inverted the diameter effect).

⚠️ Common Error

Thinking that doubling the diameter doubles the area (instead of quadrupling it, since A ∝ d²). This gives the ratio 4 : 8 : 2 instead of 4 : 8 : 1. Remember: area depends on the square of the diameter.

Q14 GRD §71 4 marks · ~5 min

A student investigates how the resistance R of a manganin wire varies with its length l. The wire has a constant cross-sectional area of 5.1 × 10⁻⁷ m². The student measures R for different lengths and plots a graph of R against l. The graph is a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 6.7 Ω m⁻¹. Use the graph to determine the resistivity of manganin.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: ρ = 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

From R = ρl/A, rearranging gives R = (ρ/A) × l. This is of the form y = mx (straight line through origin) where the gradient m = ρ/A.

Therefore: ρ = gradient × A = 6.7 Ω m⁻¹ × 5.1 × 10⁻⁷ m² = 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m

Marking Points

M1 States or implies R = ρl/A, so R = (ρ/A) × l (straight line with gradient = ρ/A)

M1 Identifies gradient of R vs l graph = ρ/A

M1 Correct substitution: ρ = 6.7 × 5.1 × 10⁻⁷

A1 ρ = 3.4 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m with correct units (accept 3.42 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m)

NOT Accepted

Using ρ = gradient/A (inverted fraction); using gradient = ρ × A (wrong relationship); omitting units; using m instead of m² for area giving ρ = 3.4 × 10⁻³ Ω m.

⚠️ Common Error

Confusing which variable goes on which axis, then writing gradient = A/ρ instead of ρ/A. Remember: if R is on the y-axis and l is on the x-axis, then gradient = ΔR/Δl = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A.

Q15 CAL §69 3 marks · ~4 min

A cell of e.m.f. 9.0 V and internal resistance 1.5 Ω is connected to an external resistor of 10.5 Ω. Calculate (a) the current in the circuit, and (b) the terminal p.d. across the cell.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: (a) I = 0.75 A; (b) V = 7.9 V.

(a) I = ε/(R + r) = 9.0 V / (10.5 Ω + 1.5 Ω) = 9.0 / 12.0 = 0.75 A

(b) V = IR = 0.75 A × 10.5 Ω = 7.9 V

(or V = ε − Ir = 9.0 − 0.75 × 1.5 = 7.875 ≈ 7.9 V)

Marking Points

M1 I = ε/(R + r) = 9.0/12.0 = 0.75 A (method mark for correct equation and total resistance)

A1 I = 0.75 A

A1 V = 7.9 V (accept 7.88 V from V = ε − Ir route; ECF from incorrect current)

NOT Accepted

Using I = ε/R (ignoring internal resistance) giving I = 0.86 A; using V = ε (ignoring internal resistance) giving V = 9.0 V; answers without units.

⚠️ Common Error

Forgetting to include the internal resistance in the total resistance. The denominator must be (R + r), not just R. Also check: terminal p.d. must be less than e.m.f. when current flows — if you get V > ε, something is wrong.

Tier 3 — IntegrationCross-topic synthesis, extended derivations, and QWC.

Q16 DER §67b, §68 4 marks · ~5 min

Starting from Kirchhoff's first and second laws and the definition of resistance R = V/I, derive the formula for the total resistance of two resistors R₁ and R₂ connected in series: Rₜ = R₁ + R₂. (Bald answer = 0 marks — every step must be shown.)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: Rₜ = R₁ + R₂ (derived from Kirchhoff's first law, Kirchhoff's second law, and V = IR).

By Kirchhoff's first law (conservation of charge), the same current I flows through both resistors since there is no junction between them.

By Kirchhoff's second law (conservation of energy), the sum of p.d.s equals the e.m.f.:

Vₜ = V₁ + V₂

Substituting V = IR for each component:

IRₜ = IR₁ + IR₂

Factoring out I:

IRₜ = I(R₁ + R₂)

Dividing both sides by I:

Rₜ = R₁ + R₂ ✓

Marking Points

M1 Same current I through both resistors (Kirchhoff's first law)

M1 Vₜ = V₁ + V₂ (Kirchhoff's second law)

M1 Substitution: IRₜ = IR₁ + IR₂, then factorising: IRₜ = I(R₁ + R₂)

A1 Divides by I to obtain Rₜ = R₁ + R₂

NOT Accepted

Stating the formula without derivation; starting from V = IR alone without citing Kirchhoff's laws; using numerical examples instead of algebraic proof; writing V₁ = I₁R₁ with different currents (current is the same in series).

⚠️ Common Error

Not explicitly citing Kirchhoff's laws as the starting point. The question specifically asks you to start from these laws. Another error is writing different subscripts for current (I₁, I₂) — in series, the current is the same throughout.

Q17 QWC §67a, §67b 6 marks · ~8 min

A circuit contains a battery of e.m.f. ε connected to three resistors: resistor P (4.0 Ω) in series with a parallel combination of resistor Q (6.0 Ω) and resistor R (12.0 Ω). A student measures the current leaving the battery as 1.50 A. Using Kirchhoff's laws, explain how the current distributes in this circuit and how the potential difference is shared between the components. Refer to each resistor by its label (P, Q, R) throughout your answer. (QWC: split rubric — 4 IC marks + 2 structure marks.)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: K1 at junction: Iᵩ = 1.00 A, Iᵣ = 0.50 A (verified: 1.00 + 0.50 = 1.50 A). K2 around loop: Vₚ = Vᵩ = Vᵣ = 6.0 V; ε = 12.0 V.

Indicative Content — 4 marks:

Mark Point required

IC1 Kirchhoff's first law applied: current of 1.50 A enters the junction and splits. Using the current divider rule: current through Q = 1.50 × 12.0/(6.0 + 12.0) = 1.00 A; current through R = 1.50 × 6.0/(6.0 + 12.0) = 0.50 A. Verified: 1.00 + 0.50 = 1.50 A ✓ (must use labels Q and R)

IC2 Physical principle of K1: conservation of charge — charge cannot accumulate at a junction

IC3 Kirchhoff's second law: Vₚ = 1.50 × 4.0 = 6.0 V; Vᵩ = 1.00 × 6.0 = 6.0 V; Vᵣ = 0.50 × 12.0 = 6.0 V. Sum of p.d.s: 6.0 + 6.0 = 12.0 V = ε (must use labels P, Q, R)

IC4 Physical principle of K2: conservation of energy — p.d. is the same across parallel components Q and R (both 6.0 V)

Structure, Precision and Linkage — 2 marks:

Mark Criterion

SP1 Each resistor is referred to by its specific label (P, Q, R) throughout the answer — generic statements without labels lose IC marks

SP2 Clear logical structure: K1 stated, applied to the specific junction, values calculated and verified; then K2 stated, applied to the specific loop, values calculated and verified; both laws explicitly linked to their physical conservation principles

NOT Accepted

"Current is conserved at junctions" without naming which junction or which resistors; "Energy is conserved" without referencing p.d. and e.m.f. specifically; "The voltages add up" without using the specific resistor labels and calculated values; any answer that does not consistently use the labels P, Q, R.

⚠️ Common Error

The MS for Jun 2022 Q15(a) was very strict: generic Kirchhoff's law statements without application to the specific resistors named in the question lost marks. Students must use the labels P, Q, R in every calculation and explanation. Writing continuous prose with logical connectives (therefore, since, because) is required for QWC marks.

Q18 QWC §71 6 marks · ~8 min

The resistance of a tungsten filament lamp increases significantly when it is operating compared to when it is cold. A student uses the cold resistance value in the equation R = ρl/A to calculate the resistivity of tungsten at its operating temperature. The student's calculated value is much lower than the accepted value at the operating temperature. Explain, using a causal chain of reasoning, why the student's calculated resistivity is incorrect. (QWC: split rubric — 4 IC marks + 2 structure marks.)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: Operating temperature raises tungsten resistivity (lattice-ion vibration mechanism), so Rₒₚₑᵣₐₜᵢₙg ≫ Rcₒₗd. Using Rcₒₗd in ρ = RA/l gives a ρ value much lower than the true ρ at the operating temperature.

Indicative Content — 4 marks:

Mark Point required

IC1 When the filament lamp operates, the temperature of the tungsten filament increases significantly because electrical energy is converted to thermal energy in the filament

IC2 Because the temperature increases, the resistivity of tungsten increases (since resistivity of metals increases with temperature due to greater lattice ion vibration)

IC3 This means the resistance at operating temperature is much greater than the cold resistance. The student uses the cold resistance in ρ = RA/l, and since Rcₒₗd ≪ Rₒₚₑᵣₐₜᵢₙg, the calculated ρ will be much lower than the true ρ at the operating temperature

IC4 To obtain the correct resistivity at the operating temperature, the student must use the resistance at that temperature (e.g. read from the I-V characteristic at the operating current), not the cold resistance

Structure — 2 marks:

Mark Criterion

S1 Coherent, sustained causal chain using connective language throughout ("because," "therefore," "which means," "so," "as a result")

S2 Each step logically follows from the previous one; no isolated or disconnected statements; the chain runs continuously from cause to final conclusion

NOT Accepted

Simple list of facts without causal connections; "The resistance changes" without explaining why (missing the temperature-resistivity mechanism for metals); bullet points (loses structure marks); stating the answer without tracing through the causal chain.

⚠️ Common Error

Writing bullet-pointed facts without connective language loses both structure marks. The key physics point that many students miss is that resistivity of metals increases with temperature (lattice vibration mechanism), and this must be stated explicitly. Using the cold resistance gives a value that is wrong because ρ at the operating temperature is genuinely higher, not because of a measurement error.

Q19 GRD §71 8 marks · ~12 min

A student investigates the resistivity of a uniform constantan wire. She measures the resistance R of wires of the same length (1.00 m) but different diameters d. Her results are:

d / mm R / Ω

0.40 2.20

0.50 1.40

0.60 0.97

0.80 0.55

1.00 0.35

(a) Explain why a graph of R against 1/d² should be plotted to determine the resistivity, rather than R against d. State the relationship you would expect. (3 marks)
(b) Calculate the additional column values of 1/d² (in m⁻²). Plot R (y-axis) against 1/d² (x-axis). Determine the gradient of your graph and use it to calculate the resistivity of constantan. (5 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer: (a) R = (4ρl/π)(1/d²) → straight line through origin; (b) ρ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

Part (a) — 3 marks:

Since A = πd²/4, we have R = ρl/A = 4ρl/(πd²). This is of the form R = (4ρl/π) × (1/d²), which is a straight line through the origin with gradient = 4ρl/π. A graph of R against d would be a curve (R ∝ 1/d²), making it impossible to determine a gradient. Plotting R against 1/d² linearises the relationship, allowing the gradient to be found and ρ calculated.

Part (b) — 5 marks:

Converting d from mm to m and calculating 1/d²:

d / mm d / m 1/d² / 10⁶ m⁻² R / Ω

0.40 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ 6.25 2.20

0.50 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ 4.00 1.40

0.60 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ 2.78 0.97

0.80 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ 1.56 0.55

1.00 1.0 × 10⁻³ 1.00 0.35

Plotting R (y-axis) against 1/d² (x-axis) gives a straight line through the origin.

Gradient = ΔR/Δ(1/d²) using a large triangle on the line of best fit:

gradient = (2.20 − 0.35) / [(6.25 − 1.00) × 10⁶] = 1.85 / (5.25 × 10⁶) = 3.52 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m²

Since gradient = 4ρl/π:

ρ = gradient × π/(4l) = 3.52 × 10⁻⁷ × π/(4 × 1.00) = 2.77 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m

Marking Points

Part (a)

M1 Derivation or statement of relationship: R = (4ρl/π)(1/d²), i.e. R ∝ 1/d²

E1 Explanation that R against d gives a curve while R against 1/d² gives a straight line through the origin

E2 Gradient of linearised graph = 4ρl/π, allowing ρ to be determined directly

Part (b)

C1 Correct conversion of d from mm to m before calculating 1/d² (critical step)

C2 Correct calculation of 1/d² values (at least 2 checked values correct)

P1 Suitable axes: R on y-axis, 1/d² on x-axis; points plotted correctly; line of best fit through origin

M2 Gradient calculated correctly from the line of best fit

A1 ρ = gradient × π/(4l) = 2.8 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m (accept 2.7–2.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m)

NOT Accepted

Plotting R against d (non-linear — defeats the purpose of linearisation); using d in mm without converting to metres for 1/d² (gives answer off by factor of 10⁶); using A = πd² (forgetting the /4) — A = πd²/4, so gradient = 4ρl/π, NOT ρl/π; forgetting to convert mm to m.

⚠️ Common Error #1

Calculating A = πd² (without /4) and then getting the wrong gradient expression. The cross-sectional area is A = π(d/2)² = πd²/4. Forgetting the factor of 4 gives ρ that is too large by a factor of 4.

⚠️ Common Error #2

Using d in mm directly when calculating 1/d². Since 1/d² has units of m⁻², the diameter must be in metres. Using mm gives 1/d² values that are 10⁶ times too large, making the gradient 10⁶ times too small and ρ 10⁶ times too small. Always convert mm → m first.

## Ch 2.4 — Electric Circuits | WPH12 Study Guide

Unit: WPH12 — IAL Physics Unit 2 • Chapter: 2.4 Electric Circuits • Spec points: 64–80

This merged study guide compiles the chapter's Definitions, Concepts, and Exam Connections into one self-contained document. Use the ☰ Index button (top-left) to jump to any section, and the 🌙 Dark button to toggle the colour scheme (your choice is remembered).

### Ch 2.4 — Electric Circuits: Definitions

Spec points 64–80 | IAL Physics WPH12

A comprehensive glossary of every examinable term in this chapter. All definitions use exam-ready language grounded in the specification and mark scheme terminology.

### 1. Electric Current and Potential Difference (Spec 64–65)

#### Electric Current (Spec 64)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Electric current (I) The rate of flow of electric charge. Current is defined as the charge passing a point per unit time: I = ΔQ/Δt. 64 15 marks, 4 sessions

Charge (Q) A fundamental property of matter; in circuits, the quantity of electricity transported. Measured in coulombs (C). One coulomb is the charge transported by a current of one ampere in one second: Q = It. 64 —

Coulomb (C) The SI unit of electric charge. Defined as the charge that passes a point in a circuit when a current of 1 ampere flows for 1 second (1 C = 1 A s). 64 —

Ampere (A) The SI unit of electric current. One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point per second (1 A = 1 C s⁻¹). 64 —

Rate of flow of charge The amount of charge passing a given point in a conductor per unit time; this is the definition of electric current. 64 —

Conventional current The flow of charge from positive to negative terminal of a cell; the direction taken as the direction of current in a circuit, opposite to the direction of electron flow. 64 —

Electron flow The actual movement of electrons in a metal conductor, from negative to positive terminal, opposite in direction to conventional current. 64 —

ΔQ/Δt The defining equation for electric current: the change in charge (ΔQ) divided by the change in time (Δt). Units: amperes (A). 64 —

Charge conservation at a point The principle that charge cannot accumulate at any point in a circuit — the current entering any point must equal the current leaving it. 64 —

I (symbol) Symbol for electric current. In the equation I = ΔQ/Δt, I is measured in amperes (A). 64 —

Q (symbol) Symbol for electric charge. In I = ΔQ/Δt, Q is measured in coulombs (C). 64 —

t (symbol) Symbol for time. In I = ΔQ/Δt, t is measured in seconds (s). 64 —

#### Potential Difference (Spec 65)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Potential difference (p.d., V) The energy transferred (work done) per unit charge between two points in a circuit: V = W/Q. It is the energy lost per coulomb of charge passing through a component. 65 14 marks, 5 sessions

Voltage A common name for potential difference; measured in volts (V). 65 —

Volt (V) The SI unit of potential difference. One volt is one joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹). 65 —

Energy transferred (W) The work done by the charge as it moves through a component; measured in joules (J). In V = W/Q, W is the energy transferred by charge Q moving through a p.d. V. 65 —

Work done per unit charge An equivalent definition of potential difference: the work done (energy transferred) when one coulomb of charge moves between two points. 65 —

V = W/Q The defining equation for potential difference: p.d. = energy transferred ÷ charge. Units: V (volts) = J (joules) ÷ C (coulombs). 65 —

p.d. across a component The energy transferred per unit charge as charge passes through that specific component; measured using a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component. 65 —

V (symbol) Symbol for potential difference (voltage). In V = W/Q, V is measured in volts (V). 65 —

W (symbol) Symbol for energy transferred or work done. In V = W/Q, W is measured in joules (J). 65 —

### 2. Resistance and Ohm's Law (Spec 66)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Resistance (R) A measure of the opposition to current flow in a conductor, defined as the ratio of potential difference across a component to the current through it: R = V/I. 66 20 marks, 8 sessions

Ohm (Ω) The SI unit of resistance. One ohm is the resistance of a component when a p.d. of 1 volt drives a current of 1 ampere through it (1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹). 66 —

R = V/I The defining equation for resistance. Resistance is the gradient of a V-I graph (or the reciprocal of the gradient of an I-V graph). 66 —

Ohm's law The principle that, for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the current through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it. 66 —

Ohmic conductor A conductor for which the current is directly proportional to the potential difference across it at constant temperature, i.e. it obeys Ohm's law and has a constant resistance. Its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin. 66 —

Constant resistance The property of an ohmic conductor: the ratio V/I remains constant for all values of current and p.d. (at constant temperature). 66 —

Directly proportional (I ∝ V) The relationship described by Ohm's law: doubling the p.d. across an ohmic conductor doubles the current through it. 66 —

Constant temperature condition The necessary condition for Ohm's law to hold; if temperature changes, resistance may change and the I-V relationship is no longer linear. 66 —

Non-ohmic conductor A conductor or component for which current is NOT directly proportional to p.d., meaning its resistance changes with current or p.d. Examples: filament lamp, thermistor, diode. 66 —

Ω (symbol) The Greek letter omega, symbol for the ohm, the SI unit of resistance. 66 —

### 3. Kirchhoff's Laws / Current and P.D. Distribution (Spec 67a, 67b)

#### Current Distribution — Kirchhoff's First Law (Spec 67a)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Kirchhoff's first law At any junction in an electrical circuit, the sum of the currents entering the junction equals the sum of the currents leaving the junction. This is a consequence of the conservation of charge. 67a 9 marks, 3 sessions

Conservation of charge The principle that electric charge cannot be created or destroyed; at any point in a circuit, the total charge flowing in equals the total charge flowing out. This is the physical basis for Kirchhoff's first law. 67a —

Junction (in a circuit) A point in a circuit where two or more conductors meet and current can divide or combine. At a junction, Kirchhoff's first law applies: ΣIᵢₙ = ΣIₒᵤₜ. 67a —

Current distribution The way current divides among parallel branches of a circuit, governed by Kirchhoff's first law. The current in each branch depends on the resistance of that branch (lower resistance → higher current). 67a —

ΣIᵢₙ = ΣIₒᵤₜ The mathematical statement of Kirchhoff's first law: the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero. 67a —

Node An alternative term for a junction in a circuit; a point where circuit elements connect. 67a —

Superposition of currents at a junction The principle that the total current at a junction is the algebraic sum of all individual currents entering and leaving; no current is lost or gained at a junction. 67a —

#### P.D. Distribution — Kirchhoff's Second Law (Spec 67b)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Kirchhoff's second law In any closed loop of an electrical circuit, the sum of the potential differences around the loop is equal to the sum of the electromotive forces in that loop. This is a consequence of the conservation of energy. 67b 7 marks, 2 sessions

Conservation of energy (in circuits) The principle that the total energy supplied by sources of e.m.f. in a closed loop equals the total energy transferred to components in that loop. This is the physical basis for Kirchhoff's second law. 67b —

Closed loop A complete conducting path around a circuit that starts and ends at the same point, passing through one or more components and/or sources of e.m.f. 67b —

P.D. distribution The way potential differences are shared among components in a series circuit, governed by Kirchhoff's second law. The sum of p.d.s across all components in series equals the total e.m.f. of the source. 67b —

ΣV = Σε The mathematical statement of Kirchhoff's second law: the sum of p.d.s around any closed loop equals the sum of e.m.f.s in that loop. 67b —

Energy per unit charge A way of understanding Kirchhoff's second law: the e.m.f. supplies a certain amount of energy per coulomb, and the p.d.s across components in the loop account for all of that energy per coulomb being transferred. 67b —

### 4. Series and Parallel Circuits (Spec 68)

#### Series Circuits (Spec 68)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Series circuit A circuit in which components are connected one after another along a single path, so the same current flows through each component. 68 23 marks, 7 sessions

Current in series The current is the same through all components connected in series (a consequence of Kirchhoff's first law — there are no junctions). 68 —

P.D. in series The total p.d. across components in series equals the sum of the individual p.d.s: Vₜₒₜₐₗ = V₁ + V₂ + ... (a consequence of Kirchhoff's second law). 68 —

Combined resistance in series The total resistance of resistors in series is the sum of the individual resistances: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ + ... 68 —

Rₛₑᵣᵢₑₛ = R₁ + R₂ + ... The formula for combining resistances in series. Adding more resistors in series always increases the total resistance. 68 —

#### Parallel Circuits (Spec 68)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Parallel circuit A circuit in which two or more components are connected across the same two points (junctions), so the p.d. across each branch is the same. 68 —

P.D. in parallel The potential difference is the same across each branch of a parallel circuit (all branches share the same two junctions). 68 —

Current in parallel The total current entering a parallel arrangement equals the sum of the currents in each branch: Iₜₒₜₐₗ = I₁ + I₂ + ... (a consequence of Kirchhoff's first law). 68 —

Combined resistance in parallel The reciprocal of the total resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances: 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... 68 —

1/Rₚₐᵣₐₗₗₑₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... The formula for combining resistances in parallel. Adding more resistors in parallel always decreases the total resistance. 68 —

Two resistors in parallel A special case: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁R₂ / (R₁ + R₂) when exactly two resistors are in parallel. 68 —

Equivalent resistance The single resistance that can replace a combination of resistors (series, parallel, or mixed) without changing the current or p.d. in the rest of the circuit. 68 —

Mixed circuit A circuit containing both series and parallel combinations of components, requiring step-by-step simplification to find the total resistance. 68 —

Branch One of the parallel paths in a parallel circuit, carrying a share of the total current determined by the resistance of that branch. 68 —

Current divider rule The principle that in a parallel circuit, the current through each branch is inversely proportional to its resistance: branches with lower resistance carry greater current. 68 —

### 5. Electrical Power and Energy (Spec 69)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Electrical power (P) The rate at which energy is transferred by an electrical device or circuit. Defined as P = VI, where V is the potential difference across the device and I is the current through it. 69 24 marks, 8 sessions

Watt (W) The SI unit of power. One watt is one joule of energy transferred per second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹ = 1 V A). 69 —

P = VI The power equation: power = potential difference × current. This is the fundamental form, from which other forms can be derived using V = IR. 69 —

P = I²R An alternative form of the power equation, derived by substituting V = IR into P = VI: P = I(IR) = I²R. Useful when current and resistance are known. 69 —

P = V²/R An alternative form of the power equation, derived by substituting I = V/R into P = VI: P = V(V/R) = V²/R. Useful when p.d. and resistance are known. 69 —

Energy transferred (W) The total electrical energy transferred in a circuit or by a component, given by W = VIt = Pt, where V is p.d., I is current, and t is time. Measured in joules (J). 69 —

W = VIt The energy equation: energy transferred = potential difference × current × time. This gives the total energy in joules. 69 —

W = Pt Energy = power × time. Gives the energy transferred when power P is delivered for time t. 69 —

Power dissipated The rate at which electrical energy is converted to other forms (e.g. thermal energy) in a component; given by P = I²R for a resistor. 69 —

Power supplied by a cell The total power output of a cell: P = Iε, where ε is the e.m.f. and I is the current. Not all of this power is delivered to the external circuit — some is dissipated in the internal resistance. 69 —

Power delivered to external circuit The useful power output delivered to the external components: Pₑₓₜ = VI = I²Rₑₓₜ, where V is the terminal p.d. 69 —

Power wasted in internal resistance The power dissipated as thermal energy inside the cell itself: Pᵢₙₜ = I²r, where r is the internal resistance. 69 —

Kilowatt-hour (kW h) A unit of electrical energy equal to the energy transferred by a power of 1 kW operating for 1 hour (1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J). Used for billing electrical energy. 69 —

### 6. I–V Characteristics (Spec 70)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data
