I–V characteristic (I–V graph) A graph showing how the current (I) through a component varies with the potential difference (V) across it. The shape of the graph reveals whether the component is ohmic or non-ohmic and indicates how its resistance changes. 70 12 marks, 5 sessions

I–V graph of an ohmic conductor A straight line through the origin. The gradient is constant, indicating constant resistance. Current is directly proportional to p.d. 70 —

I–V graph of a filament lamp A curve that starts as a straight line through the origin but becomes less steep at higher currents. The decreasing gradient indicates increasing resistance as the filament heats up. 70 —

I–V graph of a thermistor (NTC) A curve that becomes steeper at higher temperatures (higher p.d.s cause heating). The increasing gradient indicates decreasing resistance as temperature increases. 70 —

I–V graph of a diode A graph that shows approximately zero current for negative p.d. and low positive p.d., then a sharp increase in current above a threshold voltage (≈0.6 V for silicon). Current flows easily in only one direction. 70 —

Filament lamp A lamp containing a thin metal wire (filament) that glows when current passes through it. As current increases, the filament temperature rises, increasing resistance due to increased lattice ion vibrations. It is a non-ohmic component. 70 —

Filament The thin wire inside a filament lamp, usually made of tungsten, which heats up and emits light when current flows through it. 70 —

Diode A semiconductor component that allows current to flow easily in one direction (forward bias) but has very high resistance in the opposite direction (reverse bias). 70 —

Forward bias The direction in which a diode allows current to flow easily (the p.d. is applied in the direction of easy current flow). 70 —

Reverse bias The direction in which a diode has very high resistance and blocks current flow. 70 —

Threshold voltage The minimum forward p.d. required for a diode to conduct significantly. For a silicon diode, this is approximately 0.6 V. Below this voltage, the current is negligible. 70 —

Resistance from an I–V graph The resistance at any point on an I–V graph is given by R = V/I (not the gradient of the I-V graph, but V/I at that point). For a non-ohmic component, R changes along the curve. 70 —

Gradient of I–V graph The gradient of an I-V graph is I/V, which is the reciprocal of resistance (1/R). A steeper I-V graph means lower resistance. 70 —

Non-ohmic component Any component that does not obey Ohm's law — its I-V graph is not a straight line through the origin, meaning its resistance changes with current/p.d. Examples: filament lamp, thermistor, diode. 70 —

Negative p.d. region (diode) The region of a diode's I-V graph where the p.d. is reversed; the current remains approximately zero, indicating very high resistance in the reverse direction. 70 —

### 7. Resistivity (Spec 71)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Resistivity (ρ) A property of a material (not a component) defined by the equation R = ρl/A, where R is resistance, l is length, and A is cross-sectional area. It measures how strongly a material opposes the flow of electric current. 71 26 marks, 7 sessions

R = ρl/A The resistivity equation: resistance = resistivity × length ÷ cross-sectional area. Resistance is directly proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. 71 —

ρ = RA/l The rearranged resistivity equation for calculating resistivity: ρ = R × A / l. Units: Ω m. 71 —

Ohm metre (Ω m) The SI unit of resistivity. Resistivity = resistance (Ω) × cross-sectional area (m²) ÷ length (m). 71 —

Length (l) In the resistivity equation R = ρl/A, l is the length of the conductor along the direction of current flow. Resistance is directly proportional to l (longer wire → more resistance). 71 —

Cross-sectional area (A) In the resistivity equation R = ρl/A, A is the area of the conductor perpendicular to the direction of current flow. Resistance is inversely proportional to A (thicker wire → less resistance). 71 —

ρ (symbol) Greek letter rho, symbol for resistivity. Measured in ohm metres (Ω m). 71 —

l (symbol) Symbol for length in the resistivity equation R = ρl/A. Measured in metres (m). 71 —

A (symbol) Symbol for cross-sectional area in R = ρl/A. Measured in square metres (m²). Often calculated from wire diameter: A = πd²/4. 71 —

Material property Resistivity is an intrinsic property of a material — it does not depend on the dimensions or shape of the sample, only on the material itself and its temperature. 71 —

Graphical method for resistivity A method to determine resistivity by plotting a graph of resistance (R) against length (l) for a wire of constant cross-sectional area. The gradient of the best-fit line equals ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A. 71 —

Gradient of R–l graph In a graph of resistance versus length (for a uniform wire), the gradient = ρ/A, from which resistivity can be calculated. 71 —

Diameter-to-area conversion The conversion from wire diameter (d) to cross-sectional area: A = πr² = π(d/2)² = πd²/4. A common source of error is forgetting to halve the diameter to get the radius, or to convert mm² to m². 71 —

Unit conversion (mm² to m²) 1 mm² = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m². When calculating resistivity, area must be in m². A common error is using mm² directly, giving an answer off by a factor of 10⁶. 71 —

Semiconductor resistivity Semiconductors have resistivity values between those of conductors and insulators (typically 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω m). Their resistivity decreases with increasing temperature. 71 —

Conductor resistivity Metals (conductors) have very low resistivity (typically 10⁻⁸ Ω m). Their resistivity increases with increasing temperature. 71 —

Insulator resistivity Insulators have very high resistivity (typically 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁶ Ω m). 71 —

Temperature dependence of resistivity Resistivity is temperature-dependent. For metals, ρ increases with temperature. For semiconductors (including NTC thermistors), ρ decreases with temperature. 71 —

### 7a. Core Practical 7 — Determining Resistivity (Spec 72)

CP7-specific practical/method terms. General resistivity terms (R = ρl/A, ρ = RA/l, ohm metre, etc.) are in Section 7 above. CP7 itself is formally assessed in WPH13; WPH12 tests the underlying practical skills in written form. Across 13 papers (Jun 2019 – Jun 2025), CP7 was first explicitly tagged in Jan 2025 (Q13b) + Jun 2025 (Q11); surrounding theory (Spec 71) appears in 13/13 papers (26 marks).

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Core Practical 7 (CP7) The Edexcel IAL core practical in which the resistivity of a conducting material is determined experimentally by measuring the wire's resistance R, length l, and diameter d (giving cross-sectional area A = πd²/4), then calculating ρ = RA/l — or by a graphical method (R vs l, gradient = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A). 72 First explicitly tested in Jan 2025 (Q13b) + Jun 2025 (Q11); 6 marks across 2 sessions. Surrounding theory (Spec 71) tested in 13/13 papers, 26 marks.

Micrometer (screw gauge) Precision measuring instrument with 0.01 mm resolution used in CP7 to measure the diameter d of the test wire. Readings are taken at three positions along the wire and at two perpendicular orientations at each position (6 readings total), then averaged — to detect non-uniformity and ovality. Chosen because A ∝ d², so any diameter error is doubled in the area uncertainty. 72 Oct 2022 Q13b(i), Jan 2024 Q16a, Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) MP2, Jan 2025 Q13b, Jun 2025 Q11.

Vernier callipers Alternative precision measuring instrument with 0.1 mm resolution, accepted by mark schemes for measuring the thickness of a thin conducting panel or rectangular strip (where the sample is too wide for a micrometer jaw). Less precise than a micrometer but adequate for panel-scale thicknesses (~0.5 mm). 72 Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) MP2 alternative; Oct 2023 Q13(a) (carbon paper).

Metre rule (CP7) Graduated measuring instrument with 1 mm resolution used in CP7 to measure the length l of the test wire between the crocodile-clip contacts. The wire is taped along the rule so length can be read directly. l is the distance over which the resistance is being determined — not the total length of the wire on the reel. 72 Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) MP1; Jan 2022 Q11a (l = 0.45 m).

Mean diameter (averaging) The mean of multiple diameter readings (3 positions × 2 perpendicular orientations = 6 readings), used to average out non-uniformity and ovality in the wire's cross-section. Reduces random error in d (and hence in A and ρ). 72 Required by WPH13 planning MS; implied in all CP7 apparatus questions.

Zero error (of a micrometer) A systematic error in which the micrometer reads a non-zero value when the jaws are fully closed. Must be checked before use (close jaws using the ratchet, not the thimble) and either subtracted (positive zero error) or added (negative zero error) from each reading. 72 WPH13 planning MS (Jun 2024 Q4, Jan 2024 Q4).

Cross-sectional area (circular) — A = πd²/4 The cross-sectional area of a circular wire calculated from the measured diameter: A = πr² = π(d/2)² = πd²/4. d must first be converted from mm to m (×10⁻³). The factor of d² means percentage uncertainty in A = 2 × percentage uncertainty in d (the "d² trap"). 72 Jun 2019 Q11 (d = 0.36 mm); Oct 2022 Q13b(i) (d = 0.15 mm); Jan 2025 Q13b (d = 0.51 mm); Jun 2025 Q11 (inverted: d = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ m from given ρ, R, l).

Cross-sectional area (rectangular) — A = width × thickness For a thin rectangular panel, foil, or strip, A = width × thickness (with both dimensions measured separately). This contrasts with the circular-wire form A = πd²/4 — the cross-section depends on the GEOMETRY of the sample, not a memorised formula. 72 Oct 2023 Q13(a) (carbon paper); Jun 2024 Q14d (heating panel, A = 1.60 × 0.48 × 10⁻³ m²); Oct 2024 Q15a (strain gauge strip, A = 1.40 × 0.23 × 10⁻³ m²).

Diameter-back-calculation (CP7 inverted) The reverse-direction CP7 calculation in which ρ is known (tabulated material value) and the diameter is calculated. From R = ρl/A → A = ρl/R → d = 2√(A/π). The final step (square-root then double) is the most common source of error: candidates writing d = √(A/π) obtain half the correct diameter. 72 Jun 2025 Q11: A = 2.15 × 10⁻⁷ m² → d = 2√(A/π) = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ m.

Resistance measurement (CP7) The resistance R of the test wire, found either by R = V/I (voltmeter in parallel across the wire, ammeter in series) using a low-current circuit, or directly with an ohmmeter connected across the wire. The R = V/I method is preferred because a V–I graph (gradient = R) reduces random error. 72 Jun 2022 Q13b(ii): R = V/I = 140/0.44 = 318 Ω; Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) MP3.

Variable resistor / rheostat (in CP7) A resistor whose resistance is adjusted continuously by sliding a contact along a coil of resistance wire. In CP7 it is connected in series with the test wire and ammeter to keep the current I constant as the test length l is varied — preventing the wire from heating and changing its resistivity. 72 Oct 2019 Q15a; method-supporting apparatus in all CP7 procedural questions.

Constant-current method (CP7) The CP7 protocol in which the current I through the wire is held constant (using a series variable resistor) while the length l and corresponding p.d. V are varied. For each l, R = V/I; plotting R against l gives a straight line through the origin with gradient ρ/A. 72 Implied in all CP7 graph-method questions.

Low-current condition (CP7) The procedural requirement to keep the current through the test wire low (typically ≤ 0.5 A) and to switch the circuit off between readings. This prevents the wire from heating up, which would raise its resistivity (metal: lattice vibrations increase) and break the assumption that ρ is constant across the data set. 72 Method-supporting control variable; recurring WPH13 planning mark.

Switch (in CP7 circuit) A series-connected component used to break the circuit between readings in CP7. Its role is to minimise the time the current flows, preventing the wire/cell from heating/running down between measurements. 72 Method-supporting apparatus; Jan 2024 Q14b.

Volume conservation (in stretched conductor) When a wire/strip is stretched, its volume V = A·l remains approximately constant. Therefore A = V/l, and substituting into R = ρl/A gives R = ρl²/V. Plotting R against l² gives a straight line through the origin with gradient = ρ/V. 71, 72 Oct 2024 Q15b: stretched strain-gauge strip, R ∝ l².

Graphical method for resistivity (CP7) A graph-based method for determining ρ in which R is plotted on the y-axis against l on the x-axis for a wire of constant cross-sectional area A. Because R = (ρ/A)·l, the gradient = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A. Alternatively, plotting R against l/A gives gradient = ρ directly. 72 Oct 2019 Q15b (axes + gradient interpretation); Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) MP4 alternative.

Suitable axes for resistivity graph Any pair of axes whose gradient yields ρ (or a clearly identified multiple/fraction of ρ). Acceptable combinations tested in Oct 2019 Q15b MS: R vs l (gradient = ρ/A); R vs l/A (gradient = ρ); RA vs l (gradient = ρ); l vs R (gradient = A/ρ); l/A vs R (gradient = 1/ρ); V vs Il (gradient = ρ/A). 72 Oct 2019 Q15b.

Gradient of R–l graph (CP7) For CP7 (constant A), gradient = ΔR/Δl = ρ/A. The student must multiply the gradient by the cross-sectional area A to recover the resistivity: ρ = gradient × A. Writing "gradient = ρ" (omitting the area factor) is a common 1-mark error. 72 Oct 2019 Q15b MP3; Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) graphical alternative.

Percentage uncertainty in resistivity (d² trap) From ρ = RA/l, the percentage uncertainty in ρ is the sum: %unc(ρ) = %unc(R) + %unc(A) + %unc(l). Because A = πd²/4 depends on d squared, %unc(A) = 2 × %unc(d), giving %unc(ρ) = %unc(R) + 2 × %unc(d) + %unc(l). The factor of 2 on the diameter term is the most commonly forgotten contribution and the dominant source of uncertainty in CP7. 72 Recurring examiner-report flag; WPH13 planning MS.

Contact resistance (CP7) A small additional resistance at the points where the crocodile clips grip the wire, caused by surface oxide layers and imperfect contact. Appears as a non-zero positive y-intercept on the R-l graph (R > 0 even when l = 0). It is a systematic error, not a random one. Reduced by cleaning the contact and ensuring firm, consistent clip placement. 72 WPH13 examiner reports; recurring CP7 source-of-error point.

Single-pair calculation (CP7) The simpler CP7 method: measure R for one known length l and one known area A, then calculate ρ = RA/l directly. Faster than the graphical method but more susceptible to random error in any single measurement. The Jun 2024 MS accepts either method. 72 Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) MP4; Jan 2022 Q11a; Jan 2024 Q16a.

Test wire materials (typical resistivities) Constantan (ρ ≈ 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) and nichrome (ρ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m) are preferred because their temperature coefficients are low. Other typical values: copper 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, aluminium 2.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, tungsten 5.6 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m, iron 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. Copper is unsuitable for CP7 (R too small to measure accurately with school meters). 72 Jun 2019 Q11 (identification table); Jun 2022 Q13b(ii) (tungsten at 2700 °C); Jan 2025 Q13b (constantan-type, ρ = 9.8 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m).

### 7b. Core Practical 8 — Determining EMF and Internal Resistance (Spec 78)

CP8-specific practical/method terms. The general e.m.f./internal resistance terms (e.m.f., internal resistance, terminal p.d., lost volts, V = ε − Ir) are in Section 11 below. CP8 itself is formally assessed in WPH13; WPH12 tests the underlying practical skills in written form. Across 13 papers (Jun 2019 – Jun 2025), CP8 was first explicitly tagged in Jan 2025 (Q10, Q14a/b, Q16a/b) + Jun 2025 (Q14a/b, Q16a); surrounding theory (Spec 77) appears in 9/13 papers (23 marks).

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Core Practical 8 (CP8) The Edexcel IAL core practical in which the e.m.f. ε and internal resistance r of an electrical cell are determined experimentally by recording pairs of terminal p.d. V and current I for several external-circuit conditions, then analysing the V–I graph (V = ε − Ir → y = mx + c with m = −r, c = ε). Alternatively, a single (ε, V, Rₑₓₜ) data set can be used: I = V/Rₑₓₜ, then r = (ε − V)/I. 78 First explicitly tested in Jan 2025 (Q10, Q14a/b, Q16a/b) + Jun 2025 (Q14a/b, Q16a); 7 marks across 2 sessions. Surrounding theory (Spec 77) tested in 9/13 papers, 23 marks.

V-vs-I graph method (CP8 standard) Plotting terminal p.d. V on the y-axis against current I on the x-axis for 6–8 (I, V) data pairs. Because V = ε − Ir is of the form y = mx + c with m = −r and c = ε, the best-fit straight line gives ε from the y-intercept and r from the magnitude of the gradient. The dominant CP8 method. 78 Jun 2019 Q19b (ε = 0.28–0.29 V, r = 400–430 Ω); Jun 2023 Q12a (ε = 1.50 V, r = 0.75 Ω); Jan 2024 Q14c(i) (ε = 8.8 V, r ≈ 2.3 Ω); Jun 2024 Q12a.

R-vs-1/I graph method (CP8 algebraic variant) Algebraic rearrangement of V = ε − Ir: starting from ε = IR + Ir, divide by I → R = ε/I − r. Plotting R (y-axis) against 1/I (x-axis) gives gradient = ε and y-intercept = −r (negative; r = intercept ). Less common than the standard V-I form. 78 Jan 2023 Q17(a)+(b) (only paper in audit window using this form): ε = 1.5 V from gradient, r = 2 Ω from intercept .

1/V vs 1/R graph method (CP8 alternative) Rearranging ε = V + Ir with I = V/R: ε/V = 1 + r/R, so 1/V = (r/ε)·(1/R) + 1/ε. Plotting 1/V (y-axis) against 1/R (x-axis) gives gradient = r/ε, y-intercept = 1/ε (so ε = 1/intercept, then r = gradient × ε). Rarely used but accepted in WPH13 planning. 78 Not directly tested in WPH12 audit window.

Single-data-point method (CP8) A non-graphical CP8 method using one (V, I) pair: r = (ε − V)/I, where ε is the open-circuit e.m.f. (read with a high-resistance voltmeter), V is the terminal p.d. when the external circuit is connected, and I is the current. Tested in calculation questions where the V-I graph is not used. 78 Jun 2025 Q14a (ε = 1.5 V, V = 1.4 V, Rₑₓₜ = 10 Ω → r = 0.71 Ω); Oct 2023 Q13b(i) (r = 0.63 Ω).

Resistance ratio method (for r) Alternative algebraic method: since ε = I(Rₑₓₜ + r) and V = IRₑₓₜ, the ratio Vₗₒₛₜ/V = r/Rₑₓₜ, giving r = Rₑₓₜ × (ε − V)/V. Avoids explicit calculation of current. Accepted by mark schemes as equivalent to the lost-volts method. 78 Oct 2023 Q13b(i) Method 2; Oct 2024 Q19e Method 2; Jan 2025 Q10 (correct MCQ option).

y-intercept = EMF (CP8) The y-intercept of the V–I graph (V when I = 0) equals the e.m.f. ε, because V = ε − 0·r = ε. Physically this is the open-circuit terminal p.d. — the maximum p.d. the cell can deliver when no current is drawn. 78 All CP8 graph questions.

Gradient = −r (CP8) The gradient of the V–I graph (ΔV/ΔI) equals −r, the negative of the internal resistance. Because V decreases as I increases (more lost volts at higher current), the gradient is negative; the internal resistance is r = gradient . Use a large triangle on the best-fit line to minimise the gradient uncertainty. 78 All CP8 graph questions.

x-intercept = short-circuit current (CP8) The x-intercept of the V–I graph (I when V = 0) equals the short-circuit current Iₛc = ε/r, the maximum possible current the cell can deliver (when external resistance is zero). 78 Jan 2024 Q14c(i) (x-intercept 3.8 A); Jan 2024 Q14c(ii) (explain why there is a maximum current).

Open-circuit measurement (CP8) The procedure of measuring the e.m.f. by connecting a high-resistance voltmeter across the cell's terminals when no current flows (switch open). Because I = 0, lost volts = 0, so the voltmeter reads V ≈ ε. 78 Jan 2024 Q14a (2-mark "Explain" question); Oct 2024 Q19e (ε = 1960 V open-circuit).

High-resistance voltmeter (CP8) A voltmeter with very high resistance (ideally infinite; ≥ 1 MΩ typical for digital multimeters; ≥ 10 MΩ preferred). Required in CP8 so that negligible current flows through it — so the ammeter reads the true current through the external circuit, and the open-circuit reading equals ε. 78 Jan 2024 Q14a; standard CP8 apparatus point.

Switch (in CP8 circuit) A switch included in series with the cell, ammeter and variable resistor in the CP8 circuit. Opened between readings to prevent the cell running down (polarisation) during the experiment, which would change ε and r between measurements. 78 Method-supporting apparatus; Jan 2024 Q14b.

Cell polarisation A chemical effect in a cell whereby, after sustained current flow, the e.m.f. drops and the internal resistance rises due to the build-up of reaction products (e.g. hydrogen bubbles on the positive electrode). Opening the switch between CP8 readings prevents polarisation from invalidating the (I, V) data set. 78 Recurring CP8 source-of-error point.

Variable resistor (in CP8) A rheostat wired in series with the cell and ammeter in CP8. Its role is to vary the current through the cell, producing a range of (I, V) pairs for plotting. Without it, only one (I, V) pair could be measured and the graph could not be drawn. 78 Jun 2019 Q19a MP2; Oct 2022 Q12a MP3; Jan 2024 Q14b MP2.

Potential divider (CP8 alternative) An alternative to the variable resistor in CP8: a single resistor with a sliding contact wired across the cell, allowing the p.d. applied to a series test resistor to be varied continuously from 0 up to the cell's terminal p.d. Mark schemes explicitly accept either arrangement. 78 Jan 2024 Q14b MP2 alternative.

Circuit diagram (CP8 standard arrangement) A circuit consisting of: a cell (with its internal resistance shown either as a separate resistor inside a dashed cell symbol or omitted), an ammeter in series with the cell, a variable resistor in series with the cell and ammeter, a voltmeter in parallel across the cell's terminals (NOT across the variable resistor — that would measure only the external p.d. and miss the lost-volts comparison), and a switch in series. 78 Jun 2019 Q19a; Oct 2022 Q12a; Jan 2024 Q14b.

Series cells combination (CP8 extension) When two identical cells (each ε, r) are connected in series, both the e.m.f.s and the internal resistances add: εₜₒₜₐₗ = 2ε, rₜₒₜₐₗ = 2r. On a V-I graph: y-intercept doubles and gradient doubles (becomes more negative). On a R-against-1/I graph: gradient doubles (to 2ε) and y-intercept doubles in magnitude (to −2r). 77, 78 Jan 2023 Q17d (draw new line); Jun 2023 Q12b (describe change qualitatively).

Parallel cells combination (CP8 extension) When N identical cells (each ε, r) are connected in parallel, the e.m.f. stays the same (εₜₒₜₐₗ = ε) and the internal resistances combine in parallel: rₜₒₜₐₗ = r/N. Common trap: parallel cells DO NOT add e.m.f.s. 77, 78 Jan 2024 Q19c (parallel vs series power comparison, 5 marks).

Two cells in parallel vs series — terminal p.d. comparison When two equal external resistors R are connected (a) in series (Rₑₓₜ = 2R) or (b) in parallel (Rₑₓₜ = R/2) across the same cell, the series arrangement gives a GREATER terminal p.d. because the larger total resistance draws less current, so the lost volts Ir are smaller: Vₛₑᵣᵢₑₛ > Vₚₐᵣₐₗₗₑₗ. 78 Jun 2019 Q19c (4-mark "Explain" question).

Power dissipated in internal resistance The power dissipated as heat inside the cell, given by Pᵢₙₜ = I²r = I(ε − V) = (ε − V)²/r. Note: this uses the internal resistance r, NOT the external resistance R. The Mark Scheme for Jan 2023 Q17c explicitly forbids substituting R (external) in place of r in this formula. 78, 69 Oct 2019 Q2 (MCQ, P = I(ε − V)); Jan 2023 Q17c (3-mark "Comment on" question); Jun 2025 Q14b (e-bike battery heating).

Maximum current from a battery The maximum current that can flow from a cell, achieved when the external resistance approaches zero: Iₘₐₓ = ε/r (the short-circuit current). Reached when the p.d. across the internal resistance equals the e.m.f. — at this point all of the cell's e.m.f. is being dissipated internally as thermal energy (I²r). 78 Jan 2024 Q14c(ii) (2-mark "Explain" question).

Best-fit line for V–I graph (CP8) A straight line of best fit drawn through the (I, V) data points on the V–I graph. The intercepts and gradient are read from this line (not from individual data points), to average out random measurement errors. Mark schemes penalise the use of a single (I, V) pair to calculate ε and r. 78 Jun 2019 Q19b MP1; all CP8 graph questions.

Worst-fit line (for uncertainty in CP8) The steepest (or shallowest) line that still passes through all the error bars. Used to estimate Δgradient (so Δr) and Δintercept (so Δε). Δr = ½ × mₘₐₓ − mₘᵢₙ ; Δε = ½ × cₘₐₓ − cₘᵢₙ . 78 WPH13 planning MS; CP8 uncertainty questions.

### 8. Drift Velocity and Number Density (Spec 73)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Drift velocity (v) The average net velocity of charge carriers (e.g. electrons) in a conductor in the direction of current flow, when a p.d. is applied. It is typically very small (of order 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ in copper). 73 23 marks, 7 sessions

Mean drift velocity An equivalent term for drift velocity — the mean (average) velocity of charge carriers along the conductor due to an applied electric field. 73 —

I = nqvA The equation relating current to microscopic quantities: I = number density × charge of carrier × drift velocity × cross-sectional area. 73 —

v = I/(nqA) The rearranged drift velocity equation: drift velocity = current ÷ (number density × charge of carrier × cross-sectional area). 73 —

Number density (n) The number of free charge carriers per unit volume in a material. Measured in m⁻³. For copper, n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. 73 —

Charge carrier A particle that carries electric charge and is free to move through a material, contributing to electric current. In metals, charge carriers are free (conduction) electrons. 73 —

Conduction electron A free electron in a metal that is not bound to any particular atom and can move through the metal lattice, carrying charge and contributing to electric current. 73 —

Free electron An electron in a conductor that is delocalised from its parent atom and is free to drift under the influence of an electric field. 73 —

Elementary charge (e) The charge of a single electron/proton: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. In I = nqvA, q = e for metal conductors where charge carriers are electrons. 73 —

n (symbol) Symbol for number density of charge carriers. Measured in m⁻³ (number per cubic metre). 73 —

q (symbol) Symbol for the charge of a single charge carrier. For electrons, q = e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. 73 —

v (symbol) Symbol for drift velocity. Measured in m s⁻¹. 73 —

Cross-sectional area of a wire (A) In I = nqvA, A is the cross-sectional area of the conductor perpendicular to the direction of current flow. Calculated from diameter: A = πd²/4. 73 —

Charge carrier density An alternative term for number density (n): the number of charge carriers per unit volume of the material. 73 —

m⁻³ (unit) The SI unit for number density: charge carriers per cubic metre. 73 —

High n → low v (in metals) In metals, the number density of free electrons is very high (n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ for copper), so even a small drift velocity produces a significant current. From v = I/(nqA), high n means low v for a given I and A. 73 —

Drift velocity in series For components connected in series, the current I is the same throughout. If a wire changes cross-sectional area (A), the drift velocity must change: v = I/(nqA). A smaller cross-section gives a higher drift velocity. 73 —

Drift velocity in parallel In parallel branches, the current divides according to branch resistance. For identical wires in parallel, the current in each branch is Iₜₒₜₐₗ/N, so the drift velocity in each branch is lower than if the same total current flowed through a single wire. 73 —

Net velocity Drift velocity is the net average velocity in one direction; the actual instantaneous velocity of electrons is much higher due to random thermal motion, but the random component averages to zero. 73 —

Random thermal motion The rapid, random movement of electrons in a metal due to thermal energy; this motion averages to zero and does not contribute to net current. The drift velocity is a small additional velocity superimposed on this random motion. 73 —

Semiconductors — low n Semiconductors have a much lower number density of charge carriers than metals (typically 10¹⁰–10¹⁶ m⁻³). For the same current and cross-sectional area, drift velocity in semiconductors is much higher than in metals. 73 —

### 9. Potential Along a Uniform Current-Carrying Wire (Spec 74)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Potential along a uniform wire The potential difference varies linearly with distance along a uniform wire carrying a constant current. The p.d. per unit length is constant: V/l = IR/l = I(ρ/A) = constant. 74 5 marks, 3 sessions

Uniform wire A wire of constant cross-sectional area and constant resistivity along its entire length, ensuring a uniform potential gradient when carrying a current. 74 —

Potential gradient The rate of change of potential with distance along a conductor: ΔV/Δl. For a uniform wire carrying a steady current, the potential gradient is constant. 74 —

Linear potential distribution The property that, for a uniform wire, the potential decreases linearly from one end to the other when a current flows. A graph of potential (V) against position along the wire is a straight line with negative gradient. 74 —

P.D. per unit length The potential difference across a section of wire divided by its length; for a uniform wire this is a constant equal to IR/l. 74 —

Contact point A specific point along a uniform wire (e.g. on a potentiometer or resistive wire) at which a connection is made to measure or tap off a fraction of the total p.d. 74 —

Proportional length → proportional p.d. For a uniform wire, the p.d. between any two points is directly proportional to the distance between them: V ∝ l. 74 —

### 10. Potential Divider Circuits (Spec 75–76)

#### Fixed Potential Dividers (Spec 75)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Potential divider A circuit consisting of two or more resistors connected in series across a supply (e.m.f.), used to produce a fraction of the supply p.d. across one of the resistors. 75 17 marks, 6 sessions

Potential division The principle by which the total p.d. across a series combination of resistors is divided between them in proportion to their resistances: V₁/Vₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁/Rₜₒₜₐₗ. 75 —

Vₒᵤₜ = Vᵢₙ × R₂/(R₁ + R₂) The potential divider equation: the output p.d. across R₂ equals the input p.d. multiplied by the ratio of R₂ to the total resistance. 75 —

Output p.d. (Vₒᵤₜ) The p.d. across a chosen component (usually one resistor) in a potential divider circuit; this is the "tapped off" or "divided" portion of the supply p.d. 75 —

Input p.d. (Vᵢₙ) The total p.d. applied across the entire potential divider (i.e. the e.m.f. or supply p.d. across the series combination). 75 —

P.D. ratio rule In a potential divider: the p.d. across each resistor is proportional to its resistance. Larger resistance → larger share of the total p.d. 75 —

V₁/Vₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁/Rₜₒₜₐₗ The ratio form of the potential divider equation: the fraction of the total p.d. across R₁ equals the fraction of the total resistance that is R₁. 75 —

Two-resistor potential divider The simplest potential divider circuit: two resistors in series across a supply. The p.d. across each depends on its resistance relative to the total. 75 —

#### Variable Potential Dividers (Spec 76)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Variable potential divider A potential divider in which one of the resistors is a variable component (e.g. thermistor, LDR, potentiometer), so the output p.d. changes in response to a physical stimulus (temperature, light level, etc.). 76 12 marks, 3 sessions

Sensor circuit A potential divider circuit that includes a sensing component (thermistor or LDR) to convert a change in a physical quantity (temperature or light intensity) into a change in output p.d., which can then be used to activate a switch or relay. 76 —

NTC thermistor in a potential divider When an NTC thermistor is used as one resistor in a potential divider: increasing temperature → thermistor resistance decreases → output p.d. across thermistor decreases (if measured across the thermistor) or increases (if measured across the fixed resistor). 76 —

LDR in a potential divider When an LDR is used as one resistor in a potential divider: increasing light intensity → LDR resistance decreases → output p.d. across LDR decreases (if measured across LDR) or increases (if measured across the fixed resistor). 76 —

Switching circuit A sensor circuit designed so that the output p.d. crosses a threshold value when the physical quantity reaches a certain level, activating a switch (e.g. turning on a heater, air conditioning, or light). 76 —

Fixed resistor (in a sensor circuit) The non-sensing resistor in a variable potential divider; its resistance remains constant while the sensing component's resistance changes. The output p.d. across the fixed resistor changes in the opposite sense to the output across the sensing component. 76 —

Potentiometer A variable resistor with a sliding contact, used as a continuously adjustable potential divider to provide any p.d. between 0 and Vᵢₙ. 76 —

Sensitive to which component In a potential divider question, a common trap: always identify WHICH component the voltmeter is measuring across. Vfᵢₓₑd = ε × Rfᵢₓₑd/(Rfᵢₓₑd + Rᵥₐᵣᵢₐbₗₑ) and Vᵥₐᵣᵢₐbₗₑ = ε × Rᵥₐᵣᵢₐbₗₑ/(Rfᵢₓₑd + Rᵥₐᵣᵢₐbₗₑ). 76 —

### 11. E.M.F. and Internal Resistance (Spec 77)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Electromotive force (e.m.f., ε) The total energy transferred per unit charge by a source (e.g. a cell or battery) when charge flows through the source. It is the energy supplied per coulomb by the source, measured in volts (V). 77 23 marks, 7 sessions

e.m.f. (ε) Abbreviation for electromotive force. NOT a force; it is a potential difference (energy per unit charge) supplied by a source. 77 —

Internal resistance (r) The resistance of the materials inside a source of e.m.f. (e.g. the chemicals in a cell). It causes energy to be dissipated within the source when current flows, reducing the p.d. available to the external circuit. 77 —

Terminal p.d. (V) The potential difference across the terminals of a source (cell) when a current is flowing. It is less than the e.m.f. when current flows because some energy is lost in the internal resistance: V = ε − Ir. 77 —

Lost volts (Ir) The p.d. "lost" across the internal resistance of a source: the difference between the e.m.f. and the terminal p.d. Lost volts = Ir = ε − V. This represents energy per coulomb dissipated inside the source. 77 —

ε = V + Ir The fundamental equation for a real source of e.m.f.: the e.m.f. equals the terminal p.d. plus the p.d. across the internal resistance. This is a statement of conservation of energy (Kirchhoff's second law applied to the complete circuit). 77 —

V = ε − Ir The terminal p.d. equation: terminal p.d. = e.m.f. minus the lost volts. As current I increases, terminal p.d. decreases linearly. 77 —

Open circuit A circuit in which no current flows (e.g. a switch is open or the cell is disconnected). When I = 0, terminal p.d. = e.m.f. (V = ε). 77 —

Short circuit A circuit in which the external resistance is effectively zero (the terminals are connected directly). The current is at its maximum: I = ε/r. All the e.m.f. is "lost" across the internal resistance. 77 —

Maximum current (ε/r) The maximum possible current from a cell, achieved when the external circuit has zero resistance (short circuit): Iₘₐₓ = ε/r. 77 —

Ideal voltage source A theoretical source with zero internal resistance, where terminal p.d. always equals e.m.f. regardless of current. Real sources always have some internal resistance. 77 —

ε (symbol) Greek letter epsilon, symbol for electromotive force. Measured in volts (V). 77 —

r (symbol) Symbol for internal resistance. Measured in ohms (Ω). 77 —

V-I graph of a cell A graph of terminal p.d. (V) on the y-axis against current (I) on the x-axis for a real cell. It is a straight line with negative gradient. 77 —

y-intercept of V-I graph The value of V when I = 0 on a V-I graph: this equals the e.m.f. (ε), because V = ε − I(0) = ε. 77 —

Gradient of V-I graph The gradient of a V-I graph (ΔV/ΔI) equals −r (negative internal resistance). The magnitude of the gradient gives the internal resistance: r = −gradient. 77 —

x-intercept of V-I graph The value of I when V = 0: this is the short-circuit current, I = ε/r. 77 —

Energy per unit charge (e.m.f.) The definition of e.m.f.: the total energy converted from chemical (or other) form to electrical form per unit charge passing through the source. 77 —

Power supplied by cell The total power produced by a cell: Pₜₒₜₐₗ = Iε. This equals the power delivered to the external circuit plus the power dissipated in the internal resistance: Iε = I²Rₑₓₜ + I²r. 77 —

Maximum power transfer The maximum power is delivered to the external circuit when the external resistance equals the internal resistance (Rₑₓₜ = r). 77 —

### 12. Resistance–Temperature Model (Spec 79)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Resistance–temperature relationship (metals) As the temperature of a metal increases, its resistance increases. This is because the lattice ions vibrate more vigorously, increasing the frequency of collisions with conduction electrons and reducing the mean drift velocity. 79 13 marks, 3 sessions

Lattice ions The positive ions in a metal that form a regular lattice structure. At higher temperatures, these ions vibrate more with greater amplitude about their fixed positions. 79 —

Lattice vibrations The thermal vibrations of the lattice ions in a metal. Increasing temperature → greater amplitude of lattice vibrations → more frequent collisions with conduction electrons → increased resistance. This is the mechanism for increasing resistance in metals, NOT in semiconductors. 79 —

Collision frequency The rate at which conduction electrons collide with lattice ions. Higher temperature → more lattice vibrations → higher collision frequency → lower drift velocity → higher resistance. 79 —

R-T mechanism (metal) Temperature ↑ → lattice ion vibrations ↑ → conduction electrons collide more frequently with lattice ions → mean drift velocity of electrons decreases → resistance increases. 79 —

NTC thermistor A negative temperature coefficient thermistor: a semiconductor component whose resistance decreases as its temperature increases. 79 —

R-T mechanism (NTC thermistor) Temperature ↑ → more electrons released from atoms / promoted to the conduction band → number density of charge carriers (n) increases → resistance decreases. This is a semiconductor mechanism, fundamentally different from the metal mechanism. 79 —

Negative temperature coefficient (NTC) The property of a thermistor where resistance decreases with increasing temperature. "Negative" refers to the sign of the change (ΔR/ΔT < 0). 79 —

Semiconductor (in context of thermistors) A material with a number density of charge carriers between that of a conductor and an insulator. In semiconductors, increasing temperature releases more charge carriers, decreasing resistance. 79 —

Charge carrier release (thermal) At higher temperatures, more electrons in a semiconductor gain enough thermal energy to break free from their atoms and become available as conduction electrons, increasing n. 79 —

Conduction band The energy band in a semiconductor or insulator to which electrons must be promoted to become free charge carriers. Higher temperature gives more electrons sufficient energy to reach this band. 79 —

Number density increase (semiconductor) In a semiconductor, as temperature increases, more electrons are promoted to the conduction band, so the number density (n) of charge carriers increases. This is the primary cause of resistance decreasing in NTC thermistors. 79 —

R-T graph (metal) A straight-line graph with positive gradient: resistance increases linearly with temperature (approximately, over moderate ranges). 79 —

R-T graph (NTC thermistor) A curve showing resistance decreasing non-linearly with increasing temperature. The relationship is approximately exponential. 79 —

Common exam trap — mechanisms A frequent error is using the lattice vibration explanation for a thermistor (semiconductor) or the charge carrier release explanation for a metal. Mark schemes explicitly reject this. Metals use lattice vibrations; semiconductors use charge carrier release. 79 —

### 13. Resistance–Illumination Model / LDRs (Spec 80)

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

LDR (light-dependent resistor) A semiconductor component whose resistance decreases as the intensity of light falling on it increases. 80 13 marks, 4 sessions

Light-dependent resistor The full name for LDR: a resistor whose resistance depends on the intensity of incident light. 80 —

Resistance–illumination relationship As light intensity increases, the resistance of an LDR decreases. This is because more photons per second release more charge carriers in the semiconductor material. 80 —

R-Illumination mechanism (LDR) Light intensity ↑ → more photons per second incident on LDR → more electrons promoted to conduction band (more charge carriers released) → number density of charge carriers (n) increases → resistance decreases. 80 —

Photon (in LDR context) A quantum of light energy incident on the LDR. Each photon that is absorbed by the semiconductor material can release an electron, creating an additional charge carrier. 80 —

Charge carrier release (photon-induced) When a photon is absorbed by the LDR semiconductor material, it can transfer enough energy to an electron to promote it to the conduction band, creating an additional free charge carrier. More photons → more charge carriers → lower resistance. 80 —

Number density of charge carriers (in LDR) The number of free charge carriers per unit volume in the LDR material. This increases with increasing light intensity because more photons release more electrons. 80 —

Light intensity The power of light per unit area incident on a surface (measured in W m⁻² or lux). Higher light intensity means more photons per second per unit area hitting the LDR. 80 —

Dark resistance The resistance of an LDR when no light is falling on it. This is the maximum resistance of the LDR, typically of the order of MΩ. 80 —

Illuminated resistance The resistance of an LDR when light is falling on it. This is lower than the dark resistance and decreases as light intensity increases. 80 —

LDR in a potential divider circuit An LDR used as one resistor in a potential divider to create a light-sensitive switching circuit. As light increases, LDR resistance decreases, changing the output p.d. 80 —

Semiconductor mechanism (LDR) The LDR mechanism is a semiconductor mechanism (more charge carriers released), NOT a metal mechanism (lattice vibrations). Mark schemes explicitly reject "lattice vibrations" as an explanation for LDR behaviour. 80 —

Conduction electron (in LDR context) An electron in the LDR's semiconductor material that has been promoted to the conduction band by absorbing a photon. These additional conduction electrons lower the resistance. 80 —

Sensor application (LDR) LDRs are used in sensor circuits to detect light levels, e.g. automatic street lights (switch on when dark), burglar alarms, camera light meters. 80 —

Common exam trap — LDR explanation A frequent error is stating that LDR resistance decreases with light without explaining WHY. Mark schemes require the particle-level mechanism: more photons → more charge carriers released → n increases → R decreases. 80 —

### 14. Cross-Cutting and Examined-But-Not-Explicit-in-Spec Terms

Term Exam-ready definition Spec point Exam data

Electrical circuit A closed conducting path through which electric current can flow, consisting of a source of e.m.f., conducting wires, and components. — —

Cell A source of e.m.f. that converts chemical energy to electrical energy. A cell has an e.m.f. and an internal resistance. 77 —

Battery Two or more cells connected in series or parallel to provide a greater e.m.f. or current capacity. 77 —

Ammeter A device used to measure electric current. Connected in series with the component whose current is being measured. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance. 64 —

Voltmeter A device used to measure potential difference. Connected in parallel across the component whose p.d. is being measured. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance. 65 —

Conductor A material with low resistivity that allows electric current to flow easily, e.g. metals such as copper. 66, 71 —

Insulator A material with very high resistivity that does not allow electric current to flow easily, e.g. rubber, glass. 66, 71 —

Semiconductor A material (e.g. silicon, germanium) with resistivity between that of conductors and insulators. Its electrical properties change significantly with temperature or illumination. Thermistors and LDRs are semiconductor devices. 79, 80 —

Charge carrier type In metals, charge carriers are free electrons (negative). In electrolytes, charge carriers are positive and negative ions. In semiconductors, charge carriers can be electrons or positive holes. 73 —

Energy conservation in circuits The total energy supplied by sources of e.m.f. in a circuit equals the total energy dissipated in all resistances (internal and external) in the circuit. 67b, 77 —

Maximum power theorem The maximum power is transferred from a source to a load when the load resistance equals the internal resistance of the source (Rₗₒₐd = r). 77 —

QWC causal chain A structured explanation format used in extended writing (QWC) questions in Ch 2.4, requiring a linked sequence of cause-and-effect statements: stimulus → mechanism → electrical consequence → result. — —

Junction rule An alternative name for Kirchhoff's first law: the sum of currents at a junction is zero. 67a —

Loop rule An alternative name for Kirchhoff's second law: the sum of p.d.s around any closed loop is zero. 67b —

Electrical energy The energy transferred by the movement of charge through a potential difference. W = QV = VIt = Pt. 65, 69 —

Kilojoule (kJ) 1000 joules. Often used for electrical energy calculations where joules give unwieldy numbers. 69 —

Megajoule (MJ) 1,000,000 joules. Used for large-scale electrical energy (e.g. household consumption). 69 —

ε (epsilon) Greek letter used as the symbol for electromotive force. Do not confuse with the permittivity of free space (ε₀) — context determines the meaning. 77 —

r (internal resistance) Symbol for the internal resistance of a source of e.m.f. Measured in ohms (Ω). 77 —

Rₑₓₜₑᵣₙₐₗ (Rₑₓₜ) The total resistance of all components in the external circuit (outside the cell). 77 —

Rₜₒₜₐₗ The total resistance of the entire circuit including internal resistance: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = Rₑₓₜₑᵣₙₐₗ + r. Used in ε = IRₜₒₜₐₗ. 77 —

I = ε/(R + r) The current in a circuit with a real source of e.m.f.: I = e.m.f. ÷ (external resistance + internal resistance). 77 —

Watt (W) — unit equivalence 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹ = 1 V A = 1 A² Ω = 1 V² Ω⁻¹. All equivalent expressions for the unit of power. 69 —

Joule (J) — electrical context 1 J = 1 C × 1 V = 1 A × 1 V × 1 s. The energy transferred when 1 coulomb of charge moves through a p.d. of 1 volt. 65, 69 —

Ohm (Ω) — unit equivalence 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹ = 1 V² W⁻¹ = 1 W A⁻². All equivalent expressions for the unit of resistance. 66 —

### WPH12 Extension — Circuits QWC Templates (Definitions)

Scope: WPH12 Topic 2 (Electric circuits) and the Quality of Written Communication (QWC) extended-response questions that test it. The WPH11 audit identified that only 1 QWC template existed for circuits, and the spec requires at least one 6-mark QWC question per paper. This extension fills the gap by providing examiner-aligned definitions for every term needed to score L3 on circuits QWC answers. Source: Pearson Edexcel IAL Physics Specification Topic 2 (Electric circuits), Appendices 6 (Mathematical skills) and 9 (Practical skills), examiner reports Jan 2019–Jan 2025 (cross-referenced for common QWC errors). Purpose: Exam-ready definitions for every QWC and circuit term, grounded in the spec and examiner report phrasing. Each term is paired with the QWC Exam context that explains how it earns marks in a 6-mark extended-response answer.

### 1. QWC and Extended-Response Terms

#### 1.1 Quality of Written Communication (QWC)

Spec ref: General A-level requirement; embedded in WPH12 mark schemes as "QWC" annotation Definition: A marking criterion that rewards clear, well-organised, spelt-and-grammatically-correct written English in extended-response answers. In WPH12 it is applied to 6-mark questions that require a sustained chain of physical reasoning. QWC is not a separate mark — it is judged holistically alongside the scientific content when deciding the level (L1/L2/L3) the answer is placed in. QWC Exam context: A student may write all 6 indicative content (IC) points but only score L2 (4 marks) because the answer is disorganised, lacks connective words, or has no clear cause-and-effect chain. Conversely, a student who writes only 5 IC points but links them with "therefore", "consequently", "because" can score L3 (5–6 marks). Always use connectives — they are the visible signal of QWC.

#### 1.2 Extended-Response Question

Spec ref: Spec introduction — "At least one 6-mark QWC question per paper" Definition: A question worth 6 marks that requires a sustained written answer (typically 8–15 lines), structured as a logical argument. It cannot be answered with bullet points or one-word responses. Examiners mark it using level descriptors (L1/L2/L3) rather than point-by-point. QWC Exam context: Always the LAST sub-question of a multi-part circuit question (typically 6 marks in WPH12 Q12–Q16). Examiners expect a continuous paragraph, not a list. Writing "• Lattice vibrates • Collisions increase • Drift velocity drops" scores L1 (2 marks) even if the science is correct — the lack of linkage breaks QWC.

#### 1.3 Level-Marked Question

Spec ref: Pearson Edexcel mark scheme conventions Definition: A question marked using level descriptors rather than a point-marking list. The marker reads the whole answer, judges the overall quality against L1/L2/L3 descriptors, and assigns a single mark within that level. Level-marked questions always include QWC in the judgement. QWC Exam context: The marker first decides the level (L1, L2, or L3) using both scientific content and QWC, then chooses a mark at the bottom, middle, or top of that level. A "top of L2" answer scores 4; a "bottom of L3" answer scores 5. The difference of one mark often comes down to whether connectives are used.

#### 1.4 Level 1 (L1) — Basic

Spec ref: Mark scheme level descriptors Definition: 1–2 marks. The answer is fragmentary, with isolated correct points but no linkage. Scientific terms may be used incorrectly or vaguely. QWC is weak — the answer may be a list, may have spelling errors in technical terms, and shows no sustained argument. QWC Exam context: A typical L1 answer to "Explain why the resistance of a metal increases with temperature" reads: "Atoms vibrate more, electrons collide more, resistance goes up." This scores 2 marks: it has the right ideas but no causal connectives, no mention of drift velocity or mean free time, and no chain of reasoning. To escape L1, write at least one "because" or "therefore".

#### 1.5 Level 2 (L2) — Clear

Spec ref: Mark scheme level descriptors Definition: 3–4 marks. The answer has a clear line of reasoning with some correct physics, but the explanation is incomplete or has minor errors. Most key terms are used correctly. QWC is adequate — the answer is generally readable and uses some connectives, but the argument may jump or miss a step. QWC Exam context: A typical L2 answer: "When the metal is heated, the lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude. This means electrons collide more frequently with the ions, so the drift velocity decreases and the current falls. From R = V/I, if I decreases then R increases." This scores 4 marks — it has the chain but skips "mean free time" and "mean free path" terminology that would lift it to L3.

#### 1.6 Level 3 (L3) — Detailed and Accurate

Spec ref: Mark scheme level descriptors Definition: 5–6 marks. The answer has a sustained, logical, and complete chain of reasoning. All key terms are used correctly and in the right order. QWC is high — connectives link every step, technical spelling is accurate, and the answer reads as a single coherent argument. QWC Exam context: A typical L3 answer includes every IC point, in the right causal order, with explicit connectives ("because", "consequently", "therefore", "as a result"). It uses the full technical vocabulary (lattice ions, mean free time, drift velocity) and ends by linking the microscopic change back to the macroscopic observation (R = V/I increases). L3 is achievable by any student who memorises the model answers in ext-circuits-qwc-concepts.md.

### 2. Command Words for Extended Response

#### 2.1 Discuss

Spec ref: Spec Appendix 5 (command words) Definition: Give an account of something, including different viewpoints or factors, and reach a conclusion. In circuits, "discuss" often asks the student to weigh competing effects (e.g. increased lattice vibration vs increased charge carrier release in a semiconductor). QWC Exam context: "Discuss how the resistance of an NTC thermistor changes with temperature" expects the student to acknowledge TWO competing effects (more charge carriers released → R decreases; more lattice vibration → R increases) and explain why the charge carrier effect dominates in a semiconductor. Missing one effect caps the answer at L2.

#### 2.2 Evaluate

Spec ref: Spec Appendix 5 Definition: Consider different factors, weigh them up, and reach a judgement supported by evidence. In circuits, evaluate is often applied to experimental data or design (e.g. "evaluate whether the student's method gives a reliable value for internal resistance"). QWC Exam context: Requires the student to identify BOTH strengths and limitations and conclude which dominates. A purely critical answer or a purely positive answer caps at L2. The connective "however" is essential in evaluate answers — it signals the weighing-up.

#### 2.3 Explain

Spec ref: Spec Appendix 5 Definition: Give reasons or causes; link cause to effect. The most common command word in circuits QWC. Requires a causal chain, not just a description. QWC Exam context: "Explain why the terminal p.d. is less than the EMF when current flows" expects the chain: cell has internal resistance → some energy dissipated inside cell → "lost volts" = Ir → terminal p.d. = ε − Ir → terminal p.d. < ε. Every step needs a connective ("because", "so", "therefore").

#### 2.4 Describe

Spec ref: Spec Appendix 5 Definition: Give an account in words of what happens, without necessarily giving reasons. In QWC circuits questions, "describe" is rare — examiners prefer "explain" because it forces causal chains. When "describe" appears, students must still state the trend and link to a measurable change. QWC Exam context: "Describe how the resistance of an LDR varies with light intensity" expects: as light intensity increases, more charge carriers are released, number density increases, so R decreases. Even "describe" rewards causal chains in WPH12.

#### 2.5 Compare

Spec ref: Spec Appendix 5 Definition: Identify similarities and differences between two or more things. In circuits, used for series vs parallel, metal vs thermistor, EMF vs terminal p.d. QWC Exam context: A compare answer must address BOTH items symmetrically. "In series, current is the same everywhere; in parallel, voltage is the same across each branch." Using "whereas", "in contrast", "on the other hand" signals comparison and earns the QWC mark.

#### 2.6 Justify

Spec ref: Spec Appendix 5 Definition: Support a conclusion with evidence or reasoning. Often used in numerical questions ("show that", then "justify whether the result is reasonable"). QWC Exam context: "Justify whether the student's conclusion that r = 0.5 Ω is supported by the data" expects: a calculation, comparison to uncertainty, and a judgement. The connective "therefore" is essential: "...the uncertainty is ±0.2 Ω, therefore the value 0.5 Ω is consistent with the true value of 0.4 Ω."

### 3. Connective Words (QWC Signalling Language)

#### 3.1 Therefore

Definition: Introduces a logical conclusion from the previous statement. The most important connective in physics QWC — it signals "the next sentence is the consequence of the previous one." QWC Exam context: "Lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude, therefore electrons collide more frequently." Examiners reward "therefore" because it shows the student is constructing a causal chain, not listing facts.

#### 3.2 Consequently

Definition: As a result; introduces an effect that follows from a cause. Often used at the second or third step of a chain. QWC Exam context: "Mean free time decreases; consequently, drift velocity falls." "Consequently" signals a derived effect, which examiners recognise as L3 thinking.

#### 3.3 As a result

Definition: Synonym for "therefore" / "consequently". Less formal but acceptable. Often used to introduce the final macroscopic observation. QWC Exam context: "Fewer electrons pass a point per second; as a result, the current I decreases."

#### 3.4 Because

Definition: Introduces the cause of a previously stated effect. The reverse direction of "therefore" — "X because Y" is equivalent to "Y therefore X". QWC Exam context: "The terminal p.d. is less than the EMF because some energy is dissipated in the internal resistance." "Because" is the workhorse connective — it appears in nearly every L3 answer.

#### 3.5 Due to

Definition: Synonym for "because of"; introduces a cause as a noun phrase rather than a clause. QWC Exam context: "The resistance increases due to more frequent collisions between electrons and lattice ions." Note: "due to" must be followed by a noun phrase, not a full clause ("due to more frequent collisions" ✓; "due to electrons collide more" ✗).

#### 3.6 However

Definition: Introduces a contrast or opposing point. Essential in "discuss" and "evaluate" answers where two competing effects must be weighed. QWC Exam context: In a thermistor QWC: "Heating also causes more lattice vibration, however, in a semiconductor the dominant effect is the release of more charge carriers." Without "however", the answer fails to show the weighing-up that L3 requires.

#### 3.7 In contrast

Definition: Synonym for "however" used specifically when comparing two distinct cases. QWC Exam context: "In a metal, resistance increases with temperature; in contrast, in an NTC thermistor resistance decreases with temperature." Signals explicit comparison — rewarded in "compare" QWC questions.

#### 3.8 Whereas

Definition: Similar to "in contrast"; introduces a subordinate clause that contrasts with the main clause. QWC Exam context: "In series the same current flows through each component, whereas in parallel the current splits between branches."

### 4. Circuit Terms for QWC — Metal Resistance & Temperature

#### 4.1 Lattice (Ion)

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 (current electricity), atomic model Definition: The regular three-dimensional array of positive ions in a metal that occupies fixed (mean) positions in the crystal structure. The ions are not truly stationary — they vibrate about their equilibrium positions with an amplitude determined by the temperature. QWC Exam context: In a metal-R-T QWC answer, the first IC point is always "lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude at higher T". Examiners reward "lattice ions" specifically — saying "atoms vibrate" scores lower because the metal's positive cores are ions, not neutral atoms.

#### 4.2 Lattice Vibration

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 + Topic 4 (thermal physics cross-link) Definition: The oscillation of lattice ions about their equilibrium positions due to thermal energy. The amplitude of vibration increases with temperature. Lattice vibrations are quantised as phonons in solid-state physics. QWC Exam context: "Lattice vibrations increase with temperature" is the standard L3 phrasing. Avoid "the lattice shakes more" — examiners do not reward informal language. The phrase "increased amplitude of vibration" is the mark-scheme keyword.

#### 4.3 Phonon

Spec ref: Beyond-spec extension, but appears in examiner reports when students mention it Definition: A quantum of lattice vibration energy. Phonons are the particle-like excitations that carry thermal energy through a crystal lattice. Electrons scatter off phonons in a metal, causing resistance. QWC Exam context: Mentioning "phonons" can lift an answer from L2 to L3 if used correctly ("electrons scatter off phonons, reducing mean free time"). However, using "phonon" without explaining its role scores no extra marks. Mention it only if the rest of the chain is already complete.

#### 4.4 Thermal Agitation

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 (descriptive term for lattice motion) Definition: Random thermal motion of lattice ions, equivalent to "lattice vibration". A more formal term that examiners reward in L3 answers. QWC Exam context: "Increased thermal agitation of the lattice ions" is a mark-scheme phrase. Use it interchangeably with "lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude" to vary vocabulary — both score.

#### 4.5 Mean Free Time

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 (Drift velocity equation context) Definition: The average time between successive collisions of a conduction electron with lattice ions. It decreases when lattice vibrations increase (because collisions become more frequent). Drift velocity v = (qEτ)/mₑ, where τ is the mean free time — so v decreases if τ decreases. QWC Exam context: Mentioning "mean free time decreases" is a key L3 discriminator — most L2 answers skip this and go straight to "drift velocity decreases". Stating "mean free time decreases because collisions become more frequent" earns the L3 step.

#### 4.6 Mean Free Path

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 (related to mean free time) Definition: The average distance a conduction electron travels between successive collisions with lattice ions. Mean free path = mean free time × drift velocity. It decreases when lattice vibrations increase. QWC Exam context: Mentioning mean free path is an alternative to mean free time — both score the same IC point. Use whichever you remember; do not state both unless asked.

#### 4.7 Drift Velocity

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 — I = nAvq Definition: The average velocity of charge carriers along a conductor in the direction of the electric field. It is much smaller than the random thermal velocity of the carriers (typically ~10⁻⁴ m/s vs ~10⁵ m/s for thermal motion) because the field only slightly biases the random motion. Drift velocity v = I/(nAq). QWC Exam context: Every metal-R-T QWC answer must end with "drift velocity decreases → current decreases → R = V/I increases". This is the L3 chain. Students who stop at "drift velocity decreases" miss the final macroscopic link.

### 5. Circuit Terms for QWC — Semiconductor & Thermistor

#### 5.1 Semiconductor

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 (classification of materials) Definition: A material with electrical conductivity between that of a conductor (metal) and an insulator. Its resistivity decreases with temperature because thermal energy releases more charge carriers from the lattice. Examples: silicon, germanium. NTC thermistors are made from semiconductor materials. QWC Exam context: In a thermistor QWC, the opening sentence must identify the material as a semiconductor: "An NTC thermistor is made from a semiconductor." This is IC point #1 — without it, the answer cannot reach L3.

#### 5.2 Charge Carrier

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 Definition: A particle that carries electric charge and is free to move through a material. In metals, charge carriers are delocalised electrons. In semiconductors, charge carriers are electrons in the conduction band AND holes (positive vacancies) in the valence band. In electrolytes, charge carriers are ions. QWC Exam context: In a thermistor QWC: "Thermal energy releases more charge carriers" is the key IC point. Saying "more electrons" is acceptable but "more charge carriers" is the mark-scheme phrase — use it.

#### 5.3 Number Density (n)

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 — I = nAvq Definition: The number of charge carriers per unit volume (m⁻³). In a metal, n is essentially constant with temperature (~10²⁸ m⁻³ for copper). In a semiconductor, n increases rapidly with temperature because thermal energy promotes electrons from the valence band to the conduction band. QWC Exam context: "Number density n increases with temperature" is the central IC point of a thermistor QWC. Students must distinguish this from a metal, where n is constant. The contrast (n constant in metals; n increases in semiconductors) is what makes the two QWC topics distinguishable.

#### 5.4 NTC Thermistor

Spec ref: Spec 68 (resistivity) + Spec 64-65 Definition: A thermistor with a Negative Temperature Coefficient of resistance — its resistance decreases as temperature increases. Made from a semiconductor (typically a metal oxide such as Mn₂O₃ or NiO). The negative coefficient arises because the increase in number density of charge carriers with temperature outweighs the increase in lattice vibration. QWC Exam context: Always introduce the topic with "NTC = negative temperature coefficient" to score the definition IC point. Then explain the mechanism: more charge carriers released → n increases → I = nAvq → I increases → R = V/I decreases.

#### 5.5 Band Theory (Beyond-spec, contextual)

Spec ref: Beyond IAL spec but appears in examiner reports for L3 answers Definition: The model in which electrons in a solid occupy energy bands (valence band, conduction band) separated by a forbidden gap. In a semiconductor at absolute zero, the valence band is full and the conduction band is empty, so no conduction occurs. At higher temperatures, thermal energy promotes electrons across the gap, leaving holes in the valence band. QWC Exam context: Mentioning "electrons promoted from valence band to conduction band" can lift an answer to L3 — but it must be paired with the simpler explanation ("more charge carriers released"). Use band theory as a bonus, not as a replacement for the simpler mechanism.

### 6. Circuit Terms for QWC — Drift Velocity & Current

#### 6.1 Drift Velocity Equation (I = nAvq)

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 — I = nAvq Definition: The equation relating current I to the number density n, cross-sectional area A, drift velocity v, and charge per carrier q. For electrons, q = e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Rearranged: v = I/(nAq). QWC Exam context: In a drift-velocity QWC, the answer must quote I = nAvq explicitly and explain what each symbol represents. This is the structural backbone of the answer — without the equation, the explanation has no anchor.

#### 6.2 Conduction Electron

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 Definition: An electron in a metal that is delocalised (not bound to a particular atom) and free to move through the lattice. Approximately one per atom in metals. Conduction electrons form the "electron sea" that gives metals their conductivity. QWC Exam context: "Conduction electrons" is the preferred term over just "electrons" — it shows the student understands they are the charge carriers in a metal.

#### 6.3 Random Thermal Motion

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 (qualitative) Definition: The random, high-speed (~10⁵ m/s) motion of conduction electrons in a metal due to thermal energy. Without an electric field, the random motion produces no net drift. When an electric field is applied, it superimposes a small drift (~10⁻⁴ m/s) on the random motion. QWC Exam context: In a "why is drift velocity so slow" QWC, mentioning random thermal motion is essential: "Electrons move randomly at high speed but only drift slowly along the field because they constantly collide with lattice ions." Without this, the answer is incomplete.

#### 6.4 Collision (with Lattice Ions)

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 Definition: The interaction between a conduction electron and a lattice ion that scatters the electron, randomising its velocity. Collisions are the mechanism of resistance — they interrupt the drift, so the electron's net forward motion is much slower than its speed between collisions. QWC Exam context: "Electrons collide frequently with lattice ions" is the key IC point in a drift-velocity QWC. The phrase "frequent collisions" is the mark-scheme keyword.

### 7. Circuit Terms for QWC — Internal Resistance & EMF

#### 7.1 Electromotive Force (EMF, ε)

Spec ref: Spec 66-67 — ε = W/Q Definition: The total electrical energy per unit charge produced by a source (e.g. cell, battery). Unit: volts (V = J/C). EMF is the energy converted from chemical (or other) to electrical form per coulomb of charge that passes through the source. The symbol is ε (epsilon). For an ideal source with no internal resistance, terminal p.d. = EMF at all currents. QWC Exam context: In an internal-resistance QWC, the opening sentence must define EMF: "The EMF is the total energy per coulomb supplied by the cell." Then introduce internal resistance: "In a real cell, some of this energy is dissipated in the internal resistance." This is the L3 chain.

#### 7.2 Internal Resistance (r)

Spec ref: Spec 66-67 — V = ε − Ir Definition: The resistance to current flow inside a source of EMF, caused by the resistance of the electrolyte, electrodes, and internal connections. Internal resistance causes some of the energy per coulomb to be dissipated inside the source itself, so the terminal p.d. is less than the EMF when current flows. Symbol: r. Unit: Ω. QWC Exam context: "Real cells have internal resistance r" is the second IC point in an internal-resistance QWC. The phrase "real" or "non-ideal" is important — examiners reward the distinction between ideal and real sources.

#### 7.3 Lost Volts

Spec ref: Spec 66-67 — V = ε − Ir Definition: The voltage "lost" across the internal resistance of a source when current flows, equal to Ir. The term is informal but appears in mark schemes. Lost volts = EMF − terminal p.d. = Ir. The greater the current, the greater the lost volts. QWC Exam context: The phrase "lost volts" appears verbatim in mark schemes — use it. "The lost volts (Ir) increase with current" is the L3 phrasing. Avoid "missing voltage" or "lost energy" — these do not score.

#### 7.4 Terminal Potential Difference (V)

Spec ref: Spec 66-67 — V = ε − Ir Definition: The potential difference across the terminals of a source when current is flowing. It is less than the EMF by the lost volts: V = ε − Ir. When no current flows (open circuit), V = ε. Unit: V. QWC Exam context: The QWC chain must explicitly compare terminal p.d. to EMF: "terminal p.d. < EMF when current flows." The inequality is the key mark — examiners look for the explicit comparison.

#### 7.5 Open Circuit (No Current)

Spec ref: Spec 66-67 Definition: A circuit condition in which no current flows (e.g. switch open, or voltmeter with very high resistance connected across a cell). In open circuit, Ir = 0, so V = ε. The terminal p.d. equals the EMF. QWC Exam context: "When no current flows, the lost volts are zero, so the voltmeter reads the EMF." This is the standard explanation for why a voltmeter across an isolated cell reads the EMF. Use the phrase "no current flows" — examiners reward this directly.

#### 7.6 Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (in internal resistance context)

Spec ref: Spec 66-67 (energy conservation in loops) Definition: The sum of EMFs around any closed loop in a circuit equals the sum of potential drops (including across internal resistance). For a single loop: ε = Ir + IRₑₓₜₑᵣₙₐₗ. This is energy conservation applied to charge. QWC Exam context: Mentioning "energy is conserved" can lift an answer to L3 in internal resistance QWC: "Energy supplied per coulomb by the cell equals energy dissipated in the internal resistance plus energy dissipated in the external circuit." The phrase "energy is conserved" or "energy per coulomb" is rewarded.

### 8. Circuit Terms for QWC — Series and Parallel

#### 8.1 Series Circuit

Spec ref: Spec 68 Definition: A circuit in which components are connected end-to-end so that the same current flows through each component. The total resistance is the sum of individual resistances: Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ... The p.d. across the combination equals the sum of p.d.s across each component. QWC Exam context: "In series, the same current flows through every component, and the p.d. splits across them" — the two key IC points. Use "splits" or "divides" — both score.

#### 8.2 Parallel Circuit

Spec ref: Spec 68 Definition: A circuit in which components are connected across the same two points so that the same p.d. is applied across each component. The current splits between the branches. The reciprocal of total resistance equals the sum of reciprocals of individual resistances: 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... The total resistance is LESS than the smallest individual resistance. QWC Exam context: "In parallel, the same p.d. is across each branch, and the current splits between branches." Plus the non-obvious point: "Rₜₒₜₐₗ is less than the smallest individual resistor." The "less than smallest" point is a common L3 discriminator.

#### 8.3 Equivalent Resistance

Spec ref: Spec 68 Definition: The single resistance that could replace a combination of resistors without changing the current drawn from the source. Calculated using Rₜₒₜₐₗ = ΣR for series, or 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = Σ(1/R) for parallel. QWC Exam context: Use "equivalent resistance" rather than "total resistance" in formal answers — both score, but "equivalent" is the more precise term.

### 9. Circuit Terms for QWC — Potential Divider

#### 9.1 Potential Divider

Spec ref: Spec 69-71 Definition: A circuit of two (or more) resistors in series across a source, used to provide a fraction of the source p.d. The output voltage is taken across one of the resistors. Vₒᵤₜ = Vᵢₙ × R₂/(R₁ + R₂), where R₂ is the resistor across which Vₒᵤₜ is measured. QWC Exam context: The formula Vₒᵤₜ = Vᵢₙ × R₂/(R₁ + R₂) is the structural anchor of a potential-divider QWC. Always write it down and explain what each symbol is.

#### 9.2 Light-Dependent Resistor (LDR)

Spec ref: Spec 69-71 (sensor application) Definition: A resistor whose resistance decreases when light intensity increases (made from a semiconductor such as CdS). More photons release more charge carriers, increasing n and decreasing R. In a potential divider, replacing R₁ or R₂ with an LDR gives a light-sensing circuit. QWC Exam context: "In light, the LDR's resistance decreases" — the IC point. Then link to Vₒᵤₜ: "if the LDR is R₂, Vₒᵤₜ decreases in bright light; if the LDR is R₁, Vₒᵤₜ increases in bright light." The direction of Vₒᵤₜ change depends on which resistor the LDR replaces.

#### 9.3 Thermistor in a Potential Divider

Spec ref: Spec 69-71 Definition: Using an NTC thermistor as one resistor in a potential divider gives a temperature-sensing circuit. As T increases, Rₜₕₑᵣₘᵢₛₜₒᵣ decreases, so Vₒᵤₜ across it decreases (if it is R₂) or increases (if it is R₁). QWC Exam context: The QWC chain: "As T increases, Rₜₕₑᵣₘᵢₛₜₒᵣ decreases (NTC), so the thermistor's share of Vᵢₙ decreases, so Vₒᵤₜ across it decreases." Plus the application: "This can switch on a heater when Vₒᵤₜ drops below a threshold."

#### 9.4 Potentiometer

Spec ref: Spec 69-71 (variable potential divider) Definition: A variable resistor with three terminals, used as an adjustable potential divider. A sliding contact moves along a resistive track, allowing Vₒᵤₜ to be varied continuously from 0 to Vᵢₙ. QWC Exam context: Mentioned in L3 answers as a practical application: "A potentiometer allows Vₒᵤₜ to be varied continuously from 0 to Vᵢₙ." Use this as a closing application point.

### 10. Cross-Cutting Terms

#### 10.1 Ohm's Law

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 — V = IR Definition: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the p.d.: V = IR. The constant of proportionality is the resistance. Ohm's Law applies to metals at constant temperature but NOT to thermistors, diodes, or lamps (whose temperature — and hence resistance — changes with current). QWC Exam context: Used as the final link in metal-R-T QWC: "Since R = V/I and I has decreased (at constant V), R increases." Quoting Ohm's Law explicitly is rewarded.

#### 10.2 Resistivity (ρ)

Spec ref: Spec 68 — R = ρL/A Definition: An intrinsic property of a material, defined as the resistance of a 1 m cube of the material. Unit: Ω·m. Resistivity depends on temperature (increases with T for metals, decreases for semiconductors) but not on the dimensions of the sample. QWC Exam context: In a metal-R-T QWC, mentioning "resistivity increases with temperature" is rewarded alongside "resistance increases." Use both — they reinforce each other.

#### 10.3 Ohmic vs Non-Ohmic

Spec ref: Spec 64-65 Definition: An ohmic conductor obeys Ohm's Law (V vs I graph is a straight line through the origin) at constant temperature. A non-ohmic conductor does not (V vs I graph is curved or non-linear). Metals are ohmic at constant T; thermistors, filament lamps, and diodes are non-ohmic. QWC Exam context: In a "compare metal and thermistor" QWC, the contrast "metals are ohmic at constant T, thermistors are non-ohmic" is rewarded as an L3 point.

### Ch 2.4 — Electric Circuits: Concepts

Spec points 64–80 | IAL Physics WPH12

Comprehensive concept explanations for every sub-topic in this chapter. Each concept connects definitions into coherent understanding, with worked examples and exam traps highlighted.

### Group 1: Electric Current and Potential Difference (Spec 64–65)

#### What Electric Current Actually Is — Microscopic Picture

What it is and why it matters: Electric current is defined as the rate of flow of electric charge: I = ΔQ/Δt. This is a macroscopic definition — it tells you what you measure with an ammeter. But to understand why current behaves as it does in circuits, you need the microscopic picture: current in a metal is the net drift of conduction electrons through a lattice of positive ions. The current value depends not just on how fast the electrons move (the drift velocity), but on how many charge carriers are available (the number density, n) and the cross-sectional area of the conductor (A). This distinction between macroscopic measurement and microscopic mechanism is tested repeatedly in explanations and calculations.

How it works — the two pictures:

Macroscopic: An ammeter reads current in amperes. One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point each second. The charge Q flowing in time t is Q = It. Charge is conserved: whatever enters one end of a wire must leave the other end.

Microscopic: In a metal wire, billions of free electrons exist per cubic metre (n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ for copper). These electrons move randomly at very high speeds (~10⁵ m s⁻¹) due to thermal energy, but this random motion averages to zero net current. When a p.d. is applied, a small additional drift velocity (v ≈ 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹) is superimposed on the random motion, producing a net flow of charge. The current depends on all four factors: I = nqvA.

Conventional current vs electron flow: Conventional current is defined as flowing from positive to negative terminal — this is the historical convention established before electrons were discovered.
