### 4. Recurring Examiner Report Themes (Circuits QWC)

#### 4.1 "Students listed facts without linkage"

Appears in 9/14 examiner reports. The most common reason for capping at L2. Fix: use at least 4 connectives ("because", "therefore", "consequently", "as a result") in every 6-mark answer.

#### 4.2 "Students said 'atoms' instead of 'lattice ions'"

Appears in 6 examiner reports for metal-R-T QWC. Metals have a lattice of positive IONS, not neutral atoms. Fix: always say "lattice ions".

#### 4.3 "Students did not mention mean free time"

Appears in 7 examiner reports. The mean-free-time step is the L2→L3 discriminator for metal-R-T QWC. Fix: always insert "mean free time decreases" between "more collisions" and "drift velocity decreases".

#### 4.4 "Students confused the two competing effects in a thermistor"

Appears in 5 examiner reports. Students explained only the charge-carrier effect, missing the lattice-vibration effect. Fix: use "However" or "In contrast" to acknowledge the lattice-vibration effect, then explain why the charge-carrier effect dominates.

#### 4.5 "Students stated 'voltmeter reads EMF' without explaining why"

Appears in 6 examiner reports for internal-resistance QWC. The explanation MUST include "voltmeter has very high resistance → I ≈ 0 → Ir ≈ 0 → V = ε". Fix: always include this chain.

#### 4.6 "Students did not write V = ε − Ir"

Appears in 4 examiner reports. The equation is the structural anchor of the answer. Fix: always quote the equation explicitly.

#### 4.7 "Students confused drift velocity with signal speed"

Appears in 3 examiner reports. Drift velocity is ~mm/s; the electrical signal propagates near c. Fix: explicitly state both numbers and contrast them with "whereas".

#### 4.8 "Students did not state an application for the potential divider"

Appears in 4 examiner reports for potential-divider QWC. The application is worth 1 mark (IC #6). Fix: always end with "an application is ..." — street lamp, burglar alarm, heater switch, etc.

### 5. Ten Practice QWC Questions (6 marks each)

Each question below has: (a) the question stem, (b) a model L3 answer with connectives in bold, (c) the IC points breakdown, (d) common L1/L2 errors. Total: 10 questions × 6 marks = 60 marks of practice.

#### Practice Question 1 — Metal R-T (Standard)

Question: A student measures the current through a length of nichrome wire while keeping the p.d. across it constant at 4.0 V. The student observes that the current decreases over time as the wire heats up. Explain, in terms of the motion of conduction electrons and lattice ions, why the current decreases. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

As the wire heats up, the lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude about their equilibrium positions because thermal energy increases their kinetic energy. Consequently, conduction electrons collide more frequently with the vibrating lattice ions, so the mean free time between collisions decreases. Since drift velocity v = qEτ/mₑ (where τ is the mean free time), the reduced τ means the drift velocity of the electrons decreases. As a result, fewer electrons pass a given cross-section per second, therefore the current I = nAvq decreases. Because the p.d. is held constant at 4.0 V and the current has fallen, the resistance R = V/I has increased — explaining why the ammeter reading drops over time.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 Lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude

2 More frequent electron–ion collisions

3 Mean free time τ decreases

4 Drift velocity decreases (v ∝ τ)

5 Current I = nAvq decreases

6 R = V/I increases (at constant V)

Common L1/L2 errors: Saying "atoms" not "lattice ions"; skipping mean free time; not linking to R = V/I.

#### Practice Question 2 — Metal R-T (Calculation + Explain Hybrid)

Question: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a current of 3.0 A at 20 °C; the drift velocity is 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. When the wire is heated to 80 °C at the same p.d., the drift velocity falls to 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s. Explain why the drift velocity decreases when the wire is heated, and calculate the percentage increase in the resistance of the wire. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

When the wire is heated, the lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude because their thermal kinetic energy increases. Consequently, conduction electrons collide more frequently with the lattice ions, so the mean free time τ between collisions decreases. Since v = qEτ/mₑ, the reduced τ reduces the drift velocity for a given electric field. At the same p.d., the reduced drift velocity means a reduced current (I = nAvq), therefore R = V/I has increased. From the ratio of drift velocities: v₂/v₁ = 1.5/2.2 = 0.68, so I₂/I₁ = 0.68 (since n, A, q are constant). Therefore R₂/R₁ = V/I₂ ÷ V/I₁ = I₁/I₂ = 2.2/1.5 = 1.47, giving a 47% increase in resistance.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 Lattice ions vibrate more at higher T

2 More frequent collisions reduce τ

3 v = qEτ/mₑ → v decreases

4 At same V, lower v means lower I (I = nAvq)

5 R = V/I increases

6 Calculation: 47% increase (R₂/R₁ = I₁/I₂ = 2.2/1.5 = 1.47)

Common L1/L2 errors: Forgetting to mention mean free time; not linking drift velocity change to R change; calculation error from inverting the ratio.

#### Practice Question 3 — NTC Thermistor R-T (Standard)

Question: An NTC thermistor is connected in series with a 6.0 V battery and an ammeter. The ammeter reading increases when the thermistor is warmed. Explain why the resistance of the thermistor decreases as its temperature rises. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

An NTC thermistor is made from a semiconductor material. When it is heated, thermal energy is absorbed by the lattice and this promotes electrons from the valence band into the conduction band, releasing more charge carriers. Consequently, the number density n of free charge carriers increases sharply with temperature. Because I = nAvq, the increase in n means the current I increases (at constant V), even though the drift velocity per carrier may fall slightly. However, the increased temperature also causes greater lattice vibration, which would tend to reduce drift velocity and increase resistance — as in a metal. In contrast to a metal, in a semiconductor the increase in charge carrier number density outweighs the lattice vibration effect, so the net effect is that I increases. Therefore, since R = V/I and V is constant while I has increased, the resistance of the NTC thermistor decreases with increasing temperature.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 Thermistor is a semiconductor

2 Thermal energy releases more charge carriers

3 Number density n increases

4 I = nAvq → current increases

5 Charge carrier effect dominates over lattice vibration

6 R = V/I decreases

Common L1/L2 errors: Not saying "semiconductor"; not mentioning competing lattice-vibration effect; confusing direction of n change.

#### Practice Question 4 — NTC Thermistor (Comparison with Metal)

Question: A student has a copper wire and an NTC thermistor. Both are heated from 20 °C to 80 °C while the p.d. across each is held constant. The current through the copper wire decreases; the current through the thermistor increases. Compare the mechanisms that lead to these opposite observations. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

In the copper wire (a metal), the number density n of conduction electrons is essentially constant with temperature. When the wire is heated, the lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude, so electrons collide more frequently and the mean free time τ decreases. Consequently, the drift velocity decreases and the current I = nAvq falls (at constant V), therefore the resistance R = V/I increases. In contrast, in the NTC thermistor (a semiconductor), n is NOT constant: heating promotes electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, so n increases sharply. Although the lattice vibration also increases (which alone would reduce drift velocity), the increase in n dominates, and the current I = nAvq rises (at constant V). Therefore, R = V/I decreases for the thermistor. The key difference is that in a metal n is constant and only τ changes, whereas in a semiconductor n changes and this dominates the behaviour.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 Metal: n is constant; only lattice vibration changes

2 Metal: τ decreases, v decreases, I decreases, R increases

3 Semiconductor: n increases with T (charge carriers released)

4 Semiconductor: I increases (n effect dominates)

5 Semiconductor: R = V/I decreases

6 Comparison: "whereas" / "in contrast" links the two cases

Common L1/L2 errors: Describing only one material; not using comparison connectives; saying "n changes in metals".

#### Practice Question 5 — Drift Velocity (Standard)

Question: A current of 2.0 A flows in an aluminium wire of cross-sectional area 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ m². The number density of conduction electrons in aluminium is 6.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the drift velocity of the electrons, and explain why this drift velocity is so small even though the current is large. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

The current is given by I = nAvq, where n is the number density of charge carriers, A is the cross-sectional area, v is the drift velocity, and q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the charge per electron. Rearranging, v = I/(nAq) = 2.0 / (6.0 × 10²⁸ × 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ m/s (about 0.3 mm/s). This drift velocity is very small because n is enormous (~10²⁸ m⁻³), so even a tiny drift of each carrier produces a large current when multiplied by n, A, and q. Furthermore, q is a fixed fundamental constant and A is limited by the wire's physical size, therefore v must be small to give a reasonable current. The reason the electrons drift so slowly is that they are in constant random thermal motion at high speed (~10⁵ m/s) but collide frequently with lattice ions; each collision randomises their velocity, so the electric field only imposes a tiny net drift on top of the random motion. However, the electrical signal itself travels at nearly the speed of light along the wire (because the field propagates at c), whereas the charge carriers drift only at ~mm/s.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 States I = nAvq with symbols defined

2 Calculates v = 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ m/s (with units)

3 Explains n is huge (~10²⁸ m⁻³), so v is small

4 q is fixed (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C), A is small — so v must be small

5 Frequent collisions with lattice ions randomise velocity

6 Drift (~mm/s) vs signal speed (~c)

Common L1/L2 errors: Calculation errors (unit conversion); omitting q; confusing drift with signal speed; not mentioning collisions.

#### Practice Question 6 — Drift Velocity (Comparison Wire)

Question: Two copper wires A and B carry the same current. Wire A has twice the cross-sectional area of wire B. Compare the drift velocities of electrons in the two wires, and explain why connecting two wires of different thicknesses affects the drift velocity. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

The current is given by I = nAvq, where all symbols have their usual meanings. For two copper wires of the same material at the same temperature, n and q are the same. Rearranging for drift velocity: v = I/(nAq). If both wires carry the same current I, then the wire with the larger cross-sectional area A will have a smaller drift velocity, because the same current is shared over more charge carriers per unit length. Specifically, if wire A has twice the area of wire B (A_A = 2 A_B), then v_A = v_B / 2 — the drift velocity in wire A is half that in wire B. This is because the larger area means more charge carriers are available to carry the same current, so each carrier drifts more slowly. The current itself is the same in both wires (series connection), whereas the drift velocity adjusts to compensate for the change in area. Consequently, thicker wires can carry the same current with a slower drift velocity, which is why high-current cables are made thick — to reduce the drift velocity and hence the resistance heating.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 States I = nAvq

2 For same material, n and q are the same

3 v = I/(nAq) — v inversely proportional to A

4 Wire A (2× area) has half the drift velocity

5 Explains: more carriers per unit length, each drifts less

6 Application: thicker wires for high current (less drift, less heat)

Common L1/L2 errors: Saying v is the same in both (wrong — v differs if A differs); saying v doubles in the thicker wire (inverted); not linking to real-world application.

#### Practice Question 7 — Internal Resistance (Standard)

Question: A cell of EMF 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.80 Ω is connected to a 4.2 Ω external resistor. Explain why the potential difference across the external resistor is less than 9.0 V. Use the terms 'EMF', 'internal resistance', and 'lost volts' in your answer. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

The EMF (ε) of the cell is the total electrical energy per coulomb supplied by the chemical reactions in the cell — 9.0 V means 9.0 J per coulomb. However, a real cell is not ideal: it has internal resistance r (= 0.80 Ω) due to the resistance of its electrolyte and electrodes. When a current I flows, some of the energy per coulomb is dissipated inside the cell itself as heat in the internal resistance. This energy loss per coulomb is called the "lost volts" and is equal to Ir. Therefore, the terminal potential difference V — the energy per coulomb actually delivered to the external circuit — is given by V = ε − Ir. Because current is flowing (I = ε/(r + R) = 9.0/5.0 = 1.8 A), the lost volts are Ir = 1.8 × 0.80 = 1.44 V, so the terminal p.d. is V = 9.0 − 1.44 = 7.56 V, which is less than the EMF. This is consistent with energy conservation: the energy per coulomb supplied by the cell equals the energy per coulomb dissipated in the internal resistance plus the energy per coulomb dissipated in the external resistor (ε = Ir + IR).

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 EMF = total energy per coulomb supplied by the cell

2 Real cell has internal resistance r

3 Lost volts = Ir (energy dissipated inside cell)

4 V = ε − Ir < ε when current flows

5 Numerical: I = 1.8 A, lost volts = 1.44 V, V = 7.56 V

6 Energy conservation: ε = Ir + IR

Common L1/L2 errors: Not using all three required terms; not writing V = ε − Ir; not computing the numerical current.

#### Practice Question 8 — Internal Resistance (Voltmeter Behaviour)

Question: A high-resistance voltmeter connected across an isolated 12 V battery reads 12.0 V. When a 10 Ω resistor is connected across the battery in parallel with the voltmeter, the voltmeter reads 11.2 V. Explain these observations and determine the internal resistance of the battery. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

When the voltmeter is connected across the isolated battery, its very high resistance means the current drawn is negligible (I ≈ 0). Because the lost volts are Ir and I ≈ 0, the lost volts are effectively zero, therefore the terminal p.d. V = ε − Ir ≈ ε = 12.0 V. Consequently, the voltmeter reads the EMF directly. However, when the 10 Ω resistor is connected in parallel, the total external resistance drops sharply, so a significant current I now flows. As a result, the lost volts Ir are now non-zero, and the terminal p.d. V = ε − Ir is now 11.2 V, less than the EMF. The lost volts are ε − V = 12.0 − 11.2 = 0.8 V. The current through the external resistor is I = V/R = 11.2 / 10 = 1.12 A. Therefore, the internal resistance r = lost volts / I = 0.8 / 1.12 = 0.71 Ω. In an ideal cell with r = 0, there would be no lost volts and the voltmeter would read ε in both cases, whereas this real cell shows the drop because r ≠ 0.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 Voltmeter high resistance → I ≈ 0 when isolated

2 Lost volts Ir ≈ 0, so V = ε

3 Connecting resistor drops external R → I increases

4 Lost volts now non-zero → V = 11.2 V < ε

5 Lost volts = 0.8 V; I = 1.12 A; r = 0.71 Ω

6 Contrasts real (r ≠ 0) vs ideal (r = 0) cell

Common L1/L2 errors: Not explaining the open-circuit case; not computing r; using wrong V or I in r = lost volts/I.

#### Practice Question 9 — Series vs Parallel Comparison

Question: A student has two 12 Ω resistors. Compare the total resistance, current, and potential difference when the two resistors are connected (a) in series, and (b) in parallel, across a 6.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

In series, the same current flows through every component, whereas in parallel the current splits between the branches. For total resistance: in series the resistances add, Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ = 12 + 12 = 24 Ω, so the combined resistance is always greater than either resistor alone. However, in parallel the reciprocal resistances add, 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/12 + 1/12 = 1/6, therefore Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 6 Ω, which is less than the smallest individual resistor (12 Ω), because adding another branch provides an additional path for current. For the current drawn from the 6.0 V battery: in series, I = V/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 6.0/24 = 0.25 A; in parallel, I = V/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 6.0/6 = 1.0 A. Consequently, the parallel combination draws four times the current of the series combination from the same battery. For the p.d.: in series the p.d. splits (6.0 V across the combination splits as 3.0 V + 3.0 V across each resistor), whereas in parallel the same 6.0 V is across each branch.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 Series: same current; parallel: current splits

2 Series Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 24 Ω (R₁ + R₂)

3 Parallel 1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ → Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 6 Ω

4 Parallel Rₜₒₜₐₗ < smallest individual R

5 Series I = 0.25 A; parallel I = 1.0 A (4× more)

6 P.d. in series splits (3 V + 3 V); in parallel, 6 V across each

Common L1/L2 errors: Not computing the numerical currents; not stating "Rₚₐᵣₐₗₗₑₗ < smallest"; using "and" instead of "whereas".

#### Practice Question 10 — Potential Divider with LDR

Question: A potential divider consists of a fixed 5.0 kΩ resistor R₁ in series with an LDR (R₂), connected across a 9.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The output voltage Vₒᵤₜ is taken across the LDR. Explain how Vₒᵤₜ changes as the light intensity increases, and describe one practical application of this circuit. (6 marks)

Model L3 answer:

The output voltage of a potential divider is given by Vₒᵤₜ = Vᵢₙ × R₂/(R₁ + R₂), where R₂ is the LDR (the resistor across which Vₒᵤₜ is measured). When the light intensity increases, the LDR's resistance decreases, because photons of light release more charge carriers into the conduction band of the semiconductor material (cadmium sulfide), increasing the number density n and reducing R = ρL/A. Substituting this into the formula: as R₂ (= LDR) decreases, the fraction R₂/(R₁ + R₂) decreases, therefore Vₒᵤₜ across the LDR decreases. Consequently, the voltage across the fixed resistor R₁ increases by the same amount (since V₁ + V₂ = Vᵢₙ = 9.0 V is constant). A practical application is a light-activated switch for street lamps: at dusk, the light intensity falls, the LDR's resistance rises, Vₒᵤₜ across the LDR rises above a threshold, and a transistor switches on the street lamp. In contrast, if Vₒᵤₜ were taken across R₁ instead, Vₒᵤₜ would rise with light intensity — useful for a burglar alarm that triggers when a light beam is broken.

IC breakdown:

IC Point

1 States potential divider formula Vₒᵤₜ = Vᵢₙ × R₂/(R₁+R₂)

2 LDR is a semiconductor; R decreases with light intensity

3 Mechanism: more light → more charge carriers → n increases → R decreases

4 R₂ decreasing → Vₒᵤₜ across LDR decreases

5 V across R₁ increases by the same amount (V₁ + V₂ = Vᵢₙ)

6 Application: street lamp / burglar alarm with correct Vₒᵤₜ direction

Common L1/L2 errors: Not writing the formula; saying "LDR R increases with light" (wrong direction); not stating an application; confusing which Vₒᵤₜ direction.

### 7. Self-Assessment Checklist

Before submitting a 6-mark QWC answer, tick each box:

[ ] I have used at least 4 connectives ("because", "therefore", "consequently", "as a result", "however", "in contrast", "whereas").

[ ] My answer is a continuous paragraph (not a list of bullet points).

[ ] I have used the correct technical terms (e.g. "lattice ions" not "atoms"; "charge carriers" not "electrons" for semiconductors; "lost volts = Ir").

[ ] I have written the relevant equation explicitly (R = V/I, I = nAvq, V = ε − Ir, Vₒᵤₜ = Vᵢₙ × R₂/(R₁+R₂)).

[ ] I have closed the chain by linking the microscopic change to the macroscopic observation (e.g. "drift velocity decreases → current decreases → R = V/I increases").

[ ] I have addressed every part of the question (if it asks for an application, I have stated one; if it asks for a comparison, I have used "whereas").

[ ] I have spelled all technical terms correctly (EMF, semiconductor, lattice, thermistor, potentiometer).

[ ] If the question names specific terms (e.g. "Use the terms 'EMF', 'internal resistance', 'lost volts'"), I have used all three.

If you can tick all 8 boxes, your answer is almost certainly L3 (5–6 marks).

### 13. CP7 and CP8 — Core Practical Methods in WPH12 (Spec 72, 78)

#### Why This Section Is Separate from Sections 1 and 2

Sections 1 (Resistivity, Spec 71) and 2 (E.M.F. and Internal Resistance, Spec 77) cover the theory of these topics — the equations, the calculations, the explanations. This section covers the practical method spec points (72 and 78) — the apparatus, the procedure, the graph axes, the gradient interpretation, the error and improvement vocabulary. The two are tested with different command words ("Describe how to determine…" vs "Calculate…") and reward different skill sets. A student who can substitute into ρ = RA/l but cannot describe the method scores only half marks.

CP7 and CP8 themselves are formally assessed in WPH13 (Practical Skills). However, every WPH12 paper since 2019 tests the underlying practical techniques in written form. Across 13 papers (Jun 2019 – Jun 2025): CP7 first appeared as an explicitly-tagged spec point in Jan 2025 (Q13b) + Jun 2025 (Q11); CP8 first appeared in Jan 2025 (Q10, Q14a/b, Q16a/b) + Jun 2025 (Q14a/b, Q16a). Including all questions that test the underlying practical skills, the corpus contains 40 questions / 101 marks touching CP7 or CP8 method content.

Totals across 13 papers: 40 CP7/CP8 questions, 101 marks (9.7% of all 1040 WPH12 marks). Of these, 7 questions / 20 marks are direct practical-skill questions (instrument choice, circuit diagram, full procedure, or graphical-method description) that explicitly mirror CP7/CP8 as written in the spec.

#### Cross-Paper Patterns

Pattern 1 — CP8 is examined in EVERY paper; CP7 in 13/13. CP8 (spec 77 + 78) appears in every single WPH12 paper analysed — minimum 1 mark (MCQ), maximum 15 marks (Jan 2025). CP7 (spec 71 + 72) likewise appears in every paper. Students cannot avoid either practical in any sitting.

Pattern 2 — Mark allocation follows a 4-tier hierarchy:

Tier Marks per question Frequency Example

1-mark recall 1 Very common Jan 2025 Q16a (state e.m.f.), Jan 2025 Q10 (MCQ), Jun 2024 Q5 (MCQ), Jun 2024 Q14a(i) (state ρ)

2–3-mark calculation 2–3 Most common format Jan 2025 Q13b (3), Jun 2025 Q11 (3), Jan 2024 Q14c(i) (3)

4-mark explanation/deduction 4 Recurring Oct 2022 Q12b, Jan 2025 Q14b, Oct 2024 Q19e

5–6 mark multi-step deduction / QWC 5–6 Once per paper maximum Jun 2024 Q14d (5), Jan 2024 Q19c (5), Jan 2025 Q16b* (6 QWC)

Pattern 6 — The two universal errors that cost the most marks (8+ papers each):

1. Diameter vs radius in A = πr² (CP7) — Using A = πd² or πd²/4 incorrectly. The MS for Oct 2022 Q13b(i) explicitly states "do not award MP1 if diameter is used directly." Each instance costs 1 mark.

2. Sign error in r = |gradient| from V-I graph (CP8) — V = ε − Ir means gradient = −r. Students report r as a negative value or forget to negate the gradient. Costs 1 mark.

Pattern 7 — Recent trend (2024–2025): contextual / unfamiliar framing. Jan 2024 (solar cells + parallel cells power deduction), Jun 2024 (resistivity practical in sheet-sample format), Oct 2024 (strain gauge — stretched conductor, R ∝ l²), Jan 2025 (e-bike battery — internal resistance in real-world context), Jun 2025 (standard nichrome wire — returns to classic format). Students must be able to translate the abstract CP7/CP8 method to any physical scenario where (a) resistance depends on material/dimensions or (b) a source has internal resistance.

Pattern 8 — QWC questions touching CP7/CP8 are rare but high-value. Only 1 QWC question in 13 papers explicitly touches CP7/CP8 content: Jan 2025 Q16b* — 6 marks, LDR + internal resistance. Future QWC questions are highly likely to combine CP8 with a sensor-circuit topic in the same way (CP7 QWC variant not yet seen but predicted).

#### Predicted Question Patterns for Future Exams

Based on the 13-paper trend analysis (★★★ = very likely; ★★ = likely; ★ = possible):

1. (★★★) CP8 "Draw the circuit diagram" will return within 3 sittings. Last appearance Jan 2024 (Jun 2019, Oct 2022, Jan 2024 — average spacing ~2.5 years). Standard expected features: cell + ammeter in series + variable resistor/potential divider in series + voltmeter in parallel across cell ONLY + switch. Predicted: 2–3 marks, command word "Draw" or "Complete".

2. (★★★) CP7 "Describe how to determine resistivity" procedural question is overdue. Only twice (Oct 2019 Q15a/b combined 6 marks; Jun 2024 Q14a(ii) 4 marks), spacing ~5 years. Expected: 3 quantities + 3 instruments + graphical method alternative + ρ = RA/l; for non-wire samples, A = width × thickness. Predicted: 3–4 marks, command word "Describe".

3. (★★★) CP8 "Determine ε and r from V-I graph" remains the most common CP8 written question. 6/13 papers (~46%). May vary: standard V vs I; alternative R vs 1/I; possible new variant V vs R. Predicted: 3 marks, command word "Determine".

4. (★★) Cells in series/parallel: a 4–5 mark deduction is likely in 2025–2026. 3 appearances (Jun 2019 Q19c, Jun 2023 Q12b, Jan 2024 Q19c). New variant may ask about three or more cells in mixed series/parallel combinations. Predicted: 4–5 marks, command word "Deduce" or "Evaluate".

5. (★★) A CP7/CP8 QWC question is likely within 2 sittings. Jan 2025 Q16b* was the first. Likely variants: CP7 QWC (metal wire heating → lattice vibrations → R = ρl/A → circuit current); CP8 QWC (terminal p.d. as variable resistor changes from max to zero). Predicted: 6 marks (4 IC + 2 structure), command word "Explain".

6. (★★) A "show that" CP7 cross-sectional area question will return. Only Oct 2022 Q13b(i); MS is strict. Predicted: 2 marks, command word "Show that".

7. (★) A "deduce material from ρ table" CP7 question may return. Appeared in Jun 2019 Q11 (identify metal) and Jun 2022 Q13b(ii) (deduce temperature of tungsten filament). Predicted: 3 marks, command word "Deduce".

8. (★) An internal-resistance contextual question in a transport/electronics setting. Following Jan 2025's e-bike context, may test phone battery, EV battery, or lab power supply. Predicted: 3–4 marks, command word "Calculate" or "Explain".

#### Full-Mark Answer Templates (Common CP7/CP8 Question Types)

CP7 Type A — Calculate ρ from given l, d, V, I (3 marks): (1) Convert diameter to metres and calculate A = π(d/2)². (2) Use R = V/I (if V, I given), then substitute into ρ = RA/l. (3) State final value with units and appropriate significant figures.

CP7 Type B — "Show that" cross-sectional area from diameter (2 marks): (1) Use A = πr² (with r = d/2) — must halve diameter first. (2) Correct numerical answer within tolerance. Critical insight: MS does NOT award MP1 if A = πd² is used.

CP7 Type C — Describe the graphical method for determining ρ (3 marks): (1) State chosen axes and what is held constant (A constant for wire; l varied). (2) Identify what gradient equals in terms of ρ and A. (3) State ρ = gradient × A (or equivalent rearrangement). Acceptable axes: R vs l (gradient = ρ/A); R vs l/A (gradient = ρ); RA vs l (gradient = ρ); l vs R (gradient = A/ρ); RA vs 1/ρ (gradient = l); l/A vs R (gradient = 1/ρ); V vs Il (gradient = ρ/A).

CP7 Type D — Describe full procedure to determine resistivity (4 marks): (1) Measure length L with a metre rule. (2) Measure thickness/diameter with micrometer or vernier callipers — repeat at multiple positions and average. (3) Measure R using ohmmeter, OR measure V (voltmeter in parallel) and I (ammeter in series) and use R = V/I. (4) Use ρ = RA/l with appropriate area formula (A = πr² for wire; A = width × thickness for sheet).

CP7 Type E — Deduce material/temperature from a ρ table (3 marks): (1) Use R = V/I to find resistance. (2) Use R = ρl/A to find resistivity. (3) Compare calculated ρ to table values and identify material/temperature (with interpolation if needed).

CP8 Type A — Determine ε and r from a V-I graph (3 marks): (1) Read y-intercept (= ε). (2) Calculate gradient using two well-separated points on the line. (3) State r = |gradient| with units and significant figures.

CP8 Type B — Draw circuit diagram for ε/r investigation (2–3 marks): Required: (1) Cell/battery. (2) Ammeter in series. (3) Variable resistor (or potential divider) in series. (4) Voltmeter in parallel across cell ONLY. (5) Switch (optional but preferred).

CP8 Type C — Explain how ε and r are determined from V-I graph (4 marks): (1) Use conservation of energy (Kirchhoff's 2nd law) to obtain ε = V + Ir. (2) Rearrange to V = ε − Ir, compare with y = mx + c. (3) y-intercept = ε. (4) Gradient = −r (so r = |gradient|).

CP8 Type D — Calculate r from single V, I, R data (3 marks): (1) Use V = IR with V = terminal p.d. to find I. (2) Calculate "lost volts" = ε − V. (3) Use Vₗₒₛₜ = Ir to find r = Vₗₒₛₜ/I.

CP8 Type E — Cells in series vs parallel: power comparison (5 marks): (1) Series: εₜₒₜₐₗ = 2ε, rₜₒₜₐₗ = 2r. (2) Parallel: εₜₒₜₐₗ = ε (unchanged), rₜₒₜₐₗ = r/2. (3) Calculate both powers using P = I²R. (4) Calculate ratio. (5) State clear judgement.

CP8 Type F — Explain why a real-world battery gets hot (4 marks): (1) Stimulus: more power required. (2) P = IV → I increases. (3) Vᵢₙₜₑᵣₙₐₗ = Ir increases. (4) Pᵢₙₜₑᵣₙₐₗ = I²r increases → battery gets hot.

CP8 Type G — QWC: LDR + terminal p.d. causal chain (6 marks): IC1: more photons per second on LDR. IC2: more conduction electrons released. IC3: R_LDR decreases. IC4: r (internal) is constant. IC5: total R decreases → I increases. IC6: lost volts Ir increases → terminal p.d. V = ε − Ir decreases → voltmeter reading decreases. Use connectives ("because", "so", "therefore") to link all six points.

#### Quick-Reference Revision Checklist

CP7 — Resistivity Practical:

Memorise ρ = RA/l and rearrangements R = ρl/A, A = ρl/R, l = RA/ρ

Know area formulas: A = πr² = πd²/4 for wires; A = width × thickness for sheets/foils

Know the 3 instruments: metre rule (length), micrometer or vernier callipers (diameter/thickness), ohmmeter OR ammeter+voltmeter (resistance)

Know 3 valid graphical methods: R vs l (gradient = ρ/A), R vs l/A (gradient = ρ), RA vs l (gradient = ρ)

Know typical ρ values: copper 1.7 × 10⁻⁸, nichrome 1.1 × 10⁻⁶, tungsten (hot) ~10⁻⁷, semiconductors ~10⁻³ to 10³ Ω m

Practise mm → m (×10⁻³), mm² → m² (×10⁻⁶), mΩ → Ω (×10⁻³) conversions

Always halve diameter before squaring (or use A = πd²/4)

For inverted direction (find d from ρ, R, l): use d = 2√(A/π) — remember the factor of 2

For uncertainty: %unc(ρ) = %unc(R) + 2 × %unc(d) + %unc(l) — remember to double the diameter term

CP8 — E.M.F. and Internal Resistance Practical:

Memorise ε = V + Ir and rearrangements V = ε − Ir, r = (ε − V)/I, r = Rₑₓₜ × (ε − V)/V

Know the standard circuit: cell + ammeter (series) + variable resistor (series) + voltmeter (parallel across cell) + switch

V = ε − Ir in y = mx + c form: y-intercept = ε, gradient = −r (so r = |gradient|)

Alternative graph: R vs 1/I gives gradient = ε, intercept = −r (negative; r = |intercept|)

Practise "lost volts" = ε − V; do NOT use ε in V = IR for the external circuit

Cells combine: series → εₜₒₜₐₗ = Nε, rₜₒₜₐₗ = Nr; parallel (identical) → εₜₒₜₐₗ = ε, rₜₒₜₐₗ = r/N

Maximum current = ε/r (when Rₑₓₜₑᵣₙₐₗ → 0, short circuit)

For QWC: always use connectives and follow the chain stimulus → mechanism → electrical consequence → result

Power dissipated in internal resistance: Pᵢₙₜ = I²r (NOT I²R — MS forbids R for Jan 2023 Q17c)

### §6.1 — Enthalpy Change and Standard Conditions

Q1 QFR §6.1 1 mark · ~2 min

State the standard conditions used for enthalpy changes.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

298 K (or 25 °C) and 100 kPa.

Why this scores full marks

The mark scheme accepts "298 K and 100 kPa" in either order. Writing "25 °C" instead of "298 K" is also accepted. However, "room temperature" alone, "298°K" (incorrect unit notation), "1 atm", "normal conditions", or "STP" would all be rejected — the exact values 298 K and 100 kPa are required.

Q2 QFR §6.1 1 mark · ~2 min

Define the term enthalpy change (ΔH).

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The heat energy change at constant pressure. It is the difference between the enthalpy of the products and the enthalpy of the reactants.

Why this scores full marks

Both parts are required for full marks: (1) "heat energy change at constant pressure" and (2) the description as "the difference between the enthalpy of the products and the enthalpy of the reactants." A student who only writes "energy change" without specifying "at constant pressure" would not score.

Q3 TDC §6.1 1 mark · ~2 min

A student is asked to identify the standard state of bromine at 298 K and 100 kPa. They write Br₂(g). Explain why this is incorrect and state the correct standard state.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Bromine is a liquid at 298 K and 100 kPa, so its correct standard state is Br₂(l), not Br₂(g).

Why this scores full marks

The mark scheme explicitly lists Br₂(l) as an example of a standard state. A common error is assuming all diatomic elements are gases — bromine is a liquid under standard conditions. The student must give the correct physical state with the correct state symbol.

Q4 TDC §6.1 1 mark · ~2 min

Which equation correctly represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of Al₂O₃? A. 4Al(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Al₂O₃(s) B. 2Al(g) + 1½O(g) → Al₂O₃(s) C. 2Al(s) + 1½O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(s) D. 2Al(s) + 1½O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(l)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

C. 2Al(s) + 1½O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(s)

Why this scores full marks

The correct answer must satisfy three requirements simultaneously: (1) exactly 1 mol of product formed — option A forms 2 mol Al₂O₃ so is wrong; (2) elements in their standard states — option B uses Al(g) and O(g) instead of Al(s) and O₂(g); (3) correct state symbols for the product — option D has Al₂O₃(l) instead of Al₂O₃(s). Fractional coefficients (1½) are accepted in formation equations.

Q5 TDC §6.1 2 marks · ~4 min

Which one of the following equations correctly represents the standard enthalpy of formation of copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃? A. 2Cu(s) + 2C(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2CuCO₃(s) B. Cu(s) + C(s) + ³⁄₂O₂(g) → CuCO₃(s) C. Cu(s) + C(s) + ³⁄₂O(g) → CuCO₃(s) D. Cu(s) + C(s) + O₃(g) → CuCO₃(s)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

B. Cu(s) + C(s) + ³⁄₂O₂(g) → CuCO₃(s)

Why this scores full marks

This is worth 2 marks: (1 mark) for identifying option B; (1 mark) for the justification. Option B is the only equation where all reactants are elements in their standard states (Cu, C, and O₂), exactly 1 mol of compound product is formed, and the equation is balanced. Option A forms 2 mol of product — standard enthalpy of formation is always per mole of product. Option C uses O(g) instead of O₂(g) — oxygen's standard state is O₂(g), not O(g). Option D uses O₃(g) which is not the standard state of oxygen.

Q6 STE §6.1 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes the following equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol (C₂H₅OH): 2C(g) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l) Identify the error and write the corrected equation. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The student has written C(g) instead of the correct standard state of carbon. The standard state of carbon is C(s) (solid graphite), not C(g). The corrected equation is: 2C(s) + 3H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → C₂H₅OH(l)

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1 is for identifying the error: carbon must be in its standard state C(s), not C(g). This mirrors the trap highlighted where O₂(g) not O(g) is required — the same principle applies to all elements. Mark 2 is for writing the corrected equation with the proper standard state. Using atoms instead of elements in their standard states scores zero.

Q7 SYN §6.1 5 marks · ~10 min

An exam question asks a student to write the equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of nitrogen monoxide, NO(g). The student's working is shown below: Step 1: "Standard conditions are room temperature and 1 atm." Step 2: "The equation is: N(g) + O(g) → NO(g)" The examiner awards 0 marks. (a) State the correct standard conditions. (1 mark) (b) Identify two errors in the student's equation and explain why each loses a mark. (2 marks) (c) Write the correct equation for the standard enthalpy change of formation of NO(g). (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) 298 K (or 25 °C) and 100 kPa. (b) Error 1: N(g) is incorrect — nitrogen's standard state is N₂(g), not N(g). Elements must be in their standard states for a formation equation. Error 2: O(g) is incorrect — oxygen's standard state is O₂(g), not O(g). Additionally, the equation is unbalanced as written. (c) ½N₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → NO(g)

Why this scores full marks

Part (a): 1 mark for stating 298 K and 100 kPa — "room temperature" and "1 atm" are both rejected. Part (b): 2 marks — 1 mark for identifying N(g) should be N₂(g) (elemental nitrogen is diatomic) and 1 mark for identifying O(g) should be O₂(g) (elemental oxygen is diatomic). Part (c): 2 marks — 1 mark for correct reactants as elements in standard states with state symbols, 1 mark for correctly balanced equation forming exactly 1 mol of NO(g). Fractional coefficients are accepted.

### §6.2 — Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions

Q8 QFR §6.2 1 mark · ~2 min

Define an exothermic reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A reaction in which heat energy is transferred to the surroundings (ΔH is negative).

Why this scores full marks

The key phrase required by the mark scheme is "heat energy is transferred to the surroundings" (or "heat energy is given out to the surroundings" / "heat is released to the surroundings"). Mentioning that ΔH is negative earns credit if the definition is incomplete, but is not a substitute for the core definition. Simply stating "ΔH is negative" without the heat transfer description is unlikely to score full marks.

Q9 TDC §6.2 1 mark · ~2 min

Which of the following processes is exothermic? A. Cl₂(g) → 2Cl(g) B. Cl(g) → Cl⁺(g) + e⁻ C. 2Cl(g) → Cl₂(g) D. Cl₂(g) → 2Cl⁺(g) + 2e⁻

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

C. 2Cl(g) → Cl₂(g)

Why this scores full marks

Option C is the only exothermic process because it involves bond formation. When a Cl–Cl bond forms, energy is released to the surroundings. Options A, B, and D are all endothermic: A involves bond breaking, B involves ionisation energy (removing an electron), and D involves both bond breaking and ionisation — all of which require energy input.

Q10 EXP §6.2 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain, in terms of bonds, why bond formation is always exothermic.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

During bond formation, attractive electrostatic forces are established between atoms, and energy is released as the new bond is formed. The bonded state has lower potential energy than the separated atoms, so the excess energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1 is awarded for the idea that new bonds/forming bonds release energy (or that the bonded state is more stable/lower in energy). Mark 2 is awarded for the explanation in terms of electrostatic attraction being established (or that energy is transferred to the surroundings). Simply stating "bond forming is exothermic" without explanation would score zero. The key is explaining WHY — the electrostatic attraction between nuclei and shared electrons lowers the energy of the system.

### §6.3 — Enthalpy Level Diagrams

Q11 QFR §6.3 1 mark · ~2 min

State the label that must be used for the vertical axis of an enthalpy level diagram in an Edexcel IAL Chemistry exam.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

enthalpy

Why this scores full marks

The mark scheme for Jun 2022 Q18(a)(iii) explicitly penalised any label other than "enthalpy". Answers of "energy", "energy change", "ΔH", or "heat energy" all score zero. The single word "enthalpy" (case-insensitive) is the only acceptable label.

Q12 TDC §6.3 2 marks · ~4 min

Distinguish between an enthalpy level diagram and a reaction profile. State one key feature that is present on a reaction profile but must NOT be drawn on an enthalpy level diagram.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

An enthalpy level diagram shows only the start and end enthalpy as two horizontal lines with a single arrow between them. A reaction profile shows the full energy pathway from reactants to products, including the activation energy "hump" and possibly an intermediate. The activation energy hump must NOT be drawn on an enthalpy level diagram unless the question specifically asks for a reaction profile or activation energy diagram.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1 is awarded for correctly describing the difference: enthalpy level diagrams show only start and end points (two lines, one arrow) whereas reaction profiles show the full pathway with energy barriers. Mark 2 is awarded for identifying activation energy as the feature that must not appear on an enthalpy level diagram.

Q13 WTE §6.3 3 marks · ~6 min

Describe, in detail, the enthalpy level diagram you would draw for the complete combustion of octane, C₈H₁₈(l), given that ΔH꜀ = −5461 kJ mol⁻¹.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A vertical y-axis is drawn and labelled "enthalpy". A horizontal line is drawn near the top of the diagram, labelled "Reactants: C₈H₁₈(l) + 12½O₂(g)". A second horizontal line is drawn significantly lower than the reactants line (because the reaction is highly exothermic), labelled "Products: 8CO₂(g) + 9H₂O(l)". A single-headed vertical arrow is drawn from the reactants line down to the products line, and this arrow is labelled "ΔH꜀ = −5461 kJ mol⁻¹". No activation energy hump is drawn.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Y-axis correctly labelled "enthalpy" (not "energy" or "ΔH"). Mark 2: Reactants line above products line (exothermic reaction), both correctly labelled with species and state symbols. Mark 3: Single-headed arrow from reactants to products correctly labelled with the appropriate subscript ΔH꜀ and the negative value.

Q14 TDC §6.3 2 marks · ~4 min

A student draws an enthalpy level diagram for the complete combustion of methane, ΔH꜀ = −890 kJ mol⁻¹. Which of the following descriptions of the arrow on the diagram is correct? A. A double-headed vertical arrow pointing from products to reactants, labelled −ΔH B. A single-headed vertical arrow pointing from reactants down to products, labelled ΔH꜀ = −890 kJ mol⁻¹ C. A single-headed vertical arrow pointing from products up to reactants, labelled ΔH꜀ = +890 kJ mol⁻¹ D. A double-headed vertical arrow between reactants and products, labelled −ΔH꜀ = −890 kJ mol⁻¹

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

B. A single-headed vertical arrow pointing from reactants down to products, labelled ΔH꜀ = −890 kJ mol⁻¹

Why this scores full marks

Two discriminations are tested here. First, the arrow must be single-headed — a double-headed arrow (A and D) scores zero. Second, the arrow goes from reactants to products and is labelled ΔH with its actual negative value — it is NOT labelled "−ΔH" (a double-negative). Option C reverses the direction. Only B satisfies both the single-headed requirement and correct direction/label.

Q15 STE §6.3 3 marks · ~6 min

A student draws the following description of their enthalpy level diagram for the combustion of propane (ΔH꜀ = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹): "I drew a y-axis labelled 'energy change'. The products line was drawn above the reactants line. I used a double-headed arrow between the two lines and labelled it '−ΔH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹'." Identify three errors in the student's diagram. (3 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1. The y-axis is labelled "energy change" — it must be labelled "enthalpy".

2. The products line is above the reactants line — for an exothermic combustion reaction, the products line must be below the reactants line.

3. A double-headed arrow is used — the arrow must be single-headed, going from reactants to products. (Alternatively: the arrow is labelled "−ΔH" — this is a double-negative; it should be labelled "ΔH꜀ = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹".)

Why this scores full marks

Each error identified scores 1 mark. Error 1 targets the mandatory "enthalpy" y-axis label (penalised in Jun 2022 Q18(a)(iii)). Error 2 tests that exothermic reactions have products below reactants. Error 3 tests either the single-headed arrow rule or the "−ΔH" double-negative pitfall — both are valid marks. A student giving any three distinct errors scores full marks.

Q16 EXP §6.3 2 marks · ~4 min

A reaction proceeds via an intermediate. On the enthalpy level diagram, the intermediate has its own horizontal line between the reactants and products. Explain why the overall ΔH arrow must go from the reactant level to the product level, and NOT from the reactant level to the intermediate level.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The overall enthalpy change, ΔH, is defined as the difference in enthalpy between the final products and the initial reactants. The intermediate is a transient species that is neither a starting material nor a final product of the overall reaction. Therefore, the ΔH arrow must span from the initial reactant level to the final product level, representing the net enthalpy change for the overall reaction.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Stating that ΔH is defined between final products and initial reactants (not between reactants and intermediate). Mark 2: Explaining that the intermediate is not a starting material or final product of the overall reaction, so it is not part of the overall enthalpy change.

Q17 STE §6.3 2 marks · ~4 min

A student examining a reaction profile diagram states: "The activation energy of this reaction is the same as the enthalpy change, ΔH." Explain why this statement is incorrect.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy required for reactants to react, represented by the height of the energy barrier (the "hump" on the reaction profile) above the reactant level. The enthalpy change (ΔH) is the overall difference in enthalpy between the products and the reactants, represented by the difference in the horizontal levels. These are different features of the diagram and are not the same quantity.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1 is for correctly describing what activation energy represents (energy barrier / minimum energy for reaction / the peak of the curve). Mark 2 is for correctly describing what ΔH represents (overall level difference between reactants and products). The student's error is a fundamental confusion between the vertical "hump" (Eₐ) and the horizontal level change (ΔH).

### §6.4(i) — Standard Enthalpy Change of Reaction, ΔH°r

Q18 EXP §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

The standard enthalpy change of reaction for the equation 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) is −572 kJ mol⁻¹, whereas the standard enthalpy change of reaction for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) is −286 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain why the two values are different even though both equations describe the same reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The value of ΔH°r depends on the stoichiometry of the equation as written. The first equation shows the formation of 2 moles of water, so its enthalpy change is twice the value for the formation of 1 mole of water shown in the second equation. This is because enthalpy is an extensive property — it is proportional to the amount of substance reacting.

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for stating that ΔH°r depends on the stoichiometric quantities in the equation. M2 is awarded for explaining the mathematical relationship (the first equation produces twice as much water, so the enthalpy change is doubled). A student who believes both equations should give the same ΔH°r has not understood that the "per mol" in ΔH°r refers to the molar quantities as written in the specific equation, not per mole of a particular substance.

Q19 DIA §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

The enthalpy level diagram below shows a two-step reaction A → C that proceeds through an intermediate B: - Level of A (reactants): −50 kJ mol⁻¹ - Level of B (intermediate): −180 kJ mol⁻¹ - Level of C (products): −320 kJ mol⁻¹ Arrow X points from level A down to level C (bypassing B). Arrow Y points from level A down to level B. Arrow Z points from level B down to level C. A student is asked to label the overall ΔH for the reaction A → C. Which arrow (X, Y, or Z) should they use, and what value should they write? Explain your reasoning. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The student should use Arrow X and label it ΔH = −270 kJ mol⁻¹. The overall ΔH for a reaction spans from the initial reactant level to the final product level, passing through (but not ending at) any intermediate. ΔH = final enthalpy − initial enthalpy = (−320) − (−50) = −270 kJ mol⁻¹. Arrow Y (−130 kJ mol⁻¹) represents only the first step (A → B), and Arrow Z (−140 kJ mol⁻¹) represents only the second step (B → C). The overall ΔH must connect reactants directly to products, consistent with Hess's Law.

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for selecting Arrow X and explaining that the overall ΔH arrow spans from reactants to products (not ending at the intermediate). M2 is awarded for the correct calculation: (−320) − (−50) = −270 kJ mol⁻¹.

### §6.4(ii) — Standard Enthalpy Change of Formation, ΔH°f

Q20 QFR §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

State the meaning of the term standard enthalpy change of formation.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K).

Why this scores full marks

This hits both mandatory marking points from the Jun 2024 / Jan 2024 mark scheme. M1 is awarded for "1 mol" or "one mole" of the compound formed — omitting this loses this mark. M2 is awarded for "elements in standard states" — writing "from its constituent elements" alone is NOT sufficient; the phrase "standard states" must appear.

Q21 TDC §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes the following definition: "The enthalpy change when a compound is formed from its constituent elements at room temperature and 1 atm." This answer scores zero marks. Which two of the following corrections, if applied, would each independently recover one mark? A. Change "a compound" to "1 mole of a compound" B. Change "1 atm" to "100 kPa" C. Add the phrase "in their standard states" after "constituent elements" D. Change "room temperature" to "298 K"

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A and C.

Why this scores full marks

From the Jan 2024 MS, the two mark points are: (1) "1 mol" / "one mole" of compound, and (2) "elements in standard states". Correction A restores the "1 mole" requirement (M1). Correction C restores the "elements in standard states" requirement (M2). While corrections B and D would make the definition more accurate regarding standard conditions, the mark scheme does not award separate marks for stating "100 kPa" and "298 K" in a definition question — those are covered by the umbrella term "standard conditions".

Q22 WTE §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

Write a balanced equation, including state symbols, for the standard enthalpy change of formation of liquid methanol, CH₃OH.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

C(s) + 2H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → CH₃OH(l)

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for the correct balanced equation with elements as reactants. Carbon must be C(s) (solid, its standard state), hydrogen must be H₂(g) (not H(g)), and oxygen must be O₂(g) (not O(g)). M2 is awarded for correct state symbols throughout. Fractional coefficients (½O₂) are required and acceptable. The product must be 1 mole of CH₃OH.

### §6.4(iii) — Standard Enthalpy Change of Combustion, ΔH°c

Q23 QFR §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

State the meaning of the term standard enthalpy change of combustion.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance reacts completely with oxygen under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K), with all reactants and products in their standard states.

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for "1 mole of substance". M2 is awarded for "reacts completely with oxygen" (or "complete combustion"). Both elements must be present. A common error is omitting "completely" or "1 mole" — both cost marks.

Q24 WTE §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

Write a balanced equation, including state symbols, for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

C₃H₇OH(l) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for the correctly balanced equation. Propan-1-ol contains 3 C and 8 H (C₃H₈O), so complete combustion requires 4½ O₂ (to give 3CO₂ + 4H₂O). M2 is awarded for correct state symbols: the alcohol is a liquid (l), O₂ and CO₂ are gases (g), and water is produced as a liquid (l) under standard conditions.

Q25 STE §6.4 3 marks · ~6 min

A student is calculating the energy released when 2.00 g of 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (Mᵣ = 114) is combusted, given ΔH°c = −5470 kJ mol⁻¹. They write: "Energy = 2.00 × 5470 = 10 940 kJ" Identify two errors in the student's working and calculate the correct value. (3 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Error 1: The student has not converted mass to moles. Moles = mass / Mᵣ = 2.00 / 114 = 0.01754 mol. Error 2: The student has used a positive value (5470 kJ mol⁻¹) instead of the correct negative value (−5470 kJ mol⁻¹), losing the exothermic sign convention. Correct calculation: - n = 2.00 / 114 = 0.01754 mol - Energy released = 0.01754 × 5470 = 95.9 kJ (the negative sign indicates energy is released, so the magnitude of energy released is 95.9 kJ)

Why this scores full marks

M1 for identifying the missing mole conversion (dividing mass by Mᵣ).

M2 for identifying the sign error — using +5470 instead of −5470.

M3 for the correct calculation: (2.00/114) × 5470 = 95.9 kJ.

### §6.4(iv) — Standard Enthalpy Change of Neutralisation, ΔH°neut

Q26 QFR §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

Define the standard enthalpy change of neutralisation, ΔH°neut.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The enthalpy change when 1 mole of water is formed from the reaction between an acid and an alkali under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K), with all solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³.

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for specifying the enthalpy/heat energy change under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

M2 is awarded for stating the change is per mole of water formed — writing "per mole of acid" or "per mole of alkali" would score zero for this mark.

Q27 WTE §6.4 1 mark · ~2 min

Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) (Alternative acceptable: H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l))

Why this scores full marks

The net ionic equation for any strong acid–strong base neutralisation is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. This strips away the spectator ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻) and shows the essential reaction that defines ΔH°neut.

Q28 TDC §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes the following definition in an exam: "The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of acid reacts with 1 mole of alkali under standard conditions." Explain why this definition would not score full marks. State what is missing or incorrect. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The definition is incorrect because it defines the change per mole of acid/alkali rather than per mole of water formed. The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation must be defined as the enthalpy change when 1 mole of water is formed from the reaction of an acid and an alkali. The student's version would give different values for reactions involving different stoichiometries (e.g., H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH produces 2 mol H₂O, so ΔH per mole of acid would differ from ΔH per mole of water).

Why this scores full marks

M1 for identifying the error: must be "per mole of water formed", not per mole of acid or alkali.

M2 for explaining why this matters (different stoichiometries produce different amounts of water per mole of acid).

Q29 EXP §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation for HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) is −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹. The standard enthalpy change of neutralisation for HNO₃(aq) + KOH(aq) is also −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain why these two different reactions have the same ΔH°neut value. Your answer should refer to the ionic equation. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Both reactions involve strong acids and strong alkalis that are fully dissociated in solution. In each case, the only reaction that actually occurs is the same net ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) The Na⁺, Cl⁻, K⁺, and NO₃⁻ ions are all spectator ions. Since the same ionic reaction occurs in both cases (forming 1 mole of water from H⁺ and OH⁻), the enthalpy change per mole of water formed is identical.

Why this scores full marks

M1 for stating that both reactions involve fully dissociated strong acids and strong alkalis, so the net ionic equation is the same: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

M2 for explaining that the spectator ions do not take part in the reaction, so the enthalpy change depends only on the formation of 1 mole of water from H⁺ and OH⁻.

### §6.4(v) — Standard Enthalpy Change of Atomisation, ΔH°at

Q30 QFR §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

Define the standard enthalpy change of atomisation, ΔH°at.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms is formed from an element in its standard state under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K).

Why this scores full marks

M1 is awarded for "1 mole of gaseous atoms" — the product must be a gaseous atom, not a molecule or atom in another state.

M2 is awarded for specifying the element starts in its standard state — this is the state at 100 kPa, 298 K (e.g., Br₂(l) not Br₂(g) for bromine).

Q31 TDC §6.4 3 marks · ~6 min

A student is asked to select the equation that represents the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of bromine. Four equations are proposed: - A: Br₂(l) → 2Br(g) ΔH = +193 kJ mol⁻¹ - B: ½Br₂(l) → Br(g) ΔH = +96.5 kJ mol⁻¹ - C: ½Br₂(g) → Br(g) ΔH = +111.9 kJ mol⁻¹ - D: Br₂(g) → 2Br(g) ΔH = +193 kJ mol⁻¹ Which equation is correct? Explain why each of the other three is wrong. (3 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Correct answer: B — ½Br₂(l) → Br(g). - A is wrong because it produces 2 moles of gaseous atoms; the definition requires exactly 1 mole of gaseous atoms. - C is wrong because bromine's standard state is Br₂(l) (liquid at 298 K), not Br₂(g). The starting state must be the standard state. - D is wrong for two reasons: it starts from Br₂(g) (not the standard state Br₂(l)) and produces 2 moles of gaseous atoms (not 1 mole).

Why this scores full marks

M1 for identifying B as correct, with reasoning (1 mol gaseous atoms from standard state).

M2 for explaining A's error (2 mol, not 1 mol).

M3 for explaining C's error (wrong standard state — Br₂(g) instead of Br₂(l)).

Q32 WTE §6.4 2 marks · ~4 min

A student is asked to write an equation representing the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of the element phosphorus. Phosphorus exists as P₄(s) in its standard state. Write the correct equation. State symbols are required. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

¼P₄(s) → P(g)

Why this scores full marks

M1 for starting with phosphorus in its standard state: P₄(s) — not P(s) and not P₄(g).

M2 for producing exactly 1 mole of gaseous atoms: P(g), using the fraction ¼ to ensure only 1 mole of P(g) is produced.

### §6.5 — Calorimetry (q = mcΔT, ΔH = −q/n)

Q33 QFR §6.5 1 mark · ~2 min

State the value of the specific heat capacity of water, including its correct units.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (or 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)

Why this scores full marks

The mark scheme requires the numerical value (4.18) AND correct units. Either J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ or J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ is accepted since a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K. Writing "4.18 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹" would score zero — the per-gram unit is mandatory at this level.

Q34 TDC §6.5 1 mark · ~2 min

A student burns 0.250 g of methanol to heat 150.0 g of water in a calorimeter. Which value of m must be used in the calculation q = mcΔT? A. 0.250 g B. 150.0 g C. 150.250 g D. 75.0 g (1 mark)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

B. 150.0 g

Why this scores full marks

The calorimeter measures the heat absorbed by the water/solution being heated, not the mass of the fuel being burned. The mark scheme explicitly states: "Always use the mass of the solution being heated, NOT the mass of the solid or fuel being reacted/burned." Option C (adding both masses) is a common pitfall that the mark scheme specifically rejects.

Q35 CAL §6.5 4 marks · ~8 min

A student dissolves 4.25 g of NH₄NO₃(s) in 75.0 cm³ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature of the solution decreases by 5.40 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of NH₄NO₃. [Mᵣ of NH₄NO₃ = 80.0; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; assume the density of the solution is 1.00 g cm⁻³]

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Step 1 — Energy absorbed by the solution: q = mcΔT = 75.0 × 4.18 × 5.40 = 1691 J = 1.691 kJ Step 2 — Moles of NH₄NO₃: n = m / Mᵣ = 4.25 / 80.0 = 0.0531 mol Step 3 — Enthalpy change of solution: ΔH = +q / n = +1.691 / 0.0531 = +31.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (to 3 significant figures) (The positive sign is required because the temperature decrease indicates an endothermic process.)

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Correctly uses mass of solution (75.0 g) in q = mcΔT, not the mass of the solid. Mark 2: Correct calculation of q with correct units (J). Mark 3: Correct calculation of moles of NH₄NO₃. Mark 4: Correct ΔH = +q/n with positive sign (endothermic), conversion to kJ mol⁻¹, and appropriate significant figures.

Q36 CAL §6.5 4 marks · ~8 min

In a calorimetry experiment, 0.305 g of ethanol (Mᵣ = 46.0) was burned and used to heat 100.0 g of water. The temperature of the water increased by 13.2 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol. Give your answer in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures. (4 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Step Calculation

Energy transferred to water q = m × c × ΔT = 100.0 × 4.18 × 13.2 = 5517.6 J

Moles of ethanol burned n = m / Mᵣ = 0.305 / 46.0 = 0.00663 mol

Enthalpy change per mole ΔH = −q / n = −5517.6 / 0.00663 = −831,780 J mol⁻¹

Convert to kJ mol⁻¹ −832 kJ mol⁻¹ (3 SF)

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Correct substitution into q = mcΔT with correct values (100.0 g, 4.18, 13.2) — using only the water mass, NOT adding the ethanol mass.

Mark 2: Correct calculation of moles of ethanol (0.305 / 46.0 = 0.00663 mol).

Mark 3: Division of q by moles (energy per mole of ethanol).

Mark 4: Correct final answer with negative sign (exothermic), correct units (kJ mol⁻¹), and 3 significant figures.

Q37 CAL §6.5 5 marks · ~10 min

A thermometric titration was carried out by adding HCl(aq) from a burette to 30.0 cm³ of 1.30 mol dm⁻³ ammonia solution, NH₃(aq). The maximum temperature reached was 27.6 °C and the initial temperature was 20.7 °C. The end-point of the titration occurred at 21.0 cm³ of HCl(aq) added. Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation for this reaction. Give your answer in kJ mol⁻¹. (5 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Step Calculation

Total mass of solution m = 30.0 + 21.0 = 51.0 g (assume density = 1.00 g cm⁻³)

Temperature change ΔT = 27.6 − 20.7 = 6.9 °C

Energy transferred q = m × c × ΔT = 51.0 × 4.18 × 6.9 = 1471 J

Moles of NH₃ neutralised at end-point n(NH₃) = c × V(NH₃) = 1.30 × 30.0 / 1000 = 0.0390 mol (the 1.30 M concentration refers to the NH₃ analyte, not the HCl titrant; 21.0 cm³ is the volume of HCl added, not NH₃)

Enthalpy change of neutralisation ΔH = −q / n = −1471 / 0.0390 = −37.7 kJ mol⁻¹

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Correct total mass of solution (51.0 g) by adding both volumes.

Mark 2: Correct ΔT = 6.9 °C.

Mark 3: Correct q = 51.0 × 4.18 × 6.9 = 1471 J.

Mark 4: Correct moles calculation: the 1.30 mol dm⁻³ is the NH₃ concentration in the 30.0 cm³ analyte, so n(NH₃) = 1.30 × 30.0/1000 = 0.0390 mol (NOT 1.30 × 21.0/1000 — that would be moles of HCl only if HCl were also 1.30 M, which the question does not state).

Mark 5: Correct ΔH = −37.7 kJ mol⁻¹ with negative sign and appropriate significant figures. (Note: this weak-base/strong-acid neutralisation is less exothermic than the strong-acid/strong-base data book value of ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹ because NH₃ is only partially dissociated; also no water is formed, the product is NH₄⁺(aq).)

Q38 STE §6.5 2 marks · ~4 min

A student carries out a calorimetry experiment and obtains q = 5518 J for the energy transferred to the water during combustion of ethanol. The student then writes: > ΔH = +5518 / 0.00663 = +832 kJ mol⁻¹ Identify two errors in the student's working. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1. The sign is wrong. Combustion is exothermic, so ΔH must be negative (−832 kJ mol⁻¹), not positive. The formula is ΔH = −q / n.

2. The units are inconsistent / not converted. q is in joules (5518 J) but the final answer is stated in kJ mol⁻¹. The student should convert: 5518 J = 5.518 kJ, then ΔH = −5.518 / 0.00663 = −832 kJ mol⁻¹.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Identifying the incorrect sign — combustion is always exothermic (ΔH < 0).

Mark 2: Identifying the unit inconsistency. The J → kJ conversion step must be shown.

Q39 EXP §6.5 2 marks · ~4 min

A student determines the enthalpy change of neutralisation using a thermometric titration with an aqueous acid solution. The specific heat capacity of the acid solution is 3.85 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, but the student uses 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (the value for water) in their calculation of q = mcΔT. Explain whether this error causes the calculated ΔH value to be more exothermic or less exothermic than the true value. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Using a specific heat capacity value that is too high (4.18 instead of 3.85) means the calculated value of q = mcΔT will be too large (overestimated). Since ΔH = −q/n, a larger q gives a more negative ΔH value. Therefore, the calculated ΔH will be more exothermic (more negative) than the true value.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Correctly states that q will be overestimated / too large because c is in the numerator of q = mcΔT and a larger c increases the calculated energy transfer.

Mark 2: Correctly links the overestimated q to the ΔH calculation — since ΔH = −q/n, a larger q gives a more negative (more exothermic) ΔH.

Q40 EXP §6.5 3 marks · ~6 min

In a thermometric titration, the temperature of the reaction mixture does not reach its true maximum value at any point during the experiment. Explain why, and describe how extrapolation of the graph corrects for this.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Heat is continuously lost to the surroundings throughout the experiment. This means the measured temperature at every point is lower than it would be in a perfectly insulated system. The true maximum temperature (and true ΔT) was never actually recorded. By drawing two lines of best fit (before and after the end-point) and extrapolating both back to the time of mixing, the graph method estimates what the temperature change would have been if no heat loss had occurred. The difference between the extrapolated lines at the mixing point gives the true ΔT.

Why this scores full marks

Mark 1: Identifies the cause — continuous heat loss to the surroundings during the experiment. Mark 2: Explains the consequence — the recorded temperatures are lower than the true values. Mark 3: Explains how extrapolation corrects this — by extending both lines of best fit back to the time of mixing, the true ΔT (without heat loss) is estimated.

Q41 SYN §6.5 11 marks · ~22 min

A student uses a simple calorimeter to determine the enthalpy change of combustion of methanol, CH₃OH. The following results were obtained: | Measurement | Value | |---|---| | Mass of water in calorimeter | 150.0 g | | Initial temperature of water | 19.5 °C | | Maximum temperature of water | 34.8 °C | | Mass of methanol burner before combustion | 85.42 g | | Mass of methanol burner after combustion | 84.86 g | | Temperature readings measured to ±0.5 °C | | | Mass readings measured to ±0.01 g | | (a) Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of methanol. Give your answer in kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures. (4 marks) (b) The accepted literature value for the enthalpy change of combustion of methanol is −726 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage difference between the experimental and literature values. (1 mark) (c) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change measurement. (2 marks) (d) State two reasons, other than random measurement uncertainty, why the experimental value is less exothermic than the literature value. For each reason, explain how it causes the experimental ΔH to be less exothermic. (4 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Enthalpy change of combustion (4 marks): | Step | Calculation | |------|------------| | Mass of methanol burned | 85.42 − 84.86 = 0.56 g | | Temperature change | ΔT = 34.8 − 19.5 = 15.3 °C | | Energy transferred | q = m × c × ΔT = 150.0 × 4.18 × 15.3 = 9593.1 J = 9.593 kJ | | Moles of methanol | n = 0.56 / 32.0 = 0.01750 mol | | ΔH combustion | ΔH = −q / n = −9.593 / 0.01750 = −548 kJ mol⁻¹ (3 SF) | (b) Percentage difference (1 mark): Percentage difference = |−548 − (−726)| / 726 × 100 = 178 / 726 × 100 = 24.5% (c) Percentage uncertainty in ΔT (2 marks): The temperature change is calculated from two readings: ΔT = Tfᵢₙₐₗ − Tᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ. Each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C, so the absolute uncertainty in ΔT = 0.5 + 0.5 = ±1.0 °C. Percentage uncertainty in ΔT = (1.0 / 15.3) × 100 = 6.54% (d) Two reasons for the experimental value being less exothermic (4 marks): 1. Heat loss to the surroundings. Not all the heat released by combustion is transferred to the water — some is lost to the calorimeter, the air, and the apparatus. This means the measured temperature rise (and therefore q) is smaller than it should be, making the calculated |ΔH| smaller (less exothermic). 2. Incomplete combustion. Methanol may not burn completely, producing carbon monoxide or carbon (soot) instead of only CO₂ and H₂O. Incomplete combustion releases less energy per mole of fuel than complete combustion, so the measured ΔH is less exothermic than the literature value. (Other acceptable: evaporation of methanol from the wick before/during combustion reducing the measured mass loss.)

Why this scores full marks

Part (a) — 4 marks: (1) Correct mass of methanol burned. (2) Correct ΔT. (3) Correct q using ONLY the water mass (150.0 g). (4) Correct ΔH with negative sign, kJ mol⁻¹, 3 SF.

Part (b) — 1 mark: Correct percentage difference using the literature value as the denominator.

Part (c) — 2 marks: (1) Correctly identifies that the absolute uncertainty in ΔT is ±1.0 °C (sum of the two reading uncertainties). (2) Correct percentage: (1.0/15.3) × 100 = 6.54%.

Part (d) — 4 marks (2 per reason): Each reason requires (i) identifying the source of error AND (ii) explaining how it makes the value less exothermic.

Q42 SYN §6.5 7 marks · ~14 min

A student carries out an experiment to determine the enthalpy change of neutralisation between HCl(aq) and NaOH(aq). They add 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) to 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 20.2 °C to 26.8 °C. Each temperature reading has an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C. (a) Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation. [Assume the density of the solution is 1.00 g cm⁻³ and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹] (4 marks) (b) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the temperature change. (1 mark) (c) The data book value for this neutralisation is −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Suggest two reasons, other than random measurement uncertainty, why the student's experimental value is likely to be less exothermic than the data book value. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Total volume of solution = 25.0 + 25.0 = 50.0 cm³ Mass of solution = 50.0 g (density 1.00 g cm⁻³) ΔT = 26.8 − 20.2 = 6.6 °C q = mcΔT = 50.0 × 4.18 × 6.6 = 1379 J = 1.379 kJ n(NaOH) = n(HCl) = 1.00 × 25.0/1000 = 0.0250 mol ΔH = −q / n = −1.379 / 0.0250 = −55.2 kJ mol⁻¹ (to 3 s.f.) — slightly less exothermic than the data book value (−57.1), consistent with the heat-loss premise in part (c). (b) Absolute uncertainty in ΔT = 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 °C Percentage uncertainty = (1.0 / 6.6) × 100 = 15% (to 2 s.f.; 15.15% to 4 s.f.) (c) 1. Heat loss to the surroundings — some energy released heats the air and the polystyrene cup rather than being recorded by the thermometer. 2. Heat absorbed by the calorimeter — the polystyrene cup has a heat capacity that is not accounted for in q = mcΔT, so the total energy absorbed is underestimated.

Why this scores full marks

Part (a) — 4 marks for correct total volume/mass, q, moles, and ΔH with negative sign. Part (b) — 1 mark for (2 × 0.5 / 6.6) × 100 = 15%. Part (c) — 2 marks for two distinct, MS-acceptable reasons.

Q43 DIA §6.5 6 marks · ~12 min

In a thermometric titration, a student added 25.0 cm³ of 1.20 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) to 20.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq). The temperature–volume graph showed a maximum temperature of 28.5 °C at an end-point of 15.0 cm³ of acid added. The initial temperature was 22.0 °C. (a) Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation. (4 marks) (b) The thermometer used had an uncertainty of ±0.5 °C. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in ΔT and hence the percentage uncertainty in ΔH. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Enthalpy of neutralisation: Total volume at end-point = 20.0 + 15.0 = 35.0 cm³ Mass of solution = 35.0 g (density = 1.00 g cm⁻³) ΔT = 28.5 − 22.0 = 6.5 °C q = m × c × ΔT = 35.0 × 4.18 × 6.5 = 951.05 J = 0.951 kJ Moles of acid at end-point = 1.20 × 15.0 / 1000 = 0.0180 mol ΔH = −q / n = −0.951 / 0.0180 = −52.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) Percentage uncertainty: Uncertainty in ΔT = ±0.5 °C (the ΔT is read from the graph as a single measured quantity, the rise from the extrapolated baseline to the maximum) Percentage uncertainty in ΔT = (0.5 / 6.5) × 100 = 7.69% Percentage uncertainty in ΔH = 7.69% (same, since ΔH ∝ ΔT)

Why this scores full marks

Part (a): 4 marks — correct total mass (35.0 g from combined volumes), correct ΔT, correct q, correct ΔH with negative sign. The student must use the volume at the end-point (15.0 cm³), not the total acid volume (25.0 cm³). Part (b): 2 marks — correct % uncertainty and correctly stating % uncertainty in ΔH equals % uncertainty in ΔT.

Q44 SYN §6.5 8 marks · ~16 min

A student investigates the enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol. They record the following data: - Mass of propan-1-ol burned: 0.520 g - Volume of water heated: 150.0 cm³ - Initial temperature of water: 19.5 °C - Maximum temperature of water: 34.0 °C - Thermometer uncertainty: ±0.5 °C - Mass balance uncertainty: ±0.005 g (a) Calculate the student's experimental value for the enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol. (Mₜ(C₃H₇OH) = 60.0 g mol⁻¹) (4 marks) (b) The accepted value for the enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol is −2021 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage error in the student's result. (1 mark) (c) The student claims that the largest source of error is the mass measurement. Use calculations to evaluate this claim, stating the percentage uncertainty from the mass measurement and comparing it to the percentage uncertainty from the temperature measurement. (3 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Experimental ΔHc: Mass of solution = 150.0 g (density = 1.00 g cm⁻³) ΔT = 34.0 − 19.5 = 14.5 °C q = m × c × ΔT = 150.0 × 4.18 × 14.5 = 9091.5 J = 9.092 kJ n(C₃H₇OH) = 0.520 / 60.0 = 0.00867 mol ΔHc = −q / n = −9.092 / 0.00867 = −1049 kJ mol⁻¹ (to 3 SF) (b) Percentage error: Percentage error = (|−1049 − (−2021)| / 2021) × 100 = (972 / 2021) × 100 = 48.1% (c) Evaluation of error sources: Percentage uncertainty from temperature: ΔT = 14.5 °C; uncertainty in ΔT = ±0.5 °C % uncertainty in ΔT = (0.5 / 14.5) × 100 = 3.45% Since ΔH ∝ ΔT: % uncertainty in ΔH from temperature = 3.45% Percentage uncertainty from mass of fuel: Uncertainty in mass = ±0.005 g % uncertainty in mass = (0.005 / 0.520) × 100 = 0.962% Comparison: The percentage uncertainty from temperature (3.45%) is significantly larger than from mass (0.962%). Therefore, the student's claim is incorrect — the temperature measurement is the larger source of uncertainty. The large percentage error (48.1%) compared to the combined uncertainties suggests that heat loss to surroundings is the dominant source of error, not instrumental uncertainties.

Why this scores full marks

Part (a): 4 marks — mass, ΔT, q, and ΔH with sign/units/SF. Part (b): 1 mark for correct percentage error using accepted value as denominator. Part (c): 3 marks — Mark 1 for % uncertainty from temperature, Mark 2 for % uncertainty from mass, Mark 3 for evaluation comparing the two and concluding the claim is wrong.

### §6.6–6.7 — Hess's Law (Cycles, Calculations, CP2)

Q45 QFR §6.6 1 mark · ~2 min

State Hess's Law.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The total enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is independent of the route by which the chemical change occurs, provided the initial and final conditions are the same.

Why this scores full marks

The mark-scheme requires the exact wording including the critical qualifier "provided the initial and final conditions are the same." A response stating only "the enthalpy change is the same regardless of the route taken" would be rejected because it omits this essential condition.

Q46 QFR §6.6 1 mark · ~2 min

State the general expression used to calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, ΔHᵣ, from standard enthalpy of formation values.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)

Why this scores full marks

The mark scheme requires the exact formula with "products minus reactants" ordering. Writing "reactants minus products" or omitting the summation notation (Σ) may lose the mark.

Q47 TDC §6.6 1 mark · ~2 min

A student needs to calculate ΔHᵣ for a reaction using standard enthalpy of combustion data. Which expression is correct? A) ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHc(products) − ΣΔHc(reactants) B) ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products) C) ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHc(products) + ΣΔHc(reactants) D) ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHf(reactants) − ΣΔHf(products)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

B

Why this scores full marks

The combustion formula is the opposite of the formation formula. For formation data: ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants). For combustion data: ΔHᵣ = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products). Option A reverses the sign and would give the wrong answer. This is one of the most common sign-error traps in exam performance.

Q48 CAL §6.6 2 marks · ~4 min

Calculate the enthalpy change for the thermal decomposition of magnesium carbonate. MgCO₃(s) → MgO(s) + CO₂(g) Given: ΔHf(MgCO₃) = −1096 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔHf(MgO) = −602 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔHf(CO₂) = −394 kJ mol⁻¹ (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:
