### Intermolecular Forces, Redox Chemistry, and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Q1 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Describe how London forces arise between molecules.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Describe

Answer:

An instantaneous/temporary dipole arises from the asymmetrical distribution of electrons in a molecule. This induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. The attraction between the instantaneous dipole and the induced dipole is a London force.

Q2 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why a straight-chain alkane has stronger London forces than a branched isomer with the same molecular formula.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

The straight-chain isomer has greater surface area, allowing more extensive London force interactions between molecules.

Q3 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain, in terms of electrons, why larger halogen molecules (e.g. I₂) have higher boiling points than smaller ones (e.g. Cl₂).

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Larger halogen molecules have more electrons → larger electron cloud → more easily polarised → stronger London forces → more energy needed to overcome intermolecular forces → higher boiling point.

Q4 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Draw two adjacent molecules to show how an instantaneous dipole induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule. Label the instantaneous dipole and the induced dipole, and show the partial charges (δ⁺ and δ⁻).

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Draw

Answer:

Two molecules drawn adjacent. First molecule labelled "instantaneous (temporary) dipole" with δ⁺ on one end and δ⁻ on the other (due to asymmetric electron distribution). Second molecule labelled "induced dipole" with δ⁺ facing the δ⁻ of the first molecule and δ⁻ facing the δ⁺ of the first molecule. An arrow or label showing "attraction" between the opposite partial charges.

Q5 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why saying "more electrons = stronger forces" alone is insufficient for explaining London force trends, and state what additional concept is required.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

"More electrons" alone is insufficient because the mark scheme also requires the concept of polarisability. The full chain is: more electrons → larger electron cloud → more easily polarised → stronger London forces. Without "more easily polarised", the explanation is incomplete.

Q6 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

Which of the following compounds has ONLY London forces between its molecules: HF, OF₂, CF₄, PF₃?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Name

Answer:

CF₄. CF₄ is tetrahedral and symmetrical → bond dipoles cancel → no permanent dipole → London forces only.

Q7 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain the difference between BF₃ and NH₃ in terms of the intermolecular forces they experience.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel, making it non-polar — it has only London forces. NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal (due to the lone pair), so it is polar — it has London forces, permanent dipole–dipole forces, and hydrogen bonding.

Q8 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why propanal has a higher boiling point than butane, even though butane has more electrons.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Propanal has a C=O bond that creates permanent dipole–dipole forces, which are stronger than the London forces in butane. The additional permanent dipole–dipole forces in propanal outweigh the slightly stronger London forces in butane.

Q9 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Define the term hydrogen bonding.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Define

Answer:

Hydrogen bonding is a strong type of intermolecular force that occurs when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O, or N) and is attracted to a lone pair of electrons on a highly electronegative atom (F, O, or N) in a different molecule.

Q10 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why (CH₃)₃COH can form hydrogen bonds but CH₃COCH₃ (propanone) cannot, despite both containing oxygen.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

(CH₃)₃COH has an O–H bond where H is covalently bonded to the electronegative O atom, allowing hydrogen bonding to a lone pair on O of a different molecule. CH₃COCH₃ has a C=O bond but no O–H bond; the H atoms are bonded to C, which is not electronegative enough for hydrogen bonding.

Q11 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Describe what a correct diagram showing a hydrogen bond between a methanol molecule and a water molecule should include.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Draw

Answer:

The diagram must show: (1) The O—H bond of one molecule (H bonded to O, NOT to C); (2) A dashed line from H to the O atom of the other molecule, representing the hydrogen bond; (3) The O—H⋯O angle approximately 180°; (4) The lone pair on the O atom accepting the hydrogen bond should be indicated; (5) Partial charges δ⁺ on H and δ⁻ on O.

Q12 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State the two elements that must be present in a molecule for hydrogen bonding to occur.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Hydrogen bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen (any two of F, O, N).

Q13 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State whether a molecule with a C–H bond can participate in hydrogen bonding.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

No. Carbon is not electronegative enough; hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to F, O or N.

Q14 QFR 6 marks · ~12 min

Compare the intermolecular forces in H₂ and NH₃. In your answer, you should include the types of forces present, how they arise, and explain which substance liquefies more easily.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

(1) Both form London forces. (2) Temporary dipole induces dipole in adjacent molecule. (3) Weaker attraction in H₂ (electron cloud less easily polarised). (4) NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds (N very electronegative). (5) Hydrogen bond between N lone pair and δ⁺H of different molecule. (6) NH₃ liquefies more easily (due to stronger hydrogen bonding compared to London forces in H₂).

Q15 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State which compound has the higher boiling point: butan-1-ol or butane-1,4-diol. Give a reason.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Butane-1,4-diol — two hydrogen-bonding sites per molecule (more hydrogen bonding).

Q16 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) is viscous at room temperature.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Three OH groups → can form up to 3 hydrogen bonds per molecule → strong intermolecular forces → high viscosity.

Q17 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Pentan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH) has a higher boiling point than 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol ((CH₃)₃CCH₂OH). Explain why.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Both compounds have hydrogen bonding (both have one –OH group). The difference is due to London forces. Pentan-1-ol has a straight chain (greater surface area) and therefore stronger London forces than the branched 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol.

Q18 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

Arrange HF, HCl, HBr, and HI in order of increasing boiling temperature. Explain your answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

HCl < HBr < HI < HF. All hydrogen halides have London forces. London force strength increases with increasing number of electrons from HCl to HI. Only HF has hydrogen bonding. Hydrogen bonding is much stronger than London forces, so HF has the highest boiling point despite having the fewest electrons.

Q19 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

A student claims that HBr must have a higher boiling point than HF because it has more electrons and therefore stronger intermolecular forces. Evaluate this claim with reference to the types and strengths of intermolecular forces involved.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Justify

Answer:

The student's claim is incorrect. While it is true that HBr has more electrons than HF and therefore stronger London forces, HF also has hydrogen bonding (H bonded to F, the most electronegative element). Hydrogen bonding is much stronger than London forces. Therefore HF has a higher boiling point than HBr despite having fewer electrons. The student failed to consider that different TYPES of intermolecular force can override electron count comparisons.

Q20 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

For a 2-mark boiling point explanation question, why is writing "stronger intermolecular forces" alone NOT sufficient for full marks?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Write

Answer:

Because the mark scheme explicitly requires specifying WHICH type of intermolecular force (e.g. "stronger London forces" not just "stronger intermolecular forces") AND the reason (e.g. "due to greater surface area" or "more electrons"). Writing "stronger IMF" without naming the type is penalised.

Q21 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the intermolecular forces in hexane with those in water.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

Hexane has only London forces between its molecules (non-polar molecule). Water has hydrogen bonding between its molecules (H bonded to O), which is the strongest type of intermolecular force. Water also has London forces and permanent dipole–dipole forces, but hydrogen bonding is the strongest and most significant.

Q22 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why an ionic compound such as NaCl dissolves readily in water but not in hexane. Refer to the intermolecular forces involved.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Water is polar and forms ion-dipole interactions with Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, which are strong enough to separate the ions from the ionic lattice. Hexane is non-polar and can only form London forces, which are too weak to overcome the strong ionic bonds in NaCl.

Q23 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Draw a labelled diagram showing the ion-dipole interactions between Mg²⁺, SO₄²⁻ and water molecules when MgSO₄ dissolves.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Draw

Answer:

For Mg²⁺ (positive ion): the δ⁻ oxygen atom of water molecules points TOWARDS the Mg²⁺ ion; draw 4–6 water molecules surrounding Mg²⁺ with O atoms nearest.

For SO₄²⁻ (negative ion): the δ⁺ hydrogen atoms of water molecules point TOWARDS the SO₄²⁻ ion; draw water molecules with H atoms nearest the SO₄²⁻.

Must show: δ⁺ on H atoms and δ⁻ on O atom (at least once); correct orientation (O of H₂O near cation, H of H₂O near anion). Full charges (+/−) are NOT correct — these are partial charges.

Q24 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State which end of a water molecule (H or O) is attracted to a negative ion (anion) when an ionic compound dissolves.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

The δ⁺ hydrogen atoms of water are attracted to negative ions (anions).

Q25 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

For an ion-dipole diagram question, what must you show and why?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

N

Answer:

You must show δ⁺ and δ⁻ (partial charges) on water molecules at least once, because full positive/negative charges are NOT correct — ion-dipole interactions involve partial charges on the polar water molecule. Marks are deducted if full charges are shown.

Q26 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Define the term oxidising agent.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Define

Answer:

An oxidising agent is a species that causes oxidation by gaining electrons (it is itself reduced). Its oxidation number decreases.

Q27 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

In the reaction Ca + Cl₂ → CaCl₂, explain why this is a redox reaction. Include the oxidation number changes.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Ca is oxidised (0 → +2) AND Cl₂ is reduced (0 → −1). Both oxidation number changes must be shown to demonstrate that both oxidation and reduction occur.

Q28 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain the difference between the species being oxidised and the oxidising agent.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

The species being oxidised LOSES electrons and has its oxidation number INCREASED. The oxidising agent is the species that CAUSES oxidation by GAINING electrons; it is itself REDUCED. They are different species — the oxidising agent is NOT the species being oxidised.

Q29 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

−1

Q30 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State the oxidation number of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

−1

Q31 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State the oxidation number of fluorine in any compound.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

−1 (always −1 in all compounds).

Q32 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Calculate the oxidation number of vanadium in the ion VO²⁺.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Calculate

Answer:

O is −2. Let V = x. x + (−2) = +2, therefore x = +4. V = +4.

Q33 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Determine the oxidation number of Cl in ClO₂.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Determine

Answer:

O is −2. Let Cl = x. x + 2(−2) = 0, therefore x = +4. Cl = +4.

Q34 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the oxidation numbers of chromium in K₂Cr₂O₇ and K₂CrO₄. Show your working.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

In K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 → 2x = +12 → Cr = +6. In K₂CrO₄: 2(+1) + x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +6. Both have Cr = +6.

Q35 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

A student is given four compounds: HF, NaH, H₂O₂, and CH₄. (a) Deduce which compound does NOT contain any element with an oxidation number of −1. (b) For each of the remaining three compounds, identify the element with oxidation number −1 and explain why.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

(a) CH₄ (C = −4, H = +1; no element at −1). (b) HF: F has oxidation number −1 (fluorine is always −1). NaH: H has oxidation number −1 (NaH is a metal hydride; Na = +1, so H = −1). H₂O₂: O has oxidation number −1 (H₂O₂ is a peroxide; H = +1, so O = −1).

Q36 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Work out the formula of potassium manganate(VI).

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Work

Answer:

Mn(VI) indicates Mn = +6. In the manganate ion: x + 4(−2) = −2 → x = +6. K is +1, so K₂MnO₄.

Q37 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Determine the formula of barium(II) ferrate(VI).

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Determine

Answer:

BaFeO₄. Ba²⁺ and FeO₄²⁻ with Fe = +6.

Q38 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

The Roman numerals in chlorate(V) and chlorate(VII) refer to the oxidation number of chlorine. Deduce the oxidation number of chlorine in NaClO₃ (chlorate(V)) and NaClO₄ (chlorate(VII)), showing your working.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

In NaClO₃: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0 → x = +5. Cl = +5 in chlorate(V). In NaClO₄: +1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +7. Cl = +7 in chlorate(VII). The Roman numerals indicate the oxidation number of chlorine (+5 and +7).

Q39 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Define the term disproportionation as applied to a redox reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Define

Answer:

Disproportionation is a redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. The oxidation numbers of this element in the products are both higher and lower than its oxidation number in the reactant.

Q40 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

For a 3-mark disproportionation explanation, what phrase is absolutely required that will NOT be accepted if you just write "redox"?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Give

Answer:

Write "disproportionation" and state "the SAME element is both oxidised AND reduced". Writing just "redox" is explicitly ignored/penalised in mark schemes — the specific term "disproportionation" is required.

Q41 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why the reaction Cl₂ + H₂O → HClO + HCl is a disproportionation reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

The same element (Cl) is both oxidised (0 → +1 in HClO) and reduced (0 → −1 in HCl). Since the same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction, this is disproportionation.

Q42 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why the reaction IO₃⁻ + 5I⁻ + 6H⁺ → 3I₂ + 3H₂O is NOT a disproportionation reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

I in IO₃⁻ = +5 (reduced to 0 in I₂); I in I⁻ = −1 (oxidised to 0 in I₂). Not disproportionation because two DIFFERENT species are oxidised and reduced — not the SAME species.

Q43 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

Chlorine dioxide, ClO₂, contains chlorine with an oxidation number of +4. (a) Write a balanced equation for the disproportionation of ClO₂ in alkaline solution to give ClO₂⁻ and ClO₃⁻. (b) Explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

(a) 2ClO₂ + 2OH⁻ → ClO₂⁻ + ClO₃⁻ + H₂O (b) Cl is +4 in ClO₂; it is reduced to +3 in ClO₂⁻ AND oxidised to +5 in ClO₃⁻. The same element (Cl) is both oxidised and reduced.

Q44 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

In the reaction between chlorine and cold dilute sodium hydroxide: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O, deduce which species is oxidised, which is reduced, and identify the oxidising agent and reducing agent.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

Cl in Cl₂ (0) is oxidised to Cl in NaClO (+1) — oxidation number increases. Cl in Cl₂ (0) is reduced to Cl in NaCl (−1) — oxidation number decreases. Cl₂ is both the oxidising agent (gains electrons to become Cl⁻) and the reducing agent (loses electrons to become ClO⁻). This is a disproportionation reaction.

Q45 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

Show that MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O is a redox reaction by assigning oxidation numbers and identifying what is oxidised and what is reduced.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Show

Answer:

Mn in MnO₂: +4; Mn in MnCl₂: +2 (reduced, gains 2 electrons). Cl in HCl: −1; Cl in Cl₂: 0 (oxidised, loses 1 electron per Cl atom). Since oxidation numbers change, this is a redox reaction. Manganese is reduced and chlorine is oxidised.

Q46 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Write the two half-equations for the reaction between MnO₂ and HCl, given that the products are Mn²⁺, Cl₂, and H₂O.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Write

Answer:

Reduction: MnO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O; Oxidation: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

Q47 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

A student writes the following half-equation for the reduction of MnO₂ in acidic conditions: MnO₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + H₂O. Identify the error in this half-equation and write the correct balanced version.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

The equation is not balanced for oxygen or hydrogen. There are 2 oxygen atoms on the left but only 1 on the right. The correct balanced half-equation is: MnO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O (2 H₂O needed to balance oxygen, 4H⁺ needed to balance hydrogen).

Q48 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

Sodium chlorate(I) solution is left to stand and slowly disproportionates. (a) Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations for this disproportionation. (b) By multiplying and combining the half-equations, deduce the full ionic equation.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

(a) Reduction (+1 → −1): ClO⁻ + H₂O + 2e⁻ → Cl⁻ + 2OH⁻. Oxidation (+1 → +5): ClO⁻ + 4OH⁻ → ClO₃⁻ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. (b) Multiply the reduction half-equation by 2 (to give 4e⁻): 2ClO⁻ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + 4OH⁻. Add to the oxidation half-equation and cancel: 3ClO⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻.

Q49 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State how the reactivity of Group 2 metals changes down the group.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Reactivity increases down the group.

Q50 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why calcium reacts more vigorously with water than magnesium. In your answer, refer to electronic structure.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Ca has a larger atomic radius and the outer electron is more effectively shielded by more inner electron shells. This means less energy is needed to remove the outer electron (lower first ionisation energy), so calcium reacts more vigorously than magnesium.

Q51 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why Na⁺ forms a stable peroxide (Na₂O₂) but Li⁺ does not.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Larger ionic radius of Na⁺ → lower charge density → polarises O₂²⁻ less → stabilises the peroxide ion. Li⁺ has too high charge density and distorts the peroxide ion excessively, making it unstable.

Q52 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State how the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates changes down the group.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Thermal stability increases down the group.

Q53 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why Mg(NO₃)₂ is LESS thermally stable than Ca(NO₃)₂.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Mg²⁺ is smaller → higher charge density → more polarising → N–O bonds weakened more → less energy to break → decomposes more easily.

Q54 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

For a QWC question on thermal decomposition trends, what is the full polarising power explanation chain you must include?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Write

Answer:

Write the chain in order: (1) M²⁺ ionic radius increases down Group 2; (2) Charge density (charge/size ratio) decreases; (3) Polarising power decreases; (4) The cation distorts/polarises the anion less; (5) The bonds within the anion are weakened less; (6) More energy is required to decompose; (7) Thermal stability increases.

Q55 QFR 6 marks · ~12 min

Evaluate the diagonal relationship between Li and Mg by comparing the thermal decomposition of their nitrates with that of NaNO₃.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Evaluate

Answer:

4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂ and 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂ — both give the oxide, NO₂, and O₂. NaNO₃ → NaNO₂ + ½O₂ — gives the nitrite and O₂ (no NO₂). Li behaves like Group 2 because Li⁺/Mg²⁺ are smaller than Na⁺ → greater charge density → polarise nitrate more → weaken N–O bond → decompose to give NO₂.

Q56 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

Explain why the thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates produces the oxide, NO₂, and O₂, whereas Group 1 nitrates (except lithium) produce the nitrite and O₂.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Group 2 cations (M²⁺) have a higher charge than Group 1 cations (M⁺). This gives Group 2 cations a greater charge density and greater polarising power. The greater polarising power more strongly distorts the nitrate anion, weakening the N–O bonds more. This allows the nitrate to fully decompose (breaking N–O bonds completely to give the oxide and NO₂). Group 1 cations (except Li⁺) have lower charge density, so they polarise the nitrate less and only the N–O bond to oxygen is weakened enough for oxygen loss (giving the nitrite).

Q57 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

When 2.97 g of Mg(NO₃)₂ is thermally decomposed, 1200 cm³ of gas is collected at room temperature and pressure. Use this information to show that the molar gas volume is 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹. (Molar mass of Mg(NO₃)₂ = 148.3 g mol⁻¹)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Calculate

Answer:

2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂ (5 mol gas per 2 mol nitrate). n(Mg(NO₃)₂) = 2.97/148.3 = 0.02003 mol. n(gas) = 5/2 × 0.02003 = 0.05008 mol. Molar volume = 1200/0.05008 = 23 962 ≈ 24 000 cm³ mol⁻¹.

Q58 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

A sample of Mg(NO₃)₂ is heated until completely decomposed. The total volume of gas collected is 600 cm³ at room temperature and pressure. Calculate the moles of Mg(NO₃)₂ that decomposed. (Molar volume at rtp = 24000 cm³ mol⁻¹)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Calculate

Answer:

n(gas) = 600 / 24000 = 0.0250 mol. From 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂, 2 mol Mg(NO₃)₂ produces 5 mol gas. n(Mg(NO₃)₂) = (2/5) × 0.0250 = 0.0100 mol.

Q59 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State how the solubility of Group 2 hydroxides changes down the group.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Solubility increases down the group.

Q60 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State how the solubility of Group 2 sulfates changes down the group.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Solubility decreases down the group.

Q61 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

What is the most common mistake students make regarding Group 2 hydroxide and sulfate solubility trends?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Give

Answer:

Getting the trend directions WRONG: students often think hydroxide solubility decreases (it INCREASES) or sulfate solubility increases (it DECREASES). The two trends go in OPPOSITE directions.

Q62 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the solubilities of MgSO₄ and BaSO₄.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

MgSO₄ is soluble (sulfate solubility is highest at the top of Group 2) and BaSO₄ is insoluble (sulfate solubility is lowest at the bottom). BaSO₄ forms a white precipitate.

Q63 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and Group 2 sulfates.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

Group 2 hydroxide solubility INCREASES down the group: Mg(OH)₂ < Ca(OH)₂ < Sr(OH)₂ < Ba(OH)₂. Group 2 sulfate solubility DECREASES down the group: MgSO₄ > CaSO₄ > SrSO₄ > BaSO₄. These are OPPOSITE trends.

Q64 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

25.0 cm³ of a saturated solution of Ca(OH)₂ required 18.95 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ HCl for neutralisation. Calculate the solubility of Ca(OH)₂ in g dm⁻³. (Molar mass of Ca(OH)₂ = 74.1 g mol⁻¹)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Calculate

Answer:

n(HCl) = 18.95 × 10⁻³ × 0.0500 = 9.475 × 10⁻⁴ mol. n(Ca(OH)₂) = ½ × n(HCl) = 4.738 × 10⁻⁴ mol (in 25 cm³). Concentration in 1 dm³ = 4.738 × 10⁻⁴ × 1000/25 = 0.01895 mol dm⁻³. Solubility = 0.01895 × 74.1 = 1.40 g dm⁻³.

Q65 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why BaCl₂ is added to a solution in dilute HNO₃ (rather than in water) when testing for sulfate ions.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Dilute HNO₃ is added first to acidify the solution. This removes any carbonate ions (which would also form a white precipitate with Ba²⁺ as BaCO₃). BaCO₃ dissolves in acid, whereas BaSO₄ is insoluble in acid. This ensures that any white precipitate observed is BaSO₄, confirming the presence of sulfate ions.

Q66 QFR 5 marks · ~10 min

A student has an unknown Group 2 nitrate. When thermally decomposed, it produces a white solid, brown gas, and oxygen gas. When the remaining solid is added to water, a sparingly soluble suspension forms that gives a white precipitate with dilute H₂SO₄. Suggest the identity of the unknown nitrate and justify your answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Suggest

Answer:

The nitrate is Ca(NO₃)₂. Justification: (1) Brown gas (NO₂) and O₂ produced → Group 2 nitrate decomposition pattern (rules out Group 1 except Li). (2) The oxide/hydroxide formed is sparingly soluble in water → consistent with Ca(OH)₂. (3) White precipitate with H₂SO₄ → confirms Ca²⁺ (BaSO₄ would be insoluble but Ba(OH)₂ is fully soluble, so the sparingly soluble hydroxide rules out Ba; Mg(OH)₂ would be insoluble not sparingly soluble).

Q67 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

For a flame test question, what specific precaution must be taken when testing for potassium ions and why?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Give

Answer:

View through cobalt glass. This masks the yellow colour of any sodium impurity, allowing the lilac flame of K⁺ to be seen clearly.

Q68 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why different metal ions produce different flame test colours.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Different gaps between electronic energy levels → different wavelengths of light emitted when electrons return to lower energy levels.

Q69 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

A compound gives a red flame and forms a white precipitate when added to K₂SO₄(aq). The precipitate is insoluble in dilute acid. Deduce the formula of the compound.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

Red flame could be Li⁺ or Sr²⁺. Insoluble sulfate precipitate → Ba²⁺ or Sr²⁺ (MgSO₄ is soluble). Since the flame is red (not green for Ba²⁺), the cation is Sr²⁺. The compound dissolves in K₂SO₄(aq) and Sr²⁺ precipitates with SO₄²⁻, so the anion is a soluble one — the compound is Sr(NO₃)₂.

Q70 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State how the boiling temperature of the halogens changes down Group 7.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Boiling temperature increases down Group 7.

Q71 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State how the reactivity of the halogens as oxidising agents changes down Group 7.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Reactivity (oxidising power) decreases down Group 7.

Q72 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why the boiling temperature increases down Group 7 from Cl₂ to I₂.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

More electrons → larger electron cloud → more easily polarised → stronger London forces. (Not "stronger covalent bonds" — boiling involves overcoming intermolecular forces, not breaking covalent bonds.)

Q73 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why the oxidising power of halogens decreases down Group 7.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Atomic radius increases down Group 7, shielding increases, and the ability to attract electrons (electronegativity) decreases. This means the halogen molecules become less able to gain an electron and act as oxidising agents.

Q74 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the trend in reactivity down Group 7 with the trend down Group 2.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

Group 7 reactivity (as oxidising agents) DECREASES down the group. Group 2 reactivity INCREASES down the group. These are opposite trends: halogens get less reactive (less able to gain electrons) while Group 2 metals get more reactive (more easily lose electrons).

Q75 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium bromide. Explain the redox reaction that occurs, identifying what is oxidised and what is reduced.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Initially, NaBr + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HBr (acid-base reaction). Then HBr reduces H₂SO₄: H₂SO₄ + 2HBr → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O. Br⁻ (in HBr) is oxidised from −1 to 0 (in Br₂). S in H₂SO₄ is reduced from +6 to +4 (in SO₂). Products include Br₂ (red-brown fumes), SO₂ (colourless acidic gas), and H₂O.

Q76 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain the difference between the products formed when concentrated H₂SO₄ reacts with NaCl compared with NaBr.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

With NaCl: no redox occurs; only HCl gas (white fumes) is produced. Cl⁻ is too weak a reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄. With NaBr: a redox reaction occurs; Br₂ (red-brown fumes) and SO₂ (colourless gas) are produced. Br⁻ is a moderate reducing agent and reduces H₂SO₄ from S(+6) to S(+4).

Q77 QFR 5 marks · ~10 min

Three test tubes contain solid NaCl, NaBr, and NaI respectively. Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to each. (a) State the products formed with each halide. (b) Deduce the order of reducing power of the halide ions from your observations.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

(a) NaCl: HCl(g) only (white fumes, no redox). NaBr: HBr(g), Br₂ (red-brown fumes), SO₂(g) (colourless gas). NaI: HI(g), I₂ (black solid), S (yellow solid), H₂S(g), SO₂(g). (b) Reducing power: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻. Evidence: I⁻ reduces H₂SO₄ the most (to S/H₂S), Br⁻ reduces it less (to SO₂ only), and Cl⁻ does not reduce it at all. The stronger the reducing agent, the more H₂SO₄ is reduced.

Q78 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

A student claims that adding concentrated H₂SO₄ to sodium chloride produces chlorine gas. (a) Deduce whether this claim is correct. (b) The student then suggests that to produce chlorine from NaCl, they should use a stronger acid. Evaluate this suggestion.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

(a) The claim is incorrect. Adding concentrated H₂SO₄ to NaCl produces HCl gas (white fumes), NOT chlorine. Cl⁻ is too weak a reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄; only an acid-base reaction occurs. (b) The suggestion is also incorrect. The issue is not the strength of the acid but the reducing power of Cl⁻. Chloride ions are very weak reducing agents and will not reduce any common laboratory reagent to produce Cl₂. A different method is needed, such as electrolysis of molten NaCl.

Q79 QFR 1 mark · ~2 min

State the observation when aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution containing bromide ions.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

State

Answer:

Cream precipitate.

Q80 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Dilute nitric acid is added to a solution before carrying out the silver nitrate test. Explain why this step is necessary.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

To remove carbonate ions (or sulfite ions) which would also form a precipitate with silver nitrate, giving a false positive result.

Q81 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the solubility of the three silver halide precipitates in ammonia solution.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Compare

Answer:

AgCl is soluble in dilute ammonia; AgBr is soluble in concentrated ammonia only; AgI is insoluble in ammonia.

Q82 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

2.49 g of a mixture of KI and KCl is dissolved in water and excess AgNO₃ is added. 0.162 g of AgI precipitate is formed. Calculate the percentage of KI in the mixture. (M(AgI) = 234.8 g mol⁻¹; M(KI) = 166.0 g mol⁻¹)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Calculate

Answer:

n(AgI) = 0.162 / 234.8 = 6.90 × 10⁻⁴ mol; n(KI) = 6.90 × 10⁻⁴ mol (1:1 ratio); m(KI) = 6.90 × 10⁻⁴ × 166.0 = 0.1145 g; %KI = (0.1145 / 2.49) × 100 = 4.60%.

Q83 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

When aqueous iodine is shaken with cyclohexane in a separating funnel, the iodine preferentially dissolves in the cyclohexane layer. Explain why.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Iodine is a non-polar molecule. The London forces between iodine and cyclohexane are similar in strength to the London forces within iodine itself, whereas iodine cannot break the strong hydrogen bonds in water.

Q84 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

A solution is known to contain either NaCl or NaI. A student adds silver nitrate solution after acidifying with dilute nitric acid and observes a yellow precipitate. The student then adds the precipitate to cyclohexane and shakes. (a) Identify the halide ion present. (b) State what the student would observe if the yellow precipitate was AgI and excess dilute ammonia was added. (c) The student claims the yellow precipitate could be colloidal sulfur from the oxidation of sulfite by Ag⁺. Explain why the initial addition of dilute nitric acid makes this claim unlikely.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Deduce

Answer:

(a) I⁻ (iodide ions) — a yellow precipitate with AgNO₃ indicates AgI. (b) The precipitate would remain insoluble (AgI does not dissolve in ammonia). (c) Dilute nitric acid removes any sulfite ions present (by converting them to SO₂ gas) before the AgNO₃ is added, so sulfite interference is eliminated.

Q85 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

In a titration, 10.00 cm³ of solution is measured using a pipette (±0.04 cm³) and the titre is 25.00 cm³ using a burette (±0.05 cm³ per reading). Calculate the total percentage uncertainty in the concentration.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Calculate

Answer:

Pipette uncertainty = ±0.04/10.00 × 100 = ±0.40%. Burette titre uncertainty = ±0.10/25.00 × 100 = ±0.40% (titre = two readings, so uncertainty doubles). Total % uncertainty = 0.40% + 0.40% = ±0.80%.

Q86 QFR 3 marks · ~6 min

A student uses a burette with an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³ per reading. When asked to state the uncertainty in the titre volume, the student writes ±0.05 cm³. Explain why this is incorrect and state the correct value.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Suggest

Answer:

The titre volume is the DIFFERENCE between the final and initial burette readings. Since each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³ and two readings are taken, the absolute uncertainty is doubled to ±0.10 cm³. The student should write ±0.10 cm³.

Q87 QFR 2 marks · ~4 min

In a lithium-ion battery, the overall equation is: C₆Li + CoO₂ → LiCoO₂ + C₆. Describe, with reference to oxidation numbers, what happens to cobalt.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Explain

Answer:

Cobalt is reduced; its oxidation number changes from +4 (in CoO₂) to +3 (in LiCoO₂). The oxidation number decreases, meaning cobalt gains electrons.

Q88 QFR 4 marks · ~8 min

Bleach contains NaOCl. A student claims that mixing bleach with acid produces chlorine gas because "the acid reacts with the bleach." Justify this claim by writing a two-step mechanism showing how the toxic gas is produced, naming the type of reaction occurring.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Justify

Answer:

Step 1: Adding H⁺ shifts HClO ⇌ H⁺ + ClO⁻ to the LEFT, forming HClO. Step 2: HClO + Cl⁻ + H⁺ → Cl₂ + H₂O. This is a redox (comproportionation) reaction. The Cl in ClO⁻ (oxidation number +1) is reduced to Cl₂ (0), and the Cl⁻ (−1) is oxidised to Cl₂ (0). The net result is formation of toxic Cl₂(g), which is dangerous to inhale.

Q89 QFR 5 marks · ~10 min

Chlorine gas is used to produce calcium hypochlorite for swimming pool treatment via the reaction: 2Ca(OH)₂ + 2Cl₂ → Ca(ClO)₂ + CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. (a) Calculate the oxidation number of Cl in Ca(ClO)₂ and in CaCl₂. (b) Is this reaction an example of disproportionation? Justify your answer using oxidation numbers. (c) A pool requires 7.16 kg of Ca(ClO)₂. Calculate the volume of Cl₂ gas needed at rtp. (M(Ca(ClO)₂) = 143.1 g mol⁻¹; molar volume = 24000 cm³ mol⁻¹)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Command Word

Analyse

Answer:

(a) In Ca(ClO)₂: Ca = +2, O = −2, so Cl = +1. In CaCl₂: Ca = +2, Cl = −1. (b) Yes, this is disproportionation. Chlorine starts at 0 (in Cl₂) and ends up at +1 (in Ca(ClO)₂, oxidised) and −1 (in CaCl₂, reduced). The SAME element (chlorine) is both oxidised AND reduced. (c) n(Ca(ClO)₂) = 7160 / 143.1 = 50.0 mol. From the equation, 2 mol Cl₂ produces 1 mol Ca(ClO)₂. n(Cl₂) = 50.0 × 2 = 100 mol. V(Cl₂) = 100 × 24000 = 2,400,000 cm³ = 2400 dm³.

## Chapter 2.7 — Intermolecular Forces, Redox & Groups 1, 2, 7

WCH12 · Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry · Unit 2

Spec Points 7.1–8.287 Papers AnalysedJun 2022 – Oct 2024

Average ~16 marks per paper — IMFs, redox, and Group chemistry consistently tested

### Definitions

### Intermolecular Forces, Redox Chemistry, and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Specification coverage: 7.1–8.28 | Average paper weight: 38.6% (20–46 marks)
Core practicals: CP3 (volumetric analysis), CP4 (identification of Group 2 cations and Group 7 anions)

### Section 7A — Intermolecular Forces (Spec 7.1–7.6)

#### 7.1 London Forces (Induced Dipole–Dipole Forces)

Exam-ready definition:

London forces are weak intermolecular forces caused by the movement of electrons in an atom or molecule creating an instantaneous/temporary dipole, which induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom or molecule. The resulting attraction between the temporary dipole and the induced dipole is the London force. They exist between ALL atoms and molecules, whether polar or non-polar.

Key points to include for full marks: - Electrons are in constant motion → instantaneous/temporary dipole - This induces a dipole in an adjacent molecule - Attraction between temporary dipole and induced dipole - Present in ALL molecules (and atoms)

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2024 Q4 (1 mark) — Which has strongest London forces?
MS: Straight-chain alkane with most electrons (CH₃(CH₂)₇CH₃). More electrons → larger electron cloud → more easily polarised → stronger London forces.

2. Oct 2024 Q19(a)(i) (2 marks) — Describe how London forces arise.
MS: Instantaneous/temporary dipole from asymmetrical electron distribution → induced dipoles in neighbouring molecules.

3. Oct 2024 Q19(a)(ii) (1 mark) — Why HI has stronger London forces than HCl.
MS: HI has more electrons.

4. Jun 2022 Q16(d) (4 marks) — Explain HX boiling point trend.
MS: (1) All HX have London forces; (2) London force strength increases with number of electrons down the group; (3) Only HF has hydrogen bonding; (4) Hydrogen bonding is much stronger than London forces.

Common mistakes: - Writing "van der Waals forces" instead of "London forces" (Edexcel uses "London forces") - Saying "more electrons = stronger forces" without mentioning polarisability - Confusing London forces with permanent dipole–dipole forces - Saying London forces are only in non-polar molecules (they exist in ALL molecules)

#### 7.2 Permanent Dipole–Dipole Forces

Exam-ready definition:

Permanent dipole–dipole forces are intermolecular forces of attraction between the permanent dipoles of polar molecules. They arise because polar molecules have an uneven distribution of electron density, creating a permanent δ⁺ end and a permanent δ⁻ end. The δ⁺ end of one molecule attracts the δ⁻ end of another.

Key points: - Only exist in POLAR molecules - Caused by a permanent uneven distribution of electron density - Stronger than London forces but weaker than hydrogen bonding - PH₃ is an important example: non-polar P–H bonds (Δχ ≈ 0) but a polar molecule due to the lone pair

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jun 2023 Q6 (1 mark) — Butane vs propanal b.p.
MS: Propanal has a C=O bond that creates permanent dipole–dipole forces, which are stronger than the London forces in butane.

2. Jan 2023 Q4 (1 mark) — Which has only London forces?
MS: CF₄ is tetrahedral and symmetrical → no permanent dipole → London forces only. (HF has H-bonding; OF₂ and PF₃ are polar.)

3. Oct 2023 Q4 (1 mark) — Table of IMF for BF₃, CH₄, NH₃, H₂S.
MS: H₂S has London forces + permanent dipole–dipole, but NOT hydrogen bonding (S is not electronegative enough).

Common mistakes: - Confusing which molecules are polar vs non-polar (symmetrical molecules like CF₄, BF₃ are non-polar despite polar bonds) - Saying PH₃ has hydrogen bonding (P is NOT electronegative enough) - Forgetting that permanent dipole–dipole forces are additional to London forces (all molecules have London forces too)

#### 7.3 Hydrogen Bonding

Exam-ready definition:

Hydrogen bonding is a strong type of intermolecular force that occurs when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen) and is attracted to a lone pair of electrons on a highly electronegative atom (F, O, or N) in a DIFFERENT molecule.

Key points for full marks: - H must be covalently bonded to F, O, or N (NOT to C, P, S, Cl) - H is attracted to a lone pair on F, O, or N in a different molecule - Strongest type of intermolecular force (but NOT a covalent bond) - Gives anomalous properties: high b.p. of H₂O, HF, NH₃; lower density of ice

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2024 Q1 (1 mark) — Which exhibits hydrogen bonding?
MS: HF (F is highly electronegative, H bonded directly to F).

2. Jan 2023 Q5 (1 mark) — Which forms hydrogen bonding?
MS: (CH₃)₃COH — only option with O–H bond. N not bonded to H in option A; F not bonded to H in option B; C=O in option D has no O–H.

3. Jan 2023 Q6 (1 mark) — HF b.p. anomaly.
MS: HF > HI > HBr > HCl. HF highest due to H-bonding; then London forces dominate: HI > HBr > HCl.

4. Jun 2023 Q20(b) (6 marks, QWC) — Compare IMF in H₂ and NH₃.
MS indicative points: (1) Both form London forces; (2) Temporary dipole induces dipole in adjacent molecule; (3) Weaker attraction in H₂ (electron cloud less easily polarised); (4) NH₃ forms hydrogen bonds (N very electronegative); (5) H-bond between N lone pair and δ⁺H of different molecule; (6) NH₃ liquefies more easily.

5. Jun 2023 Q7 (1 mark) — Which diagram shows H-bond between methanol and water?
MS: H must be bonded to O (not C); O—H⋯O angle ~180°.

Common mistakes: - Saying H bonded to C can hydrogen bond (it CANNOT — Jan 2023 Q5 specifically tests this) - Confusing intramolecular hydrogen bonds with intermolecular ones - Saying H-bonding is a covalent bond or a type of covalent bonding - Forgetting to specify that the H is attracted to a LONE PAIR on the electronegative atom - Writing "H-bond between H and O" without specifying it is a lone pair on O

#### 7.4–7.5 Predicting Physical Properties from IMF

Key definitions:

Boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid equals the external pressure. Stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point.

Solubility depends on whether the solute–solvent intermolecular forces are similar in strength to the solute–solute and solvent–solvent forces they replace ("like dissolves like").

Rules for predicting b.p.: 1. H-bonding > permanent dipole–dipole > London forces 2. More electrons → stronger London forces → higher b.p. (for molecules with same type of IMF) 3. Less branching → greater surface area → stronger London forces → higher b.p. 4. More H-bonding sites → stronger overall IMF → higher b.p.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jun 2024 Q4(a) (1 mark) — Structural isomer with highest b.p.
MS: Least branched chain (greater surface area for London forces).

2. Jun 2024 Q4(b) (1 mark) — Compound with highest b.p. (diol vs mono-alcohol).
MS: Butane-1,4-diol — two H-bonding sites per molecule.

3. Jan 2023 Q19(b)(ii) (2 marks) — Explain b.p. difference between two alcohols.
MS: (The less branched one) has stronger London forces due to greater surface area / less branching. Must specify "London forces" and "greater surface area". MS explicitly says "Do not award just stronger intermolecular forces."

4. Jan 2023 Q19(b)(iii) (3 marks) — Solubility in ethanol vs water.
MS: (1) London forces between B and ethanol; (2) H-bonds between B and water; (3) Comparison — London forces B–EtOH stronger than/similar to those in B; OR H-bonds B–H₂O weaker than H-bonds in water.

5. Oct 2023 Q19(d) (6 marks, QWC) — Why I₂ is more soluble in hexane than water.
MS: (1) I₂ has only London forces; (2) Water forms H-bonds (strongest IMF); (3) Hexane has only London forces; (4) I₂–hexane London forces similar in strength to those broken → dissolves; (5) I₂ cannot break water H-bonds → does not dissolve.

6. Jun 2023 Q22(c)(iii) (2 marks) — Why propane-1,2,3-triol is viscous.
MS: Three OH groups → forms 3 H-bonds per molecule → strong IMF → viscous.

Common mistakes: - Writing "stronger intermolecular forces" without specifying which type (MS penalises this) - Forgetting that ALL molecules have London forces (even those with H-bonding or pd-pd forces) - Saying a molecule has "more H-bonds" when it has the same number of H-bonding sites but different branching - Confusing solubility reasoning: must compare forces formed vs forces broken, not just list forces

#### 7.6 Ion-Dipole Interactions

Exam-ready definition:

Ion-dipole interactions are the attractive forces between an ion and the permanent dipole of a polar molecule. When an ionic compound dissolves in a polar solvent (such as water), the δ⁺ hydrogen atoms of water are attracted to negative ions (anions) and the δ⁻ oxygen atoms of water are attracted to positive ions (cations). These interactions help to separate the ions from the ionic lattice, enabling dissolution.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jun 2024 Q2 (1 mark) — NaCl dissolving in water — what IMF?
MS: Ion-dipole interactions.

2. Oct 2024 Q16(c)(i) (2 marks) — Draw ion-dipole interaction diagram (Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ with water).
MS: H atoms of water near SO₄²⁻; O atom of water near Mg²⁺. Must show δ⁺/δ⁻ on water at least once.

Common mistakes: - Confusing ion-dipole with hydrogen bonding - Not showing partial charges (δ⁺/δ⁻) on the water molecule - Putting the wrong end of water near the wrong ion

### Section 8A — Redox Chemistry (Spec 8.1–8.10)

#### 8.1 Oxidation and Reduction (Definitions)

Exam-ready definitions:

Oxidation is the LOSS of electrons OR an INCREASE in oxidation number.

Reduction is the GAIN of electrons OR a DECREASE in oxidation number.

Oxidising agent is a species that CAUSES oxidation by GAINING electrons (it is itself reduced). Its oxidation number DECREASES.

Reducing agent is a species that CAUSES reduction by LOSING electrons (it is itself oxidised). Its oxidation number INCREASES.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jun 2022 Q2 (1 mark) — Identify the oxidising agent.
MS: The species that gains electrons / has its oxidation number decreased.

2. Jan 2024 Q21(b)(i) (2 marks) — Ca + Cl₂: explain redox.
MS: Ca oxidised 0→+2 AND Cl₂ reduced 0→−1. Both oxidation number changes required.

3. Oct 2023 Q19(b) (2 marks) — Show MnO₂ + HCl is redox using oxidation numbers.
MS: Mn: +4 → +2 (reduced); Cl: −1 → 0 (oxidised). Both changes must be shown.

Note: Jan 2023 Q18(a) on disproportionation of Cl₂ is listed under §8.9–8.10 (Disproportionation) below — see there for the full MS.

Common mistakes: - Writing "the oxidising agent loses electrons" (wrong — it GAINS electrons) - Confusing oxidation/oxidising agent (the agent does the OPPOSITE of what it's named) - Not showing BOTH oxidation and reduction changes when asked to "show it is redox" - Confusing the species being oxidised with the oxidising agent

#### 8.2–8.5 Oxidation Numbers

Rules for assigning oxidation numbers:

Rule Statement

1 The oxidation number of an element in its standard state is 0 (e.g., Cl₂, Na, O₂)

2 For simple monatomic ions, the oxidation number equals the charge (e.g., Na⁺ = +1, O²⁻ = −2)

3 In compounds, oxygen is usually −2 (exception: −1 in peroxides like H₂O₂, Na₂O₂)

4 In compounds, hydrogen is usually +1 (exception: −1 in metal hydrides like NaH, CaH₂)

5 Fluorine is ALWAYS −1

6 The sum of all oxidation numbers in a neutral compound equals 0; in an ion, equals the charge

Roman numeral naming convention:

The Roman numeral in a compound name (e.g., chlorate(V), manganate(VII)) indicates the oxidation number of the specified element.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2023 Q7 (1 mark) — Oxidation number of V in VO²⁺.
MS: V = +4 (O is −2, overall +2: x + (−2) = +2 → x = +4).

2. Jan 2023 Q8 (1 mark) — Formula of potassium manganate(VI).
MS: K₂MnO₄ (Mn(VI): x − 8 = −2 → x = +6; K is +1, so K₂MnO₄).

3. Jan 2024 Q6 (1 mark) — In which compound is an oxidation number −1?
MS: CH₄ has no element at −1 (H = +1, C = −4). Correct options include HF (F = −1), NaH (H = −1), H₂O₂ (O = −1).

4. Jun 2024 Q18(b)(ii) (1 mark) — Oxidation number of Cl in ClO₂.
MS: Cl = +4 (2 × (−2) + x = 0 → x = +4).

5. Jun 2022 Q4 (1 mark) — Name KClO₂ using oxidation state.
MS: Potassium chlorate(III). Cl: K = +1, 2O = −4, so Cl = +3.

6. Jun 2023 Q8 (1 mark) — Which pair has the same oxidation state?
MS: Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ and K₂CrO₄ — both have Cr = +6.

7. Jun 2023 Q9 (1 mark) — Formula of barium(II) ferrate(VI).
MS: BaFeO₄ (Ba²⁺ and FeO₄²⁻ with Fe = +6).

8. Jun 2024 Q18(b)(i) (1 mark) — Roman numerals in chlorate(V) and chlorate(VII).
MS: Oxidation number of chlorine (+5 and +7).

Common mistakes: - Forgetting the peroxide exception: O = −1 in H₂O₂, Na₂O₂ (tested in Jan 2024 Q6) - Forgetting the hydride exception: H = −1 in NaH, CaH₂ (tested in Jan 2024 Q6) - Assigning oxidation numbers to elements in their standard state as non-zero - Confusing oxidation number with charge (e.g., in CO₃²⁻, C is +4 not +2) - Not showing working for oxidation number calculations

#### 8.6–8.8 Half-Equations and Balancing Redox Equations

Exam-ready definition:

A half-equation shows either the oxidation or reduction process separately, including electrons. To combine half-equations into a full redox equation: (1) balance all atoms except H and O; (2) balance O with H₂O; (3) balance H with H⁺ (in acid) or OH⁻ (in alkali); (4) balance charge with electrons; (5) multiply half-equations so electrons cancel; (6) add the half-equations and cancel common species.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Oct 2023 Q6 (1 mark) — Balance O₂ in alkaline conditions.
MS: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ (n = 4 electrons).

2. Jun 2022 Q16(b) (4 marks) — Explain why IO₃⁻ + 5I⁻ + 6H⁺ → 3I₂ + 3H₂O is NOT disproportionation.
MS: I in IO₃⁻ = +5 (reduced to 0 in I₂); I in I⁻ = −1 (oxidised to 0 in I₂). Not disproportionation because two DIFFERENT species are oxidised and reduced — not the SAME species.

3. Jun 2024 Q18(b)(iii) (2 marks) — Deduce oxidation number range for disproportionation.
MS: Compound A disproportionates to give ClO₂ (Cl = +4, reduced) and HClO₄ (Cl = +7, oxidised); for disproportionation, Cl in compound A must lie strictly between these values, so the oxidation number is +5 or +6.

Note: Oct 2024 Q19(b)(i) on Cl₂ + H₂O disproportionation is listed under §8.9–8.10 (Disproportionation) below — see there for the full MS.

Common mistakes: - Not multiplying half-equations to make electrons equal before combining - Forgetting to add water to balance oxygen in acidic or alkaline conditions - Identifying comproportionation (reverse) as disproportionation - Not stating that the SAME element must be both oxidised AND reduced for disproportionation - Writing "redox" alone instead of "disproportionation" (explicitly ignored in Jun 2023 MS)

#### 8.9–8.10 Disproportionation

Exam-ready definition:

Disproportionation is a redox reaction in which the SAME element is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced. The oxidation numbers of this element in the products are both higher and lower than its oxidation number in the reactant.

Key disproportionation reactions to know:

Reaction Element Oxidised to Reduced to

Cl₂ + H₂O → HClO + HCl Cl (0) Cl (+1) in HClO Cl (−1) in HCl

Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O Cl (0) Cl (+1) in NaClO Cl (−1) in NaCl

3NaClO → 2NaCl + NaClO₃ Cl (+1) Cl (+5) in NaClO₃ Cl (−1) in NaCl

2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ O (−1) O (0) in O₂ O (−2) in H₂O

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2023 Q18(a) (3 marks) — Disproportionation of Cl₂ forming Ca(ClO)₂.
MS: Cl oxidised from 0 to +1 (in ClO⁻) and Cl reduced from 0 to −1 (in Cl⁻).

2. Jun 2023 Q22(c)(i) (3 marks) — Disproportionation of Cl₂ in bleach.
MS: Cl (0) → +1 in HClO/ClO⁻ (oxidised) and Cl (0) → −1 in HCl/Cl⁻ (reduced). Must state "disproportionation" not just "redox".

3. Jan 2024 Q24(b)(iii) (2 marks) — Disproportionation of NaClO.
MS: 3NaClO → 2NaCl + NaClO₃. Cl from +1 to −1 (reduced) and +1 to +5 (oxidised).

4. Oct 2024 Q19(b)(i) (3 marks) — Cl₂ + H₂O disproportionation.
MS: Same element (Cl) both oxidised (0 → +1 in HOCl) and reduced (0 → −1 in HCl).

5. Oct 2023 Q7 (1 mark) — Identify disproportionation reaction.
MS: S₂O₃²⁻ reaction where S goes from +2 to +4 and 0 simultaneously.

Common mistakes: - Confusing disproportionation with comproportionation (reverse process) - Not stating that the SAME element is both oxidised and reduced - Writing "redox" instead of "disproportionation" (explicitly penalised in Jun 2023 MS) - Not giving the correct oxidation numbers for each species - Not being able to balance disproportionation equations (e.g., 3ClO⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + ClO₃⁻)

### Section 8B — Groups 1 and 2 (Spec 8.11–8.23)

#### 8.11–8.13 Reactivity Trends

Exam-ready definitions:

Group 1 reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is more effectively shielded by more inner electron shells. This means LESS energy is needed to remove the outer electron (lower first ionisation energy), so the metals react more vigorously.

Group 2 reactivity increases down the group for the same reason: larger atomic radius and greater shielding lead to lower ionisation energies, making it easier to lose the two outer electrons.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2024 Q21(d) (6 marks, QWC) — Ca vs Mg reactivity with water.
MS: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂; Ca reacts faster than Mg; Ca has lower ionisation energy; Ca(OH)₂ more soluble → darker blue / higher pH.

2. Jan 2024 Q21(c)(i) (2 marks) — Observations of Mg(NO₃)₂ thermal decomposition.
MS: Two from: brown gas (NO₂), bubbles, solid melts, indicator turns red.

3. Jun 2023 Q10 (1 mark) — Why Na⁺ forms peroxide but Li⁺ does not.
MS: Larger ionic radius of Na⁺ → lower charge density → polarises O₂²⁻ less → stabilises peroxide. Li⁺ has too high charge density.

Common mistakes: - Saying reactivity INCREASES up the group - Confusing the reason (must mention ionisation energy AND distance/shielding) - Forgetting that Group 2 reactions with cold water are slow (Mg barely reacts), but steam reactions are vigorous

#### 8.14–8.17 Thermal Decomposition

Exam-ready definition:

Thermal decomposition is the breaking down of a compound into simpler substances when heated. For Group 2 compounds, thermal stability INCREASES down the group. This is because the M²⁺ ion gets larger down the group, decreasing its charge density and polarising power. The larger cation polarises the anion less, so less distortion of the electron cloud occurs and more energy is needed to break the bonds.

Polarising power explanation chain (high-value for QWC): 1. M²⁺ ionic radius increases down Group 2 2. Charge density (charge/size ratio) decreases 3. Polarising power decreases 4. The cation distorts/polarises the anion (e.g., CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻) less 5. The O–C or O–N bonds within the anion are weakened less 6. More energy is required to decompose the compound 7. Thermal stability increases

Thermal decomposition products:

Compound Type Group 1 (general) Group 2 (general) Li / Be (exceptions)

Carbonates M₂CO₃ → M₂O + CO₂ MCO₃ → MO + CO₂ Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂

Nitrates MNO₃ → MNO₂ + ½O₂ M(NO₃)₂ → MO + 2NO₂ + ½O₂ 4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂

Hydroxides Generally do NOT decompose (except LiOH) M(OH)₂ → MO + H₂O LiOH → Li₂O + H₂O

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2023 Q21 (6 marks, QWC) — Thermal stability of Group 1 and 2 nitrates.
MS indicative points: (IP1) Stability increases down Group 2; (IP2) Ionic radius increases / polarising power decreases; (IP3) N–O bond breaks less easily; (IP4) LiNO₃ decomposes like Group 2; (IP5) NaNO₃ equation → NaNO₂ + O₂; (IP6) Mg(NO₃)₂ equation → MgO + NO₂ + O₂.

2. Jan 2024 Q21(c)(ii) (3 marks) — Why Mg(NO₃)₂ is LESS thermally stable than Ca(NO₃)₂.
MS: Mg²⁺ smaller → higher charge density → more polarising → N–O bonds weakened more → less energy to break → decomposes more easily. Three linked points needed.

3. Jun 2024 Q6 (1 mark) — Thermal decomposition of LiNO₃ and Ca(NO₃)₂.
MS: Both give oxide + NO₂ + O₂ (Li behaves like Group 2).

4. Oct 2024 Q20(e) (6 marks, QWC) — Diagonal relationship Li/Mg (nitrate decomposition).
MS: 4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂ and 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂ (both give NO₂). NaNO₃ → NaNO₂ + ½O₂ (no NO₂). Mg²⁺/Li⁺ smaller than Na⁺ → greater charge density → polarise nitrate more → weaken N–O bond.

5. Jun 2023 Q12 (1 mark) — Mass of Mg(NO₃)₂ from gas volume.
MS: 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂ + O₂ (5 mol gas per 2 mol nitrate); n(gas) = 1200/24000; mass = 2.97 g.

Common mistakes: - Getting Group 1 nitrate products wrong (NaNO₃ → NaNO₂ + O₂, NOT oxide + NO₂) - Forgetting LiNO₃ is the EXCEPTION (decomposes like Group 2) - Saying thermal stability DECREASES down the group - Not using the polarising power argument chain (ionic radius → charge density → polarising power → bond weakening) - Wrong number of products or unbalanced equations for nitrates

#### 8.18–8.20 Solubility Trends

Exam-ready definitions:

Group 2 hydroxides: Solubility INCREASES down the group. Mg(OH)₂ is insoluble (forms a white ppt), Ca(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ is soluble.

Group 2 sulfates: Solubility DECREASES down the group. MgSO₄ is soluble, CaSO₄ is sparingly soluble, BaSO₄ is insoluble (forms a white ppt).

Group 2 carbonates: All are INSOLUBLE. Decompose on heating to give the oxide and CO₂.

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Oct 2023 Q9 (1 mark) — Which property decreases down Group 2?
MS: Solubility of sulfates DECREASES. (Other options — atomic radius and reactivity INCREASE; thermal stability INCREASES.)

2. Oct 2023 Q20(b)(ii) (2 marks) — Sr(OH)₂ vs Ca(OH)₂ solubility effect on titre.
MS: Sr(OH)₂ is MORE soluble than Ca(OH)₂ (hydroxides increase in solubility down Group 2) → higher concentration in saturated solution → greater titre value.

3. Oct 2024 Q4 (1 mark) — True statement about Group 2.
MS: First IE of Mg > Ca (correct). Ca(OH)₂ is MORE soluble (not less); MgCO₃ does decompose.

4. Oct 2023 Q20(b)(i) (4 marks) — Calculate solubility of Ca(OH)₂ in g dm⁻³.
MS: n(HCl) = 18.95 × 10⁻³ × 0.0500; n(Ca(OH)₂) = ½ × n(HCl) (in 25 cm³); scale to 1 dm³; m = 0.01895 × 74.1 = 1.40 g dm⁻³.

Common mistakes: - Getting the hydroxide trend direction WRONG (it INCREASES down the group) - Getting the sulfate trend direction WRONG (it DECREASES down the group) - Confusing the two trends - Forgetting that BaSO₄ is the classic test for sulfate ions (white ppt, insoluble in acid)

#### 8.21–8.23 Flame Tests and Qualitative Analysis

Exam-ready definition:

Flame tests are used to identify Group 1 and Group 2 metal ions. When a compound containing the metal ion is placed in a Bunsen flame, the heat excites the electrons to higher energy levels. When the electrons fall back to lower levels, they emit light of characteristic wavelengths (colours). Different metals have different gaps between energy levels, so they emit different colours.

Flame test colours:

Ion Flame Colour

Li⁺ Crimson / red

Na⁺ Yellow

K⁺ Lilac (view through cobalt glass)

Ca²⁺ Orange-red / brick-red

Sr²⁺ Red

Ba²⁺ Green

Qualitative tests:

Test Observation Ion Identified

Add dilute HCl → BaCl₂(aq) White ppt, insoluble in dilute acid SO₄²⁻ (sulfate)

Add AgNO₃(aq) White ppt (Cl⁻), cream ppt (Br⁻), yellow ppt (I⁻) Halides

Add NaOH + warm Damp red litmus turns blue NH₄⁺ (ammonium)

Add dilute acid Effervescence, CO₂ turns limewater cloudy CO₃²⁻/HCO₃⁻ (carbonate/bicarbonate)

Flame test See colours above Group 1 and 2 cations

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jun 2024 Q7 (1 mark) — Flame test colours explained.
MS: Different gaps between electronic energy levels → different wavelengths of light emitted.

2. Jun 2024 Q8 (1 mark) — Identify compound from AgNO₃ test (white ppt) + red flame.
MS: Strontium chloride (red flame = Sr; white ppt with Ag⁺ = Cl⁻).

3. Jan 2023 Q9 (1 mark) — Identify compound from red flame + white ppt with K₂SO₄.
MS: Sr(NO₃)₂ (red flame = Sr/Li; insoluble sulfate → Ba or Sr; Ba gives green flame).

4. Jan 2024 Q21(b)(iii) (1 mark) — Flame test colour of Ca.
MS: Orange-red / brick-red. NOT crimson, scarlet, or magenta.

5. Oct 2024 Q5 (1 mark) — Identify compound from red flame + colourless acidic gas on heating.
MS: CaCO₃ (red flame = Ca; CO₂ gas from carbonate decomposition).

Common mistakes: - Confusing flame colours (especially red/crimson vs brick-red, and lilac vs purple) - Saying "it turns the flame red" instead of giving the specific colour - Forgetting to view K⁺ through cobalt glass to mask Na⁺ - Confusing Ca (brick-red) with Sr (red) and Li (crimson)

### Section 8C — Group 7 (Spec 8.24–8.28)

#### 8.24–8.25 Group 7 Trends

Exam-ready definitions:

Reactivity as oxidising agents DECREASES down Group 7 because atomic radius increases, shielding increases, and the ability to attract electrons (electronegativity) decreases. This means the halogen molecules become less able to gain an electron and act as oxidising agents.

Displacement reactions: A more reactive halogen (higher up Group 7) will displace a less reactive halogen from its halide salt solution. E.g., Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.

Trend summary:

Property Direction down Group 7

Atomic radius INCREASES

Electronegativity DECREASES

Reactivity (oxidising power) DECREASES

Boiling temperature INCREASES (more electrons → stronger London forces)

Bond enthalpy (H–X) DECREASES (bond gets weaker, longer)

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2024 Q12 (1 mark) — Group 7 trends.
MS: Boiling temp ↑, electronegativity ↓, oxidising power ↓ (all three simultaneously).

2. Jun 2024 Q12 (1 mark) — Why b.p. increases down Group 7.
MS: More electrons → stronger London forces.

3. Jun 2023 Q8 (1 mark) — Which halogen displacement reaction would NOT occur?
MS: F₂ cannot be displaced by At₂ (F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent).

4. Jan 2024 Q7 (1 mark) — Which equation shows oxidation of a Group 7 element?
MS: Br₂ + F₂ → 2BrF (Br oxidised from 0 to +1).

Common mistakes: - Saying reactivity INCREASES down Group 7 (it DECREASES as oxidising agents) - Confusing "reactivity" — halogens get LESS reactive down the group (opposite to Groups 1 and 2) - Explaining b.p. increase as "stronger covalent bonds" (it is intermolecular London forces)

#### 8.26 Reactions of Halide Salts with Concentrated Sulfuric Acid

Exam-ready definitions:

When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid halides, it acts as both an acid (proton donor) and an oxidising agent. With chloride, only acid-base reaction occurs (producing HCl). With bromide, H₂SO₄ is reduced to SO₂. With iodide, H₂SO₄ is reduced further to S and/or H₂S.

Products with conc. H₂SO₄:

Halide Acid-base product Redox products Observations

NaCl(s) HCl(g) None (Cl⁻ not strong enough reducing agent) White fumes (HCl), no redox

NaBr(s) HBr(g) Br₂(l/s), SO₂(g), H₂O(l) Red-brown fumes (Br₂), colourless gas (SO₂)

NaI(s) HI(g) I₂(s), S(s), H₂S(g), SO₂(g) Black solid (I₂), yellow solid (S), colourless gas

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jan 2023 Q12 (1 mark) — Conc. H₂SO₄ + halide: greatest moles of halide oxidised.
MS: 8KI + 9H₂SO₄ → 8mol I⁻ oxidised to I₂, H₂SO₄ reduced to H₂S. (More halide oxidised than with Br⁻.)

2. Oct 2023 Q8 (1 mark) — NaBr + conc H₂SO₄ products.
MS: Br₂, HBr, SO₂. Br⁻ is moderate reducing agent → reduces H₂SO₄ to SO₂ but NOT to S or H₂S.

3. Oct 2024 Q9 (1 mark) — Conc. H₂SO₄ + solid KCl.
MS: KHSO₄ (conc. H₂SO₄ acts as acid, not oxidising agent, with chloride).

Common mistakes: - Thinking ALL halides reduce H₂SO₄ (Cl⁻ does NOT — not a strong enough reducing agent) - Getting the wrong reduction products for Br⁻ (only to SO₂, not S or H₂S) - Forgetting the acid-base reaction occurs FIRST for all halides - Confusing the colours of the products

#### 8.27 Halide Ion Tests (Silver Nitrate)

Exam-ready definition:

Silver nitrate test: Add dilute nitric acid (to remove carbonate/sulfite interferences), then add silver nitrate solution. The colour of the precipitate identifies the halide ion: - Cl⁻: White precipitate (AgCl) — soluble in dilute NH₃ - Br⁻: Cream precipitate (AgBr) — soluble in concentrated NH₃ only - I⁻: Yellow precipitate (AgI) — insoluble in NH₃

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Oct 2023 Q19(a)(i) (1 mark) — Colour of AgI precipitate.
MS: Yellow (accept "pale yellow"). AgCl dissolves in excess NH₃; AgI does not.

2. Oct 2023 Q19(a)(ii) (3 marks) — Calculate % KI in a KI/KCl mixture.
MS: M(AgI) = 234.8; n(AgI) = 0.162/234.8 = 6.90 × 10⁻⁴ mol; m(KI) = 6.90 × 10⁻⁴ × 166 = 0.1145 g; % = (0.1145/2.49) × 100 = 4.60%.

Note: Jun 2024 Q8 (AgNO₃ white ppt + red flame → SrCl₂) is listed under §8.21–8.23 (Flame Tests & Qualitative Analysis) above — see there for the full MS.

Common mistakes: - Confusing cream and yellow precipitate colours - Forgetting to add dilute HNO₃ first - Not knowing the ammonia solubility differences (used to confirm halide) - Confusing Ag⁺ test (for halides) with Ba²⁺ test (for sulfates)

#### 8.28 Halogen Extraction and Solvent Extraction

Exam-ready definitions:

Halogens can be extracted from aqueous solution using a non-polar organic solvent (e.g., cyclohexane). The halogen is more soluble in the organic solvent because the London forces between the halogen and the solvent are similar in strength to the London forces in the halogen itself, whereas the halogen cannot break the strong hydrogen bonds in water.

Colours of halogens in organic solvents:

Halogen In water In organic solvent (cyclohexane/hexane)

Cl₂ Pale green Pale green / yellow-green

Br₂ Orange / red-brown Orange / red-brown

I₂ Yellow / brown Purple / violet / pink

Real exam examples with MS answers:

1. Jun 2024 Q14 (1 mark) — Colours of cyclohexane + aqueous iodine layers.
MS: Lower layer = yellow/brown (aqueous, density >1.0); Upper layer = purple (cyclohexane, density <1.0).

2. Oct 2023 Q19(c) (2 marks) — Colours of aqueous and hexane layers after Cl₂ + KI.
MS: Aqueous layer: yellow (accept orange/brown/straw/colourless). Hexane layer: purple/pink/violet (accept lilac).

3. Oct 2024 Q10 (1 mark) — Iodine in cyclohexane colour.
MS: Purple. (Blue-black is starch-iodine complex; brown/yellow is aqueous iodine.)

Common mistakes: - Confusing aqueous and organic layer colours (especially for iodine) - Not knowing which layer is upper/lower (based on density: water >1.0, organic <1.0) - Saying "blue-black" for iodine in organic solvent (that is the starch-iodine complex)

### Core Practical Definitions (CP3 and CP4)

#### CP3 — Volumetric Analysis (Titrations)

Key definition:

A titration is a quantitative analytical technique in which a solution of known concentration (from the burette) is gradually added to a solution of unknown concentration (in the conical flask) until the reaction is complete, as indicated by a colour change in the indicator.

Indicator colours (exam-tested):

Indicator Acid Base Colour change (acid → alkali) Colour change (alkali → acid)

Methyl orange Red (pH < 3.1) Yellow (pH > 4.4) Red → orange Yellow → orange

Phenolphthalein Colourless (pH < 8.3) Pink (pH > 10.0) Colourless → pink Pink → colourless

Real exam examples:

1. Jun 2024 Q11(a) (1 mark) — Methyl orange colour change in H₂SO₄ + KOH.
MS: Red to orange (acid is red; endpoint is orange). NOT red to yellow.

2. Jun 2022 Q9(a) (1 mark) — Methyl orange colour change.
MS: Yellow → orange.

Common mistakes: - Saying methyl orange changes from red to YELLOW (endpoint is ORANGE, not yellow) - Saying phenolphthalein changes from pink to red (it goes pink → COLOURLESS) - Forgetting which indicator is used for which titration type - Confusing the direction of the colour change

#### CP4 — Identification of Group 2 Cations and Group 7 Anions

Key definition:

Qualitative analysis involves using chemical tests to identify ions present in a solution. For Group 2 cations, flame tests and precipitation reactions (with NaOH, H₂SO₄) are used. For Group 7 anions, silver nitrate (after acidification) and solvent extraction are used.
