The general shape (peak for transition state, lower level for products since exothermic) Different in the catalysed diagram: 5. The peak height / activation energy (Eₐ) — the catalysed reaction has a lower activation energy than the uncatalysed reaction

Mark Scheme

1 mark per correct "same" feature (max 2 marks for any 2 correct features)

2 marks: the different feature — lower peak / lower Eₐ in catalysed diagram Accept for "Same": "Same reactants and products"; "same direction of enthalpy change"; "both are exothermic."

Q51 SYN §9.6 4 marks · ~8 min

A student investigates the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Without a manganese(IV) oxide catalyst, the reaction takes 240 s to produce 50 cm³ of oxygen. With MnO₂ present, the same volume is produced in 45 s. (a) Calculate how many times faster the catalysed reaction is. (1 mark) (b) Describe and explain two differences between the reaction profile for the uncatalysed reaction and the catalysed reaction. (3 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) 240/45 = 5.3 times faster (1 mark). (b) Two from: - The catalysed profile has a lower peak (lower activation energy) / the uncatalysed profile has a higher peak - Both profiles have the same starting (reactant) energy level - Both profiles have the same ending (product) energy level - ΔH is the same for both reactions - The catalysed pathway represents an alternative reaction route with lower activation energy

Mark Scheme

(a) 1 mark: 5.3 (accept range 5–5.4) (b) 1 mark per correct difference (max 2) + 1 mark for explanation of at least one difference (max 3 marks total)

### Spec Point 9.7 — Catalysts and Sustainability

Q52 QFR §9.7 1 mark · ~2 min

Give one reason, in terms of energy, why using a catalyst makes an industrial process more sustainable.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Less energy needed (accept: lower temperature required / less fuel burned / reduced CO₂ emissions).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: less energy / lower temperature / reduced CO₂ emissions

Common Error

"The catalyst lowers the activation energy" is NOT a sustainability argument — it is the mechanism by which a catalyst works. "The catalyst is not used up" is also NOT a sustainability argument — it is a general property of catalysts.

Q53 TDC §9.7 2 marks · ~4 min

State two reasons, other than "the catalyst can be reused", why the use of a catalyst improves the sustainability of an industrial chemical process.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Any two of: - Less energy needed (to heat the reaction mixture to a high temperature) - A lower temperature can be used (while still achieving an acceptable rate) - Reduced CO₂ emissions (because less fuel is burned for heating) Common error to avoid: "The catalyst lowers the activation energy" or "the catalyst is not used up" are NOT sustainability arguments — they describe how a catalyst works, not why it is sustainable.

Mark Scheme

1 mark per valid sustainability reason (max 2) Accept Alternatives: "Reduced carbon footprint"; "lower energy consumption"; "fewer greenhouse gas emissions."

Q54 WTE §9.7 2 marks · ~4 min

When asked about the sustainability benefits of using a catalyst in an industrial process, a student writes: "Catalysts are sustainable because they are not used up in the reaction and can be reused." This answer would not receive credit for the sustainability argument. Explain why and give the correct sustainability reasoning.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The student's answer describes a general property of catalysts, not a sustainability argument (1 mark). The correct sustainability benefits are that using a catalyst allows the reaction to proceed at a lower temperature, which means less energy is needed, leading to reduced CO₂ emissions from burning fossil fuels (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: identifies that "not used up" is a property, not a sustainability argument

1 mark: correct sustainability reasoning — less energy / lower temperature / reduced CO₂ Exam Note: This is a high-frequency exam trap. Markers are specifically instructed not to award marks for "catalyst is not used up" or "catalyst can be reused" in sustainability questions.

Q55 EXP §9.7 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain how the use of a catalyst in an industrial process can provide a sustainability advantage. Do NOT mention that the catalyst is reused.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a lower temperature can be used (1 mark). Less energy is needed to maintain the reaction conditions, which reduces CO₂ emissions from fossil fuel combustion used to generate the energy required (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: lower temperature can be used

1 mark: less energy needed / reduced CO₂ emissions Note: The question explicitly forbids mentioning reuse. If a student still writes about reuse, it will not score, even if their sustainability argument is otherwise correct.

Q56 SYN §9.7 3 marks · ~6 min

A student is asked: "Suggest why the use of a catalyst makes an industrial process more sustainable." The student writes: "The catalyst can be reused, and it lowers the activation energy." Explain why neither part of this answer would score the mark, and give the correct answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

"The catalyst can be reused" is a true statement but it is not a sustainability argument — it describes how the catalyst functions, not its environmental benefit. "It lowers the activation energy" is the mechanism by which the catalyst works, not the sustainability benefit. The correct answer is: less energy needed (because a lower temperature can be used) / lower temperature required / less fuel burned / reduced CO₂ emissions / reduced carbon footprint.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: explains why "reused" does not score (property, not sustainability)

1 mark: explains why "lowers Eₐ" does not score (mechanism, not sustainability)

1 mark: correct sustainability answer (less energy / lower temperature / reduced CO₂)

### Spec Point 9.8 — Maxwell–Boltzmann Distribution and Catalysts

Q57 DIA §9.8 3 marks · ~6 min

Sketch a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve for a sample of gas at a fixed temperature. On your diagram, show and label the activation energy (Eₐ) without a catalyst and the activation energy with a catalyst. Shade the area representing the proportion of molecules with energy ≥ Eₐ with the catalyst.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Correctly labelled axes: energy on the x-axis and number/fraction of molecules on the y-axis

A single Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starting at the origin, peaking, and asymptotic to the energy axis

Two vertical lines labelled Eₐ(uncat) and Eₐ(cat), with Eₐ(cat) positioned to the left of Eₐ(uncat) (lower value)

Shaded area under the curve to the right of Eₐ(cat), representing the greater proportion of molecules with energy ≥ the lower activation energy

The curve itself is NOT redrawn or shifted — only the Eₐ line moves

Mark Scheme

1 mark: correctly drawn M-B curve (origin, peak, asymptotic) with labelled axes

1 mark: two Eₐ lines, Eₐ(cat) to the LEFT of Eₐ(uncat), both labelled

1 mark: shaded area beyond Eₐ(cat) showing greater proportion of molecules can react Critical Error: If the student draws TWO curves of different shapes, they lose the first mark. The curve must NOT change when a catalyst is added.

Q58 DIA §9.8 3 marks · ~6 min

Sketch two Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curves on the same axes for the same reaction mixture at the same temperature, one without a catalyst and one with a catalyst. Label the activation energy for each.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Both curves are identical (same shape, same peak position, same area under the curve) (1 mark)

A vertical line (or clearly marked position on the x-axis) labelled Eₐ (uncatalysed) is drawn further to the right (1 mark)

A second vertical line labelled Eₐ (catalysed) is drawn further to the left (lower activation energy) and the area under the curve beyond this line is shaded (or otherwise indicated) to show that a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ the (lower) activation energy (1 mark) Note: The curve itself does NOT change when a catalyst is added — only the activation energy line moves to the left.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: both curves identical (same shape, peak, area)

1 mark: Eₐ(uncat) further right than Eₐ(cat), both labelled

1 mark: shaded area showing greater proportion beyond Eₐ(cat)

Common Error

The question asks to "sketch two curves" — but they must be identical. If a student draws two visibly different curves (e.g. one taller, one shifted), they lose marks because this implies the temperature or number of molecules has changed, which it has not.

Q59 WTE §9.8 2 marks · ~4 min

A student is asked to draw a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve for a reaction mixture before and after a catalyst is added. The student draws two curves of different shapes and labels the catalysed curve with a higher peak. (i) What mistake has the student made? (ii) What should they have drawn instead?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) The student has changed the shape of the distribution curve / drawn a different curve for the catalyst. (ii) The distribution curve should remain unchanged; only the activation energy line should shift to the left (to a lower value) to show that a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ activation energy.

Mark Scheme

(i) 1 mark: identifies the error — changed the curve shape / drew a different curve

(ii) 1 mark: correct approach — single curve, only Eₐ line moves left

Common Error

Students often draw the catalysed curve as taller/narrower (resembling a lower-temperature distribution). This suggests they think the catalyst "concentrates" the energy — it does not.

Q60 TDC §9.8 3 marks · ~6 min

Compare the effects of increasing temperature and adding a catalyst on a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution diagram. In your answer, you must refer to what happens to (i) the shape of the distribution curve, (ii) the position of the activation energy line, and (iii) the proportion of molecules that can react.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) Shape of the curve: Increasing temperature changes the curve — the peak is lower and shifted to the right, with the same total area. Adding a catalyst leaves the distribution curve completely unchanged (1 mark). (ii) Activation energy line: Increasing temperature does not move the Eₐ line — it stays in the same position. Adding a catalyst moves the Eₐ line to the left (to a lower value) (1 mark). (iii) Proportion of molecules that can react: In both cases, a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ activation energy and the rate of reaction increases. However, the reason differs: for temperature the distribution has shifted so more molecules exceed the same threshold; for a catalyst the threshold itself has lowered so more of the same distribution exceeds it (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: (i) temperature changes curve; catalyst does not change curve

1 mark: (ii) temperature does not move Eₐ; catalyst moves Eₐ to the left

1 mark: (iii) both increase proportion with E ≥ Eₐ, but for different reasons This is a T3 question because it requires the student to integrate two concepts and make a nuanced comparison. It tests understanding at the highest level.

### Spec Point 9.9 — Dynamic Equilibrium

Q61 QFR §9.9 2 marks · ~4 min

State two conditions that must be satisfied for a dynamic equilibrium to be established in a reversible reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1. The reaction must take place in a closed system (so that no reactants or products can escape) and 2. The rate of the forward reaction must equal the rate of the backward reaction.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: closed system

1 mark: forward rate equals backward rate

Common Error

Students often write "the concentrations of reactants and products are equal" — this is incorrect. The concentrations are constant (unchanging), not necessarily equal.

Q62 QFR §9.9 1 mark · ~2 min

State what is meant by the term dynamic equilibrium.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a closed system where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of all reactants and products remain constant.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: reference to closed system, equal forward/backward rates, and constant concentrations (all three elements ideally, but "equal rates and constant concentrations" is sufficient for the mark)

Q63 TDC §9.9 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes: "At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of all reactants and products are equal, which is why the macroscopic properties are constant." State whether the first part of this statement is correct and explain your reasoning.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The statement is incorrect. At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are constant, not necessarily equal. The forward rate equals the backward rate, so there is no net change in concentration, but the actual concentration values depend on the equilibrium position.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: identifies the statement as incorrect

1 mark: explains that concentrations are constant, not equal

Common Error

This is one of the most frequently tested misconceptions. "Constant" means "not changing" — it does NOT mean "the same as each other."

Q64 TDC §9.9 3 marks · ~6 min

Consider the following three statements about dynamic equilibrium. For each statement, state whether it is true or false, and give a brief explanation. - Statement 1: "At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are equal." - Statement 2: "At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction." - Statement 3: "Dynamic equilibrium can be established in an open beaker."

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Statement 1: False. At equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are constant, but they are not necessarily equal.

Statement 2: True. This is the defining condition of dynamic equilibrium — the forward and backward rates are equal.

Statement 3: False. Dynamic equilibrium can only be established in a closed system where no reactants or products can escape.

Mark Scheme

1 mark per correct true/false + explanation (max 3 marks)

Q65 TDC §9.9 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the backward reaction: (i) At dynamic equilibrium. (ii) Immediately after the concentration of a reactant is increased in a system at equilibrium.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) At dynamic equilibrium: rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction. (ii) Immediately after increasing reactant concentration: rate of forward reaction is greater than rate of backward reaction (the system is no longer at equilibrium and will shift to the right to oppose the change).

Mark Scheme

(i) 1 mark: forward rate equals backward rate

(ii) 1 mark: forward rate greater than backward rate (system no longer at equilibrium) Accept for (ii): "Forward rate increases but backward rate stays the same initially, so forward > backward."

Q66 EXP §9.9 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why dynamic equilibrium can only be achieved in a closed system.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

In a closed system, no reactants or products can enter or leave. If the system were open, products could escape or reactants could be added, meaning the forward and backward rates would never become equal and concentrations would not remain constant.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: closed system prevents matter entering or leaving

1 mark: in an open system, rates would not become equal / concentrations would not be constant

Q67 EXP §9.9 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain what is meant by a dynamic equilibrium in a closed system. Why does a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium never go to completion?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

In a dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions occur at equal rates in a closed system, so the concentrations of all species remain constant (1 mark). The reaction never goes to completion because the products can react in the reverse direction (1 mark); as product concentration increases, the backward rate increases until it equals the forward rate, at which point equilibrium is established and no further net change occurs (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: forward and backward reactions occur at equal rates in a closed system

1 mark: products can react in reverse direction

1 mark: backward rate increases as product concentration increases until rates are equal

Q68 STE §9.9 2 marks · ~4 min

At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of all reactants and products remain constant. Does this mean the reaction has stopped? Explain your reasoning.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

No, the reaction has not stopped. At dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions are both still occurring but at the same rate. The concentrations are constant because the rate of formation of each substance equals its rate of consumption — this is why the equilibrium is described as dynamic.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: No / reaction has not stopped

1 mark: both forward and backward reactions still occurring at the same rate Accept Alternatives: "The word 'dynamic' tells us the reactions are still happening"; "individual molecules are still reacting but there is no overall change."

### Spec Point 9.10 — Le Chatelier's Principle

Q69 QFR §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

State Le Chatelier's principle.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

If a system at dynamic equilibrium is subjected to a change, the equilibrium position shifts to oppose (counteract) the imposed change.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: system at equilibrium is subjected to a change

1 mark: equilibrium shifts to oppose / counteract the change Accept Alternatives: "The equilibrium position moves in the direction that tends to reduce the effect of the change."

Q70 STE §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

State the effect of increasing the total pressure on the equilibrium position for each of the following reactions: (i) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (ii) H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) Equilibrium shifts to the right / moves towards the product side (fewer gas moles) (1 mark). (ii) No effect / equilibrium position unchanged (equal gas moles on both sides) (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

(i) 1 mark: shifts right / towards products (with reference to fewer gas moles)

(ii) 1 mark: no change / no effect (with reference to equal gas moles)

Common Error

Students sometimes say (ii) shifts left or right. With equal moles (2 mol → 2 mol), pressure has NO effect on the equilibrium position.

Q71 TDC §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

A student states: "Increasing the pressure of any gaseous equilibrium mixture will always increase the yield of products." State whether this is true or false and justify your answer with reference to the number of gas moles on each side of the equilibrium.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

False. Increasing the pressure causes the equilibrium to shift towards the side with fewer gas moles. The yield of products only increases if the product side has fewer gas moles than the reactant side. If the product side has more gas moles, increasing pressure decreases the yield of products.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: false

1 mark: justification — shift is to side with fewer gas moles, not always to products

Q72 TDC §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

A student states: "Decreasing the temperature of any equilibrium reaction will always increase the yield of product." Evaluate this statement.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The statement is incorrect. Decreasing the temperature only increases the yield of product when the forward reaction is exothermic. If the forward reaction is endothermic, decreasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left (towards reactants), which decreases the yield of product.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: identifies statement as incorrect

1 mark: explains with reference to exothermic vs endothermic direction

Q73 TDC §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the effect of decreasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield for the following two reactions. Reaction 1: SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) ⇌ SO₃(g) ΔH = −192 kJ mol⁻¹ Reaction 2: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

For Reaction 1: yield of SO₃ increases / equilibrium shifts to the right (exothermic direction) (1 mark). For Reaction 2: yield of H₂ decreases / equilibrium shifts to the left (exothermic direction) (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: Reaction 1 — yield increases (shifts right / exothermic direction)

1 mark: Reaction 2 — yield decreases (shifts left / exothermic direction)

Common Error

Students may say "decreasing temperature decreases yield for both reactions." This shows they have not applied Le Chatelier's principle correctly — the direction of the temperature shift depends on the enthalpy change of the reaction.

Q74 STE §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

For the equilibrium CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), state the effect of increasing the total pressure on (i) the yield of hydrogen, (ii) the rate of reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) The yield of hydrogen decreases / equilibrium shifts to the left (side with fewer gas moles) (1 mark). (ii) The rate of reaction increases (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

(i) 1 mark: yield decreases (shifts left / 2 mol gas → 4 mol gas on right)

(ii) 1 mark: rate increases Note: Part (ii) tests the distinction between equilibrium position and rate. Increasing pressure ALWAYS increases rate (more collisions) but may increase OR decrease yield depending on gas moles.

Q75 EXP §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

Sodium hydroxide is added to the equilibrium mixture: HCrO₄⁻(aq) ⇌ CrO₄²⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq). Explain the effect on the equilibrium position.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

NaOH reacts with (removes) H⁺ ions (1 mark). The equilibrium shifts to the right to replace (oppose the removal of) H⁺ / to counteract the change (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: H⁺ is removed (by reaction with NaOH / neutralisation)

1 mark: equilibrium shifts right to oppose / to replace H⁺

Common Error

Students may say "NaOH is added so the equilibrium shifts left" — they incorrectly treat NaOH as if it were increasing the concentration of a product. The key is to identify what NaOH reacts WITH (H⁺) and then apply Le Chatelier's principle to the removal of that species.

Q76 EXP §9.10 3 marks · ~6 min

Bleach solution contains two linked equilibria: - Eq.1: ClO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HClO(aq) + OH⁻(aq) - Eq.2: HClO(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) Explain step-by-step why adding an acid such as HCl to bleach can release toxic chlorine gas. In your answer, use Le Chatelier's principle and state which equilibrium shifts and in which direction at each stage.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Adding HCl provides H⁺ ions. For Eq.1, the H⁺ ions react with OH⁻, reducing [OH⁻], so the equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the change, producing more HClO (1 mark). The increased [HClO] and the added H⁺ and Cl⁻ (from HCl) mean that for Eq.2, the equilibrium shifts to the right (to oppose the increase in [HClO], [Cl⁻], and [H⁺]), producing Cl₂(aq) which escapes as toxic Cl₂(g) (1 mark). The system responds through two linked equilibrium shifts driven by the initial addition of acid (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: Eq.1 — H⁺ reacts with OH⁻; equilibrium shifts right; more HClO produced

1 mark: Eq.2 — increased [HClO], [H⁺], [Cl⁻]; equilibrium shifts right; Cl₂ produced

1 mark: linked explanation — initial acid addition drives both shifts

Q77 EXP §9.10 2 marks · ~4 min

The steam-reforming process for hydrogen production involves the equilibrium: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g). Explain why passing excess steam through the reaction mixture increases the yield of hydrogen.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Adding excess steam increases the concentration of H₂O (a reactant) (1 mark). The equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the change, increasing the yield of hydrogen (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: concentration of H₂O increases (excess steam)

1 mark: equilibrium shifts right to oppose → increased H₂ yield

Q78 SYN §9.10 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why increasing the total pressure on a gaseous equilibrium mixture always increases the rate of reaction, but may either increase or decrease the equilibrium yield. Use an example to support your answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Increasing pressure increases the concentration (of gas molecules) (1 mark), so there are more frequent (successful) collisions per unit time, increasing the rate (1 mark). The effect on yield depends on the number of gas moles on each side: e.g. for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) increasing pressure increases yield (shifts to side with fewer gas moles), but for CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g) increasing pressure decreases yield (shifts to side with fewer gas moles / reactant side) (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: increased pressure → increased concentration → increased rate (always)

1 mark: yield depends on gas moles on each side

1 mark: specific example showing both possibilities

Q79 SYN §9.10 4 marks · ~8 min

For the equilibrium PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), where the forward reaction is endothermic: (a) State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium yield of PCl₃. (b) State and explain the effect of increasing the total pressure on the equilibrium yield of PCl₃. (c) State the effect of increasing the temperature on the rate of this reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) The equilibrium yield of PCl₃ increases. The forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (in the endothermic direction) to oppose the change, by Le Chatelier's principle. (b) The equilibrium yield of PCl₃ decreases. There is 1 mol of gas on the left (PCl₅) and 2 mol of gas on the right (PCl₃ + Cl₂). Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (to the left) to oppose the change. (c) The rate of reaction increases because molecules have more kinetic energy and a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ the activation energy.

Mark Scheme

(a) 1 mark: yield increases + explanation (forward endothermic, shift right)

(b) 1 mark: yield decreases + explanation (1 mol → 2 mol gas, shift left)

(c) 1 mark: rate increases + explanation (greater proportion with E ≥ Eₐ)

1 mark: overall quality of explanation and use of Le Chatelier's principle

Q80 SYN §9.10 3 marks · ~6 min

Chlorine reacts with water in a reversible equilibrium: Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HClO(aq) + H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). When aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to this equilibrium mixture, a colour change is observed. Use Le Chatelier's principle to explain the effect of adding sodium hydroxide on the position of this equilibrium.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Sodium hydroxide reacts with / removes H⁺ ions from the equilibrium mixture (by neutralisation) (1 mark). The equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the change / to replace the removed H⁺ (1 mark). More HClO and Cl⁻ are formed / the equilibrium yield of products increases (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: NaOH removes H⁺ (neutralisation)

1 mark: equilibrium shifts right (to oppose / replace H⁺)

1 mark: consequence — more products formed / colour change explained

Q81 SYN §9.10 3 marks · ~6 min

The following equilibria exist in ocean water: CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq) Explain why increasing the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere leads to increased acidity of ocean water. Use Le Chatelier's principle in your answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Increased atmospheric CO₂ leads to more CO₂ dissolving in the ocean, increasing the concentration of CO₂(aq) (1 mark). The first equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the change, increasing the concentration of H₂CO₃(aq). The increased [H₂CO₃] shifts the second equilibrium to the right, increasing [H⁺(aq)] (1 mark). An increase in [H⁺] means the ocean water becomes more acidic / the pH decreases (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: increased CO₂ → more dissolved CO₂(aq)

1 mark: both equilibria shift right (linked explanation)

1 mark: [H⁺] increases → more acidic / lower pH Note: This is a real-world application of Le Chatelier's principle. It links to environmental chemistry and is a common context question.

### Spec Point 9.11 — Industrial Conditions and Compromise

Q82 QFR §9.11 1 mark · ~2 min

State what is meant by the term compromise conditions in the context of an industrial chemical process.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Conditions that are a compromise between the conditions that give the maximum yield (from Le Chatelier's principle) and the conditions that give an acceptable rate (from kinetics) and are economically viable.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: reference to balancing yield and rate / economic viability Accept Alternatives: "Conditions that give an acceptable yield at an economically viable rate."

Q83 STE §9.11 2 marks · ~4 min

For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹), state the effect of increasing the temperature on (i) the yield of ammonia and (ii) the rate of reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) The yield of ammonia decreases because increasing temperature favours the endothermic (backward) reaction (shifts equilibrium to the left) (1 mark). (ii) The rate of reaction increases because a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ the activation energy (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

(i) 1 mark: yield decreases + explanation (endothermic backward favoured / shifts left)

(ii) 1 mark: rate increases + explanation (greater proportion with E ≥ Eₐ)

Common Error

Students may say "yield increases because rate increases." Yield and rate are different concepts — increasing temperature always increases rate but may decrease yield for an exothermic forward reaction.

Q84 CAL §9.11 2 marks · ~4 min

Ethanol is produced industrially by the hydration of ethene: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g). A pressure greater than 7 MPa is recommended for this process. Calculate the total moles of gas on each side of the equilibrium and hence predict and explain the effect of increasing pressure on the yield of ethanol.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Reactants: 1 + 1 = 2 mol gas; Products: 1 mol gas (1 mark). Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right (side with fewer moles of gas) to oppose the change, giving a greater yield of ethanol (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: 2 mol gas on left, 1 mol gas on right

1 mark: increasing pressure shifts right (fewer gas moles) → greater yield

Q85 EXP §9.11 3 marks · ~6 min

The Haber process for the manufacture of ammonia uses the equilibrium: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. The process is operated at approximately 450 °C, not at the lowest possible temperature. Explain why a very low temperature is not used, even though it would give a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A lower temperature would give a higher yield because the forward reaction is exothermic (1 mark). However, at very low temperatures the rate of reaction would be too slow / uneconomically slow (1 mark). A compromise temperature of approximately 450 °C is used to give a reasonable rate of reaction while maintaining an acceptable yield (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: lower temperature → higher yield (exothermic forward reaction)

1 mark: very low temperature → rate too slow / uneconomical

1 mark: compromise temperature gives acceptable yield at reasonable rate

Q86 EXP §9.11 2 marks · ~4 min

In the industrial hydration of ethene to ethanol, the equilibrium conversion at the operating conditions is less than 95%, yet the overall process achieves an ethanol yield of approximately 95%. Explain how this is achieved.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Ethanol and excess water are continuously removed from the reaction mixture by condensation/liquefaction, shifting the equilibrium to the right. Unreacted ethene is recycled back into the reactor, so it is not wasted.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: unreacted ethene is recycled

1 mark: product is continuously removed / shifts equilibrium Accept Alternatives: "The reaction mixture is condensed to separate ethanol and water from unreacted gases, which are then recycled."

Q87 EXP §9.11 3 marks · ~6 min

The reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is exothermic. In the Contact process, a compromise temperature of approximately 450 °C is used rather than room temperature. Explain why this compromise temperature is used, with reference to both the rate of reaction and the equilibrium yield of SO₃.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

At room temperature, the equilibrium yield of SO₃ would be higher (since the forward reaction is exothermic, Le Chatelier's principle predicts that lower temperature shifts equilibrium to the right). However, at room temperature the rate of reaction is too slow for the process to be economically viable. At 450 °C, the equilibrium yield of SO₃ is lower than at room temperature, but the rate of reaction is significantly faster, so the product is produced quickly enough to be economically practical. This represents a compromise between maximising yield and achieving an acceptable rate.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: lower temperature → higher yield (exothermic forward)

1 mark: lower temperature → rate too slow

1 mark: 450 °C is a compromise — reasonable yield at acceptable rate

Q88 SYN §9.11 4 marks · ~8 min

In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia. A typical operating temperature of 450 °C and a pressure of 200 atm are used, even though these conditions do not give the maximum possible yield of ammonia. Explain why these compromise conditions are used rather than the conditions that would give the maximum yield.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia (Le Chatelier's principle).

However, a lower temperature would give an unacceptably slow rate of reaction, making the process uneconomical.

A higher pressure would give a higher equilibrium yield (fewer gas moles on the product side: 4 → 2).

However, very high pressures are expensive to build and maintain (safety risks, energy costs of compressing gases).

The compromise conditions of 450 °C and 200 atm give a reasonable yield at an acceptable rate, while keeping costs manageable.

Any unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled to improve the overall yield.

Mark Scheme

1 mark: lower temperature → higher yield (exothermic forward)

1 mark: lower temperature → rate too slow / uneconomical

1 mark: higher pressure → higher yield (fewer gas moles on right)

1 mark: very high pressures expensive / dangerous; compromise needed

Q89 SYN §9.11 4 marks · ~8 min

Ethanol is manufactured by the hydration of ethene: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g) ΔH is negative. In industry, a temperature of 300 °C and a pressure of 7 MPa are used, rather than the conditions that would give the maximum theoretical yield. Explain the reasoning behind this compromise, stating the effect of both temperature and pressure on the rate of reaction and on the equilibrium yield of ethanol.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Temperature: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield (shifts right). However, at low temperatures the rate of reaction is too slow, making the process economically unviable. A moderate temperature (300 °C) gives an acceptable rate while maintaining a reasonable yield (2 marks).

Pressure: There are fewer moles of gas on the product side (2 mol → 1 mol), so a higher pressure gives a higher equilibrium yield (shifts right) and a higher rate (more concentrated gas particles). However, very high pressures (> 7 MPa) require expensive, reinforced plant and equipment. A pressure of 7 MPa is a compromise between yield, rate, and cost (2 marks).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: lower temp → higher yield (exothermic)

1 mark: lower temp → rate too slow; 300 °C is compromise

1 mark: higher pressure → higher yield (2 mol → 1 mol gas) and higher rate

1 mark: very high pressures too expensive; 7 MPa is compromise

Q90 SYN §9.11 5 marks · ~10 min

In the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹, an iron catalyst is used at approximately 450 °C and 200 atm rather than at room temperature and 1 atm. Explain the reasons for these chosen conditions. Include a sustainability argument for the use of the catalyst.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Higher temperature (450 °C) increases the rate of reaction but decreases the equilibrium yield of ammonia (forward reaction is exothermic); 450 °C is a compromise between acceptable rate and acceptable yield (1 mark). Higher pressure (200 atm) increases both the rate and the equilibrium yield of ammonia (fewer gas moles on product side) (1 mark). However, very high pressures are expensive and dangerous (1 mark). The catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, allowing a lower temperature to be used than would otherwise be needed for an acceptable rate (1 mark); this means less energy is required, reducing CO₂ emissions and making the process more sustainable (1 mark).

Mark Scheme

1 mark: temperature compromise — rate vs yield

1 mark: higher pressure → higher rate and yield (fewer gas moles)

1 mark: very high pressures are expensive/dangerous

1 mark: catalyst allows lower temperature to be used

1 mark: sustainability — less energy / reduced CO₂ emissions

## Chapter 2.8 — Kinetics and Equilibria

WCH12 · Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry · Unit 2

Spec Points 9.1–9.117 Papers AnalysedJun 2022 – Oct 2024

Average ~12 marks per paper — collision theory, Boltzmann, Le Chatelier dominate

### Definitions

#### Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12 — Spec Points 9.1–9.11

### How to Use This Guide

This file contains every definition, key fact, and exam-critical statement for Chapter 2.8. Each definition is presented in the exact wording expected by Edexcel mark schemes, followed by common pitfalls and real exam examples drawn from 7 past papers (Jun 2022 – Oct 2024). Chapter 2.8 averages 10.3 marks per paper (12.9%) — it is underrepresented, meaning every mark you secure here counts disproportionately.

### 9.1 Collision Theory

#### Core Definition

Collision theory: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with sufficient energy (equal to or greater than the activation energy) and with the correct orientation.

#### Key Sub-points

Not all collisions lead to reaction. Only those that satisfy BOTH the energy requirement AND the orientation requirement are "successful" or "effective" collisions.

The rate of reaction depends on: frequency of collisions and proportion of collisions that are successful.

#### Effects on Rate (Exam-Critical Table)

Change Effect on Collision Frequency Effect on Proportion of Successful Collisions Effect on Rate

Increase concentration (solution) ↑ (more particles per unit volume) No change ↑

Increase pressure (gas) ↑ (more particles per unit volume) No change ↑

Increase temperature ↑ (particles move faster) ↑ (more particles have E ≥ Eₐ) ↑↑

Increase surface area (solid) ↑ (more exposed particles) No change ↑

#### Exam Traps — Collision Theory

Trap Example from Papers What to Remember

"Increasing temperature increases the energy of collisions" Jun 2024 Q15(a) — Eₐ does NOT change Temperature does NOT change activation energy. It changes the proportion of molecules above Eₐ.

"Increasing pressure increases energy of particles" Jun 2024 Q15(b) (via MCQ) Pressure only increases collision frequency, not energy.

Confusing rate with equilibrium position Jan 2024 Q14 — catalysts affect rate only Increasing T/pressure may increase rate but DECREASE equilibrium yield (and vice versa).

#### Real Exam Questions

Jun 2024 Q15(a): "For which values does the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution change when temperature is increased?" Answer: Eₘₒdₑ and Eₘₑₐₙ change; Eₐ stays the same.

Jun 2024 Q15(b): "For which values change when pressure is decreased?" Answer: None — Eₐ, Eₘₒdₑ, and Eₘₑₐₙ are all unchanged. Decreasing pressure reduces the total number of molecules (lower concentration) but does NOT change Eₐ, Eₘₒdₑ, or Eₘₑₐₙ — these depend only on temperature.

### 9.2 Activation Energy

#### Core Definition

Activation energy (Eₐ): The minimum energy that particles must have for a collision to be successful (to result in a reaction).

#### Essential Details

Eₐ is an intrinsic property of a reaction — it does not change with temperature, pressure, or concentration.

A lower activation energy means a faster reaction (more molecules exceed Eₐ at any given temperature).

Eₐ is always a positive value (energy barrier to be overcome).

#### Exam Facts from Mark Schemes

When asked "what happens to the activation energy when a catalyst is added?" → Eₐ decreases (the catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy).

When asked "what happens to the activation energy when temperature increases?" → Eₐ does not change. This is the single most common MCQ distractor across all 7 papers.

#### Real Exam Questions

Jan 2023 Q17(a): "Why does the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution start at the origin?" Answer: All molecules possess some (kinetic) energy — no molecule has zero energy.

Jan 2024 Q13: "Which statement correctly describes the effect of temperature on rate?" Correct: "More particles have energy ≥ Eₐ." Distractors: "Activation energy decreases" (WRONG), "Average kinetic energy increases alone is sufficient" (WRONG — must link to Eₐ).

### 9.3(i) Measuring Rate — Rate = 1/time

#### Core Definition

Rate of reaction (initial approximation): Rate ∝ 1/time, where time is measured from the start of the reaction to a fixed point (e.g., a colour change, a precipitate appearing, a fixed volume of gas produced).

#### When This Applies

This is an approximation valid for comparing rates of similar reactions under different conditions.

It assumes the reaction progress to the chosen endpoint is consistent across conditions.

Used extensively in Core Practical 5 (comparing rates of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes using the silver nitrate test).

#### Exam Application

CP5 context (Oct 2023 Q15): "Why does C–Cl react slower than C–Br in SN2 hydrolysis?" Answer: The C–Cl bond is stronger than C–Br → higher activation energy → fewer molecules have sufficient energy → slower rate. (Bond enthalpy is the key factor, not solubility or polarity.)

#### Important Caveat

Rate = 1/time is only valid as a relative comparison. The actual instantaneous rate requires a gradient calculation (see 9.3(ii) below).

### 9.3(ii) Measuring Rate — Gradient of a Concentration–Time or Volume–Time Graph

#### Core Definition

Rate of reaction (from a graph): The instantaneous rate at any point is equal to the gradient (slope) of the tangent to the curve at that point.

#### How to Calculate

1. Draw a tangent to the curve at the required point.

2. Choose two well-separated points on the tangent line.

3. Calculate: gradient = (change in y) / (change in x)

4. Include correct units (e.g., cm³ min⁻¹, mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹).

#### Real Exam Questions

Jun 2023 Q15: "What is the rate at point X on the volume–time graph?" Answer: Draw tangent at X, calculate gradient = 1.3 cm³ min⁻¹. Common error: calculating the average rate (total volume / total time) instead of the instantaneous rate at X.

Jan 2023 Q22(e)(i): "Why is a high temperature used for NO production?" Answer: To increase the rate of reaction / more molecules have E ≥ Eₐ. (Note: this question is about rate, NOT about equilibrium yield.)

#### Graph Shapes to Know

Graph Type Shape What the Gradient Tells You

Concentration of reactant vs time Curve decreasing, flattening Gradient = rate of disappearance of reactant

Volume of gas vs time Curve increasing, flattening Gradient = rate of production of gas

Mass of product vs time Curve increasing, flattening Gradient = rate of formation of product

### 9.4 Maxwell–Boltzmann Distribution

#### Core Definition

Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution: A graph showing the distribution of kinetic energies among molecules in a gas at a given temperature. The y-axis represents the number (or fraction) of molecules, and the x-axis represents energy.

#### Key Features of the Distribution

Feature Description

Starts at the origin No molecule has zero energy (Jan 2023 Q17(a))

Peak (mode) The most probable energy (Eₘₒdₑ) — shifts right with increasing T

Asymmetric Long "tail" to the right — a small fraction of molecules have very high energies

Never reaches the x-axis The curve is asymptotic — there is no maximum energy (theoretically)

Area under the curve Represents the total number of molecules (decreases if gas is removed)

#### Effect of Temperature (MOST TESTED TOPIC in 2.8)

When temperature increases: - The peak lowers (curve flattens) - The peak shifts to the right (higher average energy) - The curve becomes broader - The area stays the same (same number of molecules) - A larger proportion of molecules now have E ≥ Eₐ - Eₐ line is unchanged

Critical exam trap: Many students incorrectly state that the distribution "moves up" or that Eₐ changes. The peak ALWAYS lowers when T increases, and Eₐ NEVER changes with temperature.

#### Real Exam Questions

Jan 2023 Q17(b): "Effect of removing some gas molecules AND cooling on the M–B distribution." Answer: Area decreases (fewer molecules) AND peak shifts left (lower temperature). Both changes must be identified.

Jun 2024 Q15(a–c): Three-part MCQ on M–B:

(a) Temperature ↑: only Eₘₒdₑ and Eₘₑₐₙ change (Eₐ unchanged) → C

(b) Pressure ↓: none of the three values change — Eₐ, Eₘₒdₑ, and Eₘₑₐₙ depend only on temperature, not pressure. Only the total number of molecules (y-axis) decreases.

(c) Catalyst added: only Eₐ changes (decreases) → A

Oct 2024 Q1(a): "What happens to the M–B curve when temperature increases?" Answer: Peak becomes lower and further right.

Oct 2024 Q1(b): "How does the Eₐ line change when a catalyst is added?" Answer: Eₐ moves left; peak stays the same.

Jun 2023 Q21(a)(i): Sketch the M–B distribution at a higher temperature. Must start at origin, have lower peak shifted right, same asymptote. Do not let the curve drop below the original low-energy region.

### 9.5 Catalysts

#### Core Definition

Catalyst: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. The catalyst is not consumed in the reaction and is regenerated at the end.

#### Key Properties (Exam-Ready)

Property Detail

Lowers activation energy Provides alternative route; Eₐ(cat) < Eₐ(uncat)

Not used up Regenerated at end of reaction

Does NOT change equilibrium position Speeds up both forward AND backward rates equally

Does NOT change the products formed Same products, same yield, just faster

Works by Providing a surface for adsorption (heterogeneous) or forming an intermediate (homogeneous)

#### Heterogeneous vs Homogeneous Catalysts

Heterogeneous catalyst: A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants (e.g. solid Fe in the Haber process with gaseous N₂ and H₂). The reaction occurs on the catalyst's surface.

Homogeneous catalyst: A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants (e.g. aqueous catalysts in solution reactions). It forms an intermediate species that then decomposes to release products and regenerate the catalyst.

#### Catalyst Effects on the M–B Distribution

The distribution curve itself does NOT change when a catalyst is added.

Only the Eₐ line shifts to the left (lower value).

This means a greater proportion of molecules now have E ≥ Eₐ(new), so more successful collisions occur per unit time.

#### Exam Facts from Mark Schemes

Jun 2023 Q14: Catalyst identification from rate data — Cu²⁺ reduced reaction time from 205 s to 75 s (catalyst), while Pb²⁺ increased it to 464 s (poison/inhibitor).

Jan 2023 Q22(d)(i): Reaction profile diagram — must show two profiles: uncatalysed (Eₐ = 290 kJ mol⁻¹) and catalysed (Eₐ = 70 kJ mol⁻¹), with correct scale and ΔH arrow.

#### Real Exam Questions

Oct 2023 Q21(b)(i): "Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of reaction, with reference to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution." Three-mark answer: 1. Catalyst provides alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy 2. Greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ (new, lower) Eₐ 3. Higher proportion of successful collisions per unit time

### 9.6 Reaction Profiles

#### Core Definition

Reaction profile (energy level diagram): A diagram showing the energy changes during a chemical reaction. The y-axis represents enthalpy (energy), and the x-axis represents the progress of the reaction (reaction coordinate).

#### Uncatalysed vs Catalysed Reaction Profiles

Energy
  ^
  |     Uncatalysed: ___----‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾
  |                 /
  |                / Ea(uncat)
  |               /
  |     Catalysed:/___--‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾
  |             /   Ea(cat)
  |            /
  |___________/________________________> Reaction progress
  |   Reactants    Products
  |         |ΔH|

#### Key Differences to Draw

Feature Uncatalysed Profile Catalysed Profile

Peak height Higher (larger Eₐ) Lower (smaller Eₐ)

ΔH Same Same

Reactant energy Same Same

Product energy Same Same

#### Real Exam Questions

Jan 2023 Q22(d)(i): Complete a reaction profile for the Haber process. Must show: 1. ΔH labelled with downward arrow (exothermic) 2. Two profiles: uncatalysed (Eₐ = 290 kJ mol⁻¹) and catalysed (Eₐ = 70 kJ mol⁻¹) 3. Correct relative scale for both Eₐ values 4. Accuracy: ±1 small square tolerance

### 9.7 Catalysts in Industry — Sustainability

#### Core Definition

Catalyst sustainability benefit: Catalysts allow industrial processes to operate at lower temperatures, reducing energy consumption and fuel costs, which in turn reduces carbon dioxide emissions and makes the process more economically and environmentally sustainable.

#### Why This Matters in Exams

When asked "Suggest why using a catalyst is more sustainable" (Jan 2023 Q22(d)(ii)):

DO say: Less energy needed / lower temperature required / less fuel burned / reduced CO₂ emissions

DO NOT say: "The catalyst can be reused" (technically true but not a sustainability argument)

DO NOT say: "It lowers the activation energy" (this is HOW it works, not WHY it's sustainable)

#### Real Exam Questions

Jan 2023 Q22(d)(ii): "Suggest why the use of a catalyst is more sustainable." Acceptable answers: less energy needed / lower temperature / less fuel. Explicitly NOT accepted: "catalyst is not used up" or "lowers Ea."

### 9.8 Catalyst Action via Maxwell–Boltzmann

#### How to Answer (3-Mark Template)

When asked to explain catalyst action with reference to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution:

Mark Required Content

1 Catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy

2 Greater proportion (or more) molecules now have energy ≥ Eₐ (new, lower value)

3 Therefore more frequent successful collisions (or higher rate of reaction)

#### Key Distinction

The distribution curve does not move or change shape when a catalyst is added.

Only the Eₐ vertical line shifts left.

This is a critical distinction from temperature changes, where the curve DOES change.

#### Common Error

Drawing a new, shifted distribution curve when a catalyst is added. This is incorrect — the curve stays the same; only the Eₐ marker moves.

### 9.9(i) Dynamic Equilibrium — Forward Rate = Backward Rate

#### Core Definition

Dynamic equilibrium: The state in a closed system where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of all reactants and products remain constant.

#### Essential Conditions for Dynamic Equilibrium

Condition Why It Matters

Closed system No reactants or products can enter or leave — matter is conserved

Reversible reaction Both forward and backward reactions must be possible

Rate forward = rate backward This is the defining feature of equilibrium

Macroscopic properties constant Concentration, pressure, colour, density remain steady

#### "Dynamic" vs "Static"

Dynamic means both reactions are STILL OCCURRING — particles are still colliding and reacting in both directions. It is NOT a state of no reaction.

Static equilibrium (which is NOT what we study) would mean both reactions have stopped.

The word "dynamic" is specifically tested — Jan 2024 Q14 asked students to identify the FALSE statement about equilibrium, and the correct answer (A) was that "catalysts affect the position of equilibrium" — which is false.

#### Real Exam Questions

Jan 2024 Q14: "Which statement about dynamic equilibrium is NOT true?" Answer: "A catalyst changes the position of equilibrium" — this is FALSE. Catalysts increase both rates equally; equilibrium position is unchanged.

### 9.9(ii) Constant Concentrations at Equilibrium

#### Core Definition

At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (not necessarily equal). This is because the forward and backward rates are equal, so any reactant consumed in the forward direction is immediately replaced by the backward reaction.

#### Key Exam Points

Constant ≠ Equal. The concentrations of reactants and products can be very different from each other — they just don't change over time.

"Position of equilibrium" describes where the equilibrium lies — if products are favoured, we say the equilibrium lies to the right; if reactants are favoured, it lies to the left.

### 9.10 Le Chatelier's Principle

#### Core Definition

Le Chatelier's principle: If a system at dynamic equilibrium is subjected to a change, the equilibrium position shifts to counteract (oppose) the imposed change.

#### Effects of Changes (Complete Table)

Change Applied Equilibrium Shift Effect on Yield Effect on Rate

Increase temperature Shifts in endothermic direction Depends on ΔH of forward reaction Rate ↑ (always)

Decrease temperature Shifts in exothermic direction Depends on ΔH of forward reaction Rate ↓ (always)

Increase pressure Shifts to side with fewer gas moles Depends on gas moles each side Rate ↑ (more collisions)

Decrease pressure Shifts to side with more gas moles Depends on gas moles each side Rate ↓

Increase [reactant] (add conc.) Shifts to right (products) Yield of products ↑ Rate ↑

Decrease [reactant] (remove) Shifts to left (reactants) Yield of products ↓ Rate ↓

Add catalyst No shift No change Rate ↑ (both directions)

#### JUSTIFICATION — The Key Exam Requirement

Edexcel mark schemes are extremely strict on Le Chatelier justifications. You must state: 1. What change is applied 2. Which direction the equilibrium shifts 3. Why (referencing the principle)

Template for full-mark answers:

"Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left (endothermic direction) because the system opposes the increase in temperature by absorbing heat. This decreases the yield of products."

#### Real Exam Questions

Oct 2023 Q11(a): "Effect of decreasing temperature on SO₂ + ½O₂ ⇌ SO₃ (ΔH = −99 kJ mol⁻¹)." Answer: Equilibrium shifts right (exothermic direction is favoured) → yield ↑ but rate ↓ → D (rate decreases, yield of SO₃ increases).

Oct 2023 Q11(b): "Effect of increasing pressure on same system (3 mol gas → 2 mol gas)." Answer: Equilibrium shifts right (fewer gas moles on product side) → yield ↑ and rate ↑ → B.

Oct 2023 Q12: "Effect of adding NaOH to HCrO₄⁻ ⇌ CrO₄²⁻ + H⁺ equilibrium." Answer: NaOH removes H⁺ → equilibrium shifts left → more yellow CrO₄²⁻ → C.

Jan 2023 Q22(a)(i): "Effect of excess steam on methane reforming." Answer: Shifts equilibrium right / increases H₂ yield. Explicitly NOT accepted: "reaction goes to completion."

Jan 2023 Q22(c): "Pressure in Haber process — advantage and disadvantage." Advantage: higher yield / faster rate. Disadvantage: more energy needed / expensive equipment required.

Jan 2023 Q22(f): "Adding water removes NO₂ from equilibrium." Answer: equilibrium shifts left (to replace the removed reactant) → yield of products (HNO₃, HNO₂) decreases. Two marks: identify removal + state shift direction.

Oct 2024 Q2(a): "Effect of decreasing temperature (ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹, endothermic forward)." Answer: Rate ↓, yield ↓ (D) — lower T disfavours the endothermic forward direction.

Oct 2024 Q2(b): "Effect of increasing pressure (more gas moles on product side)." Answer: Rate ↑, yield ↓ (B) — increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (reactants).

Oct 2024 Q19(b)(ii): "Adding NaOH to Cl₂ + H₂O equilibrium." Answer: NaOH removes H⁺ (reacts with it) → equilibrium shifts right (to replace H⁺) → produces more OCl⁻/HOCl.

Jan 2024 Q24(b)(ii): "Why does adding acid to bleach release toxic Cl₂?" Three-step answer: 1. Adding acid (H⁺) shifts Eq.1 left: H⁺ + ClO⁻ → HClO 2. This shifts Eq.2 right: HClO + Cl⁻ + H⁺ → Cl₂ + H₂O 3. Toxic Cl₂(g) is released

Jun 2023 Q22(d): "Adding H⁺ to chlorine disinfectant equilibrium." Answer: Equilibrium shifts left → toxic Cl₂ released.

#### Common Le Chatelier Pitfalls

Pitfall Papers Correct Approach

Saying equilibrium "moves to completion" Jan 2023 Equilibrium NEVER goes to completion — it shifts, not completes

Forgetting to mention rate effect Oct 2023 Q11 Some questions ask for BOTH yield AND rate effects

Confusing exo/endothermic direction Oct 2024 Q2(a) For endothermic forward: lower T → yield ↓ (shifts LEFT)

Not counting gas moles correctly Oct 2024 Q2(b) Must count TOTAL moles of GAS on each side, not atoms

Ignoring intermediate equilibrium steps Jan 2024 Q24(b)(ii) Must trace shift through each linked equilibrium

### 9.11 Industrial Compromise Conditions — Yield vs Rate

#### Core Definition

Compromise conditions: In industrial processes, the conditions chosen (temperature, pressure) represent a compromise between the conditions that give the maximum yield (from Le Chatelier's principle) and the conditions that give an acceptable rate (from kinetics/collision theory) and are economically viable.

#### The Classic Example: Haber Process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹)

Factor Le Chatelier (max yield) Kinetics (max rate) Industrial Compromise

Temperature Low T (exothermic forward favoured) High T (more E ≥ Eₐ) ~450 °C — moderate T giving acceptable rate with reasonable yield

Pressure High P (4 mol → 2 mol gas) High P (more collisions) ~200 atm — high enough for good yield, but higher P = much more expensive equipment

Catalyst No effect on position Increases rate Iron (Fe) — allows lower T to be used while maintaining rate

#### Real Exam Questions

Jun 2024 Q19(c)(i): "Explain the temperature compromise for ethene hydration (C₂H₄ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₅OH, exothermic)." Answer: Lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction (higher yield), but lower temperature gives a rate that is too slow (not economically viable). Both parts needed for 2 marks.

Jun 2024 Q19(c)(ii): "Why is >7 MPa pressure suggested?" Answer: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to give a greater yield (fewer moles of gas on product side).

Jun 2024 Q19(c)(iv): "Why not exceed 7 MPa?" Answer: Higher pressures require special/expensive plant or equipment.

Jun 2024 Q19(b): "How does overall yield reach 95% if equilibrium gives less?" Answer: Ethanol (and excess water) condenses/liquefies, and unused ethene/reactants are recycled.

Jan 2023 Q22(c): "Pressure advantage and disadvantage in Haber process." Advantage: higher yield / faster rate. Disadvantage: more energy needed / expensive equipment.

Jan 2023 Q22(h): "Suggest advantages of locating multiple processes on the same site." Any two from: cheaper to produce intermediates, transport savings, waste reduction, energy from exothermic steps used in endothermic steps, smaller workforce, less land.

#### The "Recycle" Concept

Many industrial processes achieve higher overall yields than predicted by equilibrium alone by continuously removing products and recycling unreacted reactants.

This is NOT a Le Chatelier shift — it is an engineering solution. But it often appears in equilibria questions.
