### Concepts & Worked Examples

#### Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12 — Spec Points 9.1–9.11

### How to Use This Guide

This file contains worked examples with full mark-scheme-grade answers for every major concept in Chapter 2.8. Each example is drawn from or modelled on real Edexcel past paper questions (Jun 2022 – Oct 2024). Focus especially on the Le Chatelier justifications — these are the #1 area where students lose marks.

### Worked Example 1: Maxwell–Boltzmann Distribution Sketches

#### 1A: Temperature Increase (Higher T)

Question (modelled on Jun 2023 Q21(a)(i), Jun 2024 Q15(a), Oct 2024 Q1(a)):

Sketch the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at a higher temperature on the same axes as the original.

Step-by-step drawing guide:

Fraction/Number of molecules
  ^
  |        Original T
  |       /\
  |      /  \            Higher T
  |     /    \          /
  |    /      \        /
  |   /        \      /
  |  /          \    /
  | /            \  /
  |/              \/
  +-------------------> Energy (E)
  |     Eₐ (same for both)

Critical features for full marks:

Feature Requirement Common Error

Both curves start at origin Must begin at (0, 0) Drawing the higher-T curve starting above the axis

Higher-T peak is lower and right-shifted Peak must be to the RIGHT and BELOW original Drawing the peak higher (wrong direction)

Both curves have the same area Same total number of molecules Making the higher-T curve have a larger area

Both curves approach the same asymptote Right-hand tail never reaches x-axis Drawing the higher-T curve ending abruptly

Eₐ line is unchanged Same vertical line for both curves Moving Eₐ when T changes (it doesn't!)

More area to the RIGHT of Eₐ at higher T Shade or clearly show the difference Failing to show the key consequence

Mark scheme note (Jun 2023): "Do not award if curve right of peak drops below the 300 °C line" — the right tail must extend far enough.

#### 1B: Catalyst Added (Same Temperature)

Question (modelled on Oct 2024 Q1(b), Jun 2024 Q15(c)):

On the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, show the effect of adding a catalyst.

Step-by-step drawing guide:

Fraction/Number of molecules
  ^
  |       /\
  |      /  \
  |     /    \    Eₐ(original)
  |    /      \   |
  |   /        \  |
  |  /          \ |
  | /            \|
  |/          Eₐ(catalyst)|
  +--|-----------|-------> Energy (E)
     |    |      |
     |    Shaded  |
     |    area    |
     |  (more     |
     |  molecules |
     |  above new |
     |  Eₐ)       |

Critical features:

Feature Requirement Common Error

The distribution curve is UNCHANGED Same peak, same shape, same area Drawing a new, different curve (WRONG)

Eₐ line shifts left (lower value) Draw a second vertical line to the LEFT of original Moving the curve instead of Eₐ

More molecules are now above the new (lower) Eₐ Shade the additional area Not showing the consequence

Why the curve doesn't change: The catalyst doesn't give molecules more energy. It simply lowers the energy threshold they need to exceed. The same distribution of molecular energies exists, but now more of them are "energetic enough."

#### 1C: Combined Changes — Fewer Molecules + Lower Temperature

Question (Jan 2023 Q17(b)):

Some gas is removed from the container AND the temperature is decreased. What happens to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution?

Answer: 1. Area decreases — fewer molecules in the container (total number reduced) 2. Peak shifts left (and becomes slightly higher relative to the reduced area) — lower average energy at lower temperature

Mark scheme: Both changes must be identified. Area decrease alone scores 1/2. Peak shift alone scores 1/2.

#### 1D: Pressure Decrease

Question (Jun 2024 Q15(b)):

The pressure of a gaseous system is decreased at constant temperature. Which values change?

Answer: None of these values change. Decreasing pressure reduces the total number of molecules (lower concentration) but does NOT change Eₐ, Eₘₒdₑ, or Eₘₑₐₙ — these depend only on temperature. The DISTRIBUTION SHAPE (per molecule) is unchanged; only the y-axis (number of molecules at each energy) decreases.

Mark scheme answer: Only the total number of molecules decreases; Eₐ, Eₘₒdₑ, and Eₘₑₐₙ are unchanged.

### Worked Example 2: Rate Calculations from Graph Tangents

#### 2A: Rate from a Volume–Time Graph

Question (Jun 2023 Q15):

The graph shows the volume of gas (cm³) produced against time (minutes) for a reaction. What is the rate of reaction at point X (t = 2 min)?

Method:

Volume (cm³)
  ^
30|                       .  .  .  .
  |                     .
25|                  .  ←── tangent at X
  |                .
20|             .X...............
  |           .
15|         .
10|       .
  |     .
 5|   .
  +-----|-----|-----> Time (min)
        2     4

Step 1: Draw a tangent at point X. The tangent should just touch the curve at X.

Step 2: Choose two well-separated points on the tangent: - Point 1: (0 min, 18.0 cm³) - Point 2: (4 min, 23.2 cm³)

Step 3: Calculate the gradient:

gradient = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁)
        = (23.2 − 18.0) / (4 − 0)
        = 5.2 / 4
        = 1.30 cm³ min⁻¹

(Matches the exam answer of 1.3 cm³ min⁻¹; the method is what matters.)

Step 4: Include correct units → cm³ min⁻¹ (or cm³ s⁻¹ if time is in seconds).

#### 2B: Identifying Rate from Catalyst Data

Question (Jun 2023 Q14):

Reaction time without catalyst = 205 s. Reaction time with Cu²⁺ = 75 s. Reaction time with Pb²⁺ = 464 s. Which ion acts as a catalyst?

Answer: - Cu²⁺: time decreased from 205 s to 75 s → rate increased → catalyst - Pb²⁺: time increased from 205 s to 464 s → rate decreased → poison / inhibitor

Since rate ∝ 1/time: - Without: rate ∝ 1/205 = 0.00488 - With Cu²⁺: rate ∝ 1/75 = 0.01333 (almost 3× faster) - With Pb²⁺: rate ∝ 1/464 = 0.00216 (less than half the original rate)

Mark scheme answer: Cu²⁺ is the catalyst → A.

### Worked Example 3: Le Chatelier Predictions with Full Justification

This is the most important worked example section. Edexcel consistently awards marks for the reasoning chain, not just the prediction.

#### 3A: Temperature Change — Exothermic Forward Reaction

Question (Oct 2023 Q11(a)):

For the reaction SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) ⇌ SO₃(g), ΔH = −99 kJ mol⁻¹, what is the effect of decreasing the temperature on the rate and the yield of SO₃?

Full-mark answer (2 parts required):

Effect on rate: - Decreasing temperature decreases the rate of reaction because molecules have less kinetic energy and fewer molecules have energy ≥ Eₐ.

Effect on yield: - The forward reaction is exothermic. Decreasing temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right (in the exothermic direction) to oppose the temperature decrease. This increases the yield of SO₃.

Combined answer: Rate decreases, yield of SO₃ increases → D.

Mark scheme note: Students must give BOTH the rate effect AND the yield effect. Either alone scores 0/1 for a 1-mark MCQ.

#### 3B: Temperature Change — Endothermic Forward Reaction

Question (Oct 2024 Q2(a)):

For a reaction where ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic forward), what is the effect of decreasing the temperature?

Full-mark answer: - Rate decreases (lower T → fewer E ≥ Eₐ) - Yield decreases (lower T disfavours the endothermic forward reaction → equilibrium shifts LEFT, towards reactants)

Answer: Rate ↓, yield ↓ → D.

Common trap: Students assume "lower temperature always increases yield" — this is only true for EXOTHERMIC forward reactions. For endothermic forward reactions, lower T DECREASES yield.

#### 3C: Pressure Change — Fewer Gas Moles on Product Side

Question (Oct 2023 Q11(b)):

For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) (3 mol gas → 2 mol gas), what is the effect of increasing the pressure?

Full-mark answer: - Rate increases (more molecules per unit volume → more frequent collisions) - Yield of SO₃ increases (increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles → shifts right, from 4 mol to 2 mol)

Answer: Rate ↑, yield ↑ → B.

#### 3D: Pressure Change — More Gas Moles on Product Side

Question (Oct 2024 Q2(b)):

For a reaction where the product side has MORE gas moles than the reactant side, what is the effect of increasing the pressure?

Full-mark answer: - Rate increases (always, with pressure) - Yield decreases (increasing pressure favours the side with FEWER gas moles → shifts LEFT, towards reactants)

Answer: Rate ↑, yield ↓ → B.

Common trap: Students always assume "higher pressure = higher yield" — this is only true if the product side has fewer gas moles. Always COUNT THE GAS MOLES on each side first.

#### 3E: Concentration Change — Removing a Reactant

Question (Jan 2023 Q22(f)):

In the equilibrium 2NO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HNO₃(aq) + HNO₂(aq), water is added (which removes NO₂ from the gas phase by dissolving it). What happens?

Full-mark answer (2 marks): 1. Adding water removes NO₂ (reactant) from the equilibrium mixture 2. The equilibrium shifts to the left (towards reactants) to oppose the removal (to replace the removed NO₂) 3. This decreases the yield of products (HNO₃ and HNO₂)

Mark scheme requirement: Must identify what is removed AND the direction of shift. Either alone = 1/2.

#### 3F: Adding a Base to an Acid-Dependent Equilibrium

Question (Oct 2024 Q19(b)(ii), modelled on Jan 2024 Q24(b)(ii)):

The equilibrium is Cl₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HClO(aq) + HCl(aq). What happens when NaOH is added?

Full-mark answer: 1. NaOH reacts with / removes H⁺ (from HCl) from the equilibrium 2. The equilibrium shifts to the right (to replace the removed H⁺) 3. This produces more HClO (and more Cl⁻ as Cl⁻ is also in the system)

Extended version (Jan 2024 Q24(b)(ii), 3 marks): 1. Adding acid adds H⁺, shifting Eq.1 left: H⁺ + ClO⁻ → HClO 2. This causes Eq.2 to shift right: HClO + Cl⁻ + H⁺ → Cl₂ + H₂O 3. Toxic Cl₂(g) is released

#### 3G: The Industrial Compromise — Full Worked Example

Question (Jun 2024 Q19(c), 7 marks total):

Ethene hydration: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g), ΔH is negative (exothermic). (i) Explain the temperature compromise (2 marks) (ii) Why is a pressure > 7 MPa suggested? (2 marks) (iii) Why not exceed 7 MPa? (1 mark) (iv) Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using more water (2 marks)

(i) Temperature compromise (2 marks): - The forward reaction is exothermic, so lower temperature would give a higher yield (shifts equilibrium right) - However, lower temperature gives a rate that is too slow to be economically viable - Therefore a compromise temperature is used

(ii) Pressure > 7 MPa (2 marks): - There are 2 mol of gas on the left (reactants) and 1 mol on the right (products) - Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right (fewer gas moles on product side), giving a greater yield of ethanol

(iii) Why not exceed 7 MPa (1 mark): - Higher pressures require special/expensive plant or equipment - (Also accepted: much higher energy costs to generate and maintain high pressure)

(iv) More water — advantage and disadvantage (2 marks): - Advantage: Pushes equilibrium to the right (increases yield) — water is a reactant - Disadvantage: More water is condensed with the ethanol product, making separation more difficult (or: catalyst may be washed from its support)

### Worked Example 4: Reaction Profile Diagrams

Question (Jan 2023 Q22(d)(i), 3 marks):

Complete the reaction profile for the catalytic oxidation of NH₃ to NO. The uncatalysed activation energy is 290 kJ mol⁻¹ and the catalysed activation energy is 70 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH = −905 kJ mol⁻¹.

Step-by-step drawing:

Energy (kJ mol⁻¹)
  ^
  |  Reactants
  |  ________          Uncatalysed pathway
  |         \          ___
  |          \        /   \  ΔH = −905 kJ mol⁻¹
  |           \      /     \__________ Products
  |            \    /
  |             \  /  <-- Catalysed pathway
  |              \/
  |    Ea(cat)=70    Ea(uncat)=290
  +----------------------------------> Reaction progress

Marking points (3 marks): 1. ΔH labelled with a downward arrow from reactants to products 2. Two humps (profiles): the uncatalysed one much taller (Eₐ = 290), the catalysed one much shorter (Eₐ = 70) 3. Correct relative scale — the catalysed peak must be visibly much lower than the uncatalysed peak 4. Accuracy: ±1 small square on the graph paper

Key tips: - The reactant and product energy levels are the SAME for both pathways (catalyst doesn't change ΔH) - Only the height of the peak (activation energy) differs - Both profiles must start and end at the same levels

### Worked Example 5: Catalyst Sustainability Argument

Question (Jan 2023 Q22(d)(ii)):

Suggest why the use of a catalyst makes the industrial process more sustainable.

Full-mark answer (1 mark, choose ONE): - Less energy needed (because a lower temperature can be used while maintaining an acceptable rate) - Lower temperature required (reduces fuel consumption) - Less fuel burned (reduces CO₂ emissions) - Reduced carbon footprint

NOT accepted: - "The catalyst can be reused" — true but not a sustainability argument per se - "It lowers the activation energy" — this is the MECHANISM, not the sustainability benefit - "It increases the rate" — this is the FUNCTION, not the sustainability benefit

The key linkage: Lower Eₐ → lower T can be used → less energy/fuel → lower CO₂ emissions → more sustainable. You need the chain of reasoning.

### Worked Example 6: Catalyst Explanation Using Maxwell–Boltzmann (3 Marks)

Question (Oct 2023 Q21(b)(i), Jan 2024 Q24(d)):

Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction, with reference to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.

Full 3-mark answer:

Mark Statement

1 The catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy

2 A greater proportion of molecules now have energy ≥ Eₐ (the new, lower value)

3 Therefore there is a higher proportion of successful collisions per unit time, increasing the rate

Alternative wording for Mark 3 (accepted): - "More molecules have sufficient energy to react upon collision" - "The rate of successful collisions increases"

NOT accepted: - "The catalyst gives molecules more energy" — it doesn't - "The distribution shifts" — it doesn't - "The catalyst lowers the temperature needed" — while true in industry, this is not what the M–B diagram shows

Diagram that scores full marks (Jan 2024 Q24(d), 4 marks):

Mark Requirement

1 Labelled axes (energy on x, number/fraction of molecules on y)

2 Single Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starting at the origin

3 Catalyst provides lower Eₐ (shown as a vertical line moved to the left)

4 More particles have E ≥ Eₐ with catalyst (shaded area or clear annotation)

### Worked Example 7: Dynamic Equilibrium Misconceptions

Question (Jan 2024 Q14):

Which statement about dynamic equilibrium is NOT true? A. A catalyst changes the position of equilibrium B. At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are constant C. At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction D. Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system

Answer: A — A catalyst does NOT change the position of equilibrium. It speeds up both forward and backward reactions equally.

Why the other options ARE true: - B: Correct — concentrations are constant (but NOT necessarily equal) - C: Correct — this is the defining feature of dynamic equilibrium - D: Correct — equilibrium requires a closed system so matter cannot escape

Exam insight: This is a classic "identify the false statement" question. Students often select C or D (which are true) because they seem "too simple." Always read carefully — the question asks which is NOT true.

### Worked Example 8: Carbon Dioxide and Ocean Acidification (Equilibrium Application)

Question (Oct 2023 Q20(c), 3 marks):

Explain why increasing the concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere increases the acidity of seawater. Relevant equilibrium: CO₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq)

Full 3-mark answer:

Mark Statement

1 Increasing atmospheric CO₂ increases the concentration of dissolved CO₂ in seawater

2 This shifts the first equilibrium to the right, increasing [H₂CO₃]

3 The increased [H₂CO₃] shifts the second equilibrium to the right, increasing [H⁺], so the acidity increases

Note: Mark 3 depends on Mark 2 being correct (dependent marking).

### Worked Example 9: Ethene Hydration — Complete Industrial Equilibrium Analysis

Question (Jun 2024 Q19, 11 marks total — full question walkthrough):

Ethene is hydrated to ethanol: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g). The process uses a phosphoric acid catalyst.

(a) Identify the catalyst (1 mark): - Phosphoric(V) acid / H₃PO₄ (also accepted: sulfuric(VI) acid / H₂SO₄)

(b) How does overall yield reach 95% if equilibrium conversion is lower? (2 marks): 1. Ethanol and excess water condense/liquefy (are removed from the gas phase) 2. Unreacted ethene is recycled back into the reactor

(c)(i) Temperature compromise (2 marks): - Lower T favours the exothermic forward reaction → higher yield - But lower T gives a rate that is too slow → not economically viable - Therefore a compromise temperature is used

(c)(ii) Why > 7 MPa? (2 marks): - 2 mol gas (reactants) → 1 mol gas (product) - Higher pressure shifts equilibrium right → greater yield

(c)(iii) Waxy solid at very high pressure? (1 mark): - Poly(ethene) — formed by unintended polymerisation of ethene at extreme pressures

(c)(iv) Why not exceed 7 MPa? (1 mark): - Higher pressures require special/expensive plant or equipment

(c)(v) More water — advantage and disadvantage (2 marks): - Advantage: pushes equilibrium right → increases yield (Le Chatelier: more reactant) - Disadvantage: more water condenses with ethanol → harder to separate / catalyst washed from support

### Exam Technique Summary for Chapter 2.8

#### Le Chatelier — The 3-Step Justification Template

Whenever you are asked to "explain" the effect of a change on an equilibrium:

1. State the change applied (e.g., "temperature is decreased")

2. State the direction of shift (e.g., "equilibrium shifts to the left/right")

3. Give the reason (e.g., "to oppose the change / because the system opposes the decrease in temperature / because there are fewer gas moles on the product side")

#### Maxwell–Boltzmann — Decision Tree

When asked what happens to the M–B distribution:

What changed?
├── Temperature ↑
│   → Peak: lower, right-shifted
│   → Area: same
│   → Eₐ: unchanged
│   → Proportion above Eₐ: increases
├── Catalyst added
│   → Curve: unchanged
│   → Area: same
│   → Eₐ: decreases (shifts left)
│   → Proportion above Eₐ: increases
├── Gas removed (pressure ↓ at const T)
│   → Peak: lower (fewer molecules at all energies)
│   → Area: decreases
│   → Eₐ: unchanged (same threshold)
│   → Shape (per molecule): same
└── Pressure ↑ (more gas in same volume)
    → Peak: higher (more molecules at all energies)
    → Area: increases
    → Eₐ: unchanged
    → Shape (per molecule): same

#### Catalyst — What to Say vs What NOT to Say

Context DO Say DO NOT Say

How a catalyst works "Provides alternative pathway with lower Eₐ" "Gives molecules more energy"

M–B explanation "Greater proportion of molecules have E ≥ Eₐ" "Distribution shifts to the right"

Sustainability "Less energy needed / lower temperature / less CO₂" "Catalyst is reused" or "Lowers Eₐ"

Equilibrium effect "No effect on equilibrium position" "Shifts equilibrium"

#### Rate vs Yield — Never Confuse Them

Question Type Think About Keywords

"What happens to the rate?" Kinetics / collision theory Faster collisions, more E ≥ Eₐ, more frequent collisions

"What happens to the yield?" Le Chatelier / equilibrium position Equilibrium shifts, more product favoured

"What is the compromise?" Both Rate too slow at low T, yield too low at high T

### 3. Key Question Types

#### 3.1 Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution Sketches — Est. 12 marks total

This is the most consistently tested sub-topic in ch2.8, appearing in 6/7 papers (all except Jun 2022).

Paper Q Marks What Was Asked

Jan 2023 Q17(a) 1 MCQ: Distribution starts at origin because no molecule can have zero energy

Jan 2023 Q17(b) 1 MCQ: Fewer molecules + cooling → smaller area, peak shifts left

Jun 2023 Q21(a)(i) 1 Sketch: Higher T → starts at origin, lower peak, shifted right, same asymptote

Jan 2024 Q24(d) 4 Draw full diagram: labelled axes, single curve, show catalyst lowering Eₐ, annotate that more particles have E ≥ Eₐ with catalyst

Jun 2024 Q15(a) 1 MCQ: Higher T → Eₘₒdₑ and Eₘₑₐₙ change; Eₐ stays same

Jun 2024 Q15(b) 1 MCQ: Lower P → number of particles at ALL energy values decreases

Jun 2024 Q15(c) 1 MCQ: Catalyst → only Eₐ changes (decreases); distribution curve unchanged

Oct 2024 Q1(a) 1 MCQ: Higher T → peak becomes lower and further right

Oct 2024 Q1(b) 1 MCQ: Catalyst → Eₐ moves left (decreases), peak stays same

Full-Mark Answer Pattern: Maxwell-Boltzmann Sketch (2–4 marks)

REQUIREMENTS:
1. X-axis: "energy" or "molecular energy" (NOT "time" or "concentration")
2. Y-axis: "number of molecules" or "fraction of molecules" or "probability"
3. Curve starts at the ORIGIN (never touching x-axis again on the right)
4. Asymptotic to x-axis at high energies (curve approaches but never touches)

For HIGHER TEMPERATURE:
  • Lower, broader peak (more spread of energies)
  • Peak shifts RIGHT (higher average energy)
  • Starts at origin
  • Same asymptote

For CATALYST:
  • Distribution curve is UNCHANGED
  • Only Eₐ line shifts LEFT (lower activation energy)
  • Shade or annotate the area beyond Eₐ (both lines) to show larger area with catalyst

For LOWER PRESSURE:
  • Fewer molecules → SMALLER area under curve
  • Same shape (peak at same energy)
  • "All values decrease proportionally"

COMMON ERRORS:
  ✗ Starting above origin
  ✗ Making the curve cross the x-axis again (must be asymptotic)
  ✗ Changing the curve shape for catalyst questions (curve doesn't change — only Eₐ does)
  ✗ Shifting the peak left for higher temperature (opposite!)

Appears in every single paper (7/7), as either MCQs or structured responses.

Paper Q Marks What Was Asked

Jan 2023 Q22(c) 2 Pressure advantage (higher yield/rate) + disadvantage (energy cost/expensive equipment)

Jan 2023 Q22(f) 2 Adding water removes NO₂ → equilibrium shifts right → more NO₂ yield

Oct 2023 Q11(b) 1 MCQ: Increasing P → equilibrium shifts right (3 → 2 mol gas), rate ↑

Oct 2023 Q12 1 MCQ: NaOH removes H⁺ → chromate-dichromate shifts left → more yellow CrO₄²⁻

Oct 2023 Q20(c) 3 CO₂ increase → H₂CO₃ equilibrium shifts right → [H⁺] increases → acidity ↑

Jan 2024 Q24(b)(ii) 3 Acid added to bleach: Eq.1 shifts left (HClO forms) → Eq.2 shifts right (Cl₂ released)

Jun 2024 Q19(c)(i) 2 Exothermic → lower T favoured but rate too slow → temperature compromise

Jun 2024 Q19(c)(ii) 2 >7 MPa → fewer gas molecules on product side → higher yield

Oct 2024 Q2(a) 1 MCQ: Endothermic forward → lower T → rate ↓, yield ↓

Oct 2024 Q2(b) 1 MCQ: More gas moles on product side → increasing P favours reactants → yield ↓

Oct 2024 Q19(b)(ii) 2 NaOH removes H⁺ from Cl₂ + H₂O → equilibrium shifts right

Full-Mark Answer Pattern: Le Chatelier Explanation (2–3 marks)

TWO-MARK STRUCTURE:
  1. IDENTIFY the change (e.g. "increasing temperature")
  2. STATE the shift (e.g. "equilibrium shifts to the LEFT/RIGHT")
  3. LINK to the effect (e.g. "yield of product INCREASES/DECREASES")
  4. (Optional) Give the OPPOSING effect on rate

THREE-MARK STRUCTURE (requires cause + reasoning):
  1. State the change
  2. State which direction is favoured and WHY (exothermic/endothermic, or gas moles)
  3. State the consequence for yield

TEMPERATURE:
  ↑T → favours ENDOTHERMIC direction → shifts away from heat
  ↓T → favours EXOTHERMIC direction → shifts toward heat

PRESSURE:
  ↑P → favours side with FEWER gas molecules
  ↓P → favours side with MORE gas molecules

CONCENTRATION:
  Adding reactant → shifts RIGHT (toward products)
  Removing product → shifts RIGHT (toward products)
  Adding product → shifts LEFT (toward reactants)

#### 3.3 Reaction Profile Diagrams — Est. 6 marks total

Paper Q Marks What Was Asked

Jan 2023 Q22(d)(i) 3 Draw uncatalysed + catalysed profiles with quantitative Eₐ labels (70 vs 290 kJ mol⁻¹)

Jan 2023 Q22(d)(ii) 1 Catalyst sustainability advantage: less energy needed / lower temperature

NOTE (R945): Jun 2024 Q1 (enthalpy level diagram) was previously listed here but is a ch2.6 Energetics question, not ch2.8. Removed.

Full-Mark Answer Pattern: Reaction Profile (3–4 marks)

REQUIREMENTS:
1. Y-axis: "enthalpy" (NOT "energy" or "ΔH")
2. X-axis: "reaction progress" or "extent of reaction"
3. Uncatalysed curve: higher peak (higher Eₐ)
4. Catalysed curve: lower peak (lower Eₐ)
5. Both curves start and end at same energy (ΔH is the same)
6. Label Eₐ(catalyst) < Eₐ(uncatalyst) if values given
7. ΔH arrow between reactant and product levels (if exothermic, products lower)

### 4. Common Errors and Misconceptions

#### 4.1 Catalyst Misconceptions (Tested in 4/7 Papers!)

Paper Q Misconception Tested

Jun 2022 Q10(a) Catalyst does NOT increase average kinetic energy — only temperature does

Jan 2023 Q22(d)(ii) Sustainability advantage is "less energy needed", NOT "catalyst is reused" or "lowers Ea"

Jan 2024 Q14 Catalyst does NOT affect position of equilibrium — only rate

Jun 2024 Q15(c) Catalyst only changes Eₐ — distribution curve is UNCHANGED

Must memorise:

What a catalyst DOES:
  ✓ Provides alternative reaction pathway
  ✓ Lowers activation energy
  ✓ Increases rate of both forward AND backward reactions equally
  ✓ Does NOT get used up
  ✓ Can be recycled/reused

What a catalyst does NOT do:
  ✗ Change the position of equilibrium
  ✗ Change the equilibrium constant
  ✗ Change the yield of product
  ✗ Change the average kinetic energy of molecules
  ✗ Change the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve shape
  ✗ Change ΔH of the reaction

#### 4.2 Activation Energy Misconceptions

Paper Q Misconception

Jan 2024 Q13 Activation energy does NOT change with temperature — more particles simply HAVE enough energy

Jun 2024 Q15(a) Higher T changes Eₘₒdₑ and Eₘₑₐₙ but NOT Eₐ

Jun 2024 Q15(c) Catalyst changes ONLY Eₐ — nothing else on the distribution changes

Jan 2024 Q13 "Kinetic energy increases" alone is insufficient — must say "more particles have E ≥ Eₐ"

Critical distinction:

TEMPERATURE increases → distribution CHANGES → Eₐ stays same → MORE particles exceed Eₐ
CATALYST added         → distribution UNCHANGED → Eₐ DECREASES → MORE particles exceed Eₐ

Both increase rate, but by DIFFERENT MECHANISMS

#### 4.3 Le Chatelier Common Errors

Error Paper Correct

"Equilibrium shifts to completion" Jan 2023 Q22(a)(i) Equilibrium shifts but NEVER goes to completion

Mixing up rate vs yield All papers Higher T often increases rate BUT decreases yield (for exothermic)

Forgetting endothermic/exothermic direction Oct 2024 Q2(a) Must identify which direction is endothermic FIRST

Wrong gas mole counting Jun 2024 Q19(c)(ii), Oct 2024 Q2(b) Count TOTAL gas molecules on each side, not just different types

Not stating OPPOSING effects Jan 2023 Q22(c) Temperature compromise: low T favoured but rate too slow

#### 4.4 Maxwell-Boltzmann Sketching Errors

Error Paper Correct

Curve doesn't start at origin Jun 2023 Q21(a)(i) ALWAYS starts at origin (no molecule has zero energy)

Curve crosses x-axis again All Must be asymptotic — never touches x-axis on right side

Wrong peak direction for higher T Multiple Higher T = peak shifts RIGHT (higher energy), NOT left

Changing distribution for catalyst Jun 2024 Q15(c), Oct 2024 Q1(b) Catalyst does NOT change the distribution — only lowers Eₐ line

Shading wrong area Jan 2024 Q24(d) Shade area BEYOND Eₐ line (above activation energy), not below

### 7. Quick-Reference: What Changes vs What Stays the Same

Condition Eₐ Distribution Curve Eₐ line position Equilibrium Position Rate

Higher T Same Shifts right, lower peak Same Depends (favours endo) ↑

Lower T Same Shifts left, taller peak Same Depends (favours exo) ↓

Catalyst ↓ UNCHANGED Shifts LEFT NO CHANGE ↑

Higher P Same Same shape (more molecules per unit volume) Same Favours fewer gas moles ↑

Higher [reactant] Same Same Same Shifts RIGHT ↑

### 8. Predictions for Future Papers

1. Expect 8–14 marks — ch2.8 is consistently the smallest chapter but NEVER absent

2. MCQs are reliable: 2–4 MCQ marks on Maxwell-Boltzmann and/or Le Chatelier

3. If Section C is industrial: expect 8–12 embedded marks (Le Chatelier, catalyst, compromise)

4. If Section C is organic: expect only MCQ marks (4–6 total)

5. MUST know the catalyst misconception cold — tested in 4/7 papers, including as a FALSE statement MCQ

6. Maxwell-Boltzmann sketches are almost certain; practice higher T, lower P, and catalyst variations

7. Le Chatelier explanations always require a chain: change → direction of shift → reason → consequence

Kc equilibrium constant calculations — not in spec points 9.1–9.11

Rate equations / rate-determining step — not in Unit 2 (Unit 4 / WCH14)

Kp (gas equilibrium constant) — not in Unit 2

Half-life concepts — not in Unit 2

### 11. Checklist: Am I Exam-Ready for ch2.8?

□ Can I sketch a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution with correct axes and shape?
□ Can I modify the sketch correctly for higher T (broader, lower peak, shifted right)?
□ Can I modify the sketch correctly for a catalyst (curve unchanged, Eₐ line shifts left)?
□ Can I modify the sketch correctly for lower P (smaller area, same shape)?
□ Can I explain Le Chatelier for temperature changes (with endo/exo direction)?
□ Can I explain Le Chatelier for pressure changes (count gas moles)?
□ Can I explain Le Chatelier for concentration changes?
□ Do I know that catalysts do NOT change equilibrium position or yield?
□ Do I know that activation energy does NOT change with temperature?
□ Can I draw a reaction profile with uncatalysed and catalysed pathways?
□ Can I explain the temperature/yield vs rate compromise in industrial processes?
□ Can I calculate a rate from the gradient of a tangent on a concentration–time graph?
□ Do I know that rate = 1/time is only valid for initial rate comparisons?
