### Spec Point 10.1 — Substitution and Elimination Reactions

Q1 QFR §10.1 1 mark · ~2 min

Define the term hydrolysis as applied to halogenoalkanes.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A substitution reaction in which a halogenoalkane reacts with water (or aqueous hydroxide) to form an alcohol. (1)

Q2 TDC §10.1 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare substitution and elimination reactions by completing the table below. | Feature | Substitution | Elimination | |---------|-------------|-------------| | What happens to atoms/groups | (a) | (b) | | Bond formed in organic product | (c) | (d) |

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) An atom/group is replaced by a different atom/group (½) (b) A small molecule (e.g. H₂O, HX) is removed (½) (c) No new C=C bond / single bonds only (½) (d) A C=C double bond is formed (½) (Award 1 mark for each correct pair: (a)+(b) = 1 mark; (c)+(d) = 1 mark)

Q3 EXP §10.1 3 marks · ~6 min

Classify each of the following reactions as substitution, elimination, addition, or oxidation. Give one reason for each classification. (i) CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH(aq) → CH₃CH₂OH + NaBr (ii) CH₃CHBrCH₃ + KOH(ethanol) → CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O + KBr (iii) CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) Substitution — the Br atom is replaced by an OH group on the same carbon (1) (ii) Elimination — HBr is removed and a C=C double bond is formed (1) (iii) Oxidation — the functional group changes from alcohol to aldehyde (loss of H / gain of O) (1)

### Spec Point 10.2 — Nucleophile Identity in the AgNO₃ Test

Q4 WTE §10.2 1 mark · ~2 min

A student observes a precipitate forming when 1-bromobutane is added to aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol. The student concludes: "The silver ion (Ag⁺) acted as the nucleophile in this reaction." State whether this conclusion is correct, and if not, identify the actual nucleophile.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Incorrect. The nucleophile is H₂O (water). Ag⁺ acts to precipitate the halide ion (Br⁻) as AgBr; it is not the nucleophile. (1)

Q5 EXP §10.2 3 marks · ~6 min

Reaction of a halogenoalkane with aqueous silver nitrate involves two distinct roles. (a) Identify the species that acts as the nucleophile and state what is formed when it attacks the halogenoalkane. (2 marks) (b) Identify the role of Ag⁺ in this reaction. (1 mark)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) The nucleophile is H₂O (water) (1). It attacks the electrophilic carbon, forming an alcohol (1). (Accept: substitution product / hydroxyl group replaces halogen) (b) Ag⁺ reacts with the displaced halide ion (X⁻) to form an insoluble silver halide precipitate (AgX) (1), which provides the visible observation used to compare reactivity of different halogenoalkanes.

### Spec Point 10.3 — Reactivity Trend: Bond Enthalpy, Not Polarity

Q6 WTE §10.3 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes: "The hydrolysis of iodomethane is faster than the hydrolysis of fluoromethane because the C–I bond is more polar than the C–F bond." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct explanation.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Error: the C–I bond is the least polar, not the most polar (1). Correct explanation: the C–I bond has a lower bond enthalpy / is weaker than the C–F bond, leading to a lower activation energy for bond breaking (1).

Q7 EXP §10.3 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why the rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes increases in the order: RCl < RBr < RI. Your answer should include reference to bond enthalpy and activation energy.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Mean bond enthalpy decreases from C–Cl to C–Br to C–I / C–I bond is the weakest (1). The weaker the C–X bond, the lower the activation energy for the rate-determining step (1). A lower activation energy means a greater proportion of molecules have energy ≥ Eₐ (Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution), leading to more frequent successful collisions per second (1).

Q8 WTE §10.3 2 marks · ~4 min

A student explains the reactivity trend by saying "reactivity increases down Group 17 because the halogens become less electronegative." Explain why this is NOT the accepted explanation and state what should be said instead.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Electronegativity/polarity does not determine the rate of SN2 reactions (1). The correct explanation is that the C–X bond enthalpy decreases down the group (C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I), giving a lower activation energy and therefore a faster reaction (1).

Q9 EXP §10.3 4 marks · ~8 min

A student is asked to explain why fluoromethane is the least reactive halogenoalkane in hydrolysis. The student writes: "The C–F bond is the most polar, so the carbon is most electrophilic and most susceptible to nucleophilic attack, therefore fluoromethane should react fastest." Evaluate this explanation. In your answer you should: identify what is correct about the student's statement, identify what is incorrect or incomplete, and provide a complete and correct explanation.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Correct: the C–F bond is the most polar (largest electronegativity difference), so the carbon atom does carry the greatest δ⁺ charge and is the most electrophilic (1). Incorrect/incomplete: the student assumes that greater electrophilicity (from polarity) determines reactivity, but this is not the dominant factor in hydrolysis (1). Complete explanation: the C–F bond has the highest mean bond enthalpy (485 kJ mol⁻¹), requiring the most energy to break and giving the highest activation energy (1). Therefore, despite being the most polar, fluoromethane reacts slowest because bond enthalpy, not bond polarity, is the dominant factor controlling the rate of hydrolysis (1).

### Spec Point 10.4 — Nucleophiles and the SN2 Mechanism

Q10 TDC §10.4 2 marks · ~4 min

(a) Define the term nucleophile. (1) (b) State the number of steps in an SN2 mechanism. (1)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) An electron-pair donor (1) [accept: a species that donates a pair of electrons to form a new covalent bond] (b) One (1) [accept: one step / concerted / single step]

Q11 WTE §10.4 2 marks · ~4 min

A student draws a curly arrow from the negative charge symbol on OH⁻ towards the carbon in an SN2 mechanism. Explain why this is incorrect and state what should be drawn instead.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The curly arrow must originate from a lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom, not from the negative charge symbol (1). The negative charge is a consequence of the extra electron, not the electrons themselves — the arrow represents the movement of the electron pair (1).

Q12 DIA §10.4 3 marks · ~6 min

Draw the SN2 mechanism for the hydrolysis of bromoethane with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Your mechanism should include: curly arrows to show the movement of electron pairs, the transition state, and the products.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Curly arrow from lone pair on O of OH⁻ to the electrophilic carbon of bromoethane AND curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br (1). Transition state drawn with the central carbon bonded to five groups in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, with partial/dashed bonds to both the incoming OH group and the outgoing Br (1). Products shown: ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and Br⁻ (1).

Q13 TDC §10.4 2 marks · ~4 min

State TWO differences between the transition state and the products of an SN2 reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Any two from: the transition state has five groups around the central carbon (trigonal bipyramidal) whereas the product has four groups (tetrahedral) (1); the transition state is not isolable whereas the products are stable, separate species (1); the transition state has a partial bond to both the nucleophile and the leaving group whereas the product has a complete bond to the nucleophile only (1).

Q14 WTE §10.4 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writing an SN2 mechanism uses a half-headed (fishhook) arrow from the C–Br bond to Br. Why would this be penalised in an Edexcel exam?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A half-headed (fishhook) arrow represents the movement of a single electron (homolytic fission) (1). The C–Br bond in an SN2 mechanism breaks by heterolytic fission (both electrons go to Br), so a full-headed curly arrow must be used (1).

Q15 DIA §10.4 3 marks · ~6 min

Draw a reaction profile diagram (potential energy vs reaction coordinate) showing two curves: one for the SN2 hydrolysis of 1-chlorobutane and one for 1-iodobutane. Label the activation energies and explain the difference.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Both curves start at the same (or similar) reactant energy level and end at the same product energy level

The 1-iodobutane curve has a lower activation energy (Eₐ) peak than the 1-chlorobutane curve (1)

Label Eₐ(I) < Eₐ(Cl) on the diagram (1)

Explanation: C–I bond has lower bond enthalpy than C–Cl, so less energy is required to break the C–X bond in the rate-determining step; the 1-iodobutane reaction is therefore faster at the same temperature (1)

### Spec Point 10.5 — Reactions of Halogenoalkanes

Q16 QFR §10.5 2 marks · ~4 min

State the systematic name of the halogenoalkane with the formula (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1-bromo-2-methylpropane (2)

Q17 TDC §10.5 2 marks · ~4 min

Compare the products of the reaction of 1-bromopropane with (i) NaOH(aq) and (ii) KCN(ethanol). In each case, state the product name and the number of carbon atoms in the product.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) NaOH(aq) → propan-1-ol, 3 carbon atoms (1). (ii) KCN(ethanol) → butanenitrile, 4 carbon atoms (the nitrile adds one carbon to the chain) (1).

Q18 EXP §10.5 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why the reaction of a halogenoalkane with KCN is particularly useful in organic synthesis. Refer to the carbon chain length in your answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The cyanide ion (CN⁻) acts as a nucleophile and substitutes the halogen on the halogenoalkane (1). The CN group contains a carbon atom, so the product (a nitrile) has one more carbon in the chain than the starting halogenoalkane (1). This extends the carbon chain by one carbon, which is valuable for building larger organic molecules (1).

Q19 WTE §10.5 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes that the reaction of 1-chloropentane with KCN in aqueous solution produces pentanenitrile. Explain why this is incorrect and state the actual product under aqueous conditions.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Under aqueous conditions, water (or hydroxide from water) acts as the nucleophile, so the product is pentan-1-ol (via hydrolysis), not the nitrile (1). To obtain pentanenitrile, the reaction must be carried out in ethanol as the solvent, not aqueous solution (1).

Q20 QFR §10.5 1 mark · ~2 min

State the name of the organic product when 1-bromopropane reacts with excess ammonia.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Propylamine (CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂) (1).

Q21 EXP §10.5 2 marks · ~4 min

Explain why the reaction of 1-bromopropane with ammonia requires TWO steps in the mechanism, unlike the reaction with NaOH(aq) which occurs in one step.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Ammonia (NH₃) is a neutral nucleophile, so when it attacks the electrophilic carbon, it forms a positively charged intermediate (CH₃CH₂CH₂N⁺H₃) because nitrogen now has four bonds (1). A second NH₃ molecule is needed to remove a proton (H⁺) from this intermediate, forming the neutral amine product and NH₄⁺ (1). In contrast, OH⁻ is already negatively charged and the product (alcohol) is neutral directly.

Q22 WTE §10.5 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes the product of Step 1 of the ammonia reaction as CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₃ (without a positive charge on N). Explain why this would lose a mark.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

After the nitrogen of NH₃ forms a bond to carbon, it has four bonds and a positive charge (N⁺) — it is a propylammonium ion, not a neutral amine (1). Omitting the positive charge on nitrogen shows a failure to recognise that nitrogen now has four covalent bonds and carries a formal positive charge (1).

Q23 SYN §10.5 4 marks · ~8 min

Describe the full two-step mechanism for the reaction of 1-bromopropane with excess ammonia. In your answer, show all curly arrows, name all intermediates and products, and state the conditions.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Step 1: Lone pair on N of NH₃ attacks the electrophilic carbon (Cδ⁺) of 1-bromopropane; simultaneous curly arrow from C–Br bond to Br (1). Forms propylammonium ion (CH₃CH₂CH₂N⁺H₃) and Br⁻ (1). Step 2: A second NH₃ molecule acts as a base; curly arrow from lone pair on N to H⁺ on the ammonium ion; curly arrow from N–H bond to N⁺ (1). Forms propylamine (CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂) and NH₄⁺ (1). Conditions (required for full marks but no separate mark — counted within Step 1/2): ethanol as solvent, heat under pressure in a sealed tube, excess ammonia. (Any one of these conditions may be stated; the 4 marks are all awarded for the two-step mechanism above.)

Q24 EXP §10.5 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain TWO key distinctions between the conditions used for (R1) hydrolysis to form an alcohol and (R3) reaction with ammonia to form an amine.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Distinction 1: R1 uses aqueous solvent (water) because water is the nucleophile in hydrolysis; R3 uses ethanol as solvent because aqueous conditions would cause competing hydrolysis of the halogenoalkane (1). Distinction 2: R1 is carried out under reflux (heating with condenser, open to atmosphere); R3 requires heating under pressure in a sealed tube because ammonia is a gas and needs to be kept in contact with the halogenoalkane at elevated temperature (1). Both R1 and R3 are nucleophilic substitution but require different practical conditions (1).

### Spec Point 10.6 — Classification of Halogenoalkanes

Q25 QFR §10.6 2 marks · ~4 min

Classify each of the following halogenoalkanes as primary, secondary or tertiary. (i) 1-bromopropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (ii) Cyclohexyl bromide

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) Primary (1) — the carbon bearing the bromine is bonded to one other carbon atom. (ii) Secondary (1) — the carbon bearing the bromine is bonded to two ring carbon atoms.

### Spec Point 10.7 — Aqueous vs Ethanolic KOH

Q26 TDC §10.7 4 marks · ~8 min

Complete the table to compare the reactions of a halogenoalkane with KOH. | Condition | Type of solvent | Type of reaction | Organic product | |-----------|----------------|------------------|-----------------| | Heat under reflux | Aqueous | | | | Heat | Ethanolic | | |

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Condition Type of solvent Type of reaction Organic product

Heat under reflux Aqueous Substitution (1) Alcohol (1)

Heat Ethanolic Elimination (1) Alkene (1)

Q27 WTE §10.7 1 mark · ~2 min

A student writes: "Heating 1-bromopropane with aqueous KOH produces propene." Identify the error in this statement.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Aqueous KOH gives substitution (hydrolysis) producing an alcohol (propan-1-ol); elimination to give propene requires ethanolic KOH (1).

Q28 STE §10.7 2 marks · ~4 min

State the organic product formed when 2-bromopropane reacts with: (i) aqueous NaOH heated under reflux (ii) ethanolic KOH heated

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(i) Propan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₃) (1) (ii) Propene (CH₃CH=CH₂) (1)

Q29 EXP §10.7 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why 1-chlorobutane would give the slowest precipitate in an AgNO₃ in ethanol test compared to (CH₃)₃CI, (CH₃)₂CHBr, and CH₃CH₂CH₂Br.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1-Chlorobutane is primary (favouring the slower SN2 mechanism rather than SN1) (1) AND contains chlorine, which forms the strongest C–X bond (highest bond enthalpy, highest activation energy) among Cl, Br, and I (1). Both factors (primary structure AND strong C–Cl bond) result in the slowest rate of hydrolysis, hence the slowest precipitate formation (1).

### Spec Point 10.8 — Ammonia Reaction Conditions and Elimination Products

Q30 TDC §10.8 3 marks · ~6 min

Compare the conditions required for the reaction of a halogenoalkane with aqueous sodium hydroxide (hydrolysis) with those required for reaction with ammonia to form a primary amine. Your answer should include the solvent, heating method and a reason for any difference.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Aqueous NaOH: dissolved in water (or aqueous ethanol), heated under reflux (1). Ammonia: dissolved in alcoholic ammonia (ethanol solvent), heated under pressure / in a sealed tube (1). Reason: ammonia is a gas and would escape from an open reflux system, so a sealed tube is required to maintain sufficient concentration / pressure of NH₃ (1).

Q31 EXP §10.8 2 marks · ~4 min

Even when a large excess of ammonia is used, the yield of the primary amine from the reaction of a halogenoalkane with ammonia is relatively low. Explain why.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The primary amine product (R–NH₂) itself contains a lone pair on nitrogen and can act as a nucleophile (1). It can undergo further nucleophilic substitution with unreacted halogenoalkane to form a secondary amine, tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium salt, reducing the yield of the desired primary amine (1).

Q32 SYN §10.8 4 marks · ~8 min

A student carries out two experiments on 2-bromobutane. Experiment 1: 2-bromobutane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Experiment 2: 2-bromobutane is warmed with potassium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol. (a) For each experiment, state the reaction type and name the nucleophile. (2 marks) (b) For Experiment 2, the student expects the major organic product to be but-1-ene but the major product is actually but-2-ene. Explain why but-2-ene is the major product. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Experiment 1: Substitution (1); nucleophile = OH⁻ (1) Experiment 2: Elimination (1); base = OH⁻ (1) (Note: in elimination, OH⁻ acts as a base (abstracting H⁺), not a nucleophile; accept "OH⁻" for both experiments) (b) But-2-ene is the more substituted alkene (it has more alkyl groups attached to the C=C double bond) (1), making it more stable than but-1-ene (1). (Accept: Zaitsev's rule — the alkene with the greater number of alkyl groups on the C=C bond is favoured)

Q33 SYN §10.8 4 marks · ~8 min

2-Bromobutane (CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃) undergoes elimination with hot, concentrated ethanolic KOH. (a) State the reaction type. (b) Name the alkene products formed. (c) For each product, state whether it shows E/Z stereoisomerism, giving a reason.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Elimination (1). (b) But-1-ene and but-2-ene (1). (c) But-2-ene: YES, it shows E/Z isomerism because each carbon of the C=C has two different groups (CH₃ and H on each carbon) (1). But-1-ene: NO, one carbon of the C=C has two H atoms (CH₂=), so E/Z isomerism is not possible (1).

Q34 CAL §10.8 3 marks · ~6 min

CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₂CH₂CH₃ undergoes elimination with hot ethanolic KOH. (a) Name the two alkene products (without stereoisomers). (b) State the total number of alkene products including stereoisomers.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Hex-2-ene and hex-3-ene (1 each, 2 marks). (b) 4 products total (hex-2-ene has E and Z stereoisomers; hex-3-ene has E and Z stereoisomers) (1).

### Spec Point 10.9 — Reaction with KCN

Q35 CAL §10.9 3 marks · ~6 min

2-bromopropane (C₃H₇Br) is reacted with excess KCN dissolved in ethanol and heated. (a) Give the IUPAC name of the organic product. (b) How many carbon atoms does the product contain? (c) Write the equation for this reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) 2-methylpropanenitrile (1). (b) 4 carbon atoms (1). (c) CH₃CHBrCH₃ + KCN → CH₃CH(CN)CH₃ + KBr (1). The CN⁻ replaces Br via SN2, extending the carbon chain by one carbon.

Q36 SYN §10.9 4 marks · ~8 min

1-bromopropane is reacted with KCN in ethanol to give compound A. Compound A is then reduced to give compound B, which is a primary amine. (a) Give the structural formula of A. (b) Give the name and structural formula of B. (c) Compare the number of carbon atoms in B with the original 1-bromopropane and explain why.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) A is CH₃CH₂CH₂CN (butanenitrile) (1). (b) B is butan-1-amine / CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂ (1). (c) B contains 4 carbon atoms compared to 3 in 1-bromopropane (1). This is because the KCN reaction introduces a –CN group, which extends the carbon chain by one carbon atom; reduction of the nitrile converts –CN to –CH₂NH₂, retaining the additional carbon (1).

### Spec Point 10.10 — Silver Nitrate Test

Q37 QFR §10.10 2 marks · ~4 min

State the colour of the precipitate formed when silver nitrate in ethanol is added to (a) 1-bromobutane and (b) 1-iodobutane at room temperature.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Cream (1) (b) Yellow (1)

Q38 EXP §10.10 3 marks · ~6 min

When silver nitrate in ethanol is added separately to 1-chlorobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-iodo-2-methylpropane at room temperature, the iodo-compound gives a precipitate most rapidly. Explain this observation in terms of both bond enthalpy and the mechanism involved.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The C–I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy / is the weakest bond of the three, so it has the lowest activation energy for bond breaking, making it the fastest to react (1). Additionally, 2-iodo-2-methylpropane is a tertiary halogenoalkane, which undergoes SN1 via a carbocation intermediate; the tertiary carbocation is the most stable due to electron-donating alkyl groups / positive inductive effect, further increasing the rate (2).

### Spec Point 10.11 — Silver Oxide

Q39 EXP §10.11 3 marks · ~6 min

(a) Complete the ionic equation for the dissolution of silver oxide: Ag₂O + H₂O → (b) In the silver nitrate test, some students incorrectly state that Ag⁺ directly attacks the carbon–halogen bond. Describe the correct mechanism, identifying the nucleophile and the role of Ag⁺.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) 2Ag⁺ + 2OH⁻ (1). (b) The nucleophile is H₂O, which attacks the electrophilic carbon of the C–X bond in an SN2 (or SN1 for tertiary) substitution reaction, displacing X⁻ (1). Ag⁺ then reacts with the halide ion (X⁻) to form an insoluble precipitate (AgX), giving the visual observation; Ag⁺ does NOT act as the nucleophile (1).

### Spec Point 10.12 — Order of Reactivity

Q40 QFR §10.12 1 mark · ~2 min

State the order of reactivity for the hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes, from slowest to fastest.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I (1)

Q41 SYN §10.12 4 marks · ~8 min

Four halogenoalkanes are available: A = 1-chlorobutane, B = 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, C = 1-iodobutane, D = 2-iodo-2-methylpropane. Predict which of these four will hydrolyse most rapidly with aqueous KOH, giving TWO reasons for your choice.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

D (2-iodo-2-methylpropane) will hydrolyse most rapidly (1). Reason 1: It is a tertiary halogenoalkane, which reacts via the SN1 mechanism forming a relatively stable tertiary carbocation intermediate, whereas primary halogenoalkanes react by the slower SN2 mechanism (1). Reason 2: The C–I bond has a lower bond enthalpy (238 kJ mol⁻¹) than the C–Cl bond (339 kJ mol⁻¹), giving a lower activation energy for C–X bond breaking (1). Both the structural factor (tertiary > primary) and the bond enthalpy factor (iodine > chlorine) favour D as the fastest (1).

### Spec Point 10.13 — SN2 and SN1 Mechanisms

Q42 TDC §10.13 3 marks · ~6 min

Compare the SN2 and SN1 mechanisms in terms of: (a) number of steps, (b) the intermediate formed, and (c) rate dependence on reactant concentrations.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) SN2 is a one-step (concerted) mechanism; SN1 is a two-step mechanism (1). (b) SN2 has a transition state (five groups around carbon, transient and not isolable); SN1 has a carbocation intermediate (trigonal planar, transient but long-lived enough to be detected spectroscopically in favourable cases) (1). (c) SN2 rate depends on both [halogenoalkane] and [nucleophile]; SN1 rate depends on [halogenoalkane] only (1).

### Spec Point 10.14 — Core Practical 5: Comparing Rates of Hydrolysis

Q43 EXP §10.14 4 marks · ~8 min

In Core Practical 5, a student uses silver nitrate solution in ethanol to compare the rates of hydrolysis of 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane. (a) State two variables that must be kept constant to ensure a fair test. (2 marks) (b) The precipitate forms fastest for 1-iodobutane. With reference to the role of water, explain the overall process occurring in this test. (2 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Any two from: same temperature / same concentration of AgNO₃ / same volume of AgNO₃ / same concentration of halogenoalkane / same volume of halogenoalkane (2). (b) Water acts as the nucleophile (electron-pair donor), attacking the electrophilic carbon of the halogenoalkane in an SN2 substitution, displacing the halide ion (X⁻) (1); the released X⁻ then reacts with Ag⁺(aq) to form the insoluble precipitate AgX, the appearance of which signals that hydrolysis has occurred (1).

### Spec Point 10.15 — Naming Alcohols

Q44 DIA §10.15 2 marks · ~4 min

A student is asked to name the alcohol with the structure CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. State the correct IUPAC name. Explain why the locant number must be included.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Butan-2-ol (1). The locant number is required because the –OH group could be on carbon-1 or carbon-2 of the four-carbon chain; including the locant (2) distinguishes this isomer from butan-1-ol (1).

### Spec Point 10.16 — Classification and Naming of Alcohols

Q45 QFR §10.16 2 marks · ~4 min

Classify each of the following alcohols as primary, secondary, or tertiary: (a) (CH₃)₂CHOH (b) (CH₃)(C₂H₅)(OH)C–CH₂CH₃

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Secondary (the –OH carbon is attached to two other carbon atoms) (1) (b) Tertiary (the –OH carbon is attached to three other carbon atoms) (1)

Q46 QFR §10.16 2 marks · ~4 min

Name the following alcohol, giving the full systematic IUPAC name: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂OH

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

3-methylbutan-1-ol (1 mark for correct methyl position, 1 mark for correct –ol position and stem name; allow "3-methylbutan-1-ol" only)

### Spec Point 10.17 — Tests for Alcohols

Q47 WTE §10.17 1 mark · ~2 min

A student writes in their notes: "Bromine water (Br₂) can be used to test for the presence of an alcohol, as it decolourises when an –OH group is present." Is this statement correct? Give a reason for your answer.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

No (1). Bromine does not react with aliphatic alcohols; it reacts with C=C double bonds (alkenes) via electrophilic addition, so a negative bromine-water test does not rule out the presence of an alcohol.

Q48 WTE §10.17 2 marks · ~4 min

A student states: "PCl₅ only reacts with primary and secondary alcohols, just like acidified potassium dichromate(VI)." Identify the error in this statement and correct it.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Error: PCl₅ does NOT only react with primary and secondary alcohols (1). Correction: PCl₅ reacts with all alcohol types (primary, secondary, and tertiary), whereas acidified potassium dichromate(VI) only oxidises primary and secondary alcohols (tertiary alcohols are not oxidised) (1).

Q49 QFR §10.17 1 mark · ~2 min

State the observation when phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅) is added to an alcohol.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Misty white fumes of hydrogen chloride (HCl) are produced. (1)

Q50 SYN §10.17 5 marks · ~10 min

Three students propose different tests to identify the –OH group in three alcohols: menthol (secondary), linalool (tertiary, also has C=C), and citronellol (primary, also has C=C). Evaluate each student's suggestion: - Student 1: Use acidified potassium dichromate(VI) - Student 2: Use acidified potassium manganate(VII) - Student 3: Use PCl₅ Which test is best and why?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Student 1 (K₂Cr₂O₇): Works for menthol (secondary → orange to green) and citronellol (primary → orange to green) but not linalool (tertiary — no colour change). Not a valid test for all three. (1)

Student 2 (KMnO₄): Not specific for –OH; would also react with the C=C bonds in linalool and citronellol, giving false positives. Not diagnostic. (1)

Student 3 (PCl₅): Best test — produces misty fumes of HCl with all alcohols (primary, secondary, tertiary) by reacting with the –OH group specifically; does not react with C=C bonds. (2)

Therefore Student 3's suggestion is the most reliable for identifying –OH in all three compounds. (1)

### Spec Point 10.18 — Infrared Spectroscopy

Q66 TDC §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

Compare the infrared absorption of the O–H bond in an alcohol with that in a carboxylic acid. In your answer, refer to the wavenumber range and the appearance (broad/sharp) of each.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Alcohol O–H: 3750–3200 cm⁻¹, broad (1); Carboxylic acid O–H: 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, very broad (1); The carboxylic acid O–H absorption extends to lower wavenumbers and is broader due to extensive hydrogen bonding / dimer formation (1).

Q67 TDC §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

A student makes the following claim: "An IR peak at approximately 1700 cm⁻¹ indicates the presence of a C=C bond, and an IR peak at approximately 1640 cm⁻¹ indicates the presence of a C=O bond." Evaluate this claim by stating whether each part is correct or incorrect, giving the correct wavenumber range for each bond type.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

"1700 cm⁻¹ indicates C=C" — INCORRECT (1); C=C absorbs at 1680–1620 cm⁻¹ (1); "1640 cm⁻¹ indicates C=O" — INCORRECT; C=O absorbs at 1680–1750 cm⁻¹ (depending on the carbonyl type: aldehyde 1740–1720, ketone 1720–1700, carboxylic acid 1725–1700, ester 1750–1730) (1). The student has confused/swapped the wavenumber ranges for C=O and C=C.

Q68 WTE §10.18 2 marks · ~4 min

A student examines an IR spectrum and observes a broad absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. The student concludes: "This broad O–H peak means the compound is an alcohol." Identify the error in the student's reasoning and give the correct conclusion.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Error: a broad O–H absorption extending to 2500 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of a carboxylic acid, NOT an alcohol (1); Correct conclusion: the compound contains a carboxylic acid group (1). Alcohol O–H absorbs in the range 3750–3200 cm⁻¹ and, although also broad, does not extend as far to low wavenumbers.

Q69 WTE §10.18 2 marks · ~4 min

A student observes an IR peak at 1700 cm⁻¹ and states "this peak confirms the presence of a C=C double bond." Explain why this is incorrect and state the correct assignment.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

A peak at 1700 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of C=O (carbonyl), not C=C (1). C=C stretches appear at a lower wavenumber range: 1669–1645 cm⁻¹ (1). Confusing these is a common error — the C=O bond has a larger dipole moment and absorbs at higher wavenumber than C=C.

Q70 DIA §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

An IR spectrum of an unsaturated hydrocarbon shows three significant absorptions: - P at approximately 3090 cm⁻¹ - Q at approximately 2900 cm⁻¹ - R at approximately 1650 cm⁻¹ Identify the bond responsible for each absorption. You must specify the type of carbon–hydrogen bond where relevant.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

P: C–H stretching in alkene (1); Q: C–H stretching in alkane (1); R: C=C stretching in alkene (1). Just "C–H stretch" for P or Q is insufficient — must specify "in alkene" or "in alkane".

Q71 CAL §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

An unknown compound shows IR absorptions at 3415 cm⁻¹ (medium, sharp) and 2250 cm⁻¹ (sharp). Which compound from the following is most likely to be the unknown? Give a reason for your choice. A: CH₃CH₂COOH B: H₂NCH₂CH₂C≡N C: CH₃COCH₃ D: CH₃CH₂OH

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

B: H₂NCH₂CH₂C≡N (1); Absorption at 3415 cm⁻¹ corresponds to N–H stretch (in amine) (1); Absorption at 2250 cm⁻¹ corresponds to C≡N stretch (nitrile group) (1).

Q72 TDC §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

Use the following IR absorption ranges to complete the table distinguishing between five functional groups: | Functional Group | Key Absorption 1 (cm⁻¹) | Key Absorption 2 (cm⁻¹) | |---|---|---| | Alcohol | | | | Aldehyde | | | | Ketone | | | | Carboxylic acid | | | | Ester | | |

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Functional Group Key Absorption 1 Key Absorption 2

Alcohol O–H stretch 3750–3200 (broad) C–O stretch 1000–1300

Aldehyde C=O stretch 1740–1720 C–H stretch 2775–2700

Ketone C=O stretch 1720–1700 (No distinctive second absorption)

Carboxylic acid O–H stretch 2500–3300 (very broad) C=O stretch 1725–1700

Ester C=O stretch 1750–1730 C–O stretch 1300–1000

(1 mark per correct row, max 3)

Q73 EXP §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

An IR spectrum shows: a sharp peak at 2255 cm⁻¹, C–H stretches at 2950–2850 cm⁻¹, and no O–H absorption. Identify the functional group present and explain your reasoning using the IR decision tree approach.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

No broad absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ → not a carboxylic acid (1)

Sharp absorption at 2255 cm⁻¹ (within 2250–2215 cm⁻¹) → C≡N (nitrile) (1)

C–H stretches at 2950–2850 cm⁻¹ → alkane C–H; no O–H absorption rules out alcohol or carboxylic acid

The compound contains a nitrile functional group (1)

Q74 EXP §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

The IR spectrum of an unknown compound shows C–H stretches at 3080 cm⁻¹ and 2960 cm⁻¹. Explain why two different C–H stretching frequencies are observed and identify what structural feature causes this. How does this information help narrow down the identity of the compound?

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The C–H stretch at 3080 cm⁻¹ is in the alkene C–H range (3100–3000 cm⁻¹), indicating sp² hybridised C–H bonds (1). The C–H stretch at 2960 cm⁻¹ is in the alkane C–H range (2950–2850 cm⁻¹), indicating sp³ hybridised C–H bonds (1). Two different C–H frequencies indicate the compound contains both alkene and alkane C–H groups — i.e. an unsymmetrical alkene with an alkyl chain. This narrows the identity to an alkene (not a pure alkane) and rules out compounds containing only one type of C–H environment (1).

Q75 EXP §10.18 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why the O–H absorption in a carboxylic acid appears as a very broad band at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ rather than a sharper peak. In your answer, refer to hydrogen bonding and the structure of carboxylic acid dimers.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers in the liquid and solid state — two molecules linked by two O–H···O hydrogen bonds (1). This strong, extensive hydrogen bonding creates a wide range of O–H bond strengths and vibrational energies, resulting in a very broad absorption (1). The hydrogen bonding also weakens the O–H bond, shifting the absorption to lower wavenumbers compared to a free O–H — this broad, low-wavenumber O–H is a key diagnostic feature distinguishing carboxylic acids from alcohols (1).

Q76 SYN §10.18 4 marks · ~8 min

Two compounds, P and Q, both have Mᵣ = 60. P shows IR absorptions at: 3400 cm⁻¹ (broad), 2950–2850 cm⁻¹, and 1050 cm⁻¹. Q shows IR absorptions at: 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ (very broad), 2950–2850 cm⁻¹, and 1710 cm⁻¹. The mass spectrum of P shows a significant peak at m/z 31; the mass spectrum of Q shows a significant peak at m/z 45. Identify P and Q, explaining how each piece of spectral evidence supports your identification.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Compound P: O–H at 3400 cm⁻¹ (in alcohol range 3750–3200, NOT carboxylic acid range) → alcohol; no C=O absorption; C–O at 1050 cm⁻¹ (alcohol C–O range 1300–1000); fragment m/z 31 = CH₂OH⁺ (primary alcohol fragment). P = propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) (2)

Compound Q: Very broad O–H at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ (carboxylic acid range); C=O at 1710 cm⁻¹ (carboxylic acid carbonyl); fragment m/z 45 = COOH⁺ (carboxylic acid fragment). Q = ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) (2)

### Spec Point 10.19 — Dehydration of Alcohols

Q51 TDC §10.19 3 marks · ~6 min

State the reagent and conditions required for the dehydration of an alcohol to form an alkene. Give the classification of this reaction.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Reagent: concentrated phosphoric(V) acid OR concentrated sulfuric acid (1); Conditions: heat to approximately 170 °C (1). Classification: elimination (1). NOTE: Both H₃PO₄ and H₂SO₄ are accepted by Edexcel as dehydrating agents for alcohols. "Concentrated" must be stated.

### Spec Point 10.20 — Oxidation of Alcohols

Q52 TDC §10.20 3 marks · ~6 min

Compare the products formed when propan-1-ol is reacted with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under (a) distillation conditions and (b) reflux conditions. Explain why different products are obtained.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) Under distillation: propanal (aldehyde) is formed (1); (b) Under reflux (with excess oxidising agent): propanoic acid (carboxylic acid) is formed (1). Explanation: under distillation, the aldehyde has a lower boiling point than the alcohol, so it distils off as it forms, preventing further oxidation (1); under reflux, the condenser returns vapour to the flask, allowing prolonged heating and complete oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

Q53 WTE §10.20 2 marks · ~4 min

A student writes: "When a primary alcohol is heated with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, it always produces a carboxylic acid." Explain the error in this statement and state the additional information needed for it to be correct.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The primary alcohol produces a carboxylic acid only under reflux conditions with excess oxidising agent (1); if distillation is used, the product is an aldehyde (1), because the aldehyde distils off before it can be further oxidised.

Q54 QFR §10.20 1 mark · ~2 min

State what is observed when acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is added to a tertiary alcohol and gently warmed.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

No colour change / the solution remains orange (1) — tertiary alcohols are not oxidised by dichromate(VI).

Q55 EXP §10.20 3 marks · ~6 min

Explain why tertiary alcohols are not oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI), whereas primary and secondary alcohols are.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Oxidation of an alcohol requires the carbon bearing the –OH group to have at least one hydrogen atom attached, which can be removed (along with the –OH) to form a C=O bond (1). In a tertiary alcohol, the carbon bearing the –OH has no hydrogen atoms bonded to it (it is bonded to three alkyl groups) (1), so no C=O bond can form and no oxidation occurs (1).

Q56 EXP §10.20 2 marks · ~4 min

A student oxidises propan-2-ol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux and collects the product by distillation. Explain why the product is the same regardless of which collection method is used.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, which is oxidised to a ketone (propanone) (1). Ketones cannot be further oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI), so the product is propanone under both distillation and reflux conditions (1).

Q57 STE §10.20 3 marks · ~6 min

State the product and the observable change when propan-2-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Give the expected IR absorption range for the key bond in the product.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Product: propanone (acetone) (1); Observable change: orange to green (1). Expected IR absorption for the C=O bond in the ketone product: 1720–1700 cm⁻¹ (accept 1680–1750 cm⁻¹) (1). NOTE: A common trap is giving a C=C range (~1640 cm⁻¹) instead of C=O.

Q58 EXP §10.20 2 marks · ~4 min

State the colour change observed when a primary alcohol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and link this to the oxidation state change of chromium.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Colour changes from orange to green (1). Chromium is reduced from Cr(VI) in dichromate (orange) to Cr(III) in the chromium(III) ions (green) (1).

Q59 TDC §10.20 2 marks · ~4 min

Distinguish between the C=O IR absorption ranges for an aldehyde and a ketone. State a range for each.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Aldehyde C=O: 1740–1720 cm⁻¹ (1). Ketone C=O: 1720–1700 cm⁻¹ (1).

Q60 SYN §10.20 4 marks · ~8 min

Two products are obtained by oxidising propan-1-ol under different conditions. Product A (from distillation) shows IR absorptions at 1730 cm⁻¹ and a doublet at 2820 and 2720 cm⁻¹. Product B (from reflux) shows IR absorptions at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ (very broad) and 1710 cm⁻¹. Identify both products, assign each IR absorption, and explain how the different conditions led to different products.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Product A (distillation) = propanal (aldehyde): 1730 cm⁻¹: C=O stretch in aldehyde (range 1740–1720 cm⁻¹); 2820 & 2720 cm⁻¹: characteristic aldehyde C–H doublet (range 2775–2700 cm⁻¹). Distillation removes the volatile aldehyde (bp 49 °C) from the reaction mixture before further oxidation. (2)

Product B (reflux) = propanoic acid (carboxylic acid): 2500–3300 cm⁻¹: very broad O–H of carboxylic acid (hydrogen-bonded dimer); 1710 cm⁻¹: C=O of carboxylic acid (~1700 cm⁻¹). Reflux keeps the product in contact with K₂Cr₂O₇, so the aldehyde intermediate is further oxidised to the carboxylic acid. (2)

Q61 EXP §10.20 3 marks · ~6 min

A student oxidises ethanol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux and obtains ethanoic acid. A second student oxidises ethanol under distillation conditions and obtains ethanal. Explain the role of each technique in determining the product, and state the oxidation state change of the relevant carbon atom in each case.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Reflux: the condenser returns volatile products to the flask, so ethanal remains in contact with the oxidising agent and is further oxidised to ethanoic acid; carbon oxidation state changes from −1 (in ethanol) to +3 (in ethanoic acid) (1½)

Distillation: the low-boiling ethanal (bp 21 °C) is distilled off as it forms, removing it from the oxidising agent and preventing further oxidation; carbon oxidation state changes from −1 (in ethanol) to +1 (in ethanal) (1½)

(Award 1½ marks for each fully-correct bullet; maximum 3 marks total.)

### Spec Point 10.21 — [O] Calculations

Q62 CAL §10.21 3 marks · ~6 min

A compound contains two primary hydroxyl groups and one secondary hydroxyl group. Calculate the total number of [O] atoms required for complete oxidation of all oxidisable groups using acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Each primary –OH → carboxylic acid requires 2[O] (1); each secondary –OH → ketone requires 1[O] (1). Total = (2 × 2) + (1 × 1) = 5[O] (1).

Q63 SYN §10.21 4 marks · ~8 min

Outline the systematic steps you would follow to determine the structure of an unknown organic compound, given its mass spectrum (M⁺ at m/z 86), IR spectrum (broad absorption 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, peak at 1700 cm⁻¹, peak at 1650 cm⁻¹), and the results of bromine water and sodium carbonate tests.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1. Molecular formula: M⁺ = 86; from combustion data or empirical formula × n, deduce C₄H₆O₂ (1)

2. IR analysis: broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ = O–H in carboxylic acid; peak at ~1700 cm⁻¹ = C=O (carbonyl); peak at ~1650 cm⁻¹ = C=C (alkene) (1)

3. Chemical tests: bromine water decolourised confirms C=C; effervescence with Na₂CO₃ confirms –COOH (1)

4. Structural assembly: C₄H₆O₂ with COOH and C=C → but-2-enoic acid (CH₃CH=CHCOOH) (1)

5. Mass spec confirmation: fragment at m/z 45 (COOH⁺) supports carboxyl group; fragment at m/z 41 (C₃H₅⁺) supports alkene portion

### Spec Point 10.22 — IR Absorptions for C=O and C=C

Q77 QFR §10.22 2 marks · ~4 min

State the wavenumber range for the C=O absorption in a ketone, and the wavenumber range for the C=C absorption in an alkene.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

C=O (ketone): 1720–1700 cm⁻¹ (1); C=C (alkene): 1680–1620 cm⁻¹ (1). Accept either order.

Q78 STE §10.22 2 marks · ~4 min

Propan-1-ol is oxidised using acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under distillation conditions. State the wavenumber range of the IR absorption that would identify the organic product and name the bond responsible.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

1740–1720 cm⁻¹ (1); C=O stretch / C=O bond in an aldehyde (1). Accept "C=O" alone for bond name; must give range for the mark.

### Spec Point 10.23 — Conversion of Alcohols to Chloroalkanes

Q64 TDC §10.23 3 marks · ~6 min

A student writes: "To convert any alcohol to a chloroalkane, either PCl₅, concentrated HCl, or concentrated H₂SO₄ + KCl can be used." Evaluate the accuracy of this statement for primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The statement is incorrect for primary alcohols (1). PCl₅ reacts with all classes of alcohol to give a chloroalkane (1). Concentrated HCl reacts readily with tertiary alcohols to give chloroalkanes, but primary alcohols require a ZnCl₂ catalyst (Lucas reagent) to react with HCl / do not react readily with HCl alone (1). Concentrated H₂SO₄ + KCl generates HCl in situ and behaves similarly to concentrated HCl.

Q65 WTE §10.23 2 marks · ~4 min

An exam question asks: "Which reagent(s) can convert a tertiary alcohol directly to a chloroalkane?" A student selects only PCl₅ and rejects both concentrated HCl and concentrated H₂SO₄ + KCl. Identify the error in the student's reasoning.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The student is incorrect (1). All three reagents work for converting a tertiary alcohol to a chloroalkane: PCl₅ reacts with all alcohols, concentrated HCl reacts readily with tertiary alcohols, and concentrated H₂SO₄ + KCl generates HCl in situ (1).

### Spec Point 10.24 — Mass Spectrometry

Q79 QFR §10.24 2 marks · ~4 min

Define the term base peak as used in mass spectrometry.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The tallest peak in the mass spectrum / the peak assigned 100% relative abundance (1) / corresponding to the most stable fragment ion (1).

Q80 QFR §10.24 1 mark · ~2 min

State what is represented by the molecular ion peak (M⁺) in a mass spectrum.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The M⁺ peak represents the molecular ion — the original molecule that has lost one electron but has not fragmented (1).

Q81 CAL §10.24 3 marks · ~6 min

The mass spectrum of a compound shows a molecular ion peak at m/z 86. The empirical formula of the compound is C₂H₃O. Deduce the molecular formula of the compound.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Mᵣ from M⁺ peak = 86 (1). Empirical formula mass of C₂H₃O = (2 × 12) + (3 × 1) + 16 = 43 (1). Multiplier = 86 / 43 = 2, therefore molecular formula = C₄H₆O₂ (1).

Q82 EXP §10.24 3 marks · ~6 min

In a mass spectrum, the molecular ion peak (M⁺) has a relative abundance of 82% and the M+1 peak has a relative abundance of 3.3%. (a) Explain the origin of the M+1 peak. (b) Use the data to determine the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) The M+1 peak is caused by molecules containing one carbon-13 (¹³C) atom instead of carbon-12 (¹²C), due to the natural abundance of ¹³C (~1.1%) (1). (b) The ratio of M+1 to M⁺ is (3.3 / 82) × 100% ≈ 4.0%; number of carbon atoms ≈ (M+1/M⁺ ratio) / 1.1% = 4.0 / 1.1 ≈ 4 carbon atoms (2). (Methodology consistent with Q84: the M+1/M⁺ ratio is divided by 1.1% to estimate the carbon count.)

Q83 DIA §10.24 3 marks · ~6 min

The mass spectrum of a compound shows a molecular ion peak at m/z 60 and a prominent fragment ion peak at m/z 31. Identify the compound and explain how each piece of evidence supports your identification.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (1). The M⁺ peak at m/z 60 corresponds to C₃H₈O (Mᵣ = 60) (1). The peak at m/z 31 corresponds to CH₂OH⁺, which is characteristic of a primary alcohol formed by α-cleavage adjacent to the –OH group (1).

Q84 CAL §10.24 3 marks · ~6 min

A student analysing the mass spectrum of compound X sees a small peak at m/z 87, one mass unit higher than the M⁺ peak at m/z 86. Explain the origin of the m/z 87 peak, state the natural abundance of the isotope responsible, and explain how the M+1 peak can be used to estimate the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

The peak at m/z 87 is the M+1 peak, caused by the natural presence of carbon-13 (¹³C) — one ¹²C is replaced by ¹³C, increasing M⁺ by 1 (1). The natural abundance of ¹³C is approximately 1.1% (1). For a molecule with n carbon atoms, M+1/M⁺ ≈ n × 1.1%; so if the ratio is about 4.4%, the molecule contains approximately 4 carbon atoms (1).

Q85 QFR §10.24 2 marks · ~4 min

State the fragment ion responsible for a peak at (a) m/z 31 and (b) m/z 45 in a mass spectrum. State the functional group each indicates.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) m/z 31 = CH₂OH⁺ → indicates a primary alcohol (1). (b) m/z 45 = COOH⁺ → indicates a carboxylic acid (1).

Q86 SYN §10.24 5 marks · ~10 min

An organic compound X has Mᵣ = 60. The mass spectrum of X shows a base peak at m/z 31. The infrared spectrum of X shows a broad absorption covering 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. A student concludes that X is propan-1-ol. (a) Explain why the mass spectrum data is consistent with propan-1-ol. (2 marks) (b) Explain why the student's conclusion is incorrect based on the IR data, and suggest a more likely identity for X. (3 marks)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) M⁺ at m/z 60 is consistent with C₃H₈O (Mᵣ = 60) (1). The base peak at m/z 31 corresponds to CH₂OH⁺, formed by α-cleavage characteristic of a primary alcohol (1). (b) The broad absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of the O–H stretch in a carboxylic acid, NOT an alcohol (1). An alcohol O–H stretch is a broad absorption in the range 3750–3200 cm⁻¹ (data-booklet value) and does not extend as far to lower wavenumbers (1). A more likely identity for X is ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH (Mᵣ = 60), which would show a broad carboxylic O–H stretch and a characteristic fragment at m/z 45 (COOH⁺) (1).

### Spec Point 10.27 — Carboxylic Acid Identification

Q87 QFR §10.27 1 mark · ~2 min

State the reagent used in test-tube reactions to identify a carboxylic acid by effervescence.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Sodium carbonate / Na₂CO₃ (1)

Q88 EXP §10.27 4 marks · ~8 min

Two isomeric compounds, ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃), both have Mᵣ = 46. Describe a test-tube reaction that could distinguish between them and state the expected observations for each compound.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

Add acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to each compound and warm (1)

Ethanol (a primary alcohol): orange solution turns green as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺; ethanol is oxidised to ethanal/ethanoic acid (1)

Methoxymethane (an ether): no colour change; ethers cannot be oxidised by dichromate(VI) (1)

Alternatively: add PCl₅ — ethanol gives misty white fumes of HCl (has –OH); methoxymethane does not (no –OH group, ether C–O–C does not react with PCl₅ in the same way) (1). Accept either test with correct observations for both compounds.

### Spec Point 10.28 — Determination of Mᵣ by Volatilisation

Q89 CAL §10.28 3 marks · ~6 min

A volatile liquid Y is vapourised to determine its relative molecular mass. The following data were obtained: pressure = 98 500 Pa, volume = 7.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³, temperature = 373 K, mass of vapour = 0.115 g. Calculate Mᵣ of Y and suggest its identity. (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

n = pV / RT = (98 500 × 7.5 × 10⁻⁵) / (8.314 × 373) = 7.3875 / 3101.122 = 2.38 × 10⁻³ mol (1). Mᵣ = mass / n = 0.115 / 2.38 × 10⁻³ = 48.3 (1) (accept 47–49). Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, Mᵣ = 46 is closest; methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃, Mᵣ = 46) also possible — slightly high value suggests experimental error but identity is ethanol or methoxymethane (1).

### Spec Point 10.24+ — Additional Spectroscopy & Mechanism Questions

Q90 EXP §10.24 3 marks · ~6 min

The mass spectrum of an unknown chlorinated compound shows a molecular ion cluster with two peaks at m/z 78 and m/z 80 in an approximate ratio of 3 : 1. (a) Explain the origin of the two peaks. (b) State how the mass spectrum of 1,2-dibromoethane would differ in the molecular ion region, and give the relative heights of the three M, M+2, and M+4 peaks.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) The two peaks arise from the two naturally occurring isotopes of chlorine — ³⁵Cl (~75%) and ³⁷Cl (~25%). Each molecule contains one Cl atom, so two molecular ion peaks appear at m/z = M and M+2 in an approximately 3 : 1 ratio matching the natural isotopic abundance of chlorine (1). (b) Bromine has two isotopes — ⁷⁹Br (~51%) and ⁸¹Br (~49%) of roughly equal abundance. With two bromine atoms in 1,2-dibromoethane (CH₂BrCH₂Br, M⁺ = 186), three peaks appear at m/z 186 (M), 188 (M+2) and 190 (M+4) (1). Their relative heights follow the binomial expansion (0.51 + 0.49)² → 0.26 : 0.50 : 0.24, i.e. approximately 1 : 2 : 1 (1).

Q91 EXP §10.24 4 marks · ~8 min

The Lucas test uses concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) to distinguish between 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols by the rate of formation of the cloudy chloroalkane layer. (a) Write the equation for the reaction of butan-2-ol with HCl in the presence of ZnCl₂. (b) Explain why tertiary alcohols react fastest and primary alcohols react slowest (or not at all without heating). (c) State the visual observation that would distinguish each alcohol class.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ + HCl —(ZnCl₂)→ CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃ + H₂O (1). (b) The reaction proceeds via an SN1 mechanism through a carbocation intermediate. Tertiary alcohols form a tertiary carbocation (most stable, stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups via inductive effect and hyperconjugation), so the activation energy is lowest and the reaction is fastest (1). Primary alcohols would form a primary carbocation (least stable), so the SN1 pathway is disfavoured; the reaction is very slow at room temperature and may require heating (1). (c) Tertiary: cloudiness appears immediately (within ~1 minute); Secondary: cloudiness within 5–10 minutes; Primary: no observable reaction at room temperature (1).

Q92 SYN §10.24 4 marks · ~8 min

Account for the observation that 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary) undergoes hydrolysis via an SN1 mechanism, whereas 1-bromobutane (primary) undergoes hydrolysis via an SN2 mechanism. In your answer, refer to (a) carbocation stability, (b) steric hindrance, and (c) the rate equation expected for each substrate.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane forms a tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ that is stabilised by three electron-donating methyl groups (inductive effect + hyperconjugation), making the heterolytic C–Br bond cleavage energetically feasible — so the SN1 pathway is favoured (1). 1-bromobutane would form a primary carbocation (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂⁺) that is too unstable to form at an appreciable rate, so the concerted SN2 pathway (no carbocation) is favoured instead (1). (b) The tertiary carbon in 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is sterically hindered by three methyl groups, blocking back-side attack by the nucleophile required for SN2 — another factor favouring SN1 (1). (c) SN1 (tertiary): rate = k[halogenoalkane] (first-order, independent of [nucleophile]); SN2 (primary): rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile] (second-order overall) (1).

Q93 EXP §10.24 3 marks · ~6 min

Sodium iodide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to give a mixture of products including hydrogen iodide, iodine, hydrogen sulfide and sulfur. (a) Write the equation for the primary reaction producing HI. (b) Explain why H₂SO₄ is not a suitable acid for producing pure HI from NaI, and identify the type of reaction that the acid undergoes. (c) State the observation that would indicate the formation of iodine.

Answer & Marking Criteria

Answer:

(a) NaI(s) + H₂SO₄(l) → NaHSO₄(s) + HI(g) (1). (b) HI is a strong reducing agent and reduces H₂SO₄ (S in +6 oxidation state) to lower sulfur species such as SO₂, S or H₂S — for example: 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O (S reduced from +6 to −2; I⁻ oxidised from −1 to 0) (1). Therefore the acid is itself reduced and the products are contaminated with iodine and sulfur-containing gases — this is a redox reaction (H₂SO₄ acting as an oxidising agent, not just an acid), so pure HI cannot be prepared this way. Phosphoric acid (a non-oxidising acid) is used instead (1). (c) A brown/black colouration or violet vapour indicates iodine formation (1).

## Chapter 2.9 — Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

WCH12 · Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry · Unit 2

Spec Points 10.1–10.23+7 Papers AnalysedJun 2022 – Oct 2024

Average ~25 marks per paper — organic mechanisms, IR spectroscopy, and synthesis dominate

### Definitions

#### Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12 — Spec Points 10.1–10.23

### How to Use This Guide

This file contains every definition, classification rule, reaction condition, and spectroscopy fact for Chapter 2.9. This is the second-heaviest chapter in WCH12 (averaging 23.3 marks/paper, 29.1%). Content is organised into four sections (10A–10D) matching the specification structure. Every definition uses the exact phrasing expected by Edexcel mark schemes.

### Section 10A: General Principles of Organic Reactions

#### 10.1 Classification of Organic Reactions

Substitution: A reaction where an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by a different atom or group.

Elimination: A reaction where a small molecule (e.g., H₂O, HCl, HBr) is removed from a larger molecule, resulting in the formation of a double bond.

Addition: A reaction where two or more molecules combine to form a single, larger molecule (typically across a C=C double bond).

Oxidation: A reaction involving the loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen / loss of hydrogen). In organic chemistry, typically identified by a change in functional group (e.g., alcohol → aldehyde/carboxylic acid/ketone).

Hydrolysis: A reaction in which a molecule is broken down by reaction with water. In the context of halogenoalkanes, hydrolysis is a substitution reaction with water (or aqueous hydroxide) to form an alcohol.

#### Reaction Type Identification in Exams

Observation Reaction Type Example

OH replaces X on same carbon Substitution (SN2) 1-bromopropane + NaOH(aq) → propan-1-ol

H₂O eliminated, C=C formed Elimination 2-chlorobutane + KOH(ethanol) → but-2-ene

H₂ adds across C=C Addition C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆

Orange → green (K₂Cr₂O₇) Oxidation Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid

X replaced by OH, using water Hydrolysis Halogenoalkane + H₂O → alcohol

#### 10.2 Nucleophile — Definition

Nucleophile: An electron-pair donor that attacks an electron-deficient (electrophilic) carbon atom.

#### Common Nucleophiles in WCH12

Nucleophile Source Product Type

OH⁻ NaOH(aq) or KOH(aq) Alcohol

CN⁻ KCN or NaCN in ethanol Nitrile (extends carbon chain)

NH₃ Ammonia (in ethanol, under pressure) Primary amine

H₂O Water (slow) Alcohol (hydrolysis)

Exam fact (Jun 2023 Q17): In aqueous conditions, water (H₂O) acts as the nucleophile, NOT Ag⁺, NO₃⁻, or the solvent ethanol (if water is present).

#### 10.3 Bond Polarity and the C–X Bond

The carbon–halogen bond is polar because halogens (except iodine) are more electronegative than carbon. Iodine has the same electronegativity as carbon (2.5), so C–I is essentially non-polar. For the other halogens, this polarity creates a δ⁺ charge on carbon and a δ⁻ charge on the halogen.

This polarity makes the carbon atom electrophilic (electron-deficient) and therefore susceptible to attack by nucleophiles.

#### Electronegativity and Bond Polarity

Bond Electronegativity Difference Polarity Bond Strength (mean bond enthalpy)

C–F 1.50 (F = 4.0, C = 2.5) Most polar 485 kJ mol⁻¹ (strongest)

C–Cl 0.50 (Cl = 3.0) Polar 339 kJ mol⁻¹

C–Br 0.30 (Br = 2.8) Polar 276 kJ mol⁻¹

C–I 0.00 (I = 2.5) Non-polar 238 kJ mol⁻¹ (weakest)

Critical exam point: Bond STRENGTH (enthalpy) is the key factor determining hydrolysis rate, NOT bond polarity. The weaker the C–X bond, the lower the activation energy, the faster the reaction.

#### 10.4 SN2 Mechanism — Definition

SN2 (substitution nucleophilic bimolecular): A one-step nucleophilic substitution mechanism in which the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon from the opposite side to the leaving group, forming a transition state where the incoming nucleophile and outgoing leaving group are both partially bonded. The C–X bond breaks at the same time as the new C–Nu bond forms.

#### Key Features of SN2

Feature Detail

Steps One (concerted)

Stereocentre Inversion of configuration (Walden inversion) at chiral carbon

Kinetics Second order: rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile]

Favoured by Primary halogenoalkanes, good nucleophiles, polar aprotic solvents

Transition state Trigonal bipyramidal (5 groups around carbon)

### Section 10B: Halogenoalkanes

#### 10.5 Nomenclature of Halogenoalkanes

Halogenoalkane naming rules: 1. Identify the longest carbon chain containing the –OH or halogen-bearing carbon 2. Number the chain to give the substituent the lowest possible locant 3. Use prefixes: fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo- 4. Alphabetical order for multiple different substituents (but ignore di-, tri- prefixes)

#### Examples from Past Papers

Compound Correct Name Paper

(CH₃)₃CBr 2-bromo-2-methylpropane Jan 2024 Q23(a)(i)

CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl 1-chlorobutane Jan 2024 Q23(a)(ii)

(CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br 1-bromo-2-methylpropane Jan 2024 Q23(a)(iii)

CH₃CHClCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ 2-chlorohexane Jun 2024 Q16

CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₂CH₂CH₃ 3-bromohexane Jan 2023 Q14

#### 10.6 Classification of Halogenoalkanes: 1°, 2°, 3°

Primary (1°) halogenoalkane: The carbon bearing the halogen is attached to one (or zero) other carbon atoms.

Secondary (2°) halogenoalkane: The carbon bearing the halogen is attached to two other carbon atoms.

Tertiary (3°) halogenoalkane: The carbon bearing the halogen is attached to three other carbon atoms.

#### Classification Examples

Structure Classification Reason

CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (1-bromopropane) Primary C–Br carbon bonded to 1 other C

CH₃CHBrCH₃ (2-bromopropane) Secondary C–Br carbon bonded to 2 other C atoms

(CH₃)₃CBr (2-bromo-2-methylpropane) Tertiary C–Br carbon bonded to 3 other C atoms

Cyclohexyl bromide Secondary C–Br carbon bonded to 2 ring C atoms

Exam fact (Jun 2023 Q16): "Which compound is a tertiary halogenoalkane?" Students must count the bonds from the halogen-bearing carbon to other carbons, not just look at the overall structure.

#### 10.7 Reactions of Halogenoalkanes with KOH/NaOH

##### Hydrolysis (Aqueous Conditions) — Substitution

Feature Detail

Reagent Aqueous NaOH or KOH

Conditions Heat under reflux

Mechanism SN2 (primary) or SN1 (tertiary)

Product Alcohol

Equation R–Br + NaOH(aq) → R–OH + NaBr

##### Elimination (Ethanolic Conditions)

Feature Detail

Reagent Ethanolic NaOH or KOH (dissolved in ethanol)

Conditions Heat

Mechanism E2 (or E1 for tertiary)

Product Alkene

Equation R–CH₂–CHBr–R' + KOH(ethanol) → R–CH=CH–R' + KBr + H₂O

Critical exam distinction: - Aqueous KOH → SUBSTITUTION (alcohol product) - Ethanolic KOH → ELIMINATION (alkene product)

Exam fact (Jun 2024 Q16(a)(i)): "State the condition for elimination from 2-chlorobutane." Answer: ethanolic KOH. "In ethanol" alone is insufficient — must specify the reagent IS ethanolic KOH.

#### 10.8 Reaction of Halogenoalkanes with NH₃

Feature Detail

Reagent Ammonia (excess)

Conditions Alcoholic solvent (ethanol), heat under pressure (sealed tube)

Product Primary amine

Equation R–Br + 2NH₃ → R–NH₂ + NH₄Br

Critical exam points:

Trap Paper Correct Approach

"Heat under reflux" Jun 2023 Q19(c) — explicitly NOT awarded Must say "heat under pressure" or "in a sealed tube"

"Aqueous ammonia" Jan 2023 Q20(d)(i) Must specify alcoholic ammonia (ethanol solvent), not aqueous

Why is yield low? Jan 2023 Q20(d)(ii) Insufficient ammonia leads to further substitution (the primary amine product reacts with more halogenoalkane to form secondary amine, tertiary amine, or quaternary ammonium salt); using excess ammonia minimises this by acting as a base/nucleophile to mop up the intermediate

#### 10.9 Reaction of Halogenoalkanes with KCN

Feature Detail

Reagent KCN or NaCN

Conditions Dissolved in ethanol, heated

Mechanism SN2

Product Nitrile (one carbon LONGER than starting halogenoalkane)

Equation R–Br + KCN → R–CN + KBr

Key exam point (Oct 2024 Q17(c)(ii)): "Why is the reaction of halogenoalkanes with KCN important in organic synthesis?" Answer: It extends the carbon chain by one carbon atom.

#### 10.10 Reaction of Halogenoalkanes with AgNO₃ (Silver Nitrate Test)

Feature Detail

Reagent AgNO₃ dissolved in ethanol

Conditions Room temperature (no heating required)

Observation Precipitate forms; colour depends on halogen

Purpose Test for halogen present; also demonstrates relative rates of hydrolysis

#### Precipitate Colours

Halide Precipitate Colour Approximate Speed (1° halogenoalkane)

Chloride (Cl⁻) White Slowest

Bromide (Br⁻) Cream Medium

Iodide (I⁻) Yellow Fastest

Exam fact (Jan 2023 Q13): "Which compound gives the fastest precipitate with AgNO₃ in ethanol?" Answer: (CH₃)₃CI (tertiary iodoalkane) — both the tertiary structure (SN1 fast) and the weak C–I bond contribute to maximum rate.

#### 10.11 Ionic Equation for AgNO₃ Test

Ag₂O + H₂O → 2Ag⁺ + 2OH⁻

(Jun 2023 Q19(e)(i) — students were asked to complete this ionic equation)

#### 10.12 Rate of Hydrolysis — Bond Enthalpy Factor

The rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes depends primarily on the bond enthalpy of the C–X bond:

C–I (238 kJ mol⁻¹) < C–Br (276 kJ mol⁻¹) < C–Cl (339 kJ mol⁻¹) < C–F (485 kJ mol⁻¹)

Weaker bonds have lower activation energies, so reactions are faster.

Exam fact (Oct 2023 Q15): "Why does 1-chlorobutane react more slowly than 1-bromobutane?" Answer: The C–Cl bond is stronger than the C–Br bond → higher activation energy → slower reaction. Solubility and polarity are irrelevant to rate.

#### 10.13 Rate of Hydrolysis — Structure Factor (1° vs 3°)

Structure Mechanism Relative Rate Reason

Primary SN2 Slowest among the three (for a given halogen) Least steric hindrance favours SN2, but the C–X bond must break simultaneously with nucleophile attack (no stable carbocation forms)

Secondary SN2/SN1 Intermediate Some steric hindrance

Tertiary SN1 Fastest Forms stable carbocation intermediate; C–X bond breaks easily

Real exam application (Oct 2024 Q17(b)(ii), Jun 2024 Q16(b)(iii)): "Give TWO reasons why 2-iodo-2-methylpropane + KOH is faster than 1-chlorobutane + KOH." 1. 2-iodo-2-methylpropane is tertiary (SN1, fast) vs 1-chlorobutane is primary (SN2, slow) 2. C–I bond is weaker than C–Cl bond (lower activation energy)

Both reasons are required for full marks.

#### 10.14 Core Practical 5 — Comparing Rates of Hydrolysis

CP5: Investigate the rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes using silver nitrate solution in ethanol. Measure the time taken for a precipitate to form.

Key points for the exam: - Same temperature for all tests (ensure fair test) - Same concentration and volume of AgNO₃ - Same concentration of halogenoalkane - Time is measured from mixing to first appearance of precipitate - Rate ∝ 1/time

### Section 10C: Alcohols

#### 10.15 Nomenclature of Alcohols

Alcohol naming rules: 1. Identify the longest carbon chain containing the –OH group 2. Number the chain to give the –OH group the lowest possible locant 3. Suffix: -ol (replaces the -e of the alkane name) 4. The locant number MUST be included (e.g., "butan-2-ol", not just "butanol")

#### Examples from Past Papers

Compound Correct Name Paper

(CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂OH 3-methylbutan-1-ol Jan 2023 Q19(b)(i)

(CH₃)(C₂H₅)(OH)C–CH₂CH₃ Various tertiary alcohols C₆H₁₄O Jan 2023 Q19(a)

CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ butan-2-ol Jun 2023 Q19(d)(iv)

(CH₃)₂CHOH propan-2-ol Oct 2023 Q14(a)

CH₃CH₂CH₂OH propan-1-ol Oct 2023 Q14(b)

1-methylcyclopentanol 1-methylcyclopentanol Oct 2023 Q13(a)

4-methylhexan-3-ol 4-methylhexan-3-ol Oct 2024 Q12

#### 10.16 Classification of Alcohols: 1°, 2°, 3°

Primary alcohol: The –OH group is on a carbon attached to one (or zero) other carbon atoms.

Secondary alcohol: The –OH group is on a carbon attached to two other carbon atoms.

Tertiary alcohol: The –OH group is on a carbon attached to three other carbon atoms.

#### Classification and Oxidation Products

Type Oxidation Product(s) Can be further oxidised?

Primary (RCH₂OH) Aldehyde (RCHO) then carboxylic acid (RCOOH) Aldehyde: YES → carboxylic acid

Secondary (R₂CHOH) Ketone (R₂C=O) NO

Tertiary (R₃COH) No reaction N/A

Critical exam fact (Jun 2024 Q20(c)): Tertiary alcohols are NOT oxidised by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. This is a key distinguishing test between alcohol types.

#### 10.17 Reaction of Alcohols with PCl₅

Feature Detail

Reagent PCl₅ (phosphorus pentachloride)

Conditions Room temperature

Product Chloroalkane

Observation Misty white fumes (HCl gas evolved)

Equation R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl

Exam fact (Oct 2023 Q13(b)): PCl₅ reacts with ALL alcohol types (primary, secondary, and tertiary). K₂Cr₂O₇ only oxidises primary and secondary. Br₂ and Na₂CO₃ do NOT react with alcohols.

Exam fact (Oct 2023 Q16): Maximum mass of organic product from propane-1,2-diol + PCl₅ = 2.26 g. Both –OH groups are replaced, giving C₃H₆Cl₂.

#### 10.18 Reaction of Alcohols with H₂SO₄/KBr

Feature Detail

Reagent Concentrated H₂SO₄ + solid KBr

Conditions The conc. H₂SO₄ generates HBr in situ

Product Bromoalkane (substitution)

Mechanism Conc. H₂SO₄ acts as an acid (not oxidising agent) with Cl⁻; with Br⁻ it can also act as an oxidising agent

#### 10.19 Reaction of Alcohols with Concentrated H₃PO₄ (Dehydration)

Feature Detail

Reagent Concentrated phosphoric(V) acid (H₃PO₄)

Conditions Heat to ~170 °C

Product Alkene (elimination of water)

Classification Elimination reaction

Exam fact (Jun 2023 Q18(a)): "Which reagent for alcohol dehydration?" Answer: phosphoric(V) acid. Conc. H₂SO₄ at 50% was offered as a distractor but is too dilute for effective dehydration.

#### 10.20 Oxidation of Alcohols with Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇

Alcohol Type Reagent Conditions Product Colour Change

Primary K₂Cr₂O₇ / H₂SO₄ Distillation Aldehyde Orange → green

Primary K₂Cr₂O₇ / H₂SO₄ Reflux (excess) Carboxylic acid Orange → green

Secondary K₂Cr₂O₇ / H₂SO₄ Reflux Ketone Orange → green

Tertiary K₂Cr₂O₇ / H₂SO₄ — No reaction No change

#### Distillation vs Reflux — The Critical Distinction

Technique When Used Why Product

Distillation Primary alcohol → aldehyde Aldehyde has LOWER boiling point than the alcohol, so it distils off as it forms, preventing further oxidation Aldehyde

Reflux Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid, OR secondary alcohol → ketone Condenser returns vapour to the flask, allowing prolonged heating and complete reaction Carboxylic acid or ketone

Exam application (Oct 2023 Q14(a–b)): - Propan-2-ol under reflux, excess K₂Cr₂O₇ → propanone (ketone). IR: C=O at 1720–1700 cm⁻¹. - Propan-1-ol with distillation → propanal (aldehyde). IR: C=O at 1740–1720 cm⁻¹.

#### 10.21 [O] as Oxidising Agent Shorthand

[O] represents an oxidising agent (typically acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or acidified KMnO₄) in organic equations.

Counting [O] atoms needed (Jan 2024 Q19): - Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid: RCH₂OH + 2[O] → RCOOH + H₂O - Secondary alcohol → ketone: R₂CHOH + [O] → R₂C=O + H₂O - Tertiary alcohol: no reaction

Real exam (Jan 2024 Q19): A compound with 2 primary –OH groups and 1 secondary –OH requires: 2 × 2[O] + 1 × [O] = 5[O] total.

#### 10.22 Core Practical 7 — Oxidation of Alcohols

CP7: Oxidise a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux.

Key points: - Reflux apparatus: round-bottom flask + condenser (water in at bottom, out at top) - Distillation apparatus for aldehyde: round-bottom flask + condenser + collecting flask (no return of vapour) - Colour change: orange (Cr₂O₇²⁻) → green (Cr³⁺) - Secondary alcohols also oxidise to ketones (same conditions, same colour change)

#### 10.23 Reactions of Tertiary Alcohols with HCl

Exam fact (Jan 2024 Q18): "Which reagent(s) can convert a tertiary alcohol to a chloroalkane?" Answer: ALL THREE work: 1. PCl₅ (reacts with all alcohols) 2. Concentrated HCl (tertiary alcohols react readily — unlike primary, which need ZnCl₂ catalyst) 3. Concentrated H₂SO₄ + KCl (generates HCl in situ)

### Section 10D: Spectra

#### 10.24 Mass Spectrometry — Key Definitions

Molecular ion peak (M⁺): The peak in the mass spectrum corresponding to the unchanged molecule that has lost one electron. Its m/z value equals the relative molecular mass of the compound.

Fragmentation: The breaking of the molecular ion into smaller pieces (fragment ions) in the mass spectrometer. Each fragment has a characteristic m/z value.

Base peak: The tallest peak in the mass spectrum (100% relative abundance), corresponding to the most stable fragment ion.

#### M+1 Peak

The M+1 peak is caused by the natural abundance of carbon-13 (¹³C, ~1.1% natural abundance). The ratio of M+1 to M⁺ peak height gives an indication of the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

#### Common Fragment Ions

m/z Fragment Ion Source

15 CH₃⁺ Methyl group

17 OH⁺ Hydroxyl

29 C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺ Ethyl or aldehyde fragment

31 CH₂OH⁺ Primary alcohol (α-cleavage)

41 C₃H₅⁺ Propene-type fragment

43 CH₃CO⁺ or C₃H₇⁺ Acetyl (ketone/aldehyde) or propyl

45 COOH⁺ Carboxylic acid fragment

58 C₃H₆O⁺ Molecular ion of acetone

#### Real Exam Applications

Oct 2024 Q14(b): "Which compound gives peaks at m/z 31 (CH₂OH⁺) and m/z 60 (M⁺)?" Answer: Propan-1-ol (C₃H₈O, Mᵣ = 60). The m/z 31 fragment is characteristic of a primary alcohol (α-cleavage next to the –OH group).

Jan 2024 Q20: "Identify the compound from its mass spectrum." Answer: CH₃COCH₃ (acetone). M⁺ at m/z 58, fragments at 43 (CH₃CO⁺) and 15 (CH₃⁺).

Jan 2023 Q15: "Which compound would NOT show a prominent m/z 43 peak?" Answer: CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ — the nitrogen-containing compound fragments differently; there is no CH₃CO⁺ or (CH₃)₂CH⁺ fragment.

Oct 2023 Q21(a)(ii): "Molecular formula from mass spectrum." M⁺ at m/z 86. Empirical formula mass = 43. Molecular formula = C₄H₆O₂ (43 × 2 = 86).

Oct 2023 Q21(a)(iv): Fragment identification: - m/z 41 → C₃H₅⁺ (must include positive charge) - m/z 45 → COOH⁺ (carboxylic acid fragment)

Jun 2024 Q20(a)(ii): Mass spectrum of isoprene (C₅H₈): - m/z 68 = M⁺ (C₅H₈⁺) - m/z 53 = C₄H₅⁺ (loss of ·CH₃)

#### 10.25 IR Spectroscopy — Key Absorption Ranges

IR spectroscopy: A technique that measures the absorption of infrared radiation by molecular bonds. Different bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers (cm⁻¹), allowing identification of functional groups.

#### Essential IR Absorption Data (Data Booklet Values)

Bond / Group Wavenumber Range (cm⁻¹) Appearance

O–H (alcohol, carboxylic acid) 3550–3200 Broad (especially carboxylic acid: 2500–3300, very broad)

O–H (free, no H-bonding) 3750–3200 Sharp

N–H 3550–3200 Medium, sharper than O–H

C–H (alkane) 2950–2850 Medium-strong

C–H (alkene, arene) 3100–3000 Medium

C≡N (nitrile) 2260–2215 Sharp

C≡C (alkyne) 2150–2100 Weak/medium

C=O (aldehyde) 1740–1720 Strong

C=O (ketone) 1720–1700 Strong

C=O (carboxylic acid) 1725–1700 Strong

C=O (ester) 1750–1730 Strong

C=C (alkene) 1680–1620 Medium

C–O (alcohol, ester, carboxylic acid) 1300–1000 Strong

#### Real Exam Applications

Jan 2023 Q16: "Identify the compound with IR peaks at 3415 cm⁻¹ and 2250 cm⁻¹." Answer: H₂NCH₂CH₂C≡N (amino-nitrile). 3415 = N–H stretch; 2250 = C≡N stretch.

Oct 2024 Q15: "Which functional group gives broad O–H around 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ AND C=O around 1700 cm⁻¹?" Answer: Carboxylic acid.

Oct 2023 Q14(a): "What IR peak identifies the oxidation product of propan-2-ol (reflux, excess oxidising agent)?" Answer: C=O stretch at 1720–1700 cm⁻¹ (ketone range).

Oct 2023 Q14(b): "What IR peak identifies the oxidation product of propan-1-ol (distillation)?" Answer: C=O stretch at 1740–1720 cm⁻¹ (aldehyde range).

Jun 2024 Q20(a)(iii): IR spectrum of a terpene: identify P, Q, R peaks. - P = C–H stretching in alkene (~3000 cm⁻¹) - Q = C–H stretching in alkane (~2900 cm⁻¹) - R = C=C stretching in alkene (~1650 cm⁻¹) Critical: Must specify "in alkene" or "in alkane" — just "C–H stretch" is insufficient.

#### 10.26 Functional Group Identification from Test Results

Oct 2023 Q21(a)(iii): Combined test results identify functional groups:

Test Observation Functional Group Identified

Bromine water Decolourised C=C / alkene

Na₂CO₃ (aq) Effervescence (CO₂) –COOH / carboxylic acid

Combined: compound contains BOTH C=C and –COOH → but-2-enoic acid.

#### 10.27 Core Practical 8 — Analysis of an Unknown Organic Compound

CP8: Identify an unknown organic compound using a combination of: - Test-tube reactions (PCl₅, Br₂ water, Na₂CO₃, K₂Cr₂O₇, AgNO₃) - IR spectroscopy (functional group identification) - Mass spectrometry (molecular mass, fragmentation pattern, molecular formula)

#### 10.28 Ideal Gas Equation for Mᵣ Determination

Oct 2024 Q18(a): A volatile liquid X is vaporised and its Mᵣ determined using pV = nRT: - p = 99 000 Pa, V = 8.1 × 10⁻⁵ m³, T = 368 K, mass = 0.120 g - n = pV/RT = (99 000 × 8.1 × 10⁻⁵) / (8.314 × 368) = 2.62 × 10⁻³ mol - Mᵣ = 0.120 / 2.62 × 10⁻³ = 45.8 (accept 44–46) - Identification: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH, Mᵣ = 46) or methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃, Mᵣ = 46)
